\[ \begin{bmatrix} Z_g & -C_s & 0 \\ C_s^{\top} & 0 & B^{\top} \\ 0 & B & -Z_b(\omega) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{I}_\text{leak} \\ \boldsymbol{\varphi}_n \\ \mathbf{I}_\text{long} \end{bmatrix} \;=\; \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{I}_\text{in} \\ \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix}. \]

The earth Green's function block \(Z_g\) stays real and frequency-independent (quasi-static, \(f < 1\,\mathrm{kHz}\)) — the finite-frequency correction would have to come from a magnetic Green's function on the layered soil, which is again Carson territory (ADR-0005). The \(Z_b(\omega)\) block carries all the frequency-dependent physics introduced here.

docs.title: Frequency loop
docs.text:
When at least one conductor has inductance_model == "neumann", the solver:

  1. Discretises the geometry once and assembles \(Z_g\), the resistance vector \(R\), and the inductance matrix \(L\) — all frequency-independent.
  2. Loops over engine.frequencies. For each \(f_k\) the \(\omega = 2\pi f_k\) is plugged into \(Z_b(\omega)\) and the full complex linear system is solved with numpy.linalg.solve on the complex augmented matrix.
  3. Returns one complex potential / current entry per frequency in FieldResult.electrode_potentials[name][k] etc. — the FieldResult shape is unchanged; entries that used to be real per frequency are now genuinely complex.

When all conductors have inductance_model is None (the default), the solver keeps the historic real-only fast path: one linalg.solve over the real augmented matrix, the result broadcast across engine.frequencies. Quasi-static DC studies stay bit-exact and at the same cost.

docs.title: Self-inductance and shielded conductors
docs.text: The thin-wire self-inductance assumes a bare conductor. For a cable with a conductor inside an outer sheath the relevant self-inductance is geometrically smaller; this distinction matters for shielded MV cables but not for the bare-copper / PEN typical study. We keep the model simple: inductance_model == "neumann" always uses the bare-conductor self formula; refinements come with the cable-shield work later.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Single isolated segment — the segment's self-L matches the closed-form Grover formula above to within 0.5 % (we sweep \(\ell/a\) from 10 to 1000).
  • Two parallel coaxial segments — the Neumann quadrature reproduces \(M_\parallel(\ell, d)\) to within 1 % for separations \(d / \ell \in [0.1, 10]\).
  • Two perpendicular segments crossing in the middle — the Neumann integral evaluates to zero by symmetry (test tolerance \(10^{-9}\)).
  • DC reproducibility — at \(\omega = 0\) the inductive system collapses bit-exact to the resistive system from ADR-0003 (regression).
  • Cross-engine at \(f = 50\,\mathrm{Hz}\) — image, mom, cim, bem agree on the cluster impedance of a galvanic distributed conductor with the inductive model active to within 5 %.
  • Loop coupling — two parallel galvanic conductors (one current injection, one open-circuit measurement lead) show the expected finite open-circuit voltage at 50 Hz that scales linearly with the source current and with \(\omega\).

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
• Covers inductive coupling between the measurement lead and the current injection. The model is now physically complete for \(f < 1\,\mathrm{kHz}\) except for the Carson earth-return correction.
  • The Neumann integral is geometric only — it works on top of any of the existing electric Green's-function backends without duplicating their kernel logic.
  • Frequency-resolved FieldResults without API change: the same electrode_potentials[name][k] shape now actually depends on \(f_k\).

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
• The system becomes complex when the inductive model is enabled, doubling the per-frequency LU factorisation cost. A frequency sweep with \(N_f\) frequencies costs \(N_f\) complex solves (vs. one real solve in the resistive-only case). For a typical sweep (\(N_f \le 20\), \(N \le 5\,000\) segments) this is still well inside the 32-GB / 12-core workstation budget.
  • The mutual-inductance matrix is dense and symmetric; the same ACA/iterative roadmap that applies to the electric Z-matrix applies here. Both will be tackled together.

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
• Default behaviour (inductance_model is None) is unchanged. Existing notebooks and tests continue to produce DC results at identical cost.
  • The earth is still treated as a perfect mirror for the magnetic field — Carson finite-conductivity corrections are the subject of ADR-0005.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Grover, F. W. (1946). Inductance Calculations: Working Formulas and Tables. Dover (reprint 2004).
  • Sunde, E. D. (1968). Earth Conduction Effects in Transmission Systems, Dover, ch. 7.
  • Paul, C. R. (2010). Inductance: Loop and Partial. Wiley.
  • Carson, J. R. (1926). Wave propagation in overhead wires with ground return. Bell Syst. Tech. J. 5(4) — referenced for the follow-up ADR-0005.

docs.title: Amendment 2026.11 — image conventions, exact touching pairs, lumped conductors, skin effect (review pass 10)
docs.text:
Findings 10.20, 10.24, 10.37, 10.44, 10.46 and 10.60. The physical model of this ADR (Neumann partial inductances, complex branch block) stands; the following decisions refine it.

  1. The image is part of the earth model. The perfect-mirror image of section Earth return ("ideal earth") is one of three image conventions of build_inductance_matrix(image=...) (ImageConvention: "none", "additive", "antiparallel"). The solver builds the inductance matrix with the image of the selected earth_inductive_model: perfect_mirror → additive (this ADR), carson_series → anti-parallel (ADR-0005), sommerfeld → none (ADR-0006). An earth-return correction is defined against one image and must not be added to another (10.20). perfect_mirror has not been the default since 0.13.0.
  2. Pair integrals. Parallel, skew and perpendicular segment pairs use closed forms; pairs that share an end point (chain neighbours, bends) use Grover's vertex formula and the coaxial gap formula by default (touching="exact"), so a straight conductor keeps the inductance of the unsplit wire for every discretisation (10.46). touching="quadrature" reproduces 0.15.0.
  3. Internal inductance. Every self term carries the DC internal inductance \(\mu_0\ell/(8\pi)\) of a solid round conductor, for distributed and lumped branches alike (include_internal=True), except a cable shield (conductor_type="cable_shield"), a thin-walled tube without one (item 11, user decision Q33).
  4. Lumped and single-segment conductors. A conductor with an inductance_model that the topology keeps as one branch is one inductive branch from start to end, coupled to all others; up to 0.15.0 its inductance was dropped silently (10.24).
  5. Skin effect (opt-in). Conductor.resistance_model="skin" adds the exact internal impedance of a solid round conductor relative to the DC convention (resistance \(R_\text{ac}(f)\), internal inductance \(L_\text{int}(f)\)); the default "dc" keeps the numbers (10.37). The bare-conductor restriction of section Self-inductance and shielded conductors stands.
  6. Frequency loop. The earth-return correction is assembled once per solve for the whole frequency set (bit-identical to single-frequency assemblies, bounded cache; 10.60); the real fast path of purely galvanic worlds is unchanged.
  7. Close wires. Coincident conductors have no finite mutual inductance; find_close_wires and diagnose() report crossing, touching, interpenetrating and close wires (10.44).
  8. Wires closer than the sum of their radii (second adversarial audit). Two near-parallel segments whose axes stay closer than \(r_1 + r_2\) over a common length (coincident leads, a service drop along its PEN main) are evaluated as touching wires at the axis distance \(r_1 + r_2\), in every image convention; before, the quadrature stopped at its 1e-6 m floor (two coincident 50 m leads: 1.87 H). Close pairs that miss the closed forms — nearly parallel, crossing, skew pairs and T-junctions — are integrated semi-analytically (inner integral in closed form, graded outer panels), with touching="exact"; touching="quadrature" keeps the 0.15.0 rule. The coaxial closed forms are evaluated in one vectorised call per segment (audit A2C-5). The "5e-11" stated here holds for directions that differ by more than 1e-6 rad; see item 9 for the measured worst cases.
  9. Wires beside each other, tiny angles (third adversarial audit, A3C-1, A3C-2, A3C-4, A3C-5). The touching rule of item 8 switched a whole pair, and the decision depended on which segment was the row: a V pair of 1 m and 0.5 m at 1.5° read 0.362 or 0.503 µH, the generator's lumped in-line leads 0.134 or 0.127 Ω of measured reactance (50 Hz); tilted V and X pairs whose far ends lay just outside the cylinder kept a filament value above the self inductance (an indefinite matrix, a two-wire loop with a negative reactance). The rule now acts pointwise inside the Neumann integral: where a point of one wire lies beside the other wire (its foot on the other axis falls inside that wire) closer than \(r_1 + r_2\), that distance is used — touching wires — and where the thinner wire runs inside the thicker one (\(\rho + r_\text{thin} \le r_\text{thick}\), a core inside a cable shield) the thicker radius: a filament inside a thin tube couples to it as at the tube radius, which gives the coaxial loop inductance \(\frac{\mu_0}{2\pi}(\ln\frac{r_s}{r_c} + \frac14)\) per metre when the shield carries no internal inductance (+36 % before; since user decision Q32 the reading needs the shield to be marked, item 11). Both one-sided integrals (inner integral in closed form) are averaged, on end points in a fixed order, so every order and direction of the segments gives the same value bit for bit; the value is continuous in the geometry (4e-15 against an independent quadrature), chain neighbours and bends turning by less than 90° keep their closed forms, and 2000 random close configurations gave no indefinite matrix (700 before). Equal radii never count as one wire inside the other; for unequal radii the model steps from "inside" to "side by side" where the thinner axis leaves the thicker wire (the two describe different cables). Filaments from one vertex below 0.81° use a cancellation-free form of Grover's vertex formula (16 % off at 1.5e-6 rad before), and the close-pair rule takes the crossing point of nearly parallel axes from a cross product (9.5e-4 at 1e-8 rad before). Measured against mpmath: closed forms to round-off, vertex pairs to 4e-10 in a general orientation, close pairs 5e-11 above 1e-6 rad and 1.0e-9 at 1e-8 rad; pairs inside the parallel tolerance use the parallel closed form at the start offset (4.2e-9 for wires 1 cm apart tilted by 1e-10 rad, 1.7e-5 at 1 µm).
  10. Pairs across the surface (user decision Q27). Section Earth return ("ideal earth") applies the image to every pair, also to one segment above the soil surface (\(z < 0\), an overhead lead) and one below it (a buried PEN), for which a magnetic mirror between them has no physical basis. The numbers stay — perfect_mirror is a diagnostic baseline — but the solve emits one UserWarning per inductive assembly with the number of such pairs and the conductors on each side, pointing to sommerfeld; carson_series and sommerfeld couple such pairs through the field transmitted into the soil and do not warn. For two parallel 1 km wires, one 1 m above the surface and one 0.7 m deep and 1 m beside it, in 100 Ω·m, the additive image gives 2.28 times (50 Hz) and 2.77 times (1 kHz) the mutual reactance of sommerfeld; carson_series gives 1.12 and 1.03 times.
  11. Concentric cables by an explicit marker (user decisions Q32 and Q33). Item 9 read every thinner wire on the axis of a thicker one as a core inside a cable shield, so two separate cables of different radii drawn on one axis were one concentric cable. The reading now needs the thicker conductor to carry conductor_type="cable_shield" (the existing type tag, which selected only a plot colour before); two conductors of any other types on one axis are separate conductors and touch, as every pair lying side by side (build_inductance_matrix(..., shields=...) marks the segments at the low level). A shield is a thin-walled tube: its self terms carry no internal inductance of a solid wire, and Conductor.internal_impedance_per_length of a "dc" shield has no inductive part; the solid-round skin model (resistance_model="skin") is rejected for a shield. A 100 m coaxial pair (core 5 mm, shield 15 mm, 0.7 m deep) reads a loop inductance of 26.966 µH in a solve (perfect_mirror and sommerfeld; 26.970 µH with carson_series), whatever the sub-pieces of the two conductors (item 12), against the analytic 26.972 µH of the infinitely long coax, instead of 31.966 µH with the internal inductance of a solid shield; unmarked, the two cables read 43.472 µH (43.476 µH with carson_series), the 43.48 µH of two touching solid wires. A shield without a core loses \(\mu_0\ell/(8\pi)\) = 50 nH/m of self inductance against the same conductor without the tag (buried_lead() of the measurement generator builds its lead as a shield: the two-pole reading of a three-house network with buried feed and probe leads −2.5 % in reactance at 50 Hz and 1 kHz, the three-pole reading unchanged to 1e-6).
  12. Pieces of conductors lying beside each other (wave-1 audit of the calendar release, W1A-02). Item 9 decides per segment whether a point lies beside the partner, so a pair of sub-pieces of two conductors on one axis that do not overlap coupled as two filaments on the axis (distance 0) while the overlapping pairs coupled at the shield radius or at \(r_1 + r_2\): the pieces did not add up to the lumped pair. The 100 m coax read 26.912 / 26.852 / 26.374 / 24.608 µH in 10 / 5 / 1 / 0.25 m pieces (−0.2 … −8.7 %; every joint of the pieces cost about 6 nH), the unmarked pair 43.400 … 40.343 µH, the drops routed back along the PEN main of a golden case 3.9e-4 low in reactance at 1 kHz. Two rules now act on parallel pairs closer than touching. A thinner wire inside a cable shield (\(\delta + r_\text{thin} \le r_s\), \(\delta\) the lateral distance of the axes) couples at the shield radius at every axial offset — overlapping, end to end and apart — which is exact for a filament on the axis of a thin tube (every point of the tube is \(\sqrt{x^2 + r_s^2}\) away), so a shield made of several conductors, or a core and shield in sections, add up too. For two other conductors lying beside each other (the rule of item 9 acts on a parallel pair of their pieces), a point lies beside the partner when its foot falls inside the partner's whole conductor, not only inside the partner segment; the stretches have Grover's parallel-filament closed form. The solver passes one label per conductor (build_inductance_matrix(..., conductors=...); without labels every segment counts as a conductor of its own, the rule of item 9 in closed form). The pieces now add up to the lumped loop to 3e-12 (coax, marked and unmarked, 0.25 … 20 m pieces, all three earth-return models) and the drops along the main to 3e-15; the value stays continuous in the geometry, the same for every order and direction of the segments, and pieces of one conductor or conductors that only meet end to end on one axis (a main split at its taps) keep the filament integral (every other golden case bit-identical). The assembly of a 1 km coax in 2 m pieces takes 6.4 s instead of 5.8 s. Remaining: two unmarked cables in sections on one axis (a section of one beside a section of the other that it does not overlap) couple as filaments on the axis between the sections that do not overlap.
  13. Nearly parallel pieces (second wave-1 audit of the calendar release, W1R2-01, W1R2-03). The closed form of item 12 needs the pieces parallel within \(|\cos\varphi| \ge 1 - 10^{-9}\), about 4.5e-5 rad. A core tilted by more against its shield kept the rule of item 9 per segment, so the drift of item 12 came back in full, with a step at the tolerance: the 100 m coax read 26.966 µH in 0.25 m pieces at 4.4e-5 rad and 24.966 µH at 4.5e-5 rad (−7.4 %; −0.17 / −0.36 / −1.86 % in 10 / 5 / 1 m pieces). Pieces of two conductors that are nearly parallel — the lateral distance changes by at most the touching distance \(r_1 + r_2\) along the longer piece, and \(|\cos\varphi| \ge 0.99\); both bounds were dropped by item 14 — now get the two readings of item 12 against the partner's whole conductor with the stretches found exactly: each piece is split where the foot of its points passes an end of the partner's conductor and where the distance \(\rho(s)\) from the partner's axis crosses \(r_1 + r_2\) or \(r_\text{thick} - r_\text{thin}\) (from the closest approach of the two lines). On the stretches inside the shield and beside the partner the effective distance is constant and the integral has a closed form in the foot coordinate (\(du = \cos\varphi\,ds\)); a side that is entirely free takes the filament value of the pair, and a side with free and clamped stretches (a piece where the core leaves the touching distance, or passes an end of the partner) is integrated by the quadrature of item 9 with the conductor extents. The pieces add up to the lumped pair for tilts 0 … 1e-3 rad in 10 / 5 / 1 / 0.25 m pieces, in the matrix within 6.4e-12 (marked) and 3.1e-10 (unmarked; the largest value is the parallel closed form just below its tolerance, at 4.4e-5 rad) and in the solver (perfect_mirror and sommerfeld within 3.2e-11 marked, 3.1e-10 unmarked; under carson_series the Carson correction of one lumped pair, tiled at its mid-point distance, differed from the pieces by 1.7e-5 at 3e-4 rad and 1.3e-4 at 1e-3 rad, independent of the piece length — the correction's own tiling, not the rule; integrated per stretch since audit W1R3-07, ADR-0005 item 7). The literal proposal, the closed form at the mean lateral distance of each pair, missed by up to 1.35 % at 1.5e-4 … 7e-4 rad, where the core leaves the shield's tube inside a piece. Beyond the gate the rule of item 9 acted per segment. Where the core leaves the axis at the shield's start the touching stretch is then about one piece long, and the pieces differed from the lumped pair by 1.5e-7 (10 m pieces, 2.01e-3 rad), 6.6e-7 (1 m, 2.01e-2 rad) and 1.4e-6 (0.25 m, 8.01e-2 rad); in general the error was not small (item 14). The generator's overhead measurement leads are such a pair (the probe lead starts 10 mm beside the feed lead and ends on its axis, 2e-4 rad): their mutual in the default 5 m pieces was +1.0e-4 off the lumped one (1 m pieces +5.4e-4), now 4e-16; the probe junction potential moves by 6.5e-5 … 1.1e-4, the feed potentials and every electrode result not at all. Without labels (conductors=None) unmarked touching pieces stay per segment, while the inside reading of a marked shield needs no labels, also tilted. The pairs of two bundled conductors are evaluated in chunks of 4096 (W1R2-03; element-wise, so bit-identical): a 600 m pair in 1 m pieces peaked at 292 MiB with all pairs at once, now 30 MiB, the level before item 12.
  14. No length gate and no angular cap (third wave-1 audit of the calendar release, W1R3-01, W1R3-02). The two bounds of item 13 mixed two readings within one pair of conductors, and between a lumped pair and its pieces. Where the core crosses the shield axis at mid-length the touching stretch is two pieces long: just beyond the length gate the loop in 10 / 5 / 1 / 0.25 m pieces read −8.6e-5 / −6.4e-5 / −4.0e-5 / −3.0e-5 off the lumped pair (solver: X −7.6e-5 / −5.6e-5 in 10 / 5 m pieces under perfect_mirror and sommerfeld, homogeneous, two- and three-layer soil). Long pieces at small tilts read −1.7e-4 (2 × 50 m, 5e-4 rad), shield pieces of 15 / 1 m at 2e-3 rad −1.6e-3, and a core running 5 m beyond its shield +2.9e-5, its lumped mutual 4.4e-6 off the independent quadrature (the lumped loop stepped by −3.3e-5 at the gate). At the cap, two 2 m wires leaving one junction in 0.02 m pieces read 0 at 8.0° and −1.55e-3 at 8.2°. Decision of the coordinator: the rule acts on every pair of pieces of two conductors with a hit of the pointwise rule that is neither parallel within the closed form's tolerance nor orthogonal, at any angle and for pieces of any length; the classification of item 13 is exact at any angle. Every case above now adds up to the lumped pair within 2.2e-12, every lumped mutual equals the independent quadrature within 4.4e-16, the loop is smooth in the tilt (no step at the old gate, none at 8.1°; wires leaving a junction add up at 1° … 90° in 0.1 / 0.05 / 0.02 m pieces), and the matrices stay symmetric and positive definite. In the solver the pieces equal the lumped pair within 1.1e-15 under perfect_mirror; under sommerfeld within 1.6e-8 at 1 kHz (3.2e-7 at 10 × the old gate in 5 m pieces), the correction's own piece dependence, the same inside the old gate; under carson_series the correction of a tilted pair was tiled at the mid-point distance of each pair and the pieces differed from the lumped pair by 4.2e-4 (10 m pieces, 2e-3 rad), 1.4e-3 (5 m, 4e-3 rad), 1.9e-2 (10 m, 2e-2 rad) — the tiling, not this rule; per stretch since audit W1R3-07 (within 7.8e-6, ADR-0005 item 7). Only pairs with a piece that comes within the touching distance of the other's axis are classified (the others keep the filament value either way; bit-identical): a 600 m coax crossing at 0.05 / 0.3 rad in 1 m pieces assembles in 3.95 / 3.82 s against 3.73 / 3.66 s on the snapshot, where the gates skipped these pairs. Generated networks are bit-identical, with and without an inductive PEN.

docs.title: ADR-0005: Carson correction for the earth-return path
docs.text: Status Accepted — amended 2026.11 (review pass 10: Carson on its anti-parallel baseline, F32); see the amendment at the end of this document Date 2026-05-06 Deciders Project maintainers Scope groundfield

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-0004 added the Neumann self- and mutual-inductance integrals between distributed-conductor segments and assembled them into a per-frequency branch-impedance block

\[ Z_b(\omega) \;=\; R \;+\; j\omega\, L_\text{Neumann}. \]

For the magnetic image the earth was treated as a perfect mirror (\(\sigma_\text{earth}\to\infty\)). That is the same simplification Sunde 1968, ch. 7.4 uses for buried filaments and is known to be accurate when the relevant geometric dimension is small compared to the electromagnetic skin depth in soil

\[ \delta(\omega) \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{2}{\omega\,\mu_0\,\sigma_\text{earth}}} \;\approx\; 503\,\sqrt{\rho_\text{earth} \big/ f}\quad[\text{m}]. \]

For the quasi-static frequency window (\(f \le 1\,\mathrm{kHz}\)) and typical soil resistivities (\(\rho_\text{earth} \in [50, 5000]\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}\)) the skin depth \(\delta\) ranges from roughly 113 m (1 kHz, 50 Ωm) to 5.0 km (50 Hz, 5000 Ωm); at 50 Hz and 50 Ωm it is 503 m. The relevant geometric dimensions of an the TN low-voltage distribution network — house-to-station distance < 200 m, PEN-cable length up to 1 km, separation between measurement-lead and current injection 10–100 m — are not always small compared to \(\delta\). The perfect-mirror model therefore systematically underestimates the resistive part of the earth-return impedance and slightly overestimates the reactive part. The discrepancy is the very quantity that the research question

"diffusion field and Carson relevance for earth currents"

asks us to put a number on.

This ADR adds the Carson 1926 correction to close that gap. The result is a frequency-dependent, complex-valued addition to the branch-impedance block,

\[ Z_b(\omega) \;=\; \underbrace{R}_{\text{ohmic}} \;+\;\underbrace{j\omega\, L_\text{Neumann}^{\text{(perfect mirror)}}}_{\text{ADR-0004}} \;+\;\underbrace{\Delta Z_\text{Carson}(\omega, \sigma_\text{earth}, h_i, h_j, d_{ij})}_{\text{this ADR}}, \]

evaluated per frequency on the same per-branch endpoint geometry that ADR-0004 already exposes.

docs.title: Physical model
docs.text:
The starting point is John R. Carson, "Wave propagation in overhead wires with ground return", Bell Syst. Tech. J. 5(4) (1926), pp. 539–554. Carson solves Maxwell's equations for a straight horizontal wire above a homogeneous semi-infinite conductive half-space and writes the ground-return self-impedance correction as

\[ Z'_\text{Carson} \;=\; 4\omega\,J(2h\sqrt{\alpha},\,0), \qquad \alpha \;=\; 4\pi\lambda\omega \;\;[\text{CGS-emu}], \]

with

\[ J(p, q) \;=\; \int_0^{\infty}\!\!\bigl(\sqrt{\mu^2 + j} \;-\; \mu\bigr)\, e^{-p\mu}\cos(q\mu)\;d\mu \quad\text{(Carson eq. 29).} \]

The mutual-impedance correction between two parallel wires at heights \(h_1, h_2\) with horizontal separation \(x\) is

\[ Z'_{12,\text{Carson}} \;=\; 4\omega\,J\bigl((h_1+h_2)\sqrt{\alpha},\,x\sqrt{\alpha}\bigr). \]

In SI units this becomes (Carson eq. 30/31, converted by \(4\omega \to \omega\mu_0/\pi\) and \(\alpha = 4\pi\lambda\omega \to \omega\mu_0\sigma_\text{earth}\)):

\[ \boxed{\; \Delta Z_\text{Carson}(\omega) \;=\; \frac{\omega\mu_0}{\pi}\, \bigl[P(a,\theta) \;+\; jQ(a,\theta)\bigr], \;} \]

with the dimensionless Carson parameters

\[ a \;=\; D\sqrt{\omega\mu_0\sigma_\text{earth}} \;=\; \frac{D\sqrt{2}}{\delta(\omega)}, \qquad D \;=\; \begin{cases} 2h_i & \text{(self impedance, $\theta = 0$)} \\ \sqrt{(h_i+h_j)^2 + d_{ij}^2} & \text{(mutual impedance)} \end{cases}, \qquad \theta \;=\; \arctan\!\bigl(d_{ij}\big/(h_i+h_j)\bigr). \]

The functions \(P(a,\theta)\), \(Q(a,\theta)\) are the real and imaginary parts of the Carson integral \(J\). Their evaluation is split into three regimes following Carson's own discussion in section III of the original paper.

docs.title: Three evaluation regimes
docs.text: The functions \(P, Q\) are evaluated by selecting one of three expansions according to the magnitude of \(a\):

docs.title: Regime 1 — small a (a ≤ 0.25, leading-term form)
docs.text:
Carson eqs. 34–35:

\[ P_\text{small}(a,\theta) \;=\; \frac{\pi}{8} \;-\; \frac{a}{3\sqrt{2}}\cos\theta \;+\; \frac{a^2}{16}\cos(2\theta)\, \bigl(0.6728 + \ln(2/a)\bigr) \;+\; \frac{a^2}{16}\theta\,\sin(2\theta), \] \[ Q_\text{small}(a,\theta) \;=\; -0.0386 \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,\ln(2/a) \;+\; \frac{a}{3\sqrt{2}}\cos\theta. \]

docs.title: Regime 2 — intermediate a (0.25 < a ≤ 5, direct quadrature)
docs.text:
(Rewritten after the 2026-07-08 audit, WP-B2. The originally planned \(\sigma_i\)-series implementation was never built; the code evaluates Carson's integral \(J(p, q)\) numerically.)

Two quadrature paths, selected by the oscillation parameter \(q = a\sin\theta\):

  • \(\theta \approx 0\) (self-correction geometry): 64-node Gauss–Legendre on \([0, 30/p]\) — the integrand decays purely exponentially and the historic evaluation is machine-accurate (verified against adaptive references).
  • \(q > 0\) (mutual geometries): QUADPACK's Fourier integrator (scipy.integrate.quad with weight='cos') on \([0, \infty)\). This replaced the historic fixed-node Gauss–Legendre on \([0, 30/p]\), which failed for \(\theta \to \pi/2\) (small \(p\), unresolved \(\cos(q\mu)\) oscillation over a huge interval): the audit measured errors up to \(-36\,\%\) in \(P\) and \(+67\,\%\) in \(Q\) at buried-pair mutual geometries (\(a = 0.44\)–\(1.6\), \(\theta \approx 89°\)). The Fourier path also covers \(p = 0\) (\(\theta = \pi/2\)) exactly, where the imaginary part converges only conditionally through the oscillation. Verified to \(10^{-11}\) against an independent composite per-half-period Gauss rule with Euler acceleration (tests/test_audit_quadratures.py).

docs.title: Regime 3 — large a (a > 5, asymptotic expansion)
docs.text:
Carson eqs. 36–37:

\[ P_\text{large}(a,\theta) \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\frac{\cos\theta}{a} \;-\; \frac{\cos(2\theta)}{a^2} \;+\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\frac{\cos(3\theta)}{a^3} \;+\; \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\,\frac{\cos(5\theta)}{a^5} \;-\; \dots, \] \[ Q_\text{large}(a,\theta) \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\frac{\cos\theta}{a} \;-\; \frac{\cos(3\theta)}{a^3} \;+\; \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\,\frac{\cos(5\theta)}{a^5} \;-\; \dots \]

The truncation matches Carson's published curves (Fig. 2/3 of the original paper) within plotting accuracy for \(a \ge 5\); the regime-2/regime-3 boundary at \(a = 5\) carries the asymptote's truncation error (\(\lesssim 5\cdot10^{-4}\) absolute in \(P, Q\) at \(\theta = 80°\), smaller for steeper geometries). Two audit corrections (2026-07-08, WP-B2): the \(a^{-3}\) term of \(Q\) carries the factor \(1/\sqrt{2}\) (previously missing — \(\sim 6\cdot10^{-4}\) absolute at \(a = 8\)), and for \(\theta > 1.4\) rad (\(\approx 80°\)) the expansion degrades and the dispatcher routes through the regime-2 quadrature instead.

docs.title: Linear-system integration
docs.text:
The Carson correction enters the existing per-branch impedance block as one extra complex contribution per branch pair \((i, j)\):

\[ Z_b^{(i,j)}(\omega) \;=\; \delta_{ij}\,R^{(i)} \;+\; j\omega\, L_\text{Neumann}^{(i,j)} \;+\; \Delta Z_\text{Carson}^{(i,j)}(\omega). \]

The matrix \(\Delta Z_\text{Carson}\) is dense and symmetric (the Carson kernel is reciprocal). Assembly cost is the same as the Neumann matrix — one closed-form evaluation per \(M(M-1)/2\) pairs — but it must be rebuilt at every frequency, because the kernel itself depends on \(\omega\) through \(a\). The Neumann part stays frequency-independent and is built once, exactly as in ADR-0004.

The branch block consumed by _solve_cluster_currents is therefore formed at run time as

Z_b(omega) = R_diag + 1j * omega * L_neumann + dZ_carson(omega)

with R_diag, L_neumann precomputed and dZ_carson recomputed per frequency. The complex linear system

\[ \begin{pmatrix} Z & -C & 0 \\ C^\top & 0 & B^\top \\ 0 & B & -Z_b(\omega) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} I_e \\ \varphi_n \\ I_b \end{pmatrix} \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ I_\text{in} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \]

is solved per frequency, exactly as in ADR-0004.

docs.title: Earth-conductivity source
docs.text:
The earth conductivity \(\sigma_\text{earth}\) is taken from the soil model:

Soil model Source for \(\sigma_\text{earth}\) HomogeneousSoil \(\sigma = 1/\rho\) — exact TwoLayerSoil \(\sigma = 1/\rho_1\) (upper layer) with a runtime warning; see "Layered earth" below MultiLayerSoil \(\sigma = 1/\rho_1\) with a warning, identical strategy

For the homogeneous case the Carson series is exact (within the quasi-static / low-frequency assumption that Carson himself states: \(\omega \to 0\) and displacement currents in the dielectric neglected). For layered soils the pure Carson series is approximate; we keep it as a default for usability and document the escape hatch (mom_sommerfeld) explicitly.

docs.title: Engine-side switch
docs.text:
A new field is added to Engine:

class Engine(BaseModel):
    ...
    earth_inductive_model: Literal["perfect_mirror", "carson_series"] = "perfect_mirror"

Conductor.inductance_model = "neumann" continues to mean use the Neumann self/mutual integrals — no change. Whether the earth behaves like a perfect mirror or like a finite-σ Carson half-space is now a property of the engine rather than of each conductor, because every distributed conductor in the same world sits above the same earth. Default is "perfect_mirror" for backward compatibility (every existing test and notebook keeps its exact result).

Conductor.inductance_model = None is unchanged — the system stays real and the DC fast path is preserved bit-exact, regardless of earth_inductive_model.

docs.title: What about the electric Green's function?
docs.text: The Carson correction in this ADR addresses the magnetic image only — i.e. the mutual-impedance contribution to the longitudinal branch block. The electric image (charge image used by the existing image / image_2layer / mom kernels for the leakage current to soil) is not affected. That part already uses the appropriate static Green's function for the soil model (homogeneous, two-layer, n-layer). The two pieces are physically decoupled in the quasi-static regime: the conductive current in the wires sees the earth via the magnetic Green's function (Carson territory), the leakage current sees it via the electric Green's function (already implemented). For full electromagnetic coupling one would have to upgrade mom_sommerfeld to the Pollaczek kernel; that is left as a follow-up — see ADR-0006 (deferred).

docs.title: Deri/Semlyen complex depth
docs.text:
The Deri & Semlyen 1981 approximation replaces Carson's integral with the closed-form expression

\[ \Delta Z_\text{Deri-Semlyen}(\omega) \;=\; \frac{j\omega\mu_0}{2\pi}\, \ln\!\Bigl(\frac{D' + p}{D}\Bigr), \qquad p \;=\; 1\Big/\sqrt{j\omega\mu_0\sigma_\text{earth}}, \]

where the image is moved by a complex depth \(p\) below the soil surface. It is appealingly cheap (no series), but its accuracy degrades for short wires and for \(a \in [0.5, 5]\). We keep it as an internal sanity check in coupling/carson.py (deri_semlyen_correction) and use it in tests as a second opinion against the series implementation; we do not use it as the production code path.

docs.title: Direct numerical Sommerfeld quadrature
docs.text: Pollaczek 1926 generalises Carson to the layered half-space; the resulting integral has to be evaluated numerically. This is already implemented for the electric Green's function in solver/mom_sommerfeld.py. The magnetic Pollaczek kernel would slot into the same backend and would be the rigorous answer for the layered case. Cost: every frequency requires a 2-D Sommerfeld quadrature per segment pair — orders of magnitude slower than the closed-form Carson series. We defer this to a follow-up ADR (ADR-0006) and use mom_sommerfeld (electric only) plus Carson series (magnetic) as the typical working configuration.

docs.title: Layered earth via effective resistivity
docs.text: A pragmatic middle ground: when the soil is layered we replace \(\rho_\text{earth}\) in the Carson series by an effective resistivity \(\rho_\text{eff}(\omega)\) that interpolates between \(\rho_1\) (when \(\delta(\omega) \ll h_1\), the first-layer regime) and \(\rho_2\) (when \(\delta(\omega) \gg h_1\), the deep regime). We keep this as a future option and currently emit a runtime warning instead. The reason: the depth-blending is itself an approximation whose validity range is the same as the Pollaczek result we are trying to avoid. Better to be explicit about the approximation than to hide it inside an interpolation rule.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Every test below is implemented in tests/test_carson_coupling.py unless noted otherwise.

docs.title: Unit tests against Carson 1926
docs.text:
1. Wave-antenna example (Carson p. 552) \(h = 30\,\mathrm{ft}\), \(f = 5 \cdot 10^4\,\mathrm{Hz}\), \(\lambda = 10^{-12}\) emu → \(a = 4.0\) → \(J = 0.126 + j0.168\). Tolerance: \(\le 0.5\,\%\) relative.
  2. Wave-antenna example, second case Same geometry, \(\lambda = 10^{-14}\) emu → \(a = 0.4\) → \(J = 0.323 + j0.871\). Tolerance: \(\le 0.5\,\%\).
  3. Railway example (Carson p. 553) \(f = 25\,\mathrm{Hz}\), \(h = 30\,\mathrm{ft}\), \(x = 120\,\mathrm{ft}\), \(\lambda = 10^{-12}\) emu → \(J = 0.369 + j1.135\), \(\theta \approx 63°30'\). Tolerance: \(\le 0.5\,\%\).
  4. Tabulated curves Fig. 2/3 Spot checks at \(a \in \{0.5, 1, 2, 4\}\) and \(\theta \in \{0, \pi/4, \pi/2\}\). Tolerance: \(\le 1\,\%\) (Carson plotted on a small grid).

docs.title: Regime-boundary continuity
docs.text:
1. At \(a = 0.25\) the small-\(a\) form (regime 1) and the full series (regime 2) agree to \(\le 10^{-9}\) in \(P, Q\).
  2. At \(a = 5\) the full series (regime 2) and the asymptotic expansion (regime 3) agree to \(\le 10^{-6}\) in \(P, Q\).

docs.title: Limit checks
docs.text:
1. \(\sigma_\text{earth} \to \infty\) (perfect conductor) → \(\Delta Z_\text{Carson} \to 0\). The full assembled branch block reproduces ADR-0004 bit-exact (regression test).
  2. \(\omega \to 0\) → \(\Delta Z_\text{Carson} \to 0\). The DC solution reproduces ADR-0003 bit-exact.
  3. Frequency monotonicity — for fixed \(\sigma_\text{earth}\) and a 1 km PEN over earth the real part of the diagonal \(Z_b(\omega)\) grows monotonically with \(\omega\) in \([10\,\mathrm{Hz}, 1\,\mathrm{kHz}]\). Sanity check: ohmic earth-return contribution increases with frequency.

docs.title: Engineering benchmarks
docs.text:
1. 1 km PEN self impedance vs. Oeding + Carson lookup. Build a horizontal PEN conductor at \(h = 0.6\,\mathrm{m}\) above a homogeneous earth (\(\rho = 100\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}\)), 1 km long, radius 4 mm, run all distributed-capable backends at \(f \in \{50, 150, 500, 1000\}\,\mathrm{Hz}\). Verify \(Z_\text{self,per km}\) within 5 % of the Oeding/Tleis closed-form Carson R/X tabulation. Implementation: scripts/benchmarks/pen_1km_carson.py plus a regression test.
  2. Loop coupling open-circuit voltage with vs. without Carson. Two parallel galvanic conductors, 1 km long, separation 50 m. The injected current is 1 A on conductor 1, conductor 2 is open. The open-circuit voltage at \(f = 50\,\mathrm{Hz}\) must increase by \(\ge 5 \%\) (Carson on) compared to the perfect-mirror result. Test: test_carson_coupling.py:: test_loop_coupling_carson_increases_open_voltage.
  3. Cross-engine consistency at 50 Hz with Carson active. All distributed-capable backends (image, image_2layer, mom, cim, bem) must agree on the cluster impedance to within 5 %. fem continues to log a warning and fall back to the resistive solution.

docs.title: Layered-earth handling
docs.text:
1. Two-layer warning. Building an Engine with earth_inductive_model = "carson_series" against a TwoLayerSoil world emits a UserWarning containing the string "Carson series uses upper-layer rho_1".
  2. Carson(approx layered) vs. mom_sommerfeld. For a TwoLayerSoil with \(\rho_1 = 100\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}\), \(\rho_2 = 1000\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}\), \(h_1 = 1\,\mathrm{m}\), the Carson approximation differs from the Pollaczek/Sommerfeld reference by less than the documented bound (≤ 20 % at 50 Hz, ≤ 10 % at 1 kHz). The bound itself is a documented test artefact, not a guarantee — validated by the project's internal Carson harness.

docs.title: Cross-references
docs.text:
1. DC reproducibility — inductance_model = None keeps the system real for any setting of earth_inductive_model (regression).
  2. Bit-exact perfect-mirror regression — the full ADR-0004 test suite continues to pass with earth_inductive_model = "perfect_mirror" (default).

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
• Quantifies the relevance of the Carson correction for earth currents: "at which frequency / soil resistivity does the perfect-mirror approximation break down" can now be answered numerically — validated by the project's internal Carson harness.
  • The closed-form Carson series adds essentially zero cost (\(\mathcal{O}(M^2)\) scalar evaluations per frequency, vectorised via numpy). Frequency sweeps with \(N_f \le 20\) on relevant geometries (\(M \le 5\,000\)) remain inside the workstation budget.
  • The implementation is physically transparent: the same series Carson published in 1926, with the same regime split. Tests against Carson's own worked examples are the gold standard.
  • The earth conductivity now enters the inductance assembly explicitly, which makes the penetration depth \(\delta\) a first-class diagnostic. The new FieldResult.metadata["penetration_depth"] exposes \(\delta(\omega)\) per frequency for every engine.

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
• For layered soil the series is an approximation. We document the limit and provide a quantified comparison against mom_sommerfeld in the validation notebook. A user who needs rigor on layered soil must switch backends.
  • The branch block is rebuilt at every frequency. With Carson on and \(N_f\) frequencies, \(N\) segments, the assembly cost is \(\mathcal{O}(N_f \cdot M^2)\) closed-form evaluations on top of the existing \(\mathcal{O}(N_f \cdot N^3)\) LU. For typical (\(M \le 5\,000\), \(N_f \le 20\)) the assembly is still \(\le 10\,\mathrm{s}\) in the worst case; the LU dominates.

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
• Default behaviour (earth_inductive_model = "perfect_mirror") is unchanged. Existing notebooks, tests and benchmarks produce identical results to ADR-0004.
  • The Pollaczek kernel for the magnetic Green's function on a layered soil is deferred to ADR-0006 (open). That ADR will add solver/mom_sommerfeld.py magnetic-kernel support and will reuse the same engine.earth_inductive_model switch with a third value "sommerfeld".

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Carson, J. R. (1926). Wave propagation in overhead wires with ground return. Bell Syst. Tech. J. 5(4), 539–554. Primary source — equations 23, 25–37 are the production code path of this ADR.
  • Pollaczek, F. (1926). Über das Feld einer unendlich langen wechselstromdurchflossenen Einfachleitung. Elektrische Nachrichtentechnik 3(9), 339–360. Layered-earth extension (deferred).
  • Deri, A.; Tevan, G.; Semlyen, A.; Castanheira, A. (1981). The complex ground return plane: a simplified model for homogeneous and multi-layer earth return. IEEE Trans. PAS 100(8), 3686–3693. Used as a sanity check.
  • Oeding, D. & Oswald, B. R. (2016). Elektrische Kraftwerke und Netze, 8. Aufl., Springer. §9.4 "Erdrückleiter".
  • Tleis, N. D. (2008). Power Systems Modelling and Fault Analysis: Theory and Practice, Newnes. Ch. 3 — modern Carson series in SI units.
  • Sunde, E. D. (1968). Earth Conduction Effects in Transmission Systems, Dover. Ch. 7 — buried-wire equivalent.

docs.title: Amendment 2026.11 — Carson on its own baseline (review pass 10, F32)
docs.text:
Findings 10.20 (F32), 10.46 and 10.63.

  1. Baseline. Carson's correction is the change of the impedance of a line and its anti-parallel image in a perfectly conducting earth. Section Linear-system integration added it to the Neumann matrix of ADR-0004 with its additive perfect-mirror image, which roughly doubled the earth-return reactance: 1.66–2.25 times Carson's value for 100 m – 1 km lines and +41 % on \(|Z|\) at 1 kHz for a TN network with inductive PEN conductors (review pass 10). Since 2026.11 carson_series assembles the inductance matrix with image="antiparallel"; a 1 km isolated PEN reproduces \(l\,X'_\text{Carson}\) within 1 % (tests/test_inductive_solver_integration.py::test_carson_series_reactance_matches_carson).
  2. Regimes. The small-\(a\) regime (\(a \le 0.25\)) evaluates Carson's series to \(a^{12}\), with the sign rule read as the sign of each coefficient (the literal recursion is \(10^{-9}\) off at \(a = 0.25\)); the self-term quadrature at \(\theta = 0\) uses a graded composite rule and is at round-off; the asymptotic expansion is used only for \(a > 15\) (the boundary at \(a = 5\) jumped by up to \(9.3 \cdot 10^{-4}\)), with the sign of the \(a^{-7}\) term of \(Q\) corrected. Regime 2 therefore covers \(0.25 < a \le 15\).
  3. Cost. \(P\) and \(Q\) are memoised (bit-identical) and the corrections of all frequencies are built in one assembly.
  4. Positioning. carson_series is the fast approximation for long parallel lines over homogeneous earth; it is not a general replacement of sommerfeld, and the documentation no longer calls the two "identical".
  5. Validity domain (second adversarial audit, A2C-1). The per-metre tiling — the per-metre correction at the horizontal axis distance times the length over which the two segments overlap — is kept for near-parallel pairs (\(|\cos\varphi| > 0.99\)) of near-horizontal segments (inclination below 8.1°) on one side of the surface. A pair with one wire overhead and one buried has no anti-parallel baseline (a perfect conductor screens the soil) and couples through the field transmitted into the soil, carson_mixed_mutual_correction (Carson's \(J\) and the remainder of the buried wire's attenuation; Ametani et al. 2009). Against an independent quadrature it agrees to 4.2e-9 for x ≤ 300 m (\(q = x\sqrt{\omega\mu_0\sigma} \le 8.4\) at 1 kHz in 10 Ω·m; 1e-10 at 50 Hz) and to 1.2e-7 at x = 1 km (\(q = 28\)), where Carson's \(J\) itself is evaluated by QUADPACK's Fourier rule (the "1e-9" first stated here was measured up to 300 m). Oblique pairs and every pair and self term of a segment inclined by more than 8.1° get the Sommerfeld correction of a homogeneous earth of the same conductivity; before, an oblique pair got the per-metre value once per segment pair, which grew with the number of segments (two 1 km leads at 9°: 20× the Sommerfeld coupling). At the 8.1° boundary the result steps by the error of the per-metre model there (12 % for two 1 km leads 2 m apart at 1 kHz; 12.8 % after item 6).
  6. Order of the segments (third adversarial audit). Near-parallel pairs that are not exactly parallel were projected on the axis of the pair's first segment: reversing the segment order moved entries by up to 3.1 % of the largest one, and a pair could get an overlap in one order and none in the other. They are projected on the bisector of the two axes from the mean of the mid-points; every order and direction gives the same matrix. Exactly parallel pairs keep their projection. The step at 8.1° of item 5 becomes 12.8 % for two 1 km leads 2 m apart at 1 kHz (12.3 % with the old projection; 42 % for two 300 m leads at 50 Hz).
  7. Tilted pairs per stretch (audit W1R3-07). A near-parallel pair that is not parallel took the per-metre value at its mid-point distance for the whole overlap, so a lumped pair and its pieces differed: a core crossing its shield's axis at mid-length, loop reactance at 1 kHz, 4.3e-4 at 2e-3 rad, 1.4e-3 / 4.4e-3 / 1.9e-2 / 5.2e-2 at 4e-3 / 8e-3 / 2e-2 / 4e-2 rad. Where the pair comes close within its overlap — its smallest distance there is below 30 times the change of its horizontal offset along the overlap — the correction is integrated over the overlap with Gauss–Legendre nodes (4, plus 8 per change of the offset by \(h_i + h_j\), at most 32; on one depth no closer than touching). Elsewhere the mid-point value is exact to second order (an error of about \((\text{change}/d)^2/24\) of the entry, below 5e-5) and the pair keeps its single entry, as do pairs parallel up to round-off (bit for bit; the golden cases do not move). Lumped pair and pieces now agree within 2.9e-6 in the matrix and 8.0e-6 of the solved loop. The 100-house star has 3173 tilted entries among its 6710, none of which comes that close: it keeps every entry and its cost (integrating all of them cost 5.5 s of QUADPACK per frequency for 1.8e-6 of X).
  8. Accuracy for networks of short cables (stream w3perf, item 7). Carson's correction belongs to infinitely long lines; tiled over the pieces of short service drops (30 … 60 m at a skin depth of 159 m, 1 kHz, 100 Ω·m) it overstates the earth return of a generated LV network. Against sommerfeld with a refined discretisation (PEN in 2.5 m pieces, 1 m segments; the default sommerfeld agrees with it to 4e-5 … 1e-3, 1e-3 for the 5-house radial network), the input impedance of the generated star (100 houses) and grid (100 and 50 houses) networks with an insulated Neumann PEN reads X +9.3 … +14.9 % and R +5.5 … +10.9 % high at 1 kHz under carson_series; over the generated star, radial and grid networks of 5 … 100 houses (100 Ω·m and 30 … 200 Ω·m) X is 4 … 21 % and R up to 11 % high at 1 kHz and X 21 … 50 % and R up to 0.9 % high at 50 Hz (audits W3B-02, W3R2B-03; at 1 kHz / 50 Hz the 5-house radial network +13 % / +31 %, the 10-house radial network +20 % / +41 %, the 30-house star +17 % / +44 %, the 80-house radial network +19 % / +50 %; R of the 100-house radial network +11 % / +0.9 %). perfect_mirror reads +38 % / +40 % (10-house radial), +26 % / +37 % (30-house star), +36 % / +41 % (80-house radial) and +44 % / +45 % (5-house radial), so at 50 Hz carson_series is no closer than perfect_mirror except for the 5-house radial network. This error changes with the geometry. A change of the network is therefore reproduced by carson_series only to within that error: across the cabinet fix of audit W1B-01/02 the star's X moves by +1.18 % under carson_series and −3.54 % under sommerfeld (the refined reference: −3.54 %), across the cabinet threshold of the 100-house grid by +1.81 / −2.77 % (reference −2.77 %), of the 50-house grid by −21.6 / −18.9 % (reference −18.9 %). For such networks use sommerfeld; carson_series is the fast choice for long parallel lines.

docs.title: ADR-0006: Geometric Sommerfeld earth-return Green function
docs.text: Status Accepted — kernel corrected to the genuine Pollaczek form 2026-07-09 (audit 2026-07-08, WP-C1; see the amendment at the end of this document); amended 2026.11 (review pass 10: image-free baseline, exact layered kernel, λ grid) Date 2026-05-07 Deciders Project maintainers Scope groundfield

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-0005 added Carson 1926's earth-return correction \(\Delta Z_\text{Carson}(\omega)\) in the form

\[ \Delta Z_b^{(i,j)}(\omega) \;\approx\; z'_\text{Carson}(\omega, h_i, h_j, d_{ij})\,\cdot\,\ell_{ij}, \]

where \(z'_\text{Carson}\) is Carson's per-meter closed form and \(\ell_{ij}\) is the projected geometric length of the segment pair. This is the standard transmission-line modelling convention used in EMTP/PSCAD/ATP. It is exact for infinite parallel wires over a homogeneous earth, but it has two structural limitations that matter for typical applications:

  1. Short conductors / arbitrary geometry. Carson's per-meter formula assumes translation invariance along the wire axis. For wires whose length is comparable to the earth skin depth \(\delta\), or for non-parallel / 3-D arrangements, the per-meter closed form does not capture end effects. The typical frequency range (\(f \le 1\,\mathrm{kHz}\)) and soil resistivities (\(\rho_e \in [50, 5000]\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}\)) yield \(\delta \in [350\,\mathrm{m}, 35\,\mathrm{km}]\) — comparable to or larger than typical TN low-voltage distances. Many electrodes and short connection wires therefore live in the regime \(L \lesssim \delta\) where Carson is the wrong asymptote.
  2. Layered earth. Carson's series is rigorously derived for a homogeneous half-space. Layered configurations (\(\rho_1, \rho_2, h_1\)) appear in every typical study, and ADR-0005 handles them only with a UserWarning and the upper-layer \(\rho_1\) — a documented approximation, not a model.

This ADR establishes the rigorous geometric formulation of the earth-return inductive coupling: the vector-potential Green's function with the σ- (and layer-) dependent earth correction is integrated over the actual segment-pair geometry. ADR-0005's Carson series then becomes a fast asymptotic option, and ADR-0006 becomes the default for relevant studies where the asymptotic assumptions break down.

docs.title: Physical model
docs.text:
For a horizontal current source \(I\,d\vec{l}'\) at position \(\vec{r}'\) over (or in) a conducting half-space, the quasi-static vector-potential Green's function is

\[ G_\text{mag}(\vec{r}, \vec{r}';\,\omega,\sigma_e) \;=\; \frac{1}{R} \;+\; \int_0^{\infty}\!\frac{u_e-\lambda}{u_e+\lambda}\, e^{-\lambda(z+z')}\,J_0(\lambda\rho)\,d\lambda, \qquad u_e \;=\; \sqrt{\lambda^2 + j\omega\mu_0\sigma_e}\,, \]

with \(R = |\vec{r}-\vec{r}'|\) the direct distance, \(\rho\) the horizontal distance and \(z, z'\) the depths (positive into the soil). The integrand has the structure "reflection coefficient × exponential decay × Bessel kernel" — exactly the same family as the electric Sommerfeld kernel already implemented in solver/mom_sommerfeld.py.

The partial mutual impedance between two finite-length 3-D segments is then

\[ Z_{ij}(\omega) \;=\; j\omega\,\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\!\int_{C_i}\!\!\int_{C_j} (\hat{l}_i\cdot\hat{l}_j)\,G_\text{mag}(\vec{r}_i, \vec{r}_j;\,\omega,\sigma_e)\, dl_i\,dl_j . \]

This is the analogue of ADR-0004's Neumann integral, but with the σ-dependent kernel replacing the perfect-mirror \(1/R + 1/R'\).

docs.title: Limit checks (built into the test suite)
docs.text: Limit Result Validates \(\sigma_e \to \infty\) \(G_\text{mag}\to 1/R + 1/R'\) → ADR-0004 perfect mirror, bit-exact regression ADR-0004 unchanged \(\sigma_e \to 0\) \(G_\text{mag}\to 1/R\) → free space, no image \(\omega \to 0\) same Long parallel wires + homogeneous earth \(\int Z_{ij}\) collapses to Carson's per-m × \(\ell\) ADR-0005 recovered as asymptote Short wires over homogeneous earth \(Z_{ij}\) deviates from Carson by \(\mathcal{O}((L/\delta)^2)\) New physics captured Layered earth \(G_\text{mag}\) uses the layered reflection coefficient \(\Gamma_\text{mag}^{(n)}(\lambda)\) layered-earth studies

docs.title: Two pillars in one ADR
docs.text: This ADR explicitly addresses both homogeneous and layered earth. The implementation rolls out in two pillars, but the API and the mathematical formulation are designed for both from the start so that no second renaming is needed when the layered piece comes online.

docs.title: Pillar A — Homogeneous earth (this release)
docs.text:
The reflection coefficient is the Fresnel form

\[ \Gamma_\text{mag}^{(1)}(\lambda;\sigma_e) \;=\; \frac{u_e - \lambda}{u_e + \lambda}. \]

Implementation:

def earth_return_green_homogeneous(
    *, rho: float, z_i: float, z_j: float,
    omega: float, sigma_earth: float,
) -> complex:
    """G_mag(r, r') - 1/R, the σ-dependent earth correction."""

docs.title: Pillar B — Layered earth (same ADR, planned for the typical sweep)
docs.text:
For an n-layer earth, the reflection coefficient is built from the recursive Tagg/Sunde-style formula

\[ \Gamma_\text{mag}^{(n)}(\lambda;\rho_1,\dots,\rho_n,h_1,\dots,h_{n-1};\omega) \;=\; \frac{u_1 - \lambda - (u_1+\lambda)\,\Gamma^{(n-1)}_2(\lambda)\,e^{-2u_1 h_1}} {u_1 + \lambda - (u_1-\lambda)\,\Gamma^{(n-1)}_2(\lambda)\,e^{-2u_1 h_1}}, \]

with \(u_k = \sqrt{\lambda^2 + j\omega\mu_0\sigma_k}\). For \(n=2\) (two-layer), this collapses to a closed form that the test suite can compare against.

Implementation:

def earth_return_green_layered(
    *, rho: float, z_i: float, z_j: float,
    omega: float, layers: list[SoilLayer],
) -> complex:
    ...

HomogeneousSoil is implemented as the n=1 case of the layered function. Both share the same Sommerfeld-quadrature backend — only the reflection coefficient differs.

docs.title: Engine-side switch
docs.text:
Engine.earth_inductive_model gains a third value:

EarthInductiveModel = Literal[
    "perfect_mirror",   # ADR-0004
    "carson_series",    # ADR-0005 (asymptotic per-m Carson)
    "sommerfeld",       # ADR-0006 (geometric Sommerfeld kernel)
]

Default remains "perfect_mirror" — every existing notebook and test continues to produce its current bit-exact result. typical notebooks opt into "sommerfeld" for the production-grade runs; "carson_series" is preserved as the cheap asymptotic diagnostic and is documented as such.

docs.title: Numerics — Sommerfeld quadrature
docs.text:
Each segment-pair contributes one σ-dependent matrix entry \(\Delta Z_{ij}^{Sommerfeld}\). The double integral splits into:

  • Outer (geometry): 16×16 Gauss–Legendre over the two segment parameterisations. Reuses the _GL_NODES, _GL_WEIGHTS set in coupling/inductance.py.
  • Inner (Sommerfeld): adaptive quadrature on \([0, \lambda_\max]\) with \(\lambda_\max = M / (z_i + z_j + \rho)\) chosen so that the exponential factor \(e^{-\lambda_\max (z_i+z_j)} \le 10^{-13}\). 64-point Gauss–Legendre is the production scheme; for very small \(z_i + z_j\) (wires near the surface) we split \([0, \lambda_\max]\) into a logarithmic and a linear part to resolve the Bessel oscillations.

For horizontal segments at constant depth, the kernel \(K(\lambda) = \Gamma_\text{mag}(\lambda)\,e^{-\lambda(z_i+z_j)}\) factors out of the outer-integration loop and is computed once per segment-pair. The total cost is

\[ T_{Sommerfeld} \;=\; \mathcal{O}\bigl(N_f \cdot M^2 \cdot N_\lambda\bigr) \]

evaluations of \(J_0\) per outer node, fully vectorised through numpy. For typical (\(M \le 5000\), \(N_\lambda \le 200\), \(N_f \le 20\)) this is ≲ 5 minutes total — tolerable for the planned parameter sweeps.

docs.title: mom_sommerfeld reuse
docs.text: The existing electric Sommerfeld backend already evaluates a similar (but scalar-potential) Sommerfeld kernel. We do not fold the magnetic kernel into mom_sommerfeld's solver loop — keeping the two separate makes the code path clearer and lets ADR-0006 land without touching an existing backend. Both kernels share helper code in a new coupling/sommerfeld_inductance.py module.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
tests/test_sommerfeld_inductance.py:

  1. σ → ∞ collapses to ADR-0004: with sigma_earth = 1e9 and a buried PEN, the Sommerfeld solution agrees with the perfect- mirror solution to within \(10^{-6}\) on the cluster impedance.
  2. σ → 0 collapses to free space: with sigma_earth = 1e-9, the Sommerfeld correction is negligible compared to the self-inductance term.
  3. ω → 0 collapses to perfect mirror: at DC the correction vanishes; the full DC test suite from ADR-0003 must continue to pass.
  4. Long-wire homogeneous limit recovers Carson: for a 1 km PEN at 50 Hz, \(\rho_e = 100\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}\), sommerfeld and carson_series agree on the cluster impedance to \(\le 2\,\%\). For \(L = 10\,\mathrm{km}\) the bound sharpens to \(\le 0.5\,\%\).
  5. Short-wire deviation: for \(L = 10\,\mathrm{m}\) the Sommerfeld result deviates from the per-m × \(\ell\) Carson approximation by \(\ge 5\,\%\). The deviation grows with \(L/\delta \to 0\).
  6. Cross-engine consistency at 50 Hz with "sommerfeld" active: image, mom, cim, bem agree on the cluster impedance to within 5 %.
  7. Two-layer regression: a TwoLayerSoil world with \(\rho_2/\rho_1 = 10\) produces results that differ from the homogeneous Sommerfeld baseline by a controlled, frequency- monotone amount — i.e. the layered correction kicks in as the skin depth in the upper layer crosses \(h_1\).
  8. Two-layer textbook check: at the limit \(\rho_2/\rho_1 = 1\) the layered Sommerfeld solution reproduces the homogeneous Sommerfeld solution to within \(10^{-9}\).
  9. Field-point consistency: the potentials reported by result.potential(...) are unchanged when only the inductive model switches — the electric Green's function is independent of earth_inductive_model.

docs.title: Positive
docs.text:
• Reference computations run on a physically rigorous model. Layered earth, short wires, non-parallel geometries — all are treated correctly within the same numerical machinery.
  • The Carson series stays available as a cheap asymptotic reference. Users get a two-engine self-validation for free: if the two disagree, the geometry is outside the asymptotic regime.
  • The penetration-depth diagnostic in FieldResult.metadata becomes more meaningful — the actual physics of the layered earth is now in the kernel, so the diagnostic can be augmented with a per-pair Carson parameter \(a_{ij}\) that diagnoses which pairs are in the long-wire regime.
  • Layered-earth handling no longer needs a UserWarning — the Pollaczek/Sommerfeld kernel is the production path.

docs.title: Negative
docs.text:
• Computational cost grows by \(\mathcal{O}(N_\lambda)\) per segment-pair per frequency. Modest for typical cases (5 min sweep) but substantial for very large worlds (>10 000 segments). For those cases the asymptotic Carson model remains available as the fallback.
  • Three earth-inductive models in the engine schema increases the test matrix; we mitigate by parametrising the cross-engine tests over the model.

docs.title: Neutral
docs.text:
• Default behaviour unchanged. Existing notebooks and tests produce identical results.
  • Pillar B (layered earth) ships in the same release as Pillar A; the API is layered-aware from day one.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Sommerfeld, A. (1909). Über die Ausbreitung der Wellen in der drahtlosen Telegraphie. Ann. Phys. 28(4), 665–736.
  • Carson, J. R. (1926). Wave propagation in overhead wires with ground return. Bell Syst. Tech. J. 5(4), 539–554.
  • Pollaczek, F. (1926). Über das Feld einer unendlich langen wechselstromdurchflossenen Einfachleitung. Elektrische Nachrichtentechnik 3(9), 339–360. Layered-earth extension.
  • Wait, J. R. (1972). Electromagnetic Waves in Stratified Media, Pergamon. Ch. 3 — generalised reflection coefficients \(\Gamma^{(n)}_\text{mag}\).
  • Tleis, N. D. (2008). Power Systems Modelling and Fault Analysis, Newnes. Ch. 3 — modern Sommerfeld kernel for transmission-line modelling.
  • Stratton, J. A. (1941). Electromagnetic Theory, McGraw-Hill. §9-10 — derivation of the half-space vector potential.

docs.title: Amendment 2026-07-09 — Pollaczek kernel (audit 2026-07-08, WP-C1)
docs.text:
The 2026-07-08 physics audit found two structural defects in the kernel as originally implemented (1/R + ∫Γ e^{-λ(z+z')}J0):

  1. The primary term kept the static 1/R instead of the in-soil attenuated e^{-γR}/R. For buried conductors the attenuation is precisely where the earth-return resistance lives; the remaining (Γ-1) correction accumulated to ≈ -ωμ0/8 per metre — Carson's value with the wrong sign (verified numerically). The "Carson recovered as long-wire asymptote" row in the limit table above was never actually implemented as a test and does not hold for the historic kernel's real part.
  2. The soil-side reflection +Γ was applied to overhead conductors as well; the air-side boundary condition requires -Γ (Carson's geometry).

The implementation now dispatches per segment pair (buried–buried / overhead–overhead / mixed) with the genuine quasi-static Pollaczek kernels (see the module docstring of coupling/sommerfeld_inductance.py), keeps the mirror deduplication -1/R' and the buried direct-term attenuation (e^{-γR}-1)/R in closed form, and integrates only the smooth reflected/transmitted remainder (interpolated over ρ — the historic (16,16,nλ) tensor evaluation cost up to ~2 s per distant segment pair, now milliseconds).

Corrected limit table (regression-tested in tests/test_audit_inductive_stack.py and tests/test_sommerfeld_inductance.py):

Limit Result \(\sigma_e \to 0\) free space, no image (magnetically transparent earth) \(\sigma_e \to \infty\), overhead pair anti-parallel PEC image \(1/R - 1/R'\) (Carson baseline) \(\sigma_e \to \infty\), buried pair total coupling → 0 (conductor screened by the medium) Long parallel buried wires Pollaczek's \(\frac{j\omega\mu_0}{2\pi}[K_0(\gamma d) - K_0(\gamma D') + J_P]\), with \(\mathrm{Re} \to +\omega\mu_0/8\) per m at low frequency — validated to ~1 % (Im) / few % (Re, chain truncation)

Consequence for perfect_mirror: the default remains available and bit-stable, but it is now documented as a frequency-independent baseline whose additive image is far from the f < 1 kHz physics of buried conductors (audit finding F5) — use "sommerfeld" whenever quantitative Z(f) matters.

docs.title: Amendment 2026-07-20 — closed per-unit-length companion (references.pollaczek)
docs.text:
The kernel above assembles a PEEC segment inductance matrix: it is rigorous for arbitrary wire lengths and orientations, but a single per-unit-length line impedance \(z'(f)\) cannot be read back from it without an ill-defined return-path assumption (the self term is log-divergent in the segment length; PEEC \(\neq\) per-unit-length). Some consumers need exactly that scalar — a reduced nodal network of an earthing system whose line elements are \(L_\text{red}/z'(f)\), and an independent analytic reference for the assembled stack's earth-return reactance.

groundfield.references.pollaczek.pollaczek_self_impedance supplies it: the rigorous two-layer, buried-conductor self impedance per unit length in the closed Pollaczek/Sunde spectral-integral form \(Z' = j(\omega\mu_0/2\pi)[\ln(2h/\mathrm{GMR}) + 2\int_0^\infty e^{-2h\,u_\text{eff}(\lambda)}/(\lambda + u_\text{eff}(\lambda))\,d\lambda]\), with the Tagg/Sunde/Wait effective vertical wavenumber \(u_\text{eff} = u_1(u_2 + u_1\tanh u_1 h_1)/(u_1 + u_2\tanh u_1 h_1)\), \(u_i = \sqrt{\lambda^2 + j\omega\mu_0/\rho_i}\).

Corrected in 0.15.0 (review pass 9, finding F09)

Until 0.14.1 both this ADR and the implementation carried \(e^{-2h\lambda}\) in the exponent — Carson's air kernel, correct only because \(\gamma_\text{air}\approx 0\). For a conductor buried in the earth the Pollaczek/Sunde form requires \(e^{-2h\,u}\). The consequence of the old exponent was a systematically under-estimated earth-return resistance whose deficit grew with frequency and with burial depth (−0.5 % at 50 Hz / \(h=1\) m, −5.8 % at 1 kHz / \(h=3\) m, −54 % at 1 MHz), and — misleading at the time — an \(R'\) that sat below \(\omega\mu_0/8\) and fell with depth. Both are the opposite of the correct behaviour. That inverted trend had been recorded as a physical nuance in the 0.14.0 notes; it was the bug's signature.

It is earth-return only (same convention as references.earth_return.carson_self_impedance), reduces to Carson in the homogeneous limit, and brackets between the two homogeneous Carson bounds otherwise (deep-layer dominated below ~1 kHz). It is the analytic per-unit-length companion to this ADR's assembled kernel: the two are the same quasi-static earth-return physics reached two different ways, and a loop-closure test (tests/test_earth_return_benchmark.py) pins the assembled stack, the Pollaczek reference and the independent Tsiamitros (2005, Eq. 8) two-layer integral to within ~1 % on the Case V reactance at 1 kHz. See docs/api/references.md and tests/test_pollaczek_reference.py.

docs.title: Amendment 2026.11 — image-free baseline, exact layered kernel, resolved λ grid (review pass 10)
docs.text:
Findings 10.35, 10.36, 10.45, 10.46 (F50, F52) and 10.60.

  1. Image-free baseline. The correction is computed against free space (\(\Delta G = G - 1/R\)) and the solver builds the Neumann matrix without an image (image="none"); the numbers equal the former additive pairing to round-off. Conductors that cross the soil surface or lie in it are solved; the pair integrals are split at \(z = 0\) (F52). The image is removed exactly where another convention is requested (F50: the layered point kernel had the wrong sign).
  2. Exact layered kernel. For any number of layers the same-layer spectral amplitude uses generalised reflection coefficients and the pairs in different media a batched interface solve (10.35). Pillar B of this ADR is thereby complete: a three-layer earth whose lower two layers are equal reproduces the two-layer earth (the single-air-image form was +17 … +25 % in \(X'\)).
  3. λ grid. The logarithmic region ends before \(J_0\) oscillates, the linear region carries 16 nodes per \(J_0\) period up to four times the largest physical scale, and an exhausted node budget raises SommerfeldResolutionWarning instead of truncating silently (10.36; distant pair entries were −24 % at 200 m and +274 % at 400 m).
  4. Assembly. Geometry, λ grid and Bessel tables are built once per segment pair for the whole frequency set (10.60, bit-identical). The tabulated assembly (Engine.sommerfeld_assembly="tabulated", one table per pair of depth groups and frequency) is faster on large networks and closer to a converged reference than the per-pair rule; by the user decision of 2026-11-08 (Q16) it is the default, and the per-pair rule stays available as "exact".
  5. Pollaczek reference. references.pollaczek uses the exact two-layer amplitude and the \(K_0\) head (10.45). Benchmark B13 compares the solver's per-metre line impedance with it.
  6. Long segments (second adversarial audit, A2C-2). The correction of a segment pair was one 16 × 16 Gauss–Legendre rule, which cannot resolve \(e^{-\gamma R}\) along a segment much longer than the skin depth, and every lumped inductive conductor is one such segment (3 km at 1 kHz in 100 Ω·m: +13.4 % earth-return resistance). A segment longer than a quarter skin depth of the most conductive layer gets a composite outer rule (16 nodes per piece, at most 512 pieces, beyond that a SommerfeldResolutionWarning) and a correspondingly dense \(S(\rho)\) table. Frequencies with equal piece counts share one pass, so every frequency still equals a single-frequency assembly bit for bit; segments below the threshold keep the previous rule bit for bit.
  7. Accuracy of a segment's correction (third adversarial audit, A3C-4). The "1e-4" of item 6 was measured on buried conductors in 100 Ω·m. Against a refined rule (pieces δ/32, \(S(\rho)\) spacing 0.005), at 50 Hz and 1 kHz, 0.3 … 60 skin depths up to 3 km, buried in 100 Ω·m or in 1000/30 Ω·m and overhead at 10 m over 10 Ω·m, the exact assembly is within 5.9e-4 in the earth-return resistance and 2.4e-4 in the reactance (worst: a 3 km overhead line at 1 kHz; buried in 100 Ω·m 1.7e-4), the tabulated one within 3.3e-4 / 9.6e-5. The spacing of the \(S(\rho)\) table dominates. Below δ/4 the historic single rule reaches 4.8e-4 at δ/4, so the correction steps by 3.5e-4 (resistance) and 1.2e-5 (reactance) where the composite rule takes over; the step is kept because removing it would change every short segment.
  8. Self terms and close pairs (user decision Q34; audit W2B-05). The tensor rule of items 6 and 7 misses the kink of the integrand along the line of closest approach — of a segment with itself (the diagonal) and of two segments that come close (wires beside each other, a core in its shield) — formed by the \(\gamma^2R/2\) term of the direct part and its counterpart in \(S(\rho)\), smoothed only over the decay length \(z + z'\). That, not the table spacing, is the error of item 7 for buried conductors (with \(S\) summed exactly at every node the single rule was still 3.9e-4 off at δ/4); for two wires 1 mm apart in 30 over 1000 Ω·m it was 1.5e-3. The self term of every (plane-split) sub-segment is now the exact one-dimensional reduction \(2\int_0^L (L - u)\,g(u)\,du\) (one spectral plan per segment, as before, so \(g\) depends on \(u = |s - s'|\) only), with 16-node panels doubling from \(z + z'\) up to δ/4, uniform up to 40 δ and doubling beyond, and \(S\) summed at the nodes or, for long segments, from a cubic spline (spacing 0.02 in \(\ln(\rho + z)\)). A pair whose Gauss nodes come closer than half the longer segment gets a graded rule along the line of closest approach (outer rule over one segment split at the projections of the other's ends, inner rule split at the closest point, both graded from \(z + z'\)); one segment twice gets the self rule, so a core and its shield on one axis keep a loop without earth-return correction. Other pairs keep the tensor rule bit for bit. Against a refined rule (panels δ/128, first panel \((z + z')/16\), spacing 0.005, 1024 logarithmic λ nodes) and an independent reference (closed-form direct part, the \(\mathrm{Ji}_0\) kernel of the spectral part; audit W3B), at 50 Hz and 1 kHz from 1 m and 0.01 δ to 3 km (buried at 0.7 m in 100, 1000/30 and 30/1000 Ω·m, overhead at 10 m over 10 Ω·m), the self correction is within 1.1e-9 and has no step where the rule changes (below 3e-13); close pairs (wires 1 mm … 1 m apart, a core tilted by 1e-4 rad, collinear neighbours, a 30° junction) are within about 4e-8 (3.5e-8 for two 1 m wires 1 mm apart in 30 over 1000 Ω·m at 1 kHz, 2.7e-9 at a quarter skin depth). The logarithmic region of the λ grid has 256 nodes since audit W3B-01: with 64 the skin-scale part of \(S\) was under-resolved, and segments of 1 m … 0.01 δ were 1e-5 … 3e-4 off (about 1e-8 of a solved impedance); 256 cost nothing measurable. Cost (W2B-05): the pieces of a long sub-segment stood at different depths when it was inclined, each pair of them got its own λ grid, and the grid cache held 512 of them — one lumped conductor of 2 km from a rod at 0.5 m to a junction at 0.7 m took 28 s and 1.6 GB (about \(L^{2.7}\); 100 km more than 7.8 GB). The self rule costs \(O(L)\); a single segment is not cut into pieces; close pairs involving a long segment are evaluated whole in the tabulated assembly; λ grids above \(2^{16}\) nodes go to a cache of eight entries, and \(J_0\) tables above \(2^{21}\) entries are evaluated in row chunks (bit-identical below that size). The same conductor now solves in 1.1 s within 0.21 GB (100 km: 10.6 s, 0.24 GB; the \(J_0\) work grows 2.2-fold per doubling of the length instead of 7-fold). The λ budget of \(2^{17}\) panels resolves \(J_0\) up to \(2^{17}\cdot 2\pi\,(z + z')/30\): beyond 33 km this conductor (38 km for one at 0.7 m) warns SommerfeldResolutionWarning and is not converged, so the 100 km solve is a cost figure, not a result (audit W3B-10). The input impedance of that world is within 3.6e-7 (X) of a chain of 25 m pieces at 2 km, 1 kHz (2026.11.0: −2.0e-6, and its lumped value 2.9e-6 off in R). Five golden cases move by 8e-10 … 4.9e-7.

docs.title: ADR-0007: Cross-layer electrodes and conductors
docs.text: Status Accepted — step 1 (interface split), layer-aware post-processing and the mom lift implemented 2026-07-09 (audit WP-D; see the amendment at the end); amended 2026.11 (review pass 10: one owner per layer, slivers, reciprocity) Date 2026-05-07 Deciders Project maintainers Scope groundfield

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Every layered-soil backend currently rejects worlds in which any electrode segment crosses a layer interface:

ValueError: image_2layer: a segment lies below the layer interface
(z_max = 2.500 m, h_1 = 1.000 m). The current backend assumes all
electrodes sit in the upper layer.

This precondition exists in image_2layer, mom_sommerfeld, cim and bem. The reason is purely numerical: the Tagg/Sunde image series and the Sommerfeld kernel as currently implemented both assume source and observer in the same upper layer. The mathematical Green's function for two-layer earth supports arbitrary layer combinations, the implementation just hasn't been extended yet.

For typical applications this is a blocking limitation. Realistic geometries that we must be able to compute include:

  • Driven rods (Tiefenerder) of 1.5–3 m length at house connections that pass through the typical \(h_1 = 0.5\,\)m to \(5\,\)m upper layer into the lower one.
  • Foundation electrodes at depths around 0.8–1.5 m that may straddle a thin top layer.
  • MV cable shields routed at 1.0–1.5 m depth, often below the resistive top layer of dry-fill / paving.
  • Cable cabinets and substations with deep grounding stars.

Without cross-layer support the user has to either truncate the geometry artificially (wrong physics) or thicken the upper layer beyond physical reality (wrong soil model). Neither option is acceptable for typical cases.

docs.title: Physical model
docs.text:
For a 2-layer earth (upper layer \(\rho_1\) thick \(h_1\), lower layer \(\rho_2\) semi-infinite), the electric Green's function for a source at depth \(z_s\) observed at depth \(z\) has four pair-type cases that depend on which layer the source and the observer inhabit:

\[ G(\vec r, \vec r')\;=\;\begin{cases} G_{uu}(\vec r,\vec r') & 0\le z, z_s\le h_1 \quad\text{(both upper)} \\ G_{ul}(\vec r,\vec r') & 0\le z\le h_1,\; z_s>h_1 \\ G_{lu}(\vec r,\vec r') & z>h_1,\; 0\le z_s\le h_1 \\ G_{ll}(\vec r,\vec r') & z, z_s>h_1 \quad\text{(both lower)} \end{cases} \]

With \(G_{ul} = G_{lu}\) by reciprocity. Each of the four kernels has a closed-form Tagg/Sunde image-series representation and a direct Sommerfeld-quadrature representation, both documented in Sunde 1968 ch. 3 and Tagg 1964. In the limit \(\rho_2 = \rho_1\) all four collapse to the homogeneous kernel (K=0); in the limit \(\rho_2 \to \infty\) they collapse to "PEC at \(z = h_1\)" (no current can enter the lower layer).

docs.title: Implementation strategy — three phases
docs.text: This ADR ships Phase A in the same release. Phase B and C are explicit follow-up work documented here so the API contract is stable.

docs.title: Phase A — Discretiser split + uniform numerical kernel
docs.text:
1. Discretiser split. _discretize_electrode and _discretize_conductor get a new optional argument layer_interfaces=[h_1, h_2, ...]. When a segment would cross a layer boundary at depth \(h_k\), it is split at that depth into two segments. After this step every segment lies fully in exactly one layer; a new _Segment.layer_index field records which.
  2. Layered Green's-function kernel. A new coupling.layered_green module evaluates \(G_{ij}(\vec r, \vec r';\,\rho_1,\rho_2,h_1)\) for any pair \((i, j) \in \{u, l\}^2\) via direct Hankel-transform numerical integration of the spectral solution to the 2-layer matching problem. The kernel is consumed by all four layered backends.
  3. Lift the preconditions. z_max < h_1 is replaced by a discretiser-split call. Every segment-pair entry in the reaction matrix uses the appropriate kernel \(G_{uu}, G_{ul}, G_{ll}\) depending on the layer indices.
  4. Image-series fast path (Tagg/Sunde) is preserved for the common \(G_{uu}\) case; the slower spectral-quadrature path is used for \(G_{ul}\), \(G_{lu}\), \(G_{ll}\).

docs.title: Phase B — Closed-form image series for ll and ul (planned)
docs.text:
The Tagg/Sunde image series for \(G_{ll}\) uses the lower-to-upper reflection coefficient \(-K\) and an image structure analogous to the \(uu\) series; the \(ul\) case carries a transmission factor \((1 + K)\) and progressively deeper "transmitted-then-reflected" images. Both are derivable in closed form (Sunde 1968, eqs. 3.32–3.34) and will replace the slower spectral-quadrature path in _layered_green_kernel for typical worlds with many cross-layer segments.

Speedup target: Phase A's geometric Sommerfeld quadrature is \(\mathcal{O}(N_\lambda)\) per pair (≈ 128 spectral evaluations per pair × 9 line-line samples = 1 152 evaluations per diagonal entry, 128 per off-diagonal). Phase B's truncated image series truncates at \(|K|^n < \text{tol}\), typically 10–30 terms, with each term being a cheap \(1/r\) — speedup factor ≈ 30–100x.

API contract: no public API change. The dispatcher in _two_layer_self_kernel_factory(allow_cross_layer=True) will automatically pick the closed-form path when both \(z_i, z_j \le h_1\) + Tagg/Sunde-uu (already implemented), and the new closed-form \(ll\) and \(ul\) helpers when one or both segments are in the lower layer. The Sommerfeld quadrature stays as a sanity check.

Validation programme for Phase B (when implemented):

  1. ll vs Phase-A Sommerfeld at \(f = 0\) Hz, ρ_2/ρ_1 = 10, h_1 = 1 m, z = z_s = 2 m, s = 0.1 m → ≤ 0.5 % rel difference.
  2. ul vs Phase-A Sommerfeld in the symmetric configuration (same parameters, different z, z_s) → reciprocity check ≤ 1e-9 abs.
  3. ρ_1 = ρ_2 limit: every term beyond \(K^0\) vanishes, the series reduces to the homogeneous free-surface image — bit-exact.
  4. End-to-end: 1 km PEN on a 2-layer world with rod tip 1 m below h_1 — Phase B vs Phase A on the cluster impedance ≤ 1 % rel, wall-clock speedup ≥ 30x.

Status: deferred to a focused follow-up where the derivation can be cross-checked against Sunde 1968 and Tagg 1964 worked examples. For production-grade single-frequency runs at \(\lesssim 500\) segments, the Phase A path is acceptable (a few seconds per solve); Phase B becomes essential for the parameter-sweep phase of large parameter studies (many EFH counts × multiple soil models × multiple frequencies).

docs.title: Phase C — n \ge 3 layers (deferred)
docs.text: The MultiLayerSoil case generalises the 2-layer image series to a recursive Tagg-Sunde stack with reflection coefficients \(\Gamma_k(\lambda)\) at each interface. This is consistent with the existing image_nlayer dispatcher and the Sommerfeld formulation in solver/cim.py / solver/bem.py. Phase C is a straightforward extension once Phase A is stable.

docs.title: API impact
docs.text:
• Engine schema is unchanged.
  • World / Conductor / Electrode are unchanged.
  • _Segment gains a layer_index: int field.
  • _discretize_electrode, _discretize_conductor accept layer_interfaces and split there.
  • All four layered backends drop the if z_max >= h_1: raise check and dispatch the kernel by (layer_i, layer_j).
