docs.title: Audits W4R2A and W4R2B: round 2 on the wave-4 fixes
docs.text:
The second round tried to break the wave-4 fixes (snapshot 4eb1c2c) with the boundary elements of round 1, the axisymmetric model, mom refined and closed forms of the smoothed line source. Findings:

  • W4R2A-01, W4R2B-03 (medium): the 3-D model next to another wire. The fallback of W4A-03 sent a ring without room for its mesh block to the 3-D model, which read two diagonal rings 1.3 … 3.8 mm apart +11.4 … +14.3 % high against an estimate of 0.42 %, without a message; coaxial rings 7.5 cm apart, where the texts promised 2e-3, read +4.35e-3, 6 cm apart +1.0e-2, and below one source radius the port entries were off by up to 4.3 %; the radius correction counted other ports' wires with the observer's current.
  • W4R2A-02 (medium): the refined ring block held up to a contrast of 33; a ring touching a layer 1000 times more conductive read −1.61e-2 against an estimate of 1.07e-2, and at refinement=1 the estimate fell below the error at contrasts 100 and 1000.
  • W4R2A-03 (medium): the 3-D model neither warned nor refused a rod end at an interface (+43 % for a tip on a 1000 / 30 Ω·m interface).
  • W4R2B-01, W4R2B-02 (low–medium): on straight pieces longer than about 7 m off the coordinate axes the observer's own piece was clipped by round-off (a 20 m oblique strip −3.8e-4); an arm of the same polyline folded back at any angle but exactly parallel counted whole (a hairpin tilted by 1e-4 rad +1.41e-3, a 10° V +8.5e-4 against the same V as two strips).
  • W4R2A-04, W4R2A-05 (low): the reach of the near-interface warning lay 0.2 … 0.4 wire radii short for a thick wire on a small ring, and cut wires below a contrast of 2 read up to ±1.5 % without a warning; diagnose() with a fem engine reported a ring that the axisymmetric model solves.
  • W4R2B-04 … W4R2B-07, W4R2A-06, W4R2A-07 (low, info): resolved concrete with a thin cover ended in a bare ValueError after meshing; stale texts (level ratios, station memory, the junction table, the refusal of W4B-03); tests that failed on the base for the wrong reason.
  • B8 (open point of stream fw4int): the 3-D model is right; mom's floating port at the benchmark's 0.5 m is not converged. Refined to 1/32 m it falls by 0.20 … 0.75 % and ends 0.15 … 0.21 % above fem, and on a coaxial rod and ring the axisymmetric model confirms the 3-D transfer resistance to 1.3e-3.

Confirmed: golden 563 of 563 quantities identical in both audits; one near-interface warning per solve in every backend that should warn and none from the axisymmetric model; no false positive over 868 tests and the tutorials; the depth residual, the coaxial rings at 10 cm and the brace effect reproduce to the digit; the refusals of W4B-03 and W4B-08, the determinism of W4B-07 and the memory keys hold.

docs.title: Streams fw4r2a and fw4r2b: fixes of audits W4R2A and W4R2B
docs.text:
• fw4r2b, wires beside each other (W4R2A-01, W4R2B-03): two wires run beside each other where a point of one lies within 1.5 R of the side of the other and the two run within 30° of parallel, or where the whole of one lies within 1.5 R of another it does not meet; junctions, crossings at more than 30°, a rod on a ring and collinear pieces that meet are left alone. The model keeps such wires 1.5 R apart by a smaller source radius for the whole world and refuses them below 2.2 radii of the thickest bare wire of the world (3.3 such radii, axis to axis) before meshing, naming the wires, their distance, mom and image. Coaxial rings 4.5 … 10 cm apart lie within 1.72e-3 of the solid tori in every port entry and the bonded value, inside the estimate; 3 cm is refused by the node limit, the diagonal rings of W4R2A-01 and the ring at a rod head before meshing. The window term of another port counts only where the two wires meet; the coordinator kept this against the literal brief, since dropping it would put an L of two bonded strips 6.3e-4 below the same L as one polyline (1.0e-4 with it) without fixing any audited case.
  • fw4r2b, the own wire (W4R2B-01, -02): the axis distance comes from the cross product (the 20 m oblique strip matches its closed form to 4e-16); the own polyline counts whole only where it has turned by less than 120° (the tilted hairpin −1.9e-4, mom −2.0e-4; the jump at the threshold 1.5e-4 for 4 m arms, −1.26e-3 for 0.5 m arms, replaced in round 3 by a blend in the accumulated turn; the auditor's axis-line rule moved rings away from the solid torus and was not taken).
  • fw4r2b, the rest (W4R2B-04 … -07, W4R2A-07): resolved concrete with a thin cover is refused before meshing; the new fem_error_estimate_transfer (1.06 … 6.3 times the transfer error where the model holds; 6.3 on the coaxial analogue of B8); the B8 note says that mom at 0.5 m is not converged; the level ratios (rods 3.3 … 4.4, rings 3.0 … 3.4) and the CG refusal corrected; the W4B-01 tests fail on their base by assertion; solid_earth defaults to 2 million nodes. The AP1 station and the house mesh are unchanged to 7 digits.
  • fw4r2a, the ring block (W4R2A-02): graded towards the points where the interface cuts the wire at a narrow angle or comes closest to it, in angle and radius, from cells of 1e-3 wire radii, with 32 instead of 64 intervals. The estimate bounds the error in all 113 cases of the auditor's sweep at the default and at refinement=1; the default lies within 5.1e-5 of the boundary elements up to a contrast of 1000 (3.2e-5 at 100), at fewer nodes than before (a touching ring 151 807 nodes, 1.8 s, 0.76 GB).

docs.title: Audits W4R3A and W4R3B: round 3 on the wave-4 fixes
docs.text:
A short round on the round-2 fixes (snapshot b727b0b), with the boundary elements of rounds 1 and 2, the axisymmetric model, mom refined, image and closed forms. Findings:

  • W4R3B-01 (medium): two collinear wires of different ports with a small end gap ("stacked rods") were left alone, and an end gap up to the wire radius counted as meeting: rods 2 mm … 3 cm apart read +5.1e-2 … +6.4e-3 in a port entry and −20 % … −2.9 % in the transfer entry, far outside both estimates, without a message.
  • W4R3B-02, W4R3B-03 (low–medium): wires that meet at less than 30° (a V, a branch) were refused with the distance of a sample point; the 120° rule tested a piece's direction, not the turn along the chain (an arm turned by 360° counted whole, a spiral as one polyline +2.08e-3 against its windings, the jump at 120° up to −1.26e-3 for short arms).
  • W4R3B-04, W4R3B-05 (low): wires met at an axis distance of the smaller radius, not where their surfaces touch (a 2 m cross jumped by −7.5e-4); the refusal radius is that of the thickest bare wire of the world.
  • W4R3A-01 (low): mesh features merged only within the snap tolerance, so a ring axis a few picometres off an interface still read +35 … +44 % or failed, silently.
  • W4R3A-02 (low): the resistive side of the reach table had been measured above the wire for a thin ring only; a 55 mm wire under a 33 times more resistive layer read +1.72 % at 1.3 radii, unreported.

Confirmed: the graded ring block (the 113-case sweep bit for bit, 26 more worlds against the boundary elements, the estimate above every port entry), the rod-end warning once per solve, diagnose(), the costs, the cross-product axis distance, the 1.5 R and 30° switches for wires that do not meet, the thin-cover limit, the transfer estimate wherever the model holds (1.06 … 6.3 times the error), and the AP1 station and house mesh bit-identical in their radius correction.

docs.text:

Collinear pieces meet only without a gap, and a collinear piece of another port counts only where the wires meet. docs.title: Final documentation pass (author's request of 2026-11-16)
docs.text:
Before the release the author asked for a documentation that reads well, renders every formula on GitHub Pages, documents the whole public API, has getting-started examples, explains the physics, mathematics and numerics behind the methods, says when which engine is the better choice and where its limits are, and carries three case studies. Six streams worked on separate files (docstart, doctheory, docapi, docex1 … docex3), the coordinator integrated them and checked the formulas.

  • docstart: the home page, getting started (rod, ring, grid in homogeneous and two-layer soil, a fault with touch and step voltage, a profile, plots, every number asserted), concepts, glossary, units, and the decision guide Choosing an engine (decision path, accuracy against the benchmarks, cost measured on this machine, one table per engine of where it must not be used). It fixed the stale "uniform per electrode" of the engine table (one current per straight wire since Q30).
  • doctheory: one skeleton for the five engine pages (what it solves, method, numerics, accuracy, limits, the audit trail collapsed), the theory pages derived step by step, known limitations and warnings as one short entry per limit with the remedy. It found and fixed four errors (the skin-depth range, fem's support for return_to, junctions and voltage sources, a stale size notice, the quadrupole bound) and reported four outside its files (ADR-0005's skin depths, a code comment, the cim / bem names in an error message, the fem3d extra on the how-to index), which the coordinator fixed.
  • docapi: every name of the public __all__ lists (92 modules, 864 entries) is rendered with a docstring summary; 62 were on no page and 77 had no summary (constants and type aliases documented only by #: comments). tests/test_docs_api_coverage.py keeps it so.
  • docex1 … docex3: the case studies E01 (secondary substation and its LV network: 9.9 Ω alone, 0.29 Ω with 30 houses), E02 (single-family house: concrete moisture, rod, outer ring, image / mom / fem) and E03 (60 m × 40 m substation grid in two-layer soil against EN 50522, with the measures that make it pass). E02 found that a bare ring bonded 1 m outside a foundation mesh reads the touch voltage +5 … +16 % high with the image family (now in the known limitations and the safety docstring); E03 found the corner gap of the touch-voltage envelope below and the larger field errors of image_2layer over a resistive bottom (+45 % at mesh centres).
  • The envelope at the corners (author's decision): the 24 equally spaced directions of touch_voltage_envelope hit the rounded corners of the offset curve only for a square; the 60 m × 40 m grid read 12 % / 28 % low, on the unsafe side. The envelope now also stands on the arc around every corner of the convex hull of the wires (nine feet per corner, corners=True); on that grid it equals the maximum over 3600 directions to 1e-4. Square grids, rings and rods keep their maximum; corners=False reproduces the directions alone; no golden case uses the envelope.
  • Review W5E of the envelope fix: the collinearity tolerance of the hull grew with the absolute coordinates; at UTM coordinates a 20 m × 1 m outline collapsed to one straight wire and the maximum read 1.2 % low (W5E-01; the hull is built relative to the lower-left corner of the footprint). Two text corrections (W5E-02, -03). Checked correct: every corner foot at the distance to 1e-15 over many shapes and distances, the default within −0.07 % of dense sampling at the origin-scale coordinates.
  • Round 2, W5R2 (author's request): the fix holds — no maximum changes with the coordinates, no arc is lost, no sweep flips (425 705 hull vertices). Two low findings, both fixed: at projected coordinates the tolerance lay below the coordinates' round-off, so edge nodes of rotated outlines (also generated foundations) became corners and the number of feet depended on the coordinate system (64 instead of 44 at UTM; the maximum unchanged; W5R2-01: the tolerance includes 16 ulp of the largest coordinate). Five feet per 90° arc read a narrow outline 0.22 % low between two feet (W5R2-02: nine per corner, every probe within 0.001 %).
  • Formulas: a headless-Chromium render of the built site under the mike version path with the vendored MathJax found three formulas left raw (two docstrings split by a line that Markdown read as a list item), raw TeX in the table of contents of four headings with math, and a \texttt with an underscore. All fixed: 99 pages, 4540 formulas typeset, none with an error; tests/test_docs_math.py guards the three classes.
  • On the way: ruff format --check, a blocking CI step, failed on T08 and two test files on the base; fixed. The golden rebase (D8) had removed the v0.15.0 world JSON that tests/test_soil_models.py read; it is a fixture now. DIN 18014 is cited in its edition 2023-06.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
These case studies take the tools of the tutorials to complete engineering questions. Each one models a real type of installation and answers what a grounding engineer has to answer for it: the earthing impedance, the earth potential rise for a fault, and the touch and step voltages against the permissible values of EN 50522. Each also asks which engine to trust and why, and ends with the limits of the example.

Each example is a Jupyter notebook. The page shows the stored outputs of a complete run, and you can download the notebook and run it yourself. As in the tutorials, the key numbers are checked in assert cells against a second method: another engine, a convergence study or a closed-form estimate. If you have not used groundfield before, start with the quickstart. For the choice of engine, see choosing an engine.

Example The question E01 Secondary substation and its low-voltage network How much does the low-voltage network lower the earthing impedance of a 10/0.4 kV station, which earth potential rise and touch voltages does a fault cause, and which potentials reach the houses? E02 Single-family house What earthing resistance and touch voltage does the foundation earth electrode of a detached house give, and what do concrete moisture, the soil model, a rod or an outer ring change? E03 HV substation grid in two-layer soil Does the mesh earthing grid of a high-voltage substation meet the permissible touch voltage of EN 50522 in two-layer soil, and what makes it pass?

docs.title: E01 — Secondary substation and its low-voltage network
docs.text:
A 10/0.4 kV secondary substation earth (a ring with four rods) connected through the PEN to the foundation earth electrodes of 30 houses and two cable cabinets, in two-layer soil (200 over 30 Ω·m). The case study quantifies the global earthing effect, with numbers for 1 to 80 houses and five soils: 9.9 Ω for the station alone, 0.29 Ω with the network. It covers:

  • the earth potential rise and the touch voltages for a resonant-earthed and a low-impedance-earthed fault, against EN 50522;
  • the potentials the PEN transfers to the houses, including a house without an earth electrode;
  • what changes at 1 kHz.

It also asks how far the numbers can be trusted: a discretisation ladder, image against mom, mom against mom_sommerfeld, and what fem can and cannot do here. It runs in about one minute.

docs.title: E02 — Single-family house
docs.text:
The earthing of a detached house with a foundation earth electrode in concrete, alone, with a driven rod, or with a ring earth electrode 1 m outside, in homogeneous and two-layer soil. It shows:

  • how concrete moisture and the soil model move the earthing resistance;
  • when a rod pays off (only once it reaches a more conductive layer);
  • why an outer ring roughly halves the touch voltage and keeps working when the concrete dries out.

It turns the permissible touch voltage of EN 50522 into an admissible earth potential rise. It compares image, mom and fem and explains where they differ. It runs in about half a minute.

docs.title: E03 — HV substation grid in two-layer soil
docs.text:
A 60 m × 40 m mesh grid with corner rods carries an earth fault current of 2 kA. It sits in a resistive top layer over a conductive bottom, and in the reverse. The notebook:

  • checks the segment length;
  • compares the grid impedance and the earth potential rise with the homogeneous limits, IEEE 80 and Dwight;
  • maps the touch voltage and evaluates the step voltages;
  • assesses the design against the EN 50522 permissible touch voltage for 0.5 s, and shows the measures that make it pass in each soil: a grading conductor, perimeter rods, shoes or crushed rock.

It explains why the touch voltages near a grid come from mom, not from image_2layer. It also shows how the layer contrast moves the impedance and the touch voltage in opposite directions. It runs in about a minute.

One house is added by hand: an old building at the eastern end of the network, 11.5 m beyond the eastern cable cabinet, without an earth electrode of its own. Its PEN ends on a junction at the service connection box, a node without contact to the soil. No current flows to it, so it changes nothing else in the solution; sections 2 and 3 use it.

The station earth alone has about 9.9 Ω. Connected to the network, the fault current meets 0.29 Ω, 2.9 % of that: the network lowers the impedance by a factor of 34. Only 1.75 % of \(I_E\) leaves the soil at the station's own electrodes, 98 % at the houses. The PEN puts the station and the 30 foundations in parallel; together they cover about 240 m × 70 m, and at that size the current reaches the conductive bottom layer (the soil comparison below shows it).

This is the mechanism behind a global earthing system in the sense of EN 50522. Whether a real network qualifies as one is a separate assessment that this example does not make.

A single house on the PEN already lowers the impedance to 40 % of the station alone, five houses to 13 %, thirty to 2.9 %. Each further house helps less, because it stands in the potential funnels of the others: from 30 to 80 houses \(\lvert Z_\mathrm{in}\rvert\) falls to 47 % of its value, where \(1/n\) would give 38 %. At 1 kHz the curve flattens, because the reactance of the PEN limits how much the remote houses can help (section 4).

In every soil the network carries the fault current: its impedance is 2.3 to 14 % of the station alone. The two impedances see different soil. The station's electrodes, all within 2.5 m of the surface, see mainly the top layer; the network, some 240 m wide, sees mainly the bottom layer. The network impedance therefore follows \(\rho_2\) (0.29 Ω over 30 Ω·m, 0.46 Ω over 200 Ω·m, both with a 5 m top layer), and the reduction is largest for a resistive top over a conductive bottom and smallest the other way round. A thick resistive top layer (1000 Ω·m, 30 m) keeps the network at 2.4 Ω.

HOUSING = [(-1.5, -1.25), (1.5, -1.25), (1.5, 1.25), (-1.5, 1.25)]
WALLS = [(1.5, 0.0), (0.0, 1.25), (-1.5, 0.0), (0.0, -1.25)]


def touch_station(res, wld, k=F50):
    # Largest |U_T| in V/A at the walls of the station housing.
    u = [
        gf.touch_voltage_at_part(
            res,
            wld,
            position=p,
            bonded_to=STATION,
            exclude=[HOUSING],
            frequency_index=k,
        )[1]
        for p in WALLS
    ]
    return np.abs(np.concatenate(u)).max()


def touch_houses(res, wld, k=F50):
    # Largest |U_T| in V/A 1 m outside each foundation, one value per house.
    largest = []
    for h in HOUSES:
        _, u = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(res, wld, electrode=h, frequency_index=k)
        largest.append(np.abs(u).max())
    return np.array(largest)


def touch_old_house(res, wld, k=F50):
    # Largest |U_T| in V/A around the service connection box of the old house.
    u = gf.touch_voltage_at_part(
        res,
        wld,
        position=OLD_BOX,
        bonded_to="old_house_box",
        exclude=[OLD_HOUSE],
        frequency_index=k,
    )[1]
    return np.abs(u).max()

Two fault scenarios show what these per-ampere values mean. \(I_E\) is the part of the earth-fault current that flows into this earthing system; the share that the screens of the MV cables carry back (the reduction factor) is not computed by groundfield and is assumed to be taken off already. The permissible touch voltage \(U_{Tp}\) comes from the library's EN 50522 curve (gf.permissible_touch_voltage_en50522).

Scenario MV neutral earthing \(I_E\) fault duration \(t_f\) A resonant (Petersen coil): residual current, the network keeps running 60 A not cleared B low-impedance, or a double earth fault: cleared by protection 1000 A 0.5 s

The currents are examples, not data of a real network. The last column below is the largest \(I_E\) for which every touch voltage stays within \(U_{Tp}\).

With the network the EPR falls to 0.29 V/A, and both scenarios pass. The largest touch voltage is no longer at the station but at the old house without an earth electrode, 0.22 V/A. It sets the limits of the network: 362 A for a fault that is not cleared, 1018 A for one cleared in 0.5 s. In scenario B it reaches 221 V against 225 V, a margin of 2 %, smaller than the spread between the engines in section 5 (up to 3 % for touch voltages). In practice one would give that house an earth electrode of its own, or measure. Section 3 shows why it is the weak point.

At 50 Hz every house carries 97 to 100 % of the station's potential: the voltage drop along the PEN is small against the EPR. In scenario B the protective conductor of every house rises to 280 to 287 V against remote earth for the 0.5 s of the fault. The touch voltage at a house with a foundation earth electrode is only about half of that potential, 0.13 to 0.15 V/A, because its own electrode and its neighbours lift the ground around it. It grows towards the edge of the network, where fewer neighbours lift the ground; the largest is at a corner house, 116 m from the station.

The old house at the end of the eastern cable has the potential of the cabinet, 0.28 V/A, and 79 % of it appears as touch voltage: nothing lifts the ground under it but the far field of the network. That is the classic hazard of a transferred potential, and the foundation earth electrodes of the other houses are what keeps it small there.

At 1 kHz the picture changes: the potentials fall along the PEN, to 62 % at the far ends. What counts is the cable length from the station, not the distance; the western main joins its first house 13.5 m from the station ring, the eastern one after 3.5 m, hence the two branches near the station. The houses close to the station now carry the higher 1 kHz EPR and have the largest touch voltages, up to 0.20 V/A.

The surface potential at 50 Hz (per ampere of \(I_E\)) shows the whole village lifted with the station: every foundation sits in its own potential funnel on a common plateau.

From 50 Hz to 1 kHz the network impedance rises by 36 % to 0.40 Ω, at a phase angle of 31°; the station alone stays at 9.9 Ω. The station's own electrodes take a larger share of the current (2.7 % instead of 1.75 %), and more houses help less: going from 30 to 80 houses lowers \(\lvert Z_\mathrm{in}\rvert\) to 0.47 of its value at 50 Hz but only to 0.62 at 1 kHz.

For a planner this means: an impedance measured or computed at 50 Hz is not the impedance for the harmonics of a residual current; the touch voltage per ampere of a 1 kHz current is up to 0.20 V/A here, a third more than at 50 Hz. The rho-f model of T04 carries \(Z(f)\) into a network calculation. The earth-return model matters at these frequencies: the default sommerfeld is the reference, while carson_series reads the reactance of LV networks with short service drops too high (earth return).

docs.title: E01 — A secondary substation and its low-voltage network
docs.text:
This case study computes the earthing of a 10/0.4 kV secondary substation (German Ortsnetzstation) together with the TN low-voltage network it feeds: 30 single-family houses whose foundation earth electrodes are bonded to the station earth through the PEN conductors, in two-layer soil. It is written for grounding engineers who want numbers, and it answers five questions:

  1. How much does the low-voltage network lower the earthing impedance at the station (the global earthing effect), and how does that depend on the number of houses and on the soil?
  2. What earth potential rise and which touch voltages does an earth fault on the medium-voltage side of the station cause, with and without the network?
  3. Which potentials does the PEN transfer to the houses, and where in the network is the touch voltage largest?
  4. What changes at 1 kHz?
  5. How far can the numbers be trusted?

The building blocks are explained in the tutorials and are not repeated here: T03 (input, cluster and electrode impedance, split factor), T06 (the network generator), T04 (frequency response) and T08 (touch voltages and EN 50522). The network is one point of the parameter space of the AP1 studies (see the glossary) for which the generators were built: a station, house connections and cable cabinets in two-layer soil.

Runtime: about 70 s.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Part Model Generator setting station earth ring of 4 m radius, 0.6 m deep; four 2.5 m rods on a 2 m circle; bonded SubstationConfig default houses 30 foundation earth electrodes, 10 m × 10 m, 2 × 2 meshes, 0.8 m deep, bare residential default layout three rows of ten houses, 25 m apart, rows 30 m apart; the station in the centre ManhattanGridPlacement default cable cabinets two, at the far ends of the two halves, one 1.5 m rod each CabinetConfig default PEN copper, 78.5 mm², insulated, 0.6 m deep, inductive PenConfig(inductance_model="neumann") soil \(\rho_1\) = 200 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m, over \(\rho_2\) = 30 Ω·m TwoLayerSoilSpec

Station. The HV protective earth and the LV system earth of the station form one common earthing system, as usual in TN networks. The LV neutral, and with it the PEN of every outgoing cable, is bonded to the station earth.

Network. Each of the two cable cabinets (German KVS) has a PEN main of its own from the station (star topology). The mains run along the centre row and are joined to its houses; the houses of the outer rows are connected to the main of their half by service drops. The foundations are modelled bare; the effect of their concrete encasement is the topic of case study E02.

PEN. A wire of 5 mm radius, insulated from the soil (no leakage), cut into 5 m pieces. The pieces carry their self and mutual inductances (Neumann's formula) and the earth-return correction of the conducting soil (sommerfeld, the default). The inductance makes the network frequency dependent.

Soil. A resistive top layer (dry sand) over a conductive bottom (water-bearing ground). It is one of the soils of the AP1 study grid, in which \(\rho_1\) runs from 30 to 1000 Ω·m, \(\rho_2\) from 30 to 200 Ω·m and \(h_1\) from 5 to 30 m; section 1 varies it.

Fault. An earth fault on the MV side of the station drives a current \(I_E\) into the station earth, which returns through remote earth to the infeeding substation. The model feeds 1 A into the station cluster. The field problem is linear, so every voltage is first given per ampere of \(I_E\) (in V/A, numerically an impedance) and scaled in section 2.

Engines. Two-layer soil and wire electrodes call for the default image engine, which forwards to image_2layer: closed-form kernels, cheap, and accurate for impedances. Its current model, one uniform current per straight wire, is not accurate enough for surface potentials next to meshes and bonded clusters (T08), and both the foundations and the station are such clusters. For touch voltages the network is therefore solved a second time with mom, which carries one current per segment. Both use 1 m segments; section 5 checks that choice.

docs.title: 1 How much does the network lower the station's earthing impedance?
docs.text:
Two numbers describe the global earthing effect:

  • the resistance \(R_\mathrm{station}\) of the station earth alone, the value a planner computes for the station without its LV connections;
  • the input impedance \(Z_\mathrm{in}\) of the network seen from the station, the impedance the fault current meets: the station, every house and both cabinets in parallel through the PEN.

The split factor \(s\) is the share of \(I_E\) that leaves the soil through the station's own electrodes (T03).

docs.title: How many houses does it take?
docs.text: The generator builds the same network with 1, 5, 10, 30 and 80 houses (the smaller ones in one row through the station, the larger ones in rows of ten); each is solved at 50 Hz and at 1 kHz.

docs.title: How much does the soil matter?
docs.text: The same station and the same 30-house network in five soils of the AP1 grid, at 50 Hz:

docs.title: 2 Earth potential rise and touch voltages during an MV earth fault
docs.text:
The earth potential rise (EPR) \(U_E = \lvert Z_\mathrm{in}\rvert\,I_E\) is the potential of the station earth against remote earth. A person who touches an accessible metal part bonded to an earth electrode and stands 1 m from it bridges the touch voltage \(U_T = \varphi_\mathrm{part} - \varphi_\mathrm{feet}\) (the prospective value, see T08). The touch points:

  • the station housing, 3 m × 2.5 m in the centre of the ring: feet 1 m from the middle of each wall, all round, none inside the housing;
  • the houses with a foundation earth electrode: metal parts on the outer walls (a service connection box, a tap, a gate), feet 1 m outside the foundation in 24 directions and on the arc round each corner (touch_voltage_envelope);
  • the old house: its service connection box, feet 1 m around it, none inside the house.

They are evaluated on the mom solution, which is field-grade next to the foundations.

docs.title: 3 What potentials does the PEN transfer to the houses?
docs.text:
The PEN connects every house to the station, so every house takes part in the potential rise. Its foundation is at the potential of its cluster, \(\varphi_\mathrm{house}\), which differs from the station's only by the voltage drop along the PEN. The protective conductor carries that potential into the house: it is a transferred potential. What a person outside the house bridges is the touch voltage, the difference to the ground 1 m outside the wall.

The figure shows both for every house against its distance from the station, at 50 Hz and at 1 kHz.

docs.title: 4 What changes at 1 kHz?
docs.text: Below 1 kHz the soil stays quasi-static: an earth electrode is a resistance. What changes with frequency is the PEN: its series impedance \(R + j\omega L\) grows with the angular frequency \(\omega\), and the remote houses contribute less (T04). This matters for the harmonics of a residual earth-fault current, for earth testers that measure at a frequency other than 50 Hz, and for the frequency-dependent model of the network that a network calculation needs.

docs.title: 5 How far can the numbers be trusted?
docs.text: Three free checks have already passed: Kirchhoff's current law (the leakage currents add up to \(I_E\)), the fall of \(Z_\mathrm{in}\) with every added house, and diagnose without findings. Four more follow: the discretisation, a second current model, a second Green's function, and a method that shares no kernel with the others. The section ends with the engines' known limits that apply here.

docs.title: Discretisation
docs.text: The segment length is halved twice:

docs.title: Current model and Green's function
docs.text: image and mom share the image kernels but not the current model. mom and mom_sommerfeld share the discretisation but not the Green's function: the Tagg/Sunde image series against the Sommerfeld integral evaluated by quadrature. The first pair runs on the full network; mom_sommerfeld is slower, so it runs on a small variant with five houses.

docs.title: What fem can and cannot do here
docs.text: fem solves the volume problem by finite elements and shares no kernel with the integral engines (fem). Its axisymmetric model takes rods on one axis and rings around it, to about 1e-4, in a fraction of a second. The station's ring alone is such a world:

docs.title: Known limits of the engines that apply here
docs.text:
From the known limitations, the ones that bear on this example:

  • Uniform current per wire (image): impedances of meshes like these foundations are 0.4 to 0.7 % above one current per segment; touch and step voltages next to them are only impedance-grade, hence mom for the field values here.
  • Point kernel (mom): grounding resistances 0.9 to 1.9 % low, as measured above.
  • Earth return: carson_series reads the reactance of generated LV networks 4 to 21 % high at 1 kHz against sommerfeld; use the default.
  • Generated networks: the service drops of the outer rows pass 0.2 m above the side wires of the centre-row houses without inductive coupling to them (moved aside, at most 0.006 % with an insulated PEN); the 1 kHz reactance depends on where cables and drops meet the foundations; and the star topology with one cabinet per building group is a modelling choice: for the default 30-house network it reads a reactance at 1 kHz 55 to 64 % above that of the former cabinet strip with its parallel drops.
  • Quasi-static soil: valid below 1 kHz; impulse and lightning currents are out of scope.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Global earthing. The 30-house network lowers the impedance at the station from 9.9 Ω (the station alone) to 0.29 Ω at 50 Hz, 2.9 %; 98 % of the fault current leaves the soil at the houses. In five soils of the AP1 grid the ratio is 2.3 to 14 %; the network impedance follows the bottom layer.
  • Earth fault. With the network the EPR is 0.29 V/A; the touch voltages are 0.065 V/A at the station housing and at most 0.15 V/A at the houses with a foundation earth electrode. Scenario A (60 A, not cleared): at most 13 V against 80 V, where the station alone would give 216 V. Scenario B (1 kA, 0.5 s): 221 V against 225 V, at the old house.
  • Transferred potentials. At 50 Hz every house carries 97 to 100 % of the station's potential. A foundation earth electrode keeps the touch voltage at about half of it; at a house without one it is 79 %.
  • 1 kHz. \(\lvert Z_\mathrm{in}\rvert\) rises by 36 %, the far houses fall to 62 % of the station's potential, more houses help less, and the touch voltage per ampere near the station rises by a third.
  • Trust. 1 m segments are converged to 3e-5; image and mom agree within 1.2 % on the impedance and 3.4 % on the touch voltages; two Green's functions agree to 1e-8; fem confirms the station ring to 0.1 % and refuses the network.

docs.title: Limits of this example
docs.text:
• One generated network. The generator's defaults in one soil, one realisation: not a real network. A study runs the parameter space (house counts, penetration of foundation earth electrodes, soils) with sweeps or Monte Carlo (how-to guide Sweeps and Monte Carlo).
  • Bare foundations. The concrete encasement of real foundation earth electrodes changes their resistance (case study E02 and the concrete shells page).
  • The MV side is not modelled. No MV cable screens, no neighbouring stations connected through them, no reduction factor: \(I_E\) is an input. In a real network the cable screens connect further station earths and lower the impedance further.
  • Only this LV network. Water pipes, other utilities, neighbouring LV networks and the houses' own installations are not part of the model.
  • Touch voltages are prospective proxies. Feet 1 m from the station walls and the house foundations stand for the real touch points; no body, shoe or surface-layer resistance is included. Step voltages are not assessed (T08 shows how), nor are the stress voltages on the LV installations.
  • EN 50522 enters only through the library's permissible touch voltage curve; the scenario currents are examples.

import math
import time

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import groundfield as gf
from groundfield.generators import (
    FoundationElectrodeSpec,
    GroundingSystemSpec,
    RodElectrodeSpec,
)
from groundfield.references import ieee80

print("groundfield", gf.__version__)

R_A, COVER, DEPTH, SIDE = 0.005, 0.05, 0.8, 10.0  # m: bar radius, cover, depth, side
RHO_C = 150.0  # Ohm m: earth-moist concrete, the base case
SOILS = {
    "S1": gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0),
    "S2": gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=300.0, rho_2=30.0, h_1=2.0),
    "S3": gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=50.0, rho_2=500.0, h_1=2.0),
}
ROD = RodElectrodeSpec(length_m=6.0, depth_m=0.5, offset_xy_m=(0.0, -6.0))
RING = FoundationElectrodeSpec(style="ring", size_m=SIDE + 2.0, depth_m=DEPTH)  # bare
VARIANTS = {"A": (), "B": (ROD,), "C": (RING,)}
FOUNDATION = "house_foundation_0"  # the generators' name of the first bar


def house(soil, rho_c=RHO_C, extras=(), style="mesh"):
    # The house earth (foundation plus extras, bonded), fed with 1 A.
    # rho_c=None: the bars lie bare in the soil.
    world = gf.create_world(soil=soil, name="E02 house")
    foundation = FoundationElectrodeSpec(
        style=style,
        size_m=SIDE,
        depth_m=DEPTH,
        wire_radius_m=R_A,
        concrete_rho_ohm_m=rho_c,
        concrete_thickness_m=COVER,
    )
    spec = GroundingSystemSpec(electrodes=[foundation, *extras])
    anchor = spec.build_at(world, (0.0, 0.0), "house", np.random.default_rng(0))
    gf.create_source(world, attached_to=anchor, magnitude=1.0)
    return world


IMAGE = gf.create_engine(segment_length=0.5)  # image_2layer in two layers
MOM = gf.create_engine(backend="mom", segment_length=0.5)


def r_e(world, engine=IMAGE):
    # Earthing resistance in Ohm: the input impedance at 50 Hz.
    return engine.solve(world).input_impedance()[0].real

To separate the shell from the soil, a perfectly conducting shell (\(\rho_c\) = 1 µΩ·m, \(C \approx 0\)) gives the resistance of the thick wire of radius \(r_b\) alone. The rise above it, divided by \(C/L\), should not fall below 1: the shell term is smallest when the current leaves every metre of bar evenly, and the bonded bars choose the distribution with the least total resistance. A dry shell forces that even distribution, so the ratio should approach 1.

What the sweep says:

  • Concrete as conductive as the soil changes nothing; wetter concrete lowers \(R_E\) a little, because the soil then sees bars eleven times thicker. In S2, whose top layer (300 Ω·m) is worse than earth-moist concrete, the concrete even improves the earth.
  • Dry concrete dominates. From about \(\rho_c \approx 10\,\rho\) on, the shell term \(C/L\) outgrows the soil part, and at 5 000 Ω·m the earth has 36 … 39 Ω in all three soils: the soil hardly matters any more. Concrete that dries from earth-moist (150 Ω·m) to cycling humidity (1 000 Ω·m) already doubles the earthing resistance.
  • The decomposition holds: the rise above the thick wire is 1.055 \(C/L\) for wet concrete and tends to \(C/L\) for dry concrete, because a dry shell evens out the current over the bars.

def surface(result, x, y):
    # Surface potential at the points (x, y), in V per A.
    pts = np.column_stack([np.ravel(x), np.ravel(y), np.zeros(np.size(x))])
    return result.potential(pts).real.reshape(np.shape(x))

Under the house the ground stays at about 0.8 \(U_E\) with moist concrete: the foundation grades the potential of the floor, which is why it serves as protective bonding as well as an earth. Outside, the potential falls steeply: at the feet 1 m out, 40 % of the earth potential rise is gone in front of the middle of a wall and about half at a corner (the map). The ring 1 m outside lifts the potential exactly where people stand (0.81 instead of 0.60 \(U_E\) in front of the wall). With dry concrete the shell takes up most of the voltage, and the soil around the house hardly rises at all (0.08 \(U_E\) at the feet): the bonded parts are at \(U_E\) while the ground is close to remote earth.

def assess(soil, rho_c=RHO_C, extras=()):
    world, result, u_e = field(soil, rho_c=rho_c, extras=extras)
    _, u_t = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(result, world, electrode=FOUNDATION, n_angles=72)
    u_s = 0.0
    for start, d in ((5.0, (1.0, 0.0)), (5.0 * math.sqrt(2.0), (1.0, 1.0))):
        d = np.array(d) / np.hypot(*d)
        r = np.arange(start, 30.0, 0.05)
        phi = surface(result, r * d[0], r * d[1])
        phi_1m = surface(result, (r + 1.0) * d[0], (r + 1.0) * d[1])
        u_s = max(u_s, np.max(phi - phi_1m))
    u_t_max = np.max(np.abs(u_t))
    return {
        "R_E": u_e,
        "U_T/U_E": u_t_max / u_e,
        "U_T/I_E": u_t_max,  # V per A of earth current
        "U_S/U_E": u_s / u_e,
    }

How to read the table:

  • Touch voltage. With the foundation alone, about half the earth potential rise appears as touch voltage in S1; in S2, whose resistive top layer lets the current dive to the conductive layer, almost three quarters; in S3, whose conductive top layer spreads it sideways, under a third. The ring lowers the ratio to a third … three fifths of its value without it. The rod leaves the ratio almost unchanged: it lowers \(R_E\), so it helps where a current sets the earth potential rise (the column per ampere: −42 % in S2), not where a potential is transferred.
  • Dry concrete raises the ratio to 0.93: the touch voltage is then practically the full earth potential rise, and per ampere 13 times that of the moist foundation. The ring brings it back to 0.31.
  • Step voltages stay below the touch voltages, with their largest values just outside the foundation bars (or outside the ring).

A foundation earth electrode in moist concrete lets the house carry roughly twice \(U_{Tp}\) as earth potential rise (S1: 439 V for a fault cleared in 0.5 s, 156 V for one that is not cleared); the ring outside doubles that again. Over the water-bearing layer of S2 and with dry concrete the margin shrinks towards \(U_{Tp}\) itself. In a real TN network the neighbouring house earths and the substation raise the soil around the house as well, which lowers the touch voltage further; for the touch voltage this single house is the pessimistic end (see the case study E01 of a secondary substation with its low-voltage network).

Three independent methods, one ring:

  • image agrees with fem to a few \(10^{-4}\), in resistance and in touch voltage. On a ring the uniform current is exact by symmetry, so the only difference left is the image engine's polygon of 0.5 m chords, which lies slightly inside the circle.
  • mom lies 0.3 … 1.9 % below. Its point kernel represents each segment's current by a point source at the segment's midpoint, which reads the resistance low; this deficit does not vanish as the segments get shorter (tutorial T09).
  • The shell model is consistent. The image engine adds exactly \(C/L\); fem adds 0.1 … 0.2 % more, because on the solid torus the current is not spread evenly around the wire's circumference, and an uneven current loses more in the shell.

docs.title: E02 — A single-family house: foundation earth electrode in concrete
docs.text:
This case study models the earth of a detached single-family house: a foundation earth electrode in the concrete of the strip foundation, optionally with a driven rod or a ring earth electrode outside the foundation. It is written for the grounding engineer who wants to know what such an earth achieves, how much the concrete and the soil change it, and which of groundfield's engines to trust for which answer.

The questions

  1. What is the earthing resistance of the house, and how much do the concrete and the soil model change it?
  2. What do people around the house experience when its earth rises in potential: the potential profile, the touch voltage at the façade and the step voltage?
  3. What does a driven rod or a ring earth electrode outside the foundation add?
  4. What do the engines image / image_2layer, mom and fem give for this house, and why do they differ?

Prerequisites: the tutorials T01, T02, T08 and T09, and the page Concrete-encased electrodes. Runtime: about half a minute. An optional three-dimensional fem run near the end takes one to three minutes and up to 3.5 GB of memory more; it is switched off.

docs.title: The house and its earth
docs.text:
The house has a footprint of 10 m × 10 m and stands on a strip foundation whose base lies 0.8 m below ground. The foundation earth electrode (Fundamenterder, DIN 18014) is a round steel bar of 10 mm diameter on the axis of the strip, with 5 cm of concrete all round. It runs as a closed loop under the outer walls. The model house of groundfield's generators (the residential entry of default_building_catalog()) adds one cross-brace each way, for example under inner load-bearing walls: six straight bars of 10 m, 60 m of steel in concrete. DIN 18014 itself asks for cross-braces only where a mesh would exceed 20 m × 20 m; the next section shows what they change.

The foundation earth electrode is the earth of the house: the main earthing terminal, the protective bonding of the water and gas pipes and, in a TN-C-S system, the earthing of the PEN conductor at the service entrance all connect to it. Three variants, every part bonded to the foundation:

  • A — the foundation earth electrode alone;
  • B — A plus a driven rod, 6 m long, head 0.5 m deep, 1 m in front of the middle of the street-side wall (the service entrance; the black square in the plan below);
  • C — A plus a ring earth electrode, a bare 10 mm steel loop in the soil 1 m outside the foundation (12 m × 12 m, 0.8 m deep). Where the foundation has no contact with the soil (perimeter insulation, waterproof concrete, a bitumen seal), DIN 18014 asks for an earth electrode in the soil instead, typically such a ring, and the steel in the foundation then serves only the equipotential bonding.

Three soils:

  • S1, homogeneous 100 Ω·m, the reference;
  • S2, 300 Ω·m over 30 Ω·m with the interface 2 m deep: dry sand over a water-bearing layer (reflection factor \(K < 0\));
  • S3, 50 Ω·m over 500 Ω·m with the interface 2 m deep: loam over dry gravel (\(K > 0\)).

docs.title: Modelling choices
docs.text:
• A quasi-static field at 50 Hz. The earth of the house spans about 12 m and contains no long conductor. Below 1 kHz the soil behaves as a resistive conductor, so the earth is a resistance \(R_E\). The bonds between the bars are ideal (the generators' default), and the impedance has no imaginary part.
  • Two-layer soil, as a sounding (Wenner, Schlumberger) would give it, solved with the Tagg/Sunde image series of image_2layer, which the default engine selects by itself.
  • The engines. The default image engine (one uniform current per straight wire, exact line-source kernel) gives the resistances. mom (one current per segment) gives the field next to the house, where the image engine warns that its uniform current is only impedance-grade. fem (solid conductors in a meshed soil) is the independent reference. The segments are 0.5 m long: more than five outer radii, as the thin-wire check asks.

Concrete as a cylindrical shell (ADR-0012, after Sunde). A concrete cover of thickness \(t\) and resistivity \(\rho_c\) around a bar of radius \(r_a\) adds, per metre of bar, the radial resistance

\[ C = \frac{\rho_c}{2\pi}\,\ln\frac{r_a + t}{r_a} \qquad\text{in }\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}, \]

and the soil sees a bare wire of the outer radius \(r_b = r_a + t\) (here 55 mm). If the current leaves the \(L\) metres of encased bar evenly, the shell adds the series resistance \(C/L\). Given concrete_rho_ohm_m, the generators put \(r_b\) and \(C\) on every bar of the foundation, the cross-braces included. ADR-0012 lists fresh or wet concrete at 30 … 80 Ω·m, earth-moist concrete at 80 … 200 Ω·m, concrete in cycling humidity at 200 … 2 000 Ω·m and dry concrete at 5 000 Ω·m and more. The base case takes 150 Ω·m (earth-moist); a sweep covers the rest.

docs.title: Earthing resistance in homogeneous soil
docs.text:
The base case: the foundation earth electrode in earth-moist concrete in 100 Ω·m. Two neighbours help to read the number: the same bars bare in the soil, and the foundation without its two cross-braces. Sverak's formula of IEEE Std 80 (Eq. 57) is a plausibility check; it is an empirical fit for bare substation grids from the total conductor length \(L_T\), the area \(A\) and the depth \(h\),

\[ R_g = \rho\left[\frac{1}{L_T} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{20A}}\left(1 + \frac{1}{1 + h\sqrt{20/A}}\right)\right], \]

so it is compared with the bare bars.

docs.title: How much the concrete matters
docs.text: The concrete resistivity \(\rho_c\) is the least known input: it follows the moisture of the foundation. The sweep below runs from wet concrete (30 Ω·m) to dry concrete (10 000 Ω·m) in all three soils. The shell resistance \(C/L\) of the 60 m of encased bar is drawn for reference.

docs.title: The soil model
docs.text: A homogeneous soil is what a single measurement at a short probe spacing suggests. The table compares the two-layer soils with the homogeneous soils of their top and bottom layers.

docs.title: A rod or a ring earth electrode outside the foundation
docs.text: The earthing resistance of the three variants in the three soils, with earth-moist concrete (150 Ω·m) and with dry concrete (5 000 Ω·m):

docs.title: Potential profile, touch and step voltage
docs.text:
When the earth of the house rises to the earth potential rise \(U_E\), every part bonded to it — the main earthing terminal, the pipes, an outdoor tap, the meter cabinet — rises with it, while the soil outside lies lower. A person standing on the ground 1 m from a touched part bridges the touch voltage \(U_T = U_E - \varphi(\text{feet})\), and a person walking bridges the step voltage between two points 1 m apart (see T08).

The field is linear in the current. The ratios \(U_T/U_E\) and \(U_S/U_E\) therefore depend only on the geometry and the soil, not on the current nor on what raises the potential: a current that flows through the house earth (\(U_E = R_E I_E\)), or a potential transferred to the house via the PEN conductor from a substation in fault. The feet stand 1 m from the foundation bar, about 0.8 m in front of the façade; the inside of the footprint is not sampled, because there stands the house.

The image engine warns that its uniform current is only impedance-grade next to a bonded cluster of wires, so the field is computed with mom (the engines section below quantifies the difference).

docs.title: What the touch voltages allow
docs.text: EN 50522 limits the touch voltage \(U_{Tp}\) by the fault duration \(t_f\) (Table B.4: 225 V at 0.5 s; 80 V beyond 10 s and for an earth fault that is not cleared). It applies to earth faults in high-voltage installations; a house in a TN network meets them as a potential transferred via the PEN conductor. The low-voltage installation itself has its own rules (IEC 60364-4-41). The ratio \(U_T/U_E\) turns \(U_{Tp}\) into the largest earth potential rise the house can carry without extra measures, \(U_{E,\max} = U_{Tp} / (U_T/U_E)\):

docs.title: image against mom on the house
docs.text: The image engine carries one uniform leakage current per straight bar and integrates the line source exactly. mom gives every 0.5 m segment its own current, so the current can crowd towards the corners and ends of the bars, but evaluates each segment as a point source. The cell compares \(R_E\) and the touch-voltage ratio of variants A and C, moist concrete, in the three soils, and records the warning of the image engine.

docs.title: The segment length
docs.text: The image engine's line kernel integrates every straight bar exactly, so a square foundation gives the same resistance at every segment length. mom converges with the segment length:

docs.title: fem on a ring analogue (axisymmetric model)
docs.text: fem meshes the soil and treats each electrode as the solid body it is: a rod as a cylinder, a ring as a torus, the concrete shell as a surface conductance \(1/(2\pi r_b C)\) on the surface of radius \(r_b\). Its axisymmetric model solves rods on one vertical axis and rings around it to about \(10^{-4}\), in a fraction of a second. A square foundation is not axisymmetric, so we take a ring analogue: a circular ring with the same 40 m of encased bar as the foundation loop without cross-braces (radius \(40\,\mathrm{m}/2\pi\) = 6.37 m, 0.8 m deep) in earth-moist concrete, in the three soils. The shell rise is measured against the same ring with a perfectly conducting shell (\(C = 0\)).

docs.title: fem on the real foundation (three-dimensional model)
docs.text: Every other world — the square loop, the braces, the rod beside the foundation — needs the three-dimensional model of fem. It replaces each wire by a line source smoothed over a disc of radius source_radius, meshes the soil with tetrahedra and corrects for the wire radius analytically. It needs the optional fem3d extra and is expensive: the foundation loop without cross-braces (40 m of bar, S1, moist concrete), with a 0.1 m source radius and the mesh growth 0.6, has 1.04 million nodes on its finer mesh level. On the machine that executed this notebook it took one to three minutes, depending on what else was running, and up to 3.5 GB of memory. The cell below runs it only on request and otherwise uses the value of that run.

docs.title: What this means in practice
docs.text:
• A foundation earth electrode of a 10 m × 10 m house has about \(\rho\) / 20 m in homogeneous soil (5.0 Ω in 100 Ω·m) as long as the concrete is moist.
  • The concrete is neutral while it is about as conductive as the soil; dry concrete multiplies the earthing resistance (about 36 Ω at 5 000 Ω·m) and makes the soil irrelevant.
  • The soil model matters as much: the homogeneous soil of the top layer misjudges the earth by a factor of 2.2 … 2.6 either way, and the foundation still feels a layer 20 m down. Use a sounding that reaches a few times the size of the house.
  • A driven rod pays off when it reaches a better layer (−40 % in S2); it lowers \(R_E\) but not the touch voltage as a fraction of the earth potential rise.
  • A ring earth electrode 1 m outside lowers \(R_E\), cuts the touch voltage around the house by 40 … 67 % and keeps the earth working when the foundation dries out or is insulated.
  • Engines: image for resistances and sweeps, mom for the field next to the house, fem to confirm a result once; they agree within about 2 %.

docs.title: Limits of this example
docs.text:
• One house alone. In a TN network the house is bonded through the PEN to the substation and to every other house; the global earthing system lowers both the earthing impedance seen at the house and the touch voltages around it (case study E01).
  • The concrete model is a cylindrical shell of uniform resistivity around each bar. The real strip foundation is a block of concrete several times wider than the shell; DIN 18014 bonds the bar to the reinforcement at least every 2 m, which enlarges the electrode; and the moisture varies over the foundation and the year. Where bars meet, their shells overlap; the concrete-shells page estimates that this changes the house mesh by about 1 % or less.
  • The soil is horizontally layered and uniform in each layer: no backfill around the foundation, no frost, no seasonal moisture profile.
  • Touch voltages are prospective: no body, shoe or surface-layer resistance (EN 50522, Annex B, and gf.permissible_prospective_touch_voltage_en50522 add them). The feet stand 1 m from the bars; touched parts farther out (a bonded fence, a garden tap on a pipe) carry the house potential to places where the soil lies lower and need their own assessment with gf.touch_voltage_at_part.
  • Frequency: 50 Hz, no inductive conductor in the model; harmonics and lightning currents are outside its scope.
  • The 3-D fem reference was run once for the loop without braces in S1; the other worlds rest on the agreement of image and mom and on the axisymmetric ring analogue.

def substation(
    soil, *, meshes=MESHES, rods="corners", rod_length=ROD_LENGTH, grading=False
):
    """The substation earth, fed with I_E: grid, bonded rods, optional grading conductor."""
    world = gf.create_world(soil=soil)
    lx, ly = SIZE
    gf.create_electrode(
        world,
        "grid_mesh",
        name="grid",
        corner=(0.0, 0.0, DEPTH),
        size=SIZE,
        n_x=meshes[0],
        n_y=meshes[1],
        wire_radius=0.006,
    )
    if rods == "corners":
        heads = [(0.0, 0.0), (lx, 0.0), (lx, ly), (0.0, ly)]
    else:  # "perimeter": every 10 m along the outer conductor
        heads = [(x, y) for x in np.arange(0.0, lx + 1.0, 10.0) for y in (0.0, ly)]
        heads += [(x, y) for y in np.arange(10.0, ly, 10.0) for x in (0.0, lx)]
    for k, (x, y) in enumerate(heads):
        gf.create_electrode(
            world,
            "rod",
            name=f"rod_{k}",
            position=(x, y, DEPTH),
            length=rod_length,
            wire_radius=0.008,
        )
        gf.create_conductor(
            world, name=f"bond_{k}", start="grid", end=f"rod_{k}"
        )  # ideal
    if grading:  # a closed conductor 1 m outside the grid, 0.5 m deep, bonded
        ring = [
            (-1.0, -1.0, 0.5),
            (lx + 1, -1.0, 0.5),
            (lx + 1, ly + 1, 0.5),
            (-1.0, ly + 1, 0.5),
        ]
        gf.create_electrode(
            world, "polyline", name="grading", vertices=ring, wire_radius=0.005
        )
        gf.create_conductor(world, name="bond_grading", start="grid", end="grading")
    gf.create_source(world, attached_to="grid", magnitude=I_E)
    return world


worlds = {name: substation(soil) for name, soil in SOILS.items()}

fig, (ax_plan, ax_side) = plt.subplots(

FENCE_LINE = np.array(  # on the surface above the outer conductor, 1 m apart
    [(x, y, 0.0) for x in ALONG_X for y in (0.0, SIZE[1])]
    + [(x, y, 0.0) for y in ALONG_Y for x in (0.0, SIZE[0])]

def touch(result, world):
    """Largest |U_T| in V: outside the fence, at the mesh centres, anywhere in the yard."""
    _, u_out = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(result, world, electrode="grid")
    _, u_in = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(
        result, world, electrode="grid", interior="meshes", corners=False
    )
    u_line = np.abs(
        result.electrode_potentials["grid"][0] - result.potential(FENCE_LINE)
    )
    mesh = np.abs(u_in[N_ANGLES:]).max()
    return {
        "outside": np.abs(u_out).max(),
        "mesh": mesh,
        "yard": max(mesh, u_line.max()),
    }


def response(result, world, k):
    return {"Z_E": result.input_impedance()[k].real, **touch(result, world)}

Plausibility. Sverak's formula lies +8.9 % above mom in homogeneous soil, its usual accuracy for grids (T08 finds +11.8 % for a 20 m grid). It has no two-layer form, but the two-layer results lie between the homogeneous limits, as they must.

What the soil does. The two soils contain the same resistivities, yet their impedances differ by a factor of 2.2. A 60 m × 40 m grid drives its current tens of metres deep, so it sees mainly the lower layer: the apparent resistivity is 88 Ω·m in soil A, near the 50 Ω·m of the bottom, and 195 Ω·m in soil B, nearer the 300 Ω·m of the bottom than the 50 Ω·m around the grid. A sounding that stops a few metres deep would misjudge this grid badly.

A single 3 m rod alone would have 17 to 100 Ω, depending on the layer it stands in (Dwight's closed form for homogeneous soil): ten to a hundred times the impedance of the grid. And the corner rods stand in the potential well of the grid. Rods of 3 m therefore change \(Z_E\) little; section 7 shows what longer rods do.

The colour scale ends at the largest touch voltage outside the fence. Farther out, \(U_E - \varphi\) keeps growing towards \(U_E\), but no bonded part stands there. The maps show the two faces of a two-layer soil:

  • In soil A (resistive over conductive) the surface potential sags in every mesh. The touch voltage in the yard lies between 217 V and 552 V, highest in the corner meshes; it is above \(U_{Tp}\) = 225 V almost everywhere (9786 of 9801 points).
  • In soil B (conductive over resistive) the conductive top layer spreads the current sideways and flattens the surface potential. In the yard only the corners exceed \(U_{Tp}\), with 301 V right above the corner conductor, although \(U_E\) is more than twice as high as in soil A.

In both soils the largest touch voltage stands outside the corners, where the potential falls fastest. That is where mom matters: the current per metre is largest at the ends of the outer conductors.

The largest step voltages, 214 V in soil A and 185 V in soil B, begin at the corner and stay below the touch voltages. EN 50522:2022 rarely asks for them, and Annex A.3 gives the reason: the permissible step voltages are much higher than the permissible touch voltages, because the current from foot to foot passes the heart with a heart-current factor of only 0.04. The standard asks for the step voltages at the boundary of an installation only for high earth potential rises, and names \(U_E > 20\,U_{Tp}\) as an example (5.4.2, note 1); here \(U_E\) is below \(16\,U_{Tp}\) in both soils. groundfield has no permissible step voltage; it is not needed here.

Only a very fast protection would save the base design (0.06 s in soil A, 0.22 s in soil B). So we change the earthing system, with two measures of common practice:

  1. a grading conductor: a closed conductor 1 m outside the grid and 0.5 m deep, bonded to it, so that people outside the fence stand above a conductor;
  2. in addition, perimeter rods: 20 rods of 6 m every 10 m along the outer conductor instead of the four corner rods; they reach 4.3 m into the lower layer.

The feet above the grading conductor are only 0.5 m from it, closer than a 1 m segment is long, so the variants are solved with 0.5 m segments. The base design at 0.5 m is already in the convergence study of section 3.

What the variants show:

  • Soil B needs only the grading conductor. It raises the surface potential where the people outside the fence stand and pulls the value there from 486 V to 186 V, the yard from 300 V to 121 V: the design passes on bare contact. The perimeter rods add little in soil B, because their lower part stands in the 300 Ω·m bottom.
  • Soil A is harder: the resistive top layer leaves a large share of \(U_E\) between the grid and the surface everywhere. The grading conductor alone brings the fence to 309 V and leaves the yard at 455 V. The perimeter rods reach the conductive bottom and lower \(U_E\) itself, from 1466 V to 1138 V; the fence then passes on bare contact (189 V), but the corner meshes still have 262 V. With crushed rock in the yard (\(U_{vTp}\) = 1125 V), or shoes on the natural soil (\(U_{vTp}\) = 515 V), the design passes. Without either, smaller meshes near the corners would be the remaining measure: they lower the mesh voltage at the price of more conductor.

EN 50522 verifies a design by the calculated or measured touch voltages of the installation as built. These numbers choose the measures; the verification still follows.

For the impedance the two engines agree within 1.6 %: either serves a study of \(Z_E\) and \(U_E\). For the touch voltages the uniform current per wire of image_2layer overestimates, by up to 45 % at the mesh centres of soil B. Its step voltage at the corner is 4.5 % high in soil A but 4.7 % low in soil B, on the unsafe side. With a conductive top layer the current crowds strongly towards the ends of every conductor, which one current per wire cannot follow. Assess touch and step voltages near a grid with mom.

mom_sommerfeld evaluates the layered Green's function by numerical Sommerfeld quadrature instead of the image series, on the same discretisation as mom. Their agreement checks the series in this strong contrast:

In [22]: Copied! 
z_som = gf.create_engine(backend="mom_sommerfeld", segment_length=DS).solve(worlds["A"])
z_som = z_som.input_impedance()[0].real
print(
    f"soil A: mom {z_e['A']:.9f} Ohm, mom_sommerfeld {z_som:.9f} Ohm, "
    f"difference {abs(z_som / z_e['A'] - 1):.1e}"
)
assert abs(z_som / z_e["A"] - 1.0) < 1e-6
z_som = gf.create_engine(backend="mom_sommerfeld", segment_length=DS).solve(worlds["A"]) z_som = z_som.input_impedance()[0].real print( f"soil A: mom {z_e['A']:.9f} Ohm, mom_sommerfeld {z_som:.9f} Ohm, " f"difference {abs(z_som / z_e['A'] - 1):.1e}" ) assert abs(z_som / z_e["A"] - 1.0) < 1e-6 
soil A: mom 0.783258102 Ohm, mom_sommerfeld 0.783258128 Ohm, difference 3.3e-08

Closed forms. The library offers Sverak's formula of IEEE Std 80 for the grid resistance in homogeneous soil (section 4: +8.9 % above mom) and Dwight's formulas for single electrodes (section 4: the rods). It has no closed form for mesh or step voltages; IEEE Std 80's \(K_m\), \(K_i\) and \(K_s\) factors are not implemented. The homogeneous limits of the next section are the strongest independent check of the two-layer results.

The impedance moves monotonically from the \(\rho_2\) limit (thin upper layer) towards the \(\rho_1\) limit (thick upper layer), and slowly: even at \(h_1\) = 50 m it has not reached it, because the grid's current field reaches deeper than its size.

The touch-voltage fraction behaves the other way round, and that is the design lesson. With a resistive top over a conductive bottom (\(K < 0\)) a person outside the fence bridges up to 0.45 of \(U_E\), 1.7 times the homogeneous value: the current leaves the grid downwards, and the surface above it is pulled towards the low potential of the conductive bottom. With a conductive top over a resistive bottom (\(K > 0\)) the fraction drops below the homogeneous value. A low \(Z_E\) in soil A therefore does not mean low touch voltages, and a high \(Z_E\) in soil B does not mean high ones.

Now the contrast itself, with a 100 Ω·m upper layer of 2.5 m and the lower layer from 10 to 1000 Ω·m:

Scaling the homogeneous fraction with the two-layer impedance would understate the touch voltage by half over the conductive bottom (\(K\) = −0.82) and overstate it 2.3 times over the resistive one (\(K\) = +0.82): wrong in both directions, and on the unsafe side where the bottom conducts.
