docs.title: E03 — Earthing grid of a high-voltage substation in two-layer soil
docs.text:
This case study takes the mesh earthing grid of an outdoor high-voltage substation through the touch-voltage verification of EN 50522:2022, in two-layer soil. It is written for grounding engineers who know the standard and IEEE Std 80 and want to see how groundfield answers the design questions, which engine to trust for which quantity, and how far the numbers carry.

Questions this example answers

  1. What is the earthing impedance \(Z_E\) of the grid, and how much does the two-layer soil change it against a homogeneous estimate?
  2. Which earth potential rise \(U_E\), and which touch and step voltages, does an earth-fault current of 2 kA cause?
  3. Does the design meet the permissible touch voltage for a fault cleared in 0.5 s, and what would make it pass?
  4. Is the discretisation fine enough, and how do image_2layer, mom and the closed-form estimates compare?
  5. How do the layer contrast and the depth of the interface change the results?

The tutorials T02 (layered soil), T08 (touch and step voltages) and T09 (engines and convergence) introduce the functions used here. This example applies them to one installation.

Runtime: about 70 s.

docs.title: 1. The installation and the soil
docs.text:
Part Model Note Grid 60 m × 40 m, 12 × 8 meshes of 5 m 22 conductors, 1060 m Burial depth 0.8 m Conductor round copper, radius 6 mm 113 mm² Rods 4 × 3 m at the corners, radius 8 mm from 0.8 m to 3.8 m depth Earth-fault current \(I_E\) = 2 kA at 50 Hz flows from the grid into the soil Fault duration \(t_f\) = 0.5 s clearing time of the protection

The earth-fault current \(I_E\) is the part of the fault current that leaves the grid through the soil. The rest returns to the source over the earth wires of the overhead lines and the screens of the cables. In a real study \(I_E\) follows from the network's fault currents and these reduction factors; here it is an assumption.

The soil. A two-layer soil has an upper layer of resistivity \(\rho_1\) and thickness \(h_1\) over a half-space of resistivity \(\rho_2\). The interface reflects part of the current field with the factor

\[ K = \frac{\rho_2 - \rho_1}{\rho_2 + \rho_1}, \qquad -1 < K < 1 . \]

We take two soils with the same two resistivities in reverse order:

Soil \(\rho_1\) \(h_1\) \(\rho_2\) \(K\) For example A 300 Ω·m 2.5 m 50 Ω·m −0.71 dry sand over groundwater B 50 Ω·m 2.5 m 300 Ω·m +0.71 loam over dry gravel or rock

The grid lies in the upper layer in both soils; the rods reach 1.3 m into the lower one.

docs.title: Modelling choices
docs.text:
• The grid is one grid_mesh electrode: its 22 conductors are straight wires, connected at every crossing.
  • The rods are separate rod electrodes, bonded to the grid by ideal conductors (create_conductor without a cross-section). An ideal bond merges the electrodes into one cluster at one potential; the route of the bond does not matter.
  • One potential for the whole grid. groundfield treats an electrode as an equipotential body: the resistance and inductance of the copper are neglected. That is the usual assumption of grid design (IEEE Std 80 makes it too) for a compact copper grid at 50 Hz.
  • The source is a current \(I_E\) into the grid that returns at remote earth. The problem is linear, so every voltage scales with \(I_E\).
  • The touched parts. All metal structures in the yard (steel supports, equipment frames) are bonded to the grid, and people may stand anywhere inside the yard. The yard fence runs on the line of the outer conductor and is bonded to the grid; people outside the fence stand 1 m from it.

docs.title: The engines
docs.text:
Two engines solve thin wires in two-layer soil with the Tagg/Sunde image series:

  • image_2layer (what the default image runs for two-layer soil) gives every straight wire one uniform leakage current and integrates its potential exactly (line kernel). Its impedances are within about 1–2 % of mom, but near grids its surface potential is only impedance-grade: it cannot let the current crowd towards the ends of each wire, and it warns with UniformCurrentFieldWarning.
  • mom gives every segment its own current (piecewise constant, point matching at the segment midpoints, point kernel), so the current concentrates at the edges and corners of the grid as it does in reality. Its touch and step voltages are field-grade.

We therefore compute everything with mom and use image_2layer and mom_sommerfeld (the same discretisation, with the layered Green's function as a Sommerfeld integral) as cross-checks in section 8. fem is not used: its three-dimensional model needed 75–140 s and 4.3 GB for a station with 28 m of wire (fem engine page), and this grid has 1072 m.

docs.title: 2. Build the model
docs.text: One function builds the earthing system, so that the design variants of section 7 differ only in their arguments. The segment length DS of 1 m is justified in section 3.

docs.title: 3. Is the discretisation fine enough?
docs.text:
Before reading any number we check that it does not depend on the segment length. gf.convergence_study solves the same world with a ladder of segment lengths; a response function adds the touch voltages to the impedance. The helper touch returns the three touch voltages this example assesses:

  • outside: the largest value with the feet 1 m outside the grid, where people outside the fence stand (touch_voltage_envelope);
  • mesh: the largest value at the centres of the meshes, the mesh voltage of IEEE Std 80 (interior="meshes");
  • yard: the largest value anywhere inside the fence. It lies either at a mesh centre or on the fence line above the outer conductor, so touch also samples that line every metre. Section 5 confirms this against a dense map.

touch_voltage_envelope places the feet on 24 rays from the centre of the grid and, by default, on the arc around each of its corners, where the touch voltage is largest. The rays alone miss the corners of a 60 m × 40 m rectangle (section 5 shows by how much). The mesh centres come from a second call with corners=False, whose interior points follow right after the 24 rays.

mom needs segments shorter than about 2 m here. Its point form of the layered Green's function averages over ±0.387 segment lengths in depth; for longer segments that range would reach above the soil surface, and the engine refuses the world with BackendCapabilityError. The ladder therefore starts at 2 m.

docs.title: 4. Grid impedance and earth potential rise
docs.text:
In homogeneous soil the impedance is proportional to the resistivity, \(Z_E = \rho\, z_1\). One solve gives the impedance per Ω·m, \(z_1\), and with it both homogeneous limits: \(\rho_1 z_1\) for a very thick and \(\rho_2 z_1\) for a very thin upper layer. The two-layer impedance must lie between them. The apparent resistivity \(\rho_a = Z_E / z_1\) is the homogeneous resistivity that would give the same impedance.

Sverak's formula of IEEE Std 80 (2000, Eq. 57) is the engineering estimate for grids in homogeneous soil, with the total conductor length \(L_T\) (grid and rods), the area \(A\) and the depth \(h\):

\[ R_g = \rho\left[\frac{1}{L_T} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{20A}}\left(1 + \frac{1}{1 + h\sqrt{20/A}}\right)\right]. \]

With \(Z_E\) the earth potential rise is \(U_E = Z_E I_E\).

docs.title: 5. Touch voltages on the surface
docs.text:
The touch voltage is the difference between the potential of the touched part, here the earth potential rise \(U_E\) of the grid, and the potential of the soil surface under the feet, 1 m away:

\[ U_T = U_E - \varphi(\mathbf r_\text{feet}). \]

This is the prospective (open-circuit) value: no body current flows. We evaluate the surface potential \(\varphi\) on a grid of points 0.5 m apart that covers the yard and 5 m around it, 141 × 101 points. The grid, the rods and the feeding point are symmetric about both centre lines, so one quarter (3621 points) is computed and mirrored. Inside the yard every point is a possible standing position next to a bonded structure, so the map is the touch voltage there. Outside, \(U_E - \varphi\) is a touch voltage only where a bonded part stands within 1 m: along the fence.

docs.title: 6. Step voltages
docs.text:
A person walking near the grid bridges the step voltage between two points 1 m apart,

\[ U_S = \varphi(\mathbf r) - \varphi(\mathbf r + 1\,\mathrm m\;\hat{\mathbf e}). \]

It is largest where the surface potential falls fastest, at the corners. We evaluate it along two lines out of the grid, the diagonal through a corner and the normal through the middle of a long side, from inside the outer mesh to 12 m outside. The step points outwards; the plot shows its magnitude.

docs.title: 7. Assessment against EN 50522, and what makes the design pass
docs.text:
The permissible touch voltage across the body for \(t_f\) = 0.5 s is \(U_{Tp}\) = 225 V. EN 50522 allows additional resistances in the body circuit: the hand \(R_H\), the footwear \(R_{F1}\), and the soil or surface layer under the feet with \(R_{F2} = 1.5\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\,\rho_s\). The permissible prospective touch voltage (Annex B.4) is then

\[ U_{vTp} = U_{Tp}(t_f) + \frac{I_B(t_f)}{HF}\,\bigl(R_H + R_{F1} + 1.5\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\,\rho_s\bigr), \]

with the permissible body current \(I_B(t_f)\) of Table B.1 and the heart-current factor \(HF\) = 1 (hand to feet). We compare with three levels: bare contact (\(U_{Tp}\)); shoes of 1000 Ω on the natural topsoil; and a layer of crushed rock of 3000 Ω·m (an assumed wet value) without shoes.

docs.title: 8. Cross-checks: image_2layer, mom_sommerfeld and closed forms
docs.text: The same two worlds, solved with the default engine (image, which runs image_2layer for two-layer soil). Its touch voltages trigger the UniformCurrentFieldWarning; we record it and print it once.

docs.title: 9. Layer contrast and interface depth
docs.text: First the interface depth: the two contrasts of soils A and B with \(h_1\) from 1.5 m to 50 m. The touch voltages are shown relative to \(U_E\), as the fraction of the earth potential rise that a person bridges.

docs.title: 10. What this means for the design
docs.text:
• Measure deep. A 60 m × 40 m grid sees the soil to tens of metres: its apparent resistivity is 88 Ω·m in soil A and 195 Ω·m in soil B. The sounding must reach depths of the order of the grid size.
  • The earth potential rise is not the hazard. Soil B has more than twice the \(U_E\) of soil A but lower touch voltages (486 V against 710 V outside the fence, 301 V against 552 V in the yard). Calculate the touch voltages (EN 50522 criterion C4) with a field-grade engine.
  • Use mom for touch and step voltages near a grid. image_2layer is fine for \(Z_E\) (within 1.6 % here) but overestimates the mesh voltages by up to 45 % and, in soil B, underestimates the step voltage at a corner.
  • Check the corners. The largest touch voltages stand 1 m outside a corner and, in soil B, right above the corner conductor. The envelope samples the corners outside; touch points at the corner posts or a dense map cover the rest.
  • The measures depend on the soil. In soil B a grading conductor outside the fence is enough. In soil A rods into the conductive bottom, the grading conductor and a surface layer in the yard (or smaller corner meshes) are needed.

docs.title: Limits of this example
docs.text:
• Equipotential grid, no inductive effects. The copper's resistance and inductance are neglected, and so is the inductive coupling to the faulted line. For grids of several hundred metres, steel conductors or frequencies well above 50 Hz the potential varies along the grid, and this model does not show it.
  • The earth-fault current is given. The split of the fault current between the grid, the earth wires and the cable screens (the reduction factors) is not computed; tutorial T06 shows how a connected network shares the current. Transferred potentials (cable screens, pipes, a fence that leaves the site) are not assessed.
  • The soil is two horizontal layers from an assumed sounding, without seasonal variation or frozen ground. Three or more layers need mom_sommerfeld, and FieldResult.potential raises NotImplementedError for them, so touch voltages in three-layer soil are out of reach.
  • Crushed rock enters only as a resistance under the feet (\(R_{F2}\) of EN 50522). Its thin high-resistivity layer would be a third soil layer, which the field model does not include.
  • Point kernel of mom. Its impedance changes by about 0.2 % from 1 m to 0.25 m segments here and stays slightly below the exact value; the surface potential directly above a shallow conductor needs segments shorter than the conductor's depth (section 7).
  • EN 50522 in the library: the permissible touch voltage of Table B.4 (80 V beyond 10 s) and the prospective value of Annex B.4. The permissible step voltage (Annex A.3), the measures M (Annex E) and the global earthing system (criterion C1) are not implemented; IEEE Std 80 enters only through Sverak's resistance formula.
  • No fem reference. The 3-D model of fem is the independent reference for small clusters; a grid with 1 km of wire is far beyond its default node limit. The cross-checks here are image_2layer, mom_sommerfeld, the homogeneous limits and the closed forms.

See also the how-to assess touch voltages and the known limitations.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
This section explains what groundfield computes, with which equations, under which assumptions and how well. Read it when you want to know why a result looks the way it does, which engine to trust for a question, or how to cite the method. Every engine page states its physical model, the equations and discretisation actually implemented, its validity range and the literature; the accuracy figures are generated from the benchmark suite rather than written by hand.

Start here: Concepts for the overall picture, then Engines to choose the engine for your study and to see where each one must not be used.

Page Content Concepts the objects of a computation, what happens in a solve, what a result contains, the modelling assumptions, the reduced \(\rho\)–\(f\) model Engines which engine for which question: decision path, accuracy, cost, limits of use; the governing equations and the two current models image · image_2layer · mom · mom_sommerfeld · fem one theory page per engine Kernels point source and exact line source, the Galerkin self term, field points near wires Earth return inductive coupling of conductors: perfect mirror, Carson, Sommerfeld / Pollaczek, skin effect Concrete shells the cylindrical shell of foundation electrodes and its single mechanism Sources and measurement two-terminal sources, junctions, input / cluster / electrode impedance, the fall-of-potential loop Validation and benchmarks generated tolerance table per backend, comparison figures, kernel and field checks Performance and scaling memory model, measured run times of this release, how they were measured

The architecture decision records (ADRs) document why the code is built the way it is; each carries dated amendments where later releases changed a decision. Release 2026.11 amended ADR-0002, 0004, 0005, 0006, 0007, 0008, 0009 and 0012 and added ADR-0013 (calendar versioning), ADR-0014 (backend registry and shared solve pipeline), ADR-0015 (exact line-source kernel as default) and ADR-0016 (conforming finite elements in fem).

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: This page explains, in plain words, the objects you build a computation from, what happens when you call solve, and what a result contains. Read it once to get the overall picture; the quickstart shows the same in code, and the engines page explains the numerical methods.

docs.title: Position in the software family
docs.text:
groundmeas   ──▶   groundinsight   ◀──   groundfield
  (measurements)     (reduced network       (field model,
                      model)                 reference)

groundfield is the field-theoretical reference of the family. It computes the potential field of earthing systems in layered soil from their geometry and material data and compresses the solution into reduced models — impedance functions \(Z(\rho, f)\), multiport matrices — that groundinsight uses as building blocks of a network model, and against which groundmeas measurements can be interpreted. The field model is a reference, not the end product: every solution exposes the quantities the reduction needs.

docs.title: The data model
docs.text:
A computation separates the physics (what is in the ground) from the numerics (how it is solved). The physics lives in a World, the numerics in an Engine; world.solve(engine) returns a FieldResult.

Object What it is Created with soil model horizontal layers of constant resistivity: HomogeneousSoil(rho), TwoLayerSoil(rho_1, rho_2, h_1), MultiLayerSoil(layers); depth \(z\) positive into the soil the class itself World the physical model: one soil, and the electrodes, junctions, conductors and sources in it create_world electrode a thin wire in contact with the soil: rod, ring, strip, polyline, star, mesh, grid; optionally encased in concrete (concrete shells) create_electrode junction a node without soil contact: a cable joint, an instrument terminal create_junction conductor a branch between two nodes: an ideal bond, or a cable with resistance, optionally leaking into the soil along its length and optionally inductive create_conductor source a current or voltage source that drives a node against a second node or against remote earth (sources and measurement) create_source Engine the numerics: backend, frequencies, segment length, source kernel, earth-return model, backend options create_engine FieldResult potentials, leakage currents and impedances per frequency, the sources for evaluating the field, and the metadata that reproduces the solve world.solve(engine)

Two ideas recur everywhere:

  • Cluster. Electrodes joined by ideal conductors (a conductor without a cross_section) are one galvanic cluster with one potential. A cable with a cross-section is a branch with its own resistance between two clusters.
  • Node. Electrodes and junctions are the nodes of the conductor network. Conductors connect nodes; sources inject current at a node.

docs.title: What happens in a solve
docs.text:
world.solve(engine)
 1. check        the backend's capabilities (soil layers, kernel, concrete shells)
                 and the resource limit, before anything is allocated
 2. discretise   every wire into straight segments of at most segment_length,
                 split at layer interfaces
 3. soil         the reaction matrix: the potential every segment's current
                 causes at every other segment (Green's function of the soil)
 4. network      the nodal equations: soil matrix + Kirchhoff's current law at
                 every node + Ohm's law along every conductor + the sources
 5. result       one solution per frequency: potentials, currents, impedances,
                 point sources for the field, metadata

Below 1 kHz the soil behaves as a pure conductor: no displacement current, and a skin depth large against a low-voltage network. Step 3 is therefore the stationary current field of the electrodes in a horizontally layered half-space; it does not depend on frequency and is computed once per world. Frequency enters in step 4 through the conductors: their resistance (optionally with skin effect), partial inductances and the earth-return impedance make the network equations complex. A purely galvanic world is solved once and reused for every frequency; a world with inductive conductors is solved once per frequency, which is cheap against step 3. The engines page gives the equations, the earth-return page the conductor impedance.

The engines differ in steps 2 and 3: how many unknown currents a wire carries (one per straight wire, or one per segment) and how the Green's function is evaluated (closed-form image series, numerical Sommerfeld quadrature, or a finite-element volume mesh instead).

docs.title: What a result contains
docs.text:
Access Meaning Unit result.frequencies the frequencies of the engine, in their order Hz result.input_impedance(source) the voltage at a source over its current: what a fault or an earth tester sees Ω result.cluster_impedance(electrode) the potential of a cluster over the current it leaks itself Ω result.grounding_impedance(electrode) the potential of a cluster over one electrode's leakage current Ω result.electrode_potentials[name] the potential of an electrode against remote earth (the EPR for the source current) V result.electrode_currents[name] the current an electrode leaks into the soil A result.potential(points) the potential at any points in or on the soil (homogeneous and two-layer soil) V result.metadata backend, effective backend, kernel, version, segments, solve time, series controls, provenance —

Every quantity is a complex RMS phasor with one value per frequency (units and conventions). Touch and step voltages, current sharing, plots, sweeps and reduced models are functions that take a result: touch_voltage, step_voltage, cluster_current_balance, plot_surface_potential, sweep, fit_rho_f_standard and others (postprocess). save_result and load_result store a result with its provenance.

The three impedances coincide for a single electrode and differ in a network: the input impedance is what the feeding point sees (and what a measurement approaches), the cluster impedance is the local spreading impedance of the fed cluster. The input impedance is the default of the sweeps and fits since 2026.11; the sources page has the definitions.

docs.title: Modelling assumptions
docs.text:
• Quasi-static field for \(f \lesssim 1\) kHz: stationary current flow in the soil, no displacement current; the soil permittivity is inert.
  • Horizontally layered soil with piecewise constant resistivity; layer stacks are canonicalised (equal adjacent layers merged).
  • Thin wires: the wire radius is small against the segment length and the distance to other wires; the current flows on the axis, the potential is observed on the surface.
  • Current model: uniform leakage per unit length per straight wire of an electrode (and layer) in the image family — impedance-grade, not field-grade near grids and stars (image); one current per segment in the mom family.
  • Remote earth as the potential reference.
  • Conductor impedance from partial inductances and an earth-return correction; the Sommerfeld/Pollaczek kernel by default, Carson's series as a fast approximation for long parallel lines.

docs.title: The reduced model
docs.text:
The objective of a field computation is not only a number but a model that a network calculation can use. For one feeding point the reduced model is the impedance as a function of soil resistivity and frequency. The standard form exported to groundinsight is

\[ Z(\rho, f) = k_0 + k_1\rho + (k_2 + jk_3)\,f + (k_4 + jk_5)\,f\rho , \]

with the resistance \(k_0\) that does not scale with \(\rho\) (the share of a lower soil layer, or the series resistance of conductors), the spreading resistance \(k_1\rho\), the soil-independent loop terms \(k_2 f\), \(k_3 f\) and Carson-type earth-return terms \(k_4 f\rho\), \(k_5 f\rho\). It is fitted by weighted linear least squares to a family of solves that spans both \(\rho\) and \(f\), with relative weights by default; max_relative reports the worst pointwise error and a fit above 5 % warns. Where the six-term form cannot follow the data (strongly layered soils), a vector fit of the frequency response per \(\rho\) is the alternative. For several feeding points the reduced model is the multiport matrix of the earthing systems (solve_mutual_matrix): its entry \(Z_{ij}\) is the potential of cluster \(i\) per ampere leaking from cluster \(j\). Together with the branch admittances \(\mathbf{Y}_L\) of the network and \(\mathbf{Y}_G = \mathbf{Z}^{-1}\) it forms the nodal system \((\mathbf{Y}_L + \mathbf{Y}_G)\,\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{i}\) of the AP1 catalogue, with the node voltages \(\mathbf{u}\) and the injected currents \(\mathbf{i}\).

docs.title: Typical questions
docs.text:
groundfield is built for the dissertation questions on interconnected earthing systems of medium- and low-voltage networks:

  1. How strongly does a remote current injection influence an earthing measurement, and how is the measurement loop to be modelled?
  2. How important are coupling and return-path effects below 1 kHz?
  3. Which robust statements hold for typical distribution-network configurations, and how do they reduce to a small set of parameters?
  4. Which touch voltages arise in the fault case, and over which spectrum?

The tutorials walk through these computations; this explanation section gives the theory and the evidence behind them.

docs.title: Concrete-encased electrodes
docs.text:
This page explains how groundfield models an earth electrode embedded in concrete — the foundation earth electrode of a building above all: the shell coefficient, how each engine uses it, how far the current model of the image family is from a per-segment reference for such electrodes, and what changed against 0.15.0. Read it before you set concrete_shell_coefficient_ohm_m or a generator's concrete_rho_ohm_m, or when foundation results differ from those of 0.15.0.

A foundation earth electrode (Fundamenterder, DIN 18014) lies inside the concrete of the strip foundation: every ampere it leaks has to cross the concrete before it reaches the soil. Concrete conducts like soil — wet concrete at tens of Ω·m, dry concrete at thousands — so the encasement adds a series resistance that can be negligible or dominant depending on the moisture.

docs.title: Mathematical and physical context
docs.text:
Around a wire of radius \(r_a\) the concrete forms a cylindrical shell of thickness \(t\) (outer radius \(r_b = r_a + t\)) and resistivity \(\rho_c\); outside lies the soil. A wire that leaks the current \(I'\) per metre drives it radially through the shell: at the radius \(r\) the current density is \(I'/(2\pi r)\) and the field \(\rho_c I'/(2\pi r)\), so the voltage across the shell is \(\int_{r_a}^{r_b}\rho_c I'/(2\pi r)\,\mathrm dr\). In this cylindrically symmetric limit the shell and the soil add in series along the radius (Sunde 1968, §4.4), and per metre of wire the shell contributes

\[ R'_\text{shell} = \frac{\rho_c}{2\pi}\,\ln\frac{r_b}{r_a} \equiv C \qquad\text{(in } \Omega\cdot\text{m)}, \]

the radial resistance of one metre of shell, while the soil sees a bare wire of the enlarged radius \(r_b\). The decomposition is exact for an infinite straight wire and a good approximation for a finite electrode as long as the leakage current varies slowly along the wire on the scale of the shell — always the case below 1 kHz.

Concrete around the wire is local: modelling it as a horizontal soil layer would put concrete under the whole neighbourhood, which is why groundfield refuses the planar interpretation (ADR-0012). Fagan & Lee (1970) and Ufer (1964) measured such concrete-encased electrodes; their low resistance in moist concrete is the reason foundation electrodes work at all.

docs.title: One mechanism: the shell coefficient
docs.text:
Every electrode kind (rod, ring, strip, polyline, star, mesh, grid mesh) has the field concrete_shell_coefficient_ohm_m — the coefficient \(C\) above. The wire radius of an encased wire is the outer radius \(r_b\). The image family, solve_mutual_matrix / solve_mutual_field, mom and mom_sommerfeld consume it per segment: a segment of length \(\Delta s\) adds \(C/\Delta s\) to its own diagonal entry of the reaction matrix — the voltage drop of its share of the leakage current across its piece of shell — and nothing to the off-diagonal entries, because shells of different segments do not couple.

Under the uniform current of an owner (one straight wire, or its part in one soil layer) of length \(L\), segment \(k\) carries the share \(I\,\Delta s_k/L\) of the current \(I\), and the per-segment terms add up to \(\sum_k (C/\Delta s_k)(\Delta s_k/L)^2 = C/L\):

\[ Z(C) - Z(0) = \frac{C}{L}, \]

the lumped series resistance of the whole shell, for every electrode kind, homogeneous or layered soil, in Engine.solve and in solve_mutual_matrix alike (tests/test_concrete_shell_coefficient.py). fem consumes \(C\) as well: its axisymmetric model as the surface conductance \(1/(2\pi r_b C)\), its three-dimensional model as the radial resistance \(C\) per length between the metal and its smoothed line source (fem).

Measurements and audit trail

mom and mom_sommerfeld rejected encased electrodes up to 2026.11; they consume the shell per segment since then (next section).

docs.title: In the moment method
docs.text:
mom and mom_sommerfeld solve one pulse current \(I_k\) per segment, all segments of a node at one potential (point matching). A segment of length \(\Delta s_k\) drops \(C I_k/\Delta s_k\) across its piece of shell, so the segment system reads

\[ \bigl(K + S\bigr)\,\mathbf I = \varphi\,\mathbf 1, \qquad S = \operatorname{diag}(C_k/\Delta s_k), \qquad \sum_k I_k = I , \]

every segment at the potential \(\varphi\) of the metal, with \(K\) the soil reaction matrix (in Ω) of the wire of outer radius \(r_b\) and \(C_k\) the coefficient of segment \(k\). The reported segment potentials, and with them the node potential, are those of the metal, and the field in the soil is that of the leakage currents.

Unlike the uniform current of an owner, the current redistributes. The equipotential solution minimises the dissipation \(\mathbf I^\mathsf{T}(K + S)\mathbf I\) over \(\sum_k I_k = I\). The shell term alone is smallest for a current uniform per length, where it equals \(C I^2/L\), so the shell raises \(Z\) by at least \(C/L\); and by at most \(C/L\) plus the excess of the uniform current over the equipotential one. A dry shell evens the current out: \(Z - C/L\) is within \(5\cdot10^{-6}\) of the uniform-current value of the bare wire at \(C = 3.8\cdot10^{5}\) Ω·m for a 3 m rod, an 8 m × 6 m grid and a three-arm star.

Two methods check the implementation:

  • Same matrix physics. The image family with one owner per segment (point kernel, every segment its own uniform-current owner, all bonded) solves the same system and agrees with mom to \(7\cdot10^{-16}\). mom_sommerfeld reproduces mom to about \(10^{-8}\) where neither engine warns, and the shell increments \(Z(C) - Z(0)\) of the two engines agree to \(1.4\cdot10^{-10}\).
  • Closed forms. The segments of a ring are equivalent (its matrix is circulant), so its current stays uniform and the shell adds exactly \(C/(2\pi r)\): mom and mom_sommerfeld give it to \(10^{-14}\) in homogeneous, two-layer and three-layer soil for \(C\) = 11 … 382 Ω·m. For a 3 m rod from the surface in 100 Ω·m the reference is Sunde's decomposition with Dwight's rod formula, \(R = C/L + \frac{\rho}{2\pi L}\bigl(\ln\frac{4L}{r_b} - 1\bigr)\): the image family's uniform current (line kernel) lies 0.14 … 0.20 % above it and rises by exactly \(C/L\); mom lies below it by the point kernel's deficit (kernels), 0.8 … 2.7 % for the encased rod (details below).
Measurements and audit trail

Evidence of streams w2mom and fw2mom, tests/test_concrete_shells_mom_family.py.

  • Same matrix physics: rods, a rod through the layer interface, rings, strips, grids, outlines and stars in 100 Ω·m and in 30 / 200 Ω·m (\(h_1\) = 4 m), 5 cm of 100 Ω·m concrete. mom_sommerfeld against mom: \(10^{-9}\) … \(1.5\cdot10^{-8}\) for a 10 m grid in four two-layer soils, bare and encased (audit W2B-07); with the layer interface 0.2 m below the wires \(9\cdot10^{-8}\) under PointKernelInterfaceWarning (audit W2R2-09). That is the agreement of its Sommerfeld quadrature with the Tagg/Sunde series of mom without a shell.
  • The rod against Sunde and Dwight: 5 cm of 30 or 100 Ω·m concrete, \(r_b\) = 55 mm, 0.5 … 0.125 m segments. The point kernel's deficit grows as the segments shorten while they stay at least 2.99 wire radii long: with \(r_b\) = 55 mm the bare rod lies 2.5 / 3.5 % below Dwight's formula at 0.5 / 0.25 m segments, the encased one 1.4 … 2.7 % below Sunde's, rising by 1.008 … 1.022 \(C/L\). A segment shorter than \(2.99\,r_b\) takes the Galerkin self term on the diagonal (see mom), which lifts the deficit again: at 0.125 m (\(2.3\,r_b\)) the bare rod lies 2.4 % and the encased one 0.8 / 1.5 % below (100 / 30 Ω·m, rising by 1.022 / 1.041 \(C/L\)). With \(r_b\) = 20 mm (1.5 cm of 100 Ω·m), where 0.5 … 0.0625 m segments all stay above \(2.99\,r_b\), the deficit grows monotonically: bare 1.9 / 2.5 / 2.9 / 3.2 %, encased 1.4 / 1.8 / 2.0 / 2.2 % at 0.5 / 0.25 / 0.125 / 0.0625 m.
  • An own point-matching matrix written from the thin-wire formulas equals mom to \(2\cdot10^{-16}\) wherever every segment is that long and departs from it by −2.2 % (bare rod, \(r_b\) = 55 mm, 0.125 m), the self-term switch (audit W2B-07).

docs.title: The owner model against one current per segment
docs.text:
mom is therefore the per-segment reference against which the owner model of the image family (one uniform current per straight wire) is measured, also for encased electrodes. With 5 cm of 30 Ω·m (wet) concrete around a 5 mm wire, 1 m segments (the outline 0.5 m), grids and stars 0.5 m deep and the outline 0.8 m, the owner model lies above one current per segment by:

Geometry, soil line kernel, bare / encased point kernel against mom, bare / encased grids 10 m 2 × 2 … 40 m 8 × 8, 100 Ω·m +0.36 … +0.70 % / +0.43 … +0.68 % +0.29 … +0.66 % / +0.35 … +0.63 % the same grids, 1 000 / 100 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m +0.43 … +0.64 % / +0.64 … +0.89 % +0.33 … +0.50 % / +0.50 … +0.69 % stars of 3 … 8 arms of 10 m, 100 Ω·m +1.8 … +10.5 % / +2.7 … +13.6 % +1.6 … +10.0 % / +2.4 … +13.0 % the same stars, 1 000 / 100 Ω·m +1.6 … +12.6 % / +3.1 … +19.7 % +1.4 … +11.8 % / +2.7 … +18.8 % outline 16 m × 1 m, 100 Ω·m +0.38 % / +0.48 % +0.39 % / +0.49 %

The line-kernel column compares with one owner per segment under the line kernel; the mom column compares with the point kernel, the kernel of mom, which isolates the current model. Grids and outlines are within about 1 %, stars are not: their arm tips leak more than the uniform current allows (see image).

Measurements and audit trail

The line-kernel column repeats the numbers quoted before, which were measured against the image family's per-segment owners (confirmed to the printed digit). For the generated meshes of the next section (0.5 m segments) the owner model lies +0.42 / +0.36 / +0.31 / +0.057 / +0.004 % (line kernel) and +0.38 / +0.33 / +0.28 / +0.052 / +0.004 % (point kernel against mom) above one current per segment for the house in 100 Ω·m at \(\rho_c\) = 50 / 100 / 150 / 1 000 / 5 000 Ω·m, at most +0.57 % and +0.54 % for medium_industry (50 Ω·m); for the rectangles without cross-braces of the table further down mom gives one owner per side +0.230 % (80 m × 20 m) and +1.353 % (150 m × 3 m) above one current per segment, bare and in 5 cm of 30 Ω·m (30 / 200 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m, 1 m segments), against +0.230 / +0.231 % and +1.336 / +1.339 % with the line kernel.

docs.title: What the generators build
docs.text:
Both concrete_model settings of the generators produce the same representation:

  1. every wire of an encased foundation carries \(C\) and the radius \(r_b\) — the perimeter and, for a mesh foundation, the cross-braces (see Cross-braces of mesh foundations);
  2. rods and the other electrodes of a site stay bare (\(r_a\), \(C = 0\));
  3. no shell resistance on PEN service drops (it would count twice);
  4. substation and cabinet electrodes get \(C\) when their specification is encased;
  5. every rectangle without cross-braces (style="ring", or "mesh" with n_x = n_y = 1) is one owner per side at every orientation (user decision Q38, see Owners of a rectangle).

concrete_model therefore has no effect and is deprecated (removal no earlier than 2027.5): "distributed" still loads and warns, the default "lumped" and the files of 0.15.0 load silently; drop the argument (see Deprecations). World.concrete_shell_corrections is deprecated as well (it still loads and warns at solve; removal no earlier than 2027.5).

Why one mechanism (findings 10.12–10.14)

Up to 0.15.0 the two variants of ADR-0012 travelled different roads. The distributed variant put the shell on the wires; the lumped variant recorded a total shell resistance in the world registry World.concrete_shell_corrections, which only the TN generator turned into a series resistance on the PEN service drop. Every other path — Engine.solve of any other world, solve_mutual_matrix, solve_mutual_field, the layout builder — ignored the registry but kept the inflated wire radius. For the AP1 catalogue, which builds its foundation matrix with solve_mutual_matrix, the concrete therefore lowered the impedance instead of raising it at low soil resistivity. A lumped shell spread over a mixed site also pushed rod and brace current through the foundation's shell, and mesh braces declared unencased got the inflated radius. Up to user decision Q38 "lumped" made an axis-aligned rectangle without cross-braces a single grid-mesh owner.

The golden case mutual_foundations_lumped_concrete records the effect on a foundation matrix: its diagonal rises because the lumped shell now reaches solve_mutual_matrix; the release notes give the magnitudes for AP1-type sites. Since user decision Q38 its two square rings are one owner per side as well, so the passive one carries equalising currents among its sides: the matrix moves by a further 5.2e-4, and the field at the edges of the passive foundation by +5.5 / −4.7 % (the default line kernel at 2 m and 1 m segments, the point kernel at 1 m; the golden engine's point kernel at 2 m segments gives +5.9 / −5.1 %, an effect of the coarse segments, not of the kernel; audit R4B-13), 1.6 % of the largest value of the case's field (the norm-wise measure of the golden harness; audit D3B-02).

docs.title: Cross-braces of mesh foundations
docs.text:
A mesh foundation (FoundationElectrodeSpec(style="mesh"), the generators' default for buildings) joins its perimeter with cross-braces. DIN 18014 lays the foundation earth electrode in the concrete together with its connections, so the braces are encased like the perimeter: every wire of an encased mesh carries \(r_b\) and \(C\) (user decision of 2026.11). The shell resistance of the whole foundation is \(C/L\) over every encased wire, the per-wire shells \(C/L_j\) in parallel; concrete_shell(spec, encased_length_m=...) in groundfield.generators.materialise reports it.

The rule matters as soon as the concrete is drier than the soil. Bare braces are a bare electrode inside the concrete: however dry the concrete, the foundation could not exceed the spreading resistance of its braces alone (9.60 Ω for the house mesh below in 100 Ω·m). Encased, the shell term grows with \(\rho_c\); for \(\rho_c \gg \rho\) the current spreads over the wires in proportion to their length and \(Z \to C/L + Z_\text{soil}\), with \(Z_\text{soil}\) = 4.105 Ω for a uniform current over the 60 m of the house mesh.

The table gives the change of the input impedance when the braces are encased as well, against the bare braces (\(r_a\), no \(C\)) of the 2026.11 development line — a rule that was never released but isolates the braces; the change against 0.15.0 is in Against 0.15.0:

Mesh, soil \(\rho_c\) = 50 100 150 1 000 5 000 Ω·m house, 100 Ω·m −1.1 % −0.03 % +1.5 % +47 % +307 % house, 30 / 100 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m +1.3 % +6.2 % +12 % +154 % +861 % medium_industry, 100 Ω·m −1.3 % −0.03 % +1.6 % +46 % +298 % medium_industry, 30 / 100 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m +1.0 % +4.8 % +9.7 % +120 % +671 %

House mesh: the generators' default (10 m, 2 × 2 cells, 0.8 m deep, \(r_a\) = 5 mm, \(t\) = 5 cm); medium_industry: 20 m, 3 × 3 cells, same wire and cover. Default engine (image family, line kernel, 0.5 m segments). Concrete wetter than the soil lowers \(Z\) a little (the wire grows to \(r_b\)); concrete as conductive as the soil changes nothing but the line kernel's self term. With the point kernel an encased mesh in concrete of the soil's resistivity equals the bare mesh to round-off.

Model uncertainty. The table rests on the owner model of the image family, one uniform current per wire. With one current per segment, all segments at one potential (the moment-method reference), encasing the braces of the house mesh in 100 Ω·m changes \(Z\) by +49.6 / +321.2 % (mom, 0.25 m segments) instead of +46.9 / +307 % at \(\rho_c\) = 1 000 / 5 000 Ω·m (medium_industry: +49.5 / +313.7 % instead of +46.2 / +298 %). The owner model is 1.6 / 2.8 % high for the mesh with bare braces (house; medium_industry 2.2 / 3.6 %) and at most 0.6 % high for the encased mesh, whose shell evens out the current over the wires. The three-dimensional model of fem (each wire its own shell, the soil meshed as a volume) gives +49.1 / +318.2 % for encasing the braces of the house mesh at \(\rho_c\) = 1 000 / 5 000 Ω·m — mom +49.6 / +321.3 % and the owner model +46.9 / +307.0 % on the same world; against it the owner model is +1.6 / +2.8 % high with bare braces and +0.14 / +0.03 % with encased ones.

Measurements and audit trail
  • Earlier brace rules. In 0.15.0 every wire of an encased mesh had the radius \(r_b\), but the braces carried no \(C\): with "distributed" only the perimeter wires had the shell, with "lumped" (the default) no wire had it, and the lumped shell sat in World.concrete_shell_corrections, which Engine.solve of a house never read. The 2026.11 development line, between review pass 10 and the user decision, kept the braces bare (\(r_a\), no \(C\)).
  • Checks of the table. Engine.solve of the generated world and a hand assembly of its wires agree to 4e-16: the wires as separate shell-free electrodes of radius \(r_b\), their mutual matrix from solve_mutual_matrix, \(C/L_j\) added to its diagonal, the wires bonded (\(1/(\mathbf{1}^\mathsf{T} Z^{-1}\mathbf{1})\)). The assembly uses the solver's kernel and owner model, so it checks how the generator wires \(r_b\) and \(C\), not the numbers. An independent thin-wire boundary-element solution (its own line-source kernel and image series, audit D2B) reproduces every entry of the table to 0.02 percentage points.
  • Per-segment values. groundfield's per-segment assembly with the line kernel gives +49.2 / +318.5 % (medium_industry +49.2 / +312 %), and the boundary-element solution agrees with it to 0.02 points; an own point-matching solve of six hand-built wires (own segments, own kernel, Sunde's \(C\) by hand) reproduces mom on the generated mesh to \(4\cdot10^{-16}\) in \(Z\) (audit W2B-06; evidence of stream fw2mom). With the point kernel against mom the owner model is 1.5 / 2.7 % (house) and 2.1 / 3.5 % (medium_industry) high with bare braces; for the encased house mesh in 100 Ω·m it is 0.43 % high at 50 Ω·m and 0.004 % at 5 000 Ω·m. These owner-model numbers come from groundfield's per-segment assembly with the line kernel at 0.25 m segments; at 0.5 m segments it gives 0.42 %, and mom with its point kernel puts the image family's point kernel 0.38 % above it (see In the moment method).
  • The 3-D model of fem: 1.5 million nodes (evidence of stream w4fem3d); it confirms the per-segment value (+49.2 / +318.5 %) to 0.1 / 0.3 points, and mom lies 0.5 / 0.8 % and 0.2 / 0.06 % below it (re-measured after audit W4B-01, evidence of stream fw4fem3d).

docs.title: Overlapping shells at junctions
docs.text:
Each wire carries its own radial shell; where wires meet, the shells overlap within about \(r_b\) of the junction and each wire counts the shared concrete as its own. The three-dimensional model of fem can resolve the concrete instead (FemOptions.concrete_resistivity): a square prism of conformal radius \(r_b\) around every straight encased wire, their union the concrete, on the same mesh as the per-wire shells. The square keeps the shell's resistance to the soil, but in the shell-dominated limit its concrete is 3.8 % less resistive (its inner conformal radius is 0.914 \(r_b\)), and its faces and edges converge at first order: it reads the conductance per metre 2.8 … 4.6 % high at the default levels. So the junctions are read from differences between configurations of the same length and the same free ends — a straight 4 m bar against an L of two 2 m arms (the corner), straight 4 m and 8 m bars against a T and a crossing (user decision Q40). For a 5 mm bar with 5 cm cover, 0.8 m deep in 100 Ω·m, each junction expressed as the equivalent length of wire at the default prism faces (negative where the shared concrete leaks less than the overlapping shells):

Junction (not converged) \(\rho_c\) = 1 000 Ω·m 5 000 Ω·m corner +3.4 cm +5.7 cm crossing −5.1 cm −1.9 cm T-joint +0.6 cm +3.7 cm

These numbers are not converged: one refinement of the prism faces moved the corner to −1.5 / −1.4 cm (−4.9 / −7.1 cm), the crossing and the T-joint were not refined, and the impedance form of the same runs gives −4.0 … −6.3 cm for every junction. A junction acts like a few cm of wire, at most about \(2\,r_b\), sign not settled. With each wire's own shell an L of 4 m reads 0.35 % low, and the house mesh (60 m: 4 corners, 4 T-joints, 1 crossing) changes by about 1 % or less (0.35 … 0.85 % with every sign aligned). The image family, mom and the 3-D model agree on the per-wire shell of these configurations to 0.01 … 0.3 %. No correction is applied: the effect lies below the uncertainty of the concrete resistivity and of the resolved model.

Measurements and audit trail

Evidence of streams w4fem3d and fw4fem3d, after audit W4B-01. The inner conformal radius of the square prism is audit W4B-04, the unconverged junction numbers audit W4B-05.

docs.title: Against 0.15.0
docs.text:
The release changes encased mesh foundations against 0.15.0 by the brace rule above, by the shell that now reaches the solver for "lumped", by the owners (one per wire) and by the default line kernel. Combined change of the input impedance of the house mesh built with GroundingSystemSpec.build_at, default engine of each version (0.15.0: point kernel; 2026.11: line kernel; 0.5 m segments):

House mesh, soil concrete_model in 0.15.0 \(\rho_c\) = 50 100 150 1 000 5 000 Ω·m 100 Ω·m "lumped" +7.0 % +15.0 % +23.0 % +157 % +782 % 100 Ω·m "distributed" +2.2 % +4.2 % +6.6 % +67.9 % +399 % 30 / 100 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m "lumped" +16.5 % +33.8 % +51.0 % +341 % +1 701 % 30 / 100 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m "distributed" +4.8 % +11.8 % +20.2 % +194 % +1 045 %

In 0.15.0 the house read 4.07 Ω in 100 Ω·m with "lumped" whatever the concrete, and 7.20 Ω with "distributed" at 5 000 Ω·m; 2026.11 gives 35.9 Ω for both. Affected are generated mesh foundations with concrete_rho_ohm_m set. Worlds without a shell, ring and building-outline foundations — the AP1 catalogue among them — and the golden cases do not change by the brace rule.

Measurements and audit trail

The causes are findings 10.12–10.14 (the shell of "lumped"), 10.39 (the owners) and 10.28 (the line kernel). The line kernel contributes +0.78 % without a shell and +0.09 % at 5 000 Ω·m (100 Ω·m); with the point kernel on both versions the changes are +6.2 … +781 % ("lumped") and +1.5 … +398 % ("distributed") in 100 Ω·m. In a TN network the 0.15.0 lumped shell sat on the PEN service drop of the house: the default TN network with four such houses (TnNetworkGenerator, seed 0, 100 Ω·m, input impedance at the substation) moves by −3.8 / −5.2 / −6.5 / −13.8 / −10.7 % with "lumped" and by −0.3 / +1.0 / +2.5 / +34.5 / +120.9 % with "distributed" at \(\rho_c\) = 50 … 5 000 Ω·m (−1.7 % without a shell, from other findings). The 0.15.0 models rebuilt by hand in the release code reproduce the 0.15.0 numbers to round-off with the point kernel, and the boundary-element solution reproduces the changes to 0.08 percentage points.

docs.title: Owners of a rectangle without cross-braces
docs.text:
A rectangle without cross-braces (style="ring", or "mesh" with n_x = n_y = 1) is one uniform-current owner per side: one strip per side, bonded to the local \(-y\) side (the anchor), at every orientation, bare or encased (user decision of 2026.11, Q38). concrete_model has no effect on it (see Deprecations). A building outline (polygon_xy_m) stays one closed polyline; since the user decision Q44 (with Q30) the image family gives it one owner per side as well, so a rectangular outline equals the rectangle given by its size.

The change of the input impedance, one owner per side over one owner minus one, is never positive. The four bonded owners carry the split of the current among the sides that dissipates least (their owner matrix is symmetric and positive definite), and the single owner's split, in proportion to the side lengths, is one of those they can take; for a square the two splits coincide and nothing changes. The decrease is largest for narrow rectangles, conductive upper layers over resistive ones, and thick, wet shells. Over the 39 soils of the AP1 grid, for a 5 mm wire at 0.8 m (the generator defaults) and a short side of at least 1 m, the largest decreases found are:

Scope aspect ratio ≤ 4, sides ≤ 80 m aspect ratio ≤ 50, sides ≤ 150 m bare, homogeneous soil −0.089 % (7 m × 1.75 m) −0.330 % (25 m × 1 m) bare or shell up to 5 cm (the default), \(\rho_c\) = 30 … 1 000 Ω·m −0.320 % (80 m × 20 m, 5 cm at 30 Ω·m, 30 / 200 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m) −0.907 % (150 m × 7.75 m, bare, same soil) bare or shell up to 0.2 m, \(\rho_c\) = 30 … 1 000 Ω·m −0.686 % (4 m × 1 m, 0.2 m at 30 Ω·m, 1 000 / 30 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m) −1.529 % (16 m × 1 m, same shell, \(h_1\) = 10 m)

The field description and the generators' module docstring quote a bound with a margin over these values: per side the input impedance is lower by less than 1 % up to aspect ratio 4 (short side at least 1 m, sides up to 80 m) and 2 % up to aspect ratio 50 (short side at least 1 m, sides up to 150 m); bare or with the default 5 cm shell by less than 0.4 % and 1 %. No case of the scan gives a positive change beyond round-off (\(4\cdot10^{-16}\), for a square). Every case decreases most for the wettest concrete of the scope (30 Ω·m), and the largest cases grow with the shell thickness; drier concrete brings the two models together (−0.04 % at 5 000 Ω·m for the 16 m × 1 m case), a perfectly conducting shell separates them up to −1.66 %. A foundation at 0.5 … 1.5 m or a wire of 2.5 … 10 mm deepens the largest decreases by at most 0.10 percentage points (−0.78 % for 4 m × 1 m at 0.5 m, −0.99 % for 150 m × 7.75 m with a 10 mm wire). Below a short side of 1 m the decrease keeps growing (2 m × 0.5 m: −1.01 %, 10 m × 0.5 m: −2.22 % with the 0.2 m shell; 1.2 m × 0.3 m: −0.33 % with the default shell), which is why the scope names the short side.

At the AP1 station (the ring of 4 m × 4 m at 0.6 m with three bonded 4 m rods) the change is −0.0009 … −0.0026 % over the 39 AP1 soils, at 2 m and at 0.5 m segments: the square ring alone would not change, the rods break its symmetry. The houses of the AP1 catalogue are building outlines and did not change by Q38; one owner per side of an outline (user decision Q44) moves the twelve outlines of the tutorial T06 layout by at most −0.004 % each and the layout with the AP1 station by −0.03 … −0.40 % (5 cm of 100 Ω·m concrete or bare, four soils).

Measurements and audit trail
  • Before user decision Q38 the default concrete_model="lumped" made an axis-aligned rectangle — also one turned by a multiple of 90°, built as the axis-aligned rectangle with swapped sides — a single owner: one GridMeshElectrode, the same current density on all four sides; only "distributed" or a rotation by another angle split it (audit D3B-04). Until the decision the numbers of the table, as one owner over one per side minus one (0.089 … 1.553 %), bounded the difference between the two values of concrete_model. Before user decision Q44 a building outline was one owner, and a rectangular outline read like the single owner did.
  • The scan behind the table: 30 rectangles with short sides of 1 to 37.5 m and aspect ratios 1 to 50, bare and with 5 cm and 0.2 m shells, 61 values of \(\rho_c\), refined around each maximum, 13 524 owner matrices in all (audit R2B-01, re-run for the decision). Engine.solve of the generated rectangles (both styles) against one GridMeshElectrode with the same radius and shell reproduces the scan to the printed digit; the line kernel at 0.25 m or 1 m segments and the point kernel stay within the bound (−0.51 … −0.69 % and −1.38 … −1.53 % for the two largest cases).
  • The AP1 station: Engine.solve and the owner algebra of the seven wires agree to \(10^{-15}\). The outlines: evidence of stream w1sol.

Model uncertainty. Against one current per segment, all segments at one potential (the moment-method reference), one owner per side is the closer model, which is why the decision kept it: over the whole scope one owner per side is at most 1.4 % high, the single owner up to 2.2 % (2.16 % for 16 m × 1 m), and one current per segment is never above one owner per side nor one owner per side above one owner:

Scope (short side ≥ 1 m) aspect ratio ≤ 4, sides ≤ 80 m aspect ratio ≤ 50, sides ≤ 150 m bare +0.230 % (80 m × 20 m, 30 / 200 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m) +1.336 % (150 m × 3 m, same soil) bare or shell up to 5 cm, \(\rho_c\) = 30 … 1 000 Ω·m +0.231 % (80 m × 20 m, 5 cm of 30 Ω·m) +1.339 % (150 m × 3 m, 5 cm of 30 Ω·m) bare or shell up to 0.2 m, \(\rho_c\) = 30 … 1 000 Ω·m +0.253 % (6 m × 1.5 m, 0.2 m of 30 Ω·m, 1 000 / 30 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m) +1.347 % (150 m × 3 m, 0.2 m of 30 Ω·m)

The largest values sit at the corner of the scope, the longest and narrowest rectangle (145 m × 2.9 m: +1.335 %, 125 m × 2.5 m: +1.323 %); narrower ones than the scope allows lie higher (150 m × 1 m: +1.65 %). The values for the 0.2 m shell are uncertain by about 0.2 points, because its outer radius of 0.205 m is not thin against the segments (at the default 0.5 m, segment length over wire radius is 2.4, below the thin-wire limit of 5, and the engine warns).

Measurements and audit trail
  • Over the whole scope (audit D3B-01): 80 rectangles with short sides of 1 to 150 m, the 39 AP1 soils, bare and with 5 cm and 0.2 m shells, 61 values of \(\rho_c\), 9 360 segment matrices; segments of 0.5 m up to sides of 50 m, 1 m beyond; groundfield's per-segment assembly at 0.25 m segments. At the largest decreases of the first table one owner was 0.55 % (80 m × 20 m, bare) to 2.16 % (16 m × 1 m) high, one per side 0.23 … 0.90 % high; for the bare cases the boundary-element solution agrees to 0.001 points. 150 m × 2.9 m (aspect ratio 51.7, outside the scope) gives +1.350 % (audit R4B-06); 150 m × 1 m is audit D3B.
  • The independent boundary-element solution of audits R2B and D3B averages the potential over the wire surface. It gives the same bare and 5 cm values to 0.001 points, at the scan's segments and at half of them. For the 0.2 m shell it gives −0.594 % and −1.447 % instead of −0.686 % and −1.529 % in the first table, the same at 0.25, 0.125 and 0.083 m segments. In the second table the two solutions agree at 150 m × 3 m (+1.346 / +1.347 %); at 6 m × 1.5 m the boundary-element value grows from +0.253 % to +0.334 % when its segments are halved to 0.25 m; for the cases of the first table it lies up to 0.23 points lower at 0.25 m segments, and refining its segments to 0.083 m — shorter than the radius, which groundfield refuses — moves it by up to 0.17 points (4 m × 1 m: one owner +0.85 → +1.01 %, one per side +0.25 → +0.41 %).

docs.title: Converting between the conventions
docs.text:
The helpers in groundfield.geometry.electrodes convert between the material description, the coefficient and a lumped resistance:

Helper Formula Use concrete_shell_coefficient(rho_c, wire_radius, thickness) \(C = \frac{\rho_c}{2\pi}\ln\frac{r_a + t}{r_a}\) from concrete resistivity and cover shell_coefficient_from_resistance(electrode, R) \(C = R\,L\) from a lumped shell resistance of the whole electrode shell_resistance_from_coefficient(electrode, C=None) \(R = C/L\) the lumped resistance a coefficient represents

\(L\) is electrode.total_length(), all wires of the electrode. A lumped resistance of a site belongs to its encased wires only — every wire of the foundation, braces included, but not the bonded rods; spreading it over the rods was the error behind the mixed-site deviations of finding 10.13. With \(\rho_c = 100\) Ω·m, 5 cm cover and a 5 mm wire, \(C = (100/2\pi)\ln 11 \approx 38.2\) Ω·m, i.e. 3.8 Ω for 10 m of encased wire.

docs.title: Validity
docs.text: Condition Statement Geometry thin shell around a thin wire, not overlapping a neighbouring wire's shell along its length (at junctions the shells share a region of the size of \(r_b\), see above) Current radial through the shell; the series decomposition holds below 1 kHz for foundation sizes Concrete homogeneous \(\rho_c\) per electrode; about 30 Ω·m (wet) to tens of kΩ·m (dry), see ADR-0012 Field quantities the surface potential is that of the bare wire of radius \(r_b\) fed through the shell; the shell itself is a series element Current model against one current per segment the owner model of the image family is +0.3 … +0.9 % high for grids, at most 0.6 % for encased meshes, 1.4 % for rectangles without braces, 3.6 % for meshes with bare braces and +19.7 % for stars (table) Backends image, image_2layer, solve_mutual_*, mom, mom_sommerfeld and fem
