docs.title: Earth return and inductive coupling
docs.text:
This page explains the longitudinal impedance of the conductors of a grounding study — PEN conductors, cable screens, measurement leads, interconnections between earth electrodes — and in particular the earth-return impedance that the current returning through the soil adds to it. Read it before you give conductors an inductance_model, when you choose Engine.earth_inductive_model, or when a reactance looks suspicious.

At 50 Hz, and more so at the harmonics up to 1 kHz that matter for AP2, conductors are not only resistors: their longitudinal impedance has an inductive part, they couple magnetically to each other, and the soil closes the loop. The galvanic part of the problem (leakage, potentials in the soil) is not affected; it is explained on the engine pages.

docs.title: Mathematical and physical context
docs.text:
A conductor with inductance_model="neumann" is split into branches (one per sub-segment of discretize_segment_length, or one branch for a lumped conductor). Their longitudinal impedance matrix enters the network equations of the engine family:

\[ Z_b(\omega) = R + j\omega L + \Delta Z(\omega) , \]

the voltage drop along each branch per unit current in every branch, at the angular frequency \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Its three parts:

  • \(R\) — the diagonal of the DC resistances of the branches; with resistance_model="skin" a frequency-dependent internal-impedance correction is added (see skin effect).
  • \(L\) — the partial-inductance matrix. Between two branches \(i\) and \(j\) it is Neumann's double line integral \(L_{ij} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_i\int_j \frac{\mathrm d\mathbf l_i\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf l_j}{r}\), the magnetic flux that a unit current in one branch links with the other (\(\mu_0\) the permeability of free space, \(r\) the distance of the two line elements). groundfield evaluates it in closed form for parallel, skew, touching and coaxial pairs (Grover 1946). The self terms are those of a thin wire with the DC internal inductance \(\mu_0\ell/(8\pi)\) of a solid round conductor of length \(\ell\) (none for a cable shield, conductor_type="cable_shield", a thin-walled tube). To \(L\) belongs the image of the earth model (below).
  • \(\Delta Z\) — the earth-return correction: how much the finite conductivity of the soil changes the magnetic field of that image.

The physical scale is the skin depth of the soil,

\[ \delta = \sqrt{\frac{2\rho}{\omega\mu_0}} \approx 503\,\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{f}}\ \text{m}, \]

the depth over which an alternating field in soil of resistivity \(\rho\) decays by \(1/e\). In the frequency range of the package it lies between about 110 m (50 Ω·m, 1 kHz) and 1.6 km (500 Ω·m, 50 Hz): comparable to or larger than the extent of a low-voltage network. The return current therefore spreads deep and wide, and neither a perfect mirror nor a perfectly conducting earth describes it. FieldResult.metadata["penetration_depth"] reports \(\delta\) for every frequency of a solve with inductive conductors.

The soil-side galvanic coupling (leakage, potentials) is unaffected: the field kernel stays real and quasi-static, the earth return acts on the longitudinal impedance of conductors only.

Corrected statement

Earlier versions of this page gave the range of \(\delta\) as "about 350 m (50 Ω·m, 1 kHz) and 5 km (500 Ω·m, 50 Hz)". The formula above gives 112.5 m and 1591.5 m there (groundfield.coupling.carson.skin_depth agrees); the 159 m at 1 kHz in 100 Ω·m quoted below were right.

docs.title: The three earth models
docs.text:
Engine.earth_inductive_model selects the model. Each is the combination of an image convention for \(L\) and a correction \(\Delta Z\) defined against that very image — an earth-return correction is meaningless without the baseline it was derived for:

earth_inductive_model Image in \(L\) Correction \(\Delta Z\) Use "sommerfeld" (default since 0.13.0) none (free space) full Sommerfeld / Pollaczek kernel minus free space, every segment pair quantitative \(Z(f)\), any geometry, layered earth "carson_series" anti-parallel (perfectly conducting earth) Carson per metre on near-parallel horizontal pairs, Sommerfeld otherwise (below) long parallel lines over homogeneous earth; fast "perfect_mirror" additive (magnetic mirror) none diagnostic baseline only

docs.title: Sommerfeld (Pollaczek kernel)
docs.text:
The vector potential of an alternating line current in or above a conducting half-space is a Sommerfeld integral (Sommerfeld 1909; Pollaczek 1926 for the buried conductor, Carson 1926 for the overhead one). Take the time convention \(e^{+j\omega t}\), the soil conductivity \(\sigma = 1/\rho\), the propagation constant \(\gamma\) with \(\gamma^2 = j\omega\mu_0\sigma\), the radial wavenumber \(\lambda\) of the Hankel transform and \(u = \sqrt{\lambda^2 + \gamma^2}\). For two points at depths \(z\) and \(z'\) in homogeneous soil, at the horizontal distance \(s\) and the distance \(R\), the Green's function of the vector potential is

\[ G(s, z, z') = \frac{e^{-\gamma R}}{R} + \int_0^\infty \frac{\lambda}{u}\,\frac{u - \lambda}{u + \lambda}\, e^{-u(z+z')}\,J_0(\lambda s)\,\mathrm d\lambda : \]

the field of the source in an unbounded conducting medium, plus the field reflected at the soil surface, written as a superposition of cylindrical waves (\(J_0\) the Bessel function of order zero). The factor \((u - \lambda)/(u + \lambda)\) is the reflection coefficient of the insulating air. The earth-return correction of two segments is the change of their mutual impedance against free space,

\[ \Delta Z_{ij} = j\omega\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_i\int_j \Bigl(G - \frac{1}{R}\Bigr)\, \mathrm d\mathbf l_i\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf l_j , \]

integrated over the actual geometry of each segment pair — any length, orientation and depth — and added to an image-free Neumann matrix. For layered earth the spectral amplitude carries the generalised reflection coefficients of the stack, and overhead pairs keep Carson's air-side geometry; the amplitudes are documented in groundfield.coupling.sommerfeld_inductance. In the long-wire limit the correction gives Pollaczek's per-metre impedance, including the positive earth-return resistance of about \(\omega\mu_0/8\) per metre; for \(\sigma \to 0\) it vanishes (the soil is magnetically transparent).

docs.title: Numerics of the Sommerfeld correction
docs.text:
• Image-free baseline. The correction is built against free space, so no image has to be added and removed again. Conductors that cross the soil surface or lie in it are solved (the pair integrals are split at \(z = 0\)); with the image conventions of the other models such a segment is singular and raises.
  • Exact layered kernel. For any number of layers the same-layer amplitude uses generalised reflection coefficients and all other pairs a batched interface solve; a three-layer earth whose lower two layers are equal equals the two-layer earth exactly.
  • Resolved \(\lambda\) grid. The logarithmic region of the quadrature in \(\lambda\) ends before \(J_0\) oscillates, the linear region carries 16 nodes per \(J_0\) period up to four times the largest physical scale, and an exhausted panel budget warns (SommerfeldResolutionWarning) instead of truncating silently.
  • Multi-frequency assembly. Geometry, \(\lambda\) grid and Bessel tables are built once per pair for the whole frequency set of a solve, bit-identical to single-frequency assemblies, with a bounded cache.
  • Long segments. A single 16 × 16 rule over a segment cannot resolve \(e^{-\gamma R}\) along a segment much longer than the skin depth. A pair of segments longer than a quarter skin depth of the most conductive layer gets a composite outer rule (16 nodes per piece, at most 512 pieces, then a SommerfeldResolutionWarning) and a denser table of the spectral integral over the horizontal distance.
  • Self terms and close pairs (user decision Q34). Along the line of closest approach of a segment with itself, or of two segments that come close (wires beside each other, a core in its shield), the integrand has a kink — the \(\gamma^2R/2\) term of \((e^{-\gamma R}-1)/R\) and its counterpart in the spectral part, smoothed only over the decay length \(z + z'\) — which a tensor-product rule cannot follow. The self term of every segment is therefore the exact one-dimensional reduction \(2\int_0^L (L-u)\,g(u)\,\mathrm du\) of its double integral (\(g(u)\) the integrand at the axial separation \(u\)), with 16-node panels graded from \(z + z'\) up to a quarter skin depth, uniform up to 40 skin depths and doubling beyond. Close pairs (closest distance below half the longer segment) get a graded rule along their line of closest approach (a coinciding pair: the self rule). The self correction is within 1.1e-9 of a refined rule and of an independent reference from 1 m and 0.01 skin depths to 3 km at 50 Hz and 1 kHz (buried at 0.7 m in 100, 1000/30 and 30/1000 Ω·m, overhead at 10 m over 10 Ω·m) and continuous in the length (steps below 3e-13); close pairs are within about 4e-8 (3.5e-8 for two 1 m wires 1 mm apart in 30 over 1000 Ω·m at 1 kHz). Both rest on the 256-node logarithmic region of the \(\lambda\) grid.
  • Very long conductors. Both rules cost at most linearly in the length: one lumped conductor of 2 km from a rod to a junction, 50 Hz and 1 kHz, is solved in 1.1 s within 0.21 GB, 100 km in 10.6 s within 0.24 GB. Beyond about 33 km such a conductor is not converged and the solve warns (SommerfeldResolutionWarning; the resolved \(\lambda\) grid reaches \(2^{17}\cdot 2\pi\,(z + z')/30\), 38 km for a conductor at 0.7 m).
  • Tabulated assembly (the default since 2026.11, Engine.sommerfeld_assembly="tabulated"; user decision Q16). Sub-segments are grouped by depth, and one table of the spectral integral per pair of depth groups and frequency replaces the per-pair quadrature. It is much faster on large networks (a 30-house TN network 306 s → 12 s) and agrees with a converged reference better than the per-pair rule (sommerfeld_assembly="exact"), whose 24-node interpolation in the horizontal distance dominates its error (2e-10 against 1.2e-8 of two refined references). Measured times are on the performance page.
Measurements and audit trail

What 2026.11 changed (ADR-0006 amendment):

  • Image-free baseline (findings 10.46, F52): the numbers equal the former additive pairing to round-off.
  • Exact layered kernel (10.35): a three-layer earth whose lower two layers are equal was +17…+25 % in \(X'\) before.
  • Resolved \(\lambda\) grid (10.36): distant pair entries were off by −24 % (200 m) and +274 % (400 m) before.
  • Multi-frequency assembly (10.60).
  • Long segments (10.24, audits of 2026.11): a lumped 3 km PEN read +13.4 % earth-return resistance at 1 kHz in 100 Ω·m.
  • Self terms and close pairs (user decision Q34): up to 2026.11.0 the self correction of a buried segment was 4.8e-4 off at a quarter skin depth (growing like \(L/\delta\) below it), stepped by 3.5e-4 where the composite rule took over, and was within 5.9e-4 for longer segments; two wires 1 mm apart were 1.5e-3 off in 30 over 1000 Ω·m. With the 64 nodes of earlier builds in the logarithmic region of the \(\lambda\) grid, short segments were 1e-5 … 7.4e-5 off at 0.01 skin depths and up to 3e-4 at 1 m, about 1e-8 of a solved impedance (audit W3B-01).
  • Very long conductors: the 2 km conductor took 28 s and 1.6 GB, the 100 km one more than 7.8 GB (audit W2B-05); the limit at about 33 km is audit W3B-10.

docs.title: Carson on its own baseline
docs.text:
Carson (1926) derived the earth-return impedance of a line over homogeneous earth as a correction to the impedance of the line and its anti-parallel image in a perfectly conducting plane. The correction is \((\omega\mu_0/\pi)(P + jQ)\) per metre, where Carson's series \(P\) and \(Q\) depend on the dimensionless parameter \(a = D\sqrt{\omega\mu_0\sigma}\) — \(D\) the distance between conductor and image, \(2h\) for a self term at height or depth \(h\) — and on the angle of the image direction. It is a per-metre result for infinitely long parallel horizontal wires, so carson_series uses it only inside that validity domain:

  • Near-parallel horizontal pairs on one side of the surface — \(\lvert\cos\varphi\rvert > 0.99\) (\(\varphi\) the angle between the two segments) and both segments inclined by less than 8.1° — get the per-metre correction at their horizontal axis distance, times the length over which their projections overlap; the self term of a horizontal segment is the per-metre value times its length. Pairs that do not overlap (staggered, end to end) and collinear pieces of one wire get none: the per-metre self value on the diagonal already contains the rest of the same wire. The tiling converges under refinement. Two conductors that overlap on one axis are wires lying side by side and get the correction at the distance of touching wires, \(r_i + r_j\) (the sum of their radii).
  • Pairs across the surface — an overhead wire parallel to a buried one — have no anti-parallel baseline (a perfect conductor screens the soil). They couple through the field transmitted into the soil, carson_mixed_mutual_correction: Carson's \(J\) plus the bounded remainder of the buried wire's attenuation (Ametani et al. 2009).
  • Tilted near-parallel pairs. Where a near-parallel pair comes close within its overlap (its smallest distance there is below 30 times the change of its offset), the per-metre correction is integrated over the overlap (Gauss–Legendre nodes) instead of being taken at the mid-point distance, so a lumped pair and its pieces add up: a core crossing its shield's axis at mid-length differs by at most 8.0e-6 of the loop reactance. Other pairs keep one entry at the mid-point distance, exact to second order there.
  • Everything else — oblique pairs and every pair and self term of a segment inclined by more than 8.1° (risers, sloping leads) — gets the exact Sommerfeld correction of a homogeneous earth of the same conductivity, moved onto the anti-parallel baseline.

At the 8.1° boundary the result steps from the per-metre tiling to the Sommerfeld value, by the error of the per-metre model there: 13 % for two 1 km leads 2 m apart at 1 kHz, more for shorter leads (42 % for two 300 m leads at 50 Hz). That step is the price of keeping Carson's closed form where it is accurate; for oblique or short conductors use sommerfeld.

On this baseline a 1 km isolated PEN reproduces \(l\,X'_\text{Carson}\) within 1 % (tests/test_inductive_solver_integration.py::test_carson_series_reactance_matches_carson). Carson's small-\(a\) series is evaluated to \(a^{12}\) and the self-term quadrature at \(\theta = 0\) to round-off, so the regime boundaries are continuous; the asymptotic expansion is used for \(a > 15\).

carson_series remains an approximation for short, inclined or buried conductors and for layered soil (an effective homogeneous conductivity is used); it is the fast choice for long parallel lines over homogeneous earth, not a replacement of sommerfeld in general.

Networks of short cables. Tiled over the pieces of service drops that are shorter than the skin depth (30 … 60 m against 159 m at 1 kHz in 100 Ω·m), Carson's infinite-line correction overstates the earth return of an LV network. For the generated star, radial and grid networks of 5 … 100 houses with an insulated Neumann PEN, carson_series reads the input reactance 4 … 21 % and the resistance up to 11 % high at 1 kHz, and the reactance 21 … 50 % and the resistance up to 0.9 % high at 50 Hz; at 50 Hz it is then no closer than the diagnostic perfect_mirror for four of the five networks measured (note below). A change of such a network is reproduced by carson_series only within that error, possibly with the opposite sign. Use sommerfeld for LV networks.

Measurements and audit trail
  • Validity domain of carson_series: since the second adversarial audit of 2026.11 (A2C-1). Up to then an oblique pair got \(\sqrt{\ell_i\ell_j}\,\lvert\cos\varphi\rvert\) times the per-metre value once per segment pair, which grew with the number of segments (two 1 km leads at 9°: 20× the Sommerfeld coupling). Pairs across the surface: the solver used to treat the buried wire as an overhead wire at height \(\lvert z\rvert\), which gave 36 % too little mutual reactance for a lead 1 m above a PEN at 0.7 m depth at 1 kHz.
  • Tilted near-parallel pairs (audit W1R3-07): before, a core crossing its shield's axis at mid-length differed by 4.3e-4 of the loop reactance at 2e-3 rad and 5.2e-2 at 4e-2 rad; generated networks are unchanged by the rule.
  • 0.15.0 (finding 10.20 / F32): the solver added Carson's correction to the additive image matrix of the perfect mirror, which roughly doubled the earth-return reactance: 1.66–2.25 times Carson's value for 100 m – 1 km lines, +41 % on \(\lvert Z\rvert\) at 1 kHz for a TN network with inductive PEN conductors. Since 2026.11 the matrix is built on the anti-parallel image.
  • Networks of short cables (audits W3B-02, W3R2B-03). Soils: 100 Ω·m and two-layer soils of 30 … 200 Ω·m. Reference: sommerfeld with a refined discretisation (PEN in 2.5 m pieces, 1 m segments); the default sommerfeld agrees with it to 1e-3 for the 5-house radial network and to 4e-5 for the 80- and 100-house ones. Per network, input reactance at 1 kHz / 50 Hz: the 5-house radial network +13 % / +31 %, the 10-house radial network +20 % / +41 %, the 30-house star +17 % / +44 %, the 80-house radial network +19 % / +50 %; the 100-house radial network R +11 % / +0.9 %. At 50 Hz carson_series is no closer than perfect_mirror for the 10-house radial network, the 30-house star and the 80- and 100-house radial networks (perfect_mirror +40 / +37 / +41 / +41 % there), but closer for the 5-house radial network (perfect_mirror +45 %). The error changes with the geometry: across the cabinet fix of audit W1B-01/02 the star's reactance moves by +1.18 % under carson_series and −3.54 % under sommerfeld (the refined reference: −3.54 %), between two house spacings around the cabinet threshold of the 100-house grid by +1.81 / −2.77 % (reference −2.77 %), and of the 50-house grid by −21.6 / −18.9 % (reference −18.9 %).

docs.title: Equivalent depth of layered soil
docs.text: The complex-depth formulas of Dubanton and Deri replace a homogeneous earth by a perfectly conducting plane at the complex depth \(p = \sqrt{\rho/(j\omega\mu_0)}\) and give the line impedance in closed form. gf.penetration_depth(soil, frequencies) returns the \(p\) (and the equivalent resistivity \(j\omega\mu_0 p^2\)) for which these formulas reproduce the earth return of any layer stack: the plane-wave surface impedance of the stack over \(j\omega\mu_0\), which matches the layered surface reflection coefficient to second order in the horizontal wavenumber. Over the 39 soils of the AP1 grid, 50 Hz … 1 kHz and 0.1 … 1000 m, the earth-return correction of two overhead or buried wires is reproduced within a median of 2.2 % (the formula's own median error in homogeneous soil: 2.4 %), at most 28 … 33 % where the separation approaches \(\lvert p\rvert\); the homogeneous depth of \(\rho_1\) is off by up to 2800 %. Method and numbers: Soil. The solver's models do not use it.

docs.title: Perfect mirror
docs.text:
perfect_mirror treats the earth as a perfect magnetic mirror (additive image, no correction). It is cheap and frequency independent but far from the physics of buried conductors below 1 kHz; it was the default before 0.13.0 and is kept as a baseline for comparisons.

Its image is applied to every pair of inductive segments, also to a pair of which one segment lies above the soil surface (\(z < 0\), an overhead lead) and one below it (a buried PEN or cable). Such a pair has no magnetic mirror between them in any physical sense, so the additive image has no basis there. The numbers are kept as they are (a baseline), but the solve emits one UserWarning that counts these pairs, names the conductors on each side and points to "sommerfeld"; carson_series and sommerfeld treat such pairs through the field transmitted into the soil and do not warn. Segments in or across the surface plane are rejected under this image convention.

Measurements and audit trail

The warning on pairs across the surface exists since 2026.11 (user decision Q27).

docs.title: Conductor details
docs.text:
• Touching segments. Chain neighbours and bends share an end point where the Neumann integrand is logarithmically singular; Grover's vertex formula and the coaxial gap formula replace the 16 × 16 Gauss–Legendre rule by default (touching="exact"), so a straight conductor keeps the inductance of the unsplit wire for every discretisation (tests/test_inductive_solver_integration.py::test_inductance_is_refinement_invariant_for_a_straight_conductor). touching="quadrature" reproduces 0.15.0.
  • Lumped and single-segment conductors. A conductor with an inductance_model that the topology keeps as one branch is one inductive branch from start to end, coupled to all others.
  • Close pairs. Pairs that miss the closed forms — nearly parallel wires close together, crossing and skew pairs, a branch starting on another segment — are integrated semi-analytically (inner integral in closed form, outer Gauss–Legendre panels graded towards the near-singular points). Measured against mpmath: 5e-11 for directions that differ by more than 1e-6 rad, 1.0e-9 for filaments crossing at 1e-8 rad; filaments from one vertex to round-off on axis-parallel geometry (4e-10 in a general orientation).

  • Wires beside each other. Where a point of one wire lies beside another wire — its foot on that wire's axis falls inside it — closer than the sum of the radii \(r_i + r_j\), the filament integral is meaningless: it diverges for coincident axes (two coincident 50 m leads read 1.87 H) and exceeds the self inductance once the wires are closer than about their radius, which makes the inductance matrix indefinite (a network whose service drops ran back along the PEN main had a negative input reactance). There the distance from the other axis is taken as \(r_i + r_j\) — two wires touching side by side, as two cables in one trench lie — pointwise inside the Neumann integral, both one-sided integrals averaged.

    A core inside a shield. Where the thinner wire runs inside the thicker one and the thicker one is a cable shield (conductor_type="cable_shield", user decision Q32), the shield radius is used instead: a core inside a shield is a filament inside a thin tube and couples to it as at the tube radius, and since the shield carries no internal inductance (user decision Q33) the loop gives the coaxial inductance per metre

    \[ L'_\text{coax} = \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\Bigl(\ln\frac{r_s}{r_c} + \frac14\Bigr), \]

    the flux between the core of radius \(r_c\) and the shield of radius \(r_s\) plus the internal inductance of the solid core: 26.97 µH for 100 m with a 5 mm core and a 15 mm shield (31.97 µH with the internal inductance of a solid shield). Two unmarked conductors on one axis are separate cables and touch (43.47 µH for the same pair).

    Pieces add up to the lumped pair. A wire inside a shield couples at the shield radius at every axial offset, and for two other conductors lying beside each other a point lies beside the partner when its foot falls inside the partner's whole conductor: the sub-pieces of the two conductors then add up to the lumped pair (within 3e-12). That holds for pieces that are not parallel too, at any angle and whatever their length — a core tilted against its shield or crossing its axis, wires leaving a junction or crossing at a small angle: the stretches inside, beside and away from the partner are found exactly, and a core leaving the shield's tube along its length adds up as well. The value does not depend on the order or the direction of the segments, is continuous in the geometry, and leaves chain neighbours, bends turning by less than 90° and pairs farther apart unchanged. For unequal radii it steps where the thinner axis leaves the thicker wire, from "inside" to "side by side": the two describe different cables. Equal radii never count as one wire inside the other.

    At the low level, build_inductance_matrix(..., shields=[False, True], include_internal=[True, False], conductors=[0, 1]) does the same. The marker leaves the self terms alone, so a shield needs include_internal=False (else it keeps the 50 nH/m of a solid wire, 31.97 µH), and conductors labels the pieces of each conductor (without it every segment is a conductor of its own: unmarked touching pieces of one cable then do not add up, 40.34 instead of 43.47 µH in 0.25 m pieces, while a marked shield needs no labels). - Diagnostics. conductors.find_close_wires and diagnose() report crossing, touching, interpenetrating and close wires; diagnose() also reports inductive conductors that lie beside each other closer than touching over a stretch (category overlap), the pairs the rule above evaluates as touching wires.

Measurements and audit trail
  • Touching segments, close pairs, wires beside each other: finding 10.46. With the 16 × 16 rule close pairs were +12 % at 10 cm and up to +250 % at 1 cm for two 5 m segments.
  • Lumped and single-segment conductors (finding 10.24): up to 0.15.0 their inductance was silently dropped (a 300 m PEN read 0.0564 Ω at 1 kHz instead of 0.210 + 3.78j Ω).
  • Shields: before user decision Q33 a shield carried the internal inductance of a solid wire (31.97 µH for the coax above).
  • Pieces adding up to the lumped pair (audit W1A-02; before, the coax in 1 m pieces read 2.2 % low). Audits W1R2-01, W1R3-01 and W1R3-02 extended the rule to tilted and crossing pieces: a core tilted by 4.5e-5 rad read 7.4 % low in 0.25 m pieces, with a step at the parallel tolerance; until W1R3 the rule acted only while the lateral distance changed by at most \(r_i + r_j\) along a piece and for \(\lvert\cos\varphi\rvert \ge 0.99\), and beyond either bound the rule of the single segments mixed in: a core crossing the shield's axis at mid-length read −8.6e-5 of the loop off the lumped pair in 10 m pieces, shield pieces of mixed length −1.6e-3, two wires leaving a junction stepped by 1.5e-3 at 8.1°. The conductors labels of build_inductance_matrix: audit W1R2-08.
  • Diagnostics: finding 10.44; the overlap category of diagnose() exists since 2026.11.

docs.title: Skin effect
docs.text:
With Conductor.resistance_model="skin" (opt-in) every branch of the conductor adds \(\ell_b\,\Delta Z'_\text{skin}(f)\) to its diagonal (\(\ell_b\) the branch length): the exact internal impedance per metre of a solid round conductor of radius \(a\) and resistivity \(\rho\),

\[ Z'_\text{int} = \frac{k\rho}{2\pi a}\,\frac{I_0(ka)}{I_1(ka)},\qquad k = \sqrt{j\omega\mu_0/\rho}, \]

which describes the current crowding towards the surface of the conductor (\(I_0\), \(I_1\) the modified Bessel functions of the first kind), taken relative to the DC convention (\(R'_\text{dc}\) plus the internal inductance \(\mu_0/(8\pi)\) already in \(L\)). For 150 mm² aluminium the resistance rises by the factors 1.056, 1.231 and 1.550 at 250, 550 and 1000 Hz and the internal inductance falls to 0.740 of its DC value at 1 kHz (tests/test_skin_effect.py); the IEC 60287-1-1 skin factor agrees to about 1 %. A conductor without an inductance_model has no inductance at all, so only the resistance part applies to it. The default resistance_model="dc" keeps the numbers and the JSON of earlier releases.

Measurements and audit trail

The skin-effect model is finding 10.37 of review pass 10.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Carson: the solver's 1 km PEN against \(l\,X'_\text{Carson}\) (test above); Carson's \(P\) and \(Q\) against an independent mpmath quadrature across all regimes (tests/test_carson_pq.py).
  • Sommerfeld against Pollaczek: benchmark B13 takes the per-metre series impedance of an isolated line from the difference of a 1600 m and an 800 m line (which cancels the end effects) and compares it with the conductor-earth loop impedance of references.pollaczek; the generated numbers are on the validation page (rows pollaczek_x, pollaczek_r). Distant pair entries against an independent quadrature: tests/test_sommerfeld_accuracy.py.
  • references.pollaczek itself uses the exact two-layer amplitude and the \(K_0\) head and agrees with an independent boundary-value solution to \(10^{-7}\) (tests/test_pollaczek_layered.py).
  • Engine level: compare_engines compares complex impedances at every frequency, so a reactance mismatch between earth models cannot pass as consistent (benchmark B13 row image_vs_mom).
Measurements and audit trail

The exact two-layer amplitude of references.pollaczek is finding 10.45 (since 2026.11), the complex comparison of compare_engines finding 10.71.

docs.title: Kernels: point source and exact line source
docs.text:
This page explains how the integral engines turn the current of one wire segment into the potential at another — the kernel — and why the two kernels of groundfield differ by a systematic 1–2 % on grounding resistances. Read it when kernel="point" and kernel="line" disagree, when you compare groundfield with another program, or before you choose a segment length.

At a glance

point kernel line kernel Source of a segment its current at the midpoint its current spread uniformly along the axis Observation at the midpoint of the other segment (collocation) averaged over the other segment (Galerkin) Used by mom, mom_sommerfeld; kernel="point" of the image family the image family by default since 2026.11 (ADR-0015) Resistance of a straight wire converges to a value about 1–2 % low exact at any segment length Cost lowest about 1.1 … 5.8 times the point kernel (Cost)

docs.title: Mathematical and physical context
docs.text:
An electrode is cut into straight segments. Segment \(j\) has the length \(L_j\), the wire radius \(a_j\), the unit tangent \(\mathbf t_j\), the midpoint \(\mathbf P_j\) and the axis \(\mathbf x_j(l')\), \(0 \le l' \le L_j\). The image family assumes that it leaks its current \(I_j\) uniformly along its axis, with the line density \(I_j/L_j\) in A/m.

In homogeneous soil of resistivity \(\rho\) with an insulating surface, a point current \(I\) at \(\mathbf y\) produces at \(\mathbf x\) the potential \(\rho I/(4\pi)\) times \(1/\lvert\mathbf x - \mathbf y\rvert\) plus the same term for the mirror point of \(\mathbf y\) above the surface (the air image, which makes the surface current-free). Integrating the line density of segment \(j\) along its axis and averaging the result over the observing segment \(i\) gives the mean potential of segment \(i\),

\[ \bar\varphi_i = \frac{\rho}{4\pi}\sum_j K_{ij}\,I_j , \]

which says that the potential of every segment is a weighted sum of all segment currents; the weights \(K_{ij}\) (in 1/m) are the reaction coefficients. Exactly,

\[ K_{ij} = \frac{1}{L_i L_j}\int_{0}^{L_i}\!\!\int_{0}^{L_j} \frac{\mathrm dl\,\mathrm dl'}{\sqrt{\lvert\mathbf x_i(l) - \mathbf x_j(l')\rvert^2 + a^2}} \quad(+\text{ the same integral with the image of segment } j), \]

the mean over both segments of the potential that a unit current on one produces on the other. The reduced kernel \(1/\sqrt{r^2 + a^2}\) puts the source current on the wire axis and the observation point on the wire surface, a distance \(a\) away; this keeps the self term finite. For two different wires \(a^2 = \tfrac12(a_i^2 + a_j^2)\).

Averaging the potential with the same weights that distribute the current is the Galerkin choice. It makes \(K\) symmetric (\(K_{ij} = K_{ji}\)), so every multiport matrix built from it is reciprocal, and for a straight wire the sum over all segment pairs is the double integral over the whole wire — the result does not depend on how finely the wire is cut. A kernel is an approximation of \(K_{ij}\); the two kernels below differ in how they evaluate it.

docs.title: The point kernel
docs.text:
The point kernel (kernel="point", the only kernel of 0.15.0 and of the mom family) replaces both integrals by values at the midpoints:

  • off the diagonal the current of segment \(j\) sits at its midpoint and is observed at the midpoint of segment \(i\): \(K_{ij} \approx 1/r_{ij}\), \(r_{ij} = \lvert\mathbf P_i - \mathbf P_j\rvert\);
  • on the diagonal it takes the collocation self term \(2\ln(L_i/a_i)/L_i\) — the potential of the uniformly loaded segment at its own midpoint, \((2/L)\operatorname{arsinh}(L/2a)\), for \(L \gg a\) — plus the self image \(1/(2z_i)\) as a point image, \(z_i\) the depth of the segment.

Why it is low. Take a straight wire cut into segments of equal length \(L\) and compare one row of the matrix with the exact Galerkin entries:

  • the segment itself: exact \(K_{ii} \approx 2[\ln(2L/a) - 1]/L\) against \(2\ln(L/a)/L\), so the point kernel over-counts by \(2(1 - \ln 2)/L = +0.61/L\);
  • each adjacent collinear segment: exact \(\frac{1}{L^2}\int_0^L\!\int_L^{2L}\frac{\mathrm dl'\,\mathrm dl}{l' - l} = 2\ln 2/L\) against \(1/L\), so the two neighbours together are under-counted by \(2(2\ln 2 - 1)/L = -0.77/L\);
  • the segment \(k\) places away: exact \([(k+1)\ln(k+1) - 2k\ln k + (k-1)\ln(k-1)]/L\) against \(1/(kL)\), a deficit that falls like \(1/k^3\) and adds about \(-0.07/L\) over both sides.

The net row-sum error is about \(-0.23/L\). The row sum itself grows like \(2\ln(\ell/a)/L\) for a wire of total length \(\ell\), so the relative error of the resistance — the ratio of the two — depends on \(\ell/a\) and not on the segment length. The point kernel converges, but to a value about 1–2 % below the uniform-current solution, and a convergence study cannot see it. The generated kernel check on the validation page shows it for a rod, a ring and a strip at every segment length.

Two further consequences of the point form:

  • Short segments. The collocation self term vanishes at \(L = a\) and is too small for short segments, so a short piece acts like a short circuit. The point kernel therefore takes the Galerkin self term below \(L/a = 2.990\), where both coincide (SELF_TERM_CROSSOVER; every segment with \(L/a \ge 2.990\) keeps its value bit for bit). Every interface cut is kept, however short the piece beyond it; the self term of such a piece is evaluated without cancellation.
  • Shallow segments. The self image \(1/(2z)\) is the \(L \ll 4z\) limit of the image line; for segments longer than four times their depth it is biased high (ShallowSegmentWarning).
Measurements and audit trail

The row-sum analysis is finding 10.28 of review pass 10. Before the Galerkin self term for short segments (finding 10.32, second adversarial audit A2S-01), a sliver at a layer interface acted as a short: mom gave a rod whose tip is 9 mm below \(h_1\) 27 % less resistance than the same rod 1 mm above it.

docs.title: The exact line kernel
docs.text:
The line kernel (kernel="line", default of the image family) evaluates the double integral of \(K_{ij}\). Its inner integral, the potential of a uniformly loaded segment from \(A\) to \(B\) at a point \(X\) with the end-point distances \(R_1 = \lvert X - A\rvert\) and \(R_2 = \lvert X - B\rvert\), has the classical closed form

\[ \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L \frac{\mathrm dl}{\lvert X - A - l\,\mathbf t\rvert} = \frac{1}{L}\ln\frac{R_1 + R_2 + L}{R_1 + R_2 - L}, \]

valid for any orientation of the segment: the equipotentials of a uniformly charged segment are ellipsoids with its end points as foci. The code evaluates it without cancellation and with the reduced kernel. The outer average is computed as follows.

Self term. With \(u = l - l'\) the double integral reduces to one integral, \(K_{ii} = \frac{2}{L^2}\int_0^L \frac{L - u}{\sqrt{u^2 + a^2}}\,\mathrm du\), which is

\[ K_{ii} = \frac{2}{L}\Bigl[\operatorname{arsinh}\frac{L}{a} - \sqrt{1 + (a/L)^2} + \frac{a}{L}\Bigr], \]

the mean potential of the segment on its own surface per unit current; for \(L \gg a\) it tends to \(2[\ln(2L/a) - 1]/L\).

Near pairs — midpoint distance below six times the longer segment (NEAR_FACTOR) — are integrated exactly. Parallel pairs have a closed form (the integral of Neumann's mutual-inductance formula for parallel filaments); touching or crossing pairs use Gauss–Legendre points graded towards the point of closest approach with the exact inner line potential; separated skew pairs a plain eight-point rule.

Far pairs use the expansion of the segment average. Write a point of segment \(k\) as \(\mathbf P_k + s\,\mathbf t_k\) with \(-L_k/2 \le s \le L_k/2\) and expand \(1/\lvert\mathbf R + s\,\mathbf t\rvert\) to second order in \(s\), \(\mathbf R = \mathbf P_i - \mathbf P_j\), \(R = \lvert\mathbf R\rvert\). The linear term averages to zero and the mean of \(s^2\) is \(L_k^2/12\), which leaves

\[ \frac{1}{R} + \frac{L_i^2(3c_i^2 - 1) + L_j^2(3c_j^2 - 1) - 12a^2}{24R^3}, \qquad c_k = \frac{\mathbf R\cdot\mathbf t_k}{R}, \]

the point form \(1/R\), the quadrupole term of each segment's length (\(c_k\) is the cosine between the segment and the line joining the midpoints) and the radius term \(-a^2/(2R^3)\) of \(1/\sqrt{R^2 + a^2}\). The remainder is of order \((L/R)^4\).

The switch between exact and far form is a blend (user decision D2): pairs between six and 7.5 segment lengths (SWITCH_FACTOR) take \(w\,K_\text{exact} + (1 - w)\,K_\text{far}\), the weight \(w\) falling from 1 to 0 with zero slope at both ends (smoothstep in \(R^2\)). The result is continuous in the geometry: it spreads by at most 1e-13 over local offsets of 0.1 m … 8.8 km, and the solve at UTM coordinates lies as close to the local one as with the point kernel (3e-11 in \(Z\)).

Images. The air image is a mirrored segment and is treated like a source segment. The Tagg / Sunde images of a two-layer soil lie at least \(2(h_1 - z)\) away (\(h_1\) the thickness of the top layer); they get the treatment of direct pairs — exact near, blended, far form with the quadrupole term — with two differences:

  • Transverse distance. An image line that passes the wire at a transverse distance \(\rho_\perp\) acts with its potential averaged over the wire's circumference. By the two-dimensional mean-value property — the average of \(\ln\lvert x - y\rvert\) over a circle of radius \(a\) around \(x\) is \(\ln\max(\rho, a)\), \(\rho = \lvert x - y\rvert\) — that average is its value on the axis for \(\rho_\perp \ge a\). The exact integral of an image pair therefore uses \(\max(\rho_\perp, a)\) in place of \(\sqrt{\rho_\perp^2 + a^2}\), which keeps the reduced kernel for a collinear image (\(\rho_\perp = 0\), a rod against its own image), and the far form of images has no radius term. A ring 1 cm above a 1000 / 30 Ω·m interface then lies within −0.004 % of its exact thin ring.
  • Reach of the quadrupole term. The quadrupole term of an image is tapered off between 60 and 120 segment lengths of vertical distance between observer and image (IMAGE_QUADRUPOLE_REACH). At 60 segment lengths it is at most \(1/(6\cdot 60^2)\) of the image's point value (\(1/(12\cdot 60^2)\) for horizontal wires), of the order of the far form's remainder at the switch: the image series of a high contrast has hundreds of images, of which few are close. An image is evaluated only on the pairs whose longer segment reaches it, and in the reaction matrix, which is symmetric, on its upper half.

Engine.image_far_field = "point" keeps far images as point sources (see Cost). On the cross-layer path of image_2layer the layered correction is the exact image expansion of the two-layer Green's function (Sunde) in every layer combination, and its images get the same treatment on top of the spectral point values; pairs in different layers carry the transmitted resistivity \(2\rho_1\rho_2/(\rho_1+\rho_2)\), which keeps the matrix reciprocal.

Measurements and audit trail
  • Radius term of the far form. Up to wave 3 of the 2026.11 work the far form had no radius term: it was \(a^2/(2R^2)\) — 1.4e-6 at six segment lengths of 0.5 m — away from the exact pairs it joins.
  • One-step switch. Before user decision D2 the form switched at six segment lengths in one step — where the pairs six segments apart on a straight wire sit exactly. Round-off of the coordinates decided their form, and the same world at different positions spread by up to 4.4e-7 in the impedance (a 12 m strip) and, in two-layer soil with an image distance of six segment lengths, by 1e-5 … 2.6e-5 (audit W2B-01/-02).
  • Far Tagg / Sunde images. Up to wave 3 of the 2026.11 work they were point sources beyond six segment lengths, which left a straight strip in two-layer soil up to 5e-4 off and the potential above it up to 1 % off.
  • Transverse distance (audit W3A-02). The reduced kernel on images left out \(a^2/(2d^2)\) of an image \(d\) away, so a ring 1 cm above a 1000 / 30 Ω·m interface read +1.60 % against its exact thin ring.
  • Reach of the far-image work (audit W3A-01). Before, a few long pieces among short segments extended the reach of every pair.
  • Bound of the tapered term. Earlier texts gave \(1/(8\cdot 60^2)\) of the image's point value at the start of the taper, which holds for horizontal wires; the largest size, reached for a vertical wire and its collinear image, is \(1/(6\cdot 60^2)\) (the bound \(\lvert w\rvert(L^2 + 3a^2)/(6\,\mathrm dz^2)\) that the code uses to skip images, IMAGE_QUADRUPOLE_TOL).

docs.title: Accuracy of the line kernel
docs.text:
For a straight wire the line kernel is exact at any segment length, in homogeneous and in two-layer soil, up to the \((L/R)^4\) remainder of the far form and the reduced kernel that the soil-surface image keeps: a 10 m strip in 1000 / 50 Ω·m with \(h_1\) = 1 m is within 3.6e-6 of its closed-form uniform-current resistance (images axis to axis) for segment lengths of 0.125 … 2 m, not monotonically (the same strip in homogeneous soil: within 2.1e-6), and a rod through the layer interface is within 1.4e-6 of its exact two-owner value at every segment length. A ring converges like the square of the segment length, because its chords approximate the circle.

What remains against the true thin-wire solution is the uniform-current ansatz itself: for the 3 m rod of benchmark B2 the line kernel sits about +0.9 % above the thin-wire value at every segment length (generated numbers on the validation page). The point kernel's −1 … −2 % kernel error partly cancels that ansatz error on impedances, which is why the old numbers looked closer to some references than they were.

Measurements and audit trail

The strip and rod numbers are those of audit W3A (4 soils, 3 rods).

docs.title: Field points
docs.text:
After the solve, FieldResult.potential evaluates the field with the kernel of the solve. With the line kernel that is the exact line potential near a segment and the point form plus the quadrupole term \(L_j^2(3c_j^2 - 1)/(24R^3)\) farther away, blended like the reaction matrix and for the Tagg/Sunde images as well (sources in the lower layer of a two-layer soil are evaluated in point form by the spectral kernel). Every PointSource of a line-kernel result carries its unit tangent (direction), so a stored result is re-evaluated with line sources; results written by 0.15.0 have no direction and are evaluated with the point kernel.

Near a wire the difference is large: on the surface of a rod discretised at 0.5 m the point form spikes at every segment midpoint (16 … 177 V around an electrode potential of 32 V), while the line form is smooth and its surface average equals the electrode potential (tests/test_line_kernel.py::test_line_potential_is_equipotential_on_the_wire_surface). Surface potentials next to a wire — touch and step voltages — therefore need the line kernel.

Measurements and audit trail

The spikes of the point form on the wire surface are finding 10.33 of review pass 10.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
The exact near pairs and the quadrupole far field over all \(N^2\) pairs make the line kernel more expensive than the point kernel. A solve of 16 house grids (\(N\) = 1920 segments) takes 3.8 times as long as with the point kernel in homogeneous soil and 1.6 times in two-layer soil (\(h_1\) = 5 m) with numba installed (it is used automatically, extra fast), 5.8 and 1.4 times without; the extra time grows with \(N^2\). The blended switch adds the integrals of the pairs between six and 7.5 segment lengths, and in two-layer soil every image within reach carries the far-field term, evaluated only on the pairs whose longer segment reaches it and, in the reaction matrix, on its upper half, with one division per evaluation. A 40-house network in 1000 / 30 Ω·m with \(h_1\) = 1.5 m (82 images within reach) takes 1.8 times the solve before wave 3 of the 2026.11 work with numba and 3.6 times without.

Engine.image_far_field = "point" keeps far images as point sources and leaves out their far-field term; the near image pairs stay Galerkin integrals. It takes 1.1 … 1.3 times the solve before wave 3 on house grids within the upper layer. The 40-house network solves on the cross-layer path (its transformer rods reach below \(h_1\)): 0.91 times the solve before wave 3 and 0.49 times the default with numba. Below thin top layers the near image pairs remain, 1.5 … 2.4 times the solve before wave 3 (0.51 … 0.74 times the default). The performance page has the table. kernel="point" remains available and reproduces the numbers of 0.15.0.

Measurements and audit trail

Audit W3A-01 measured the far-image work before its restriction to the pairs that reach an image: a few long pieces among short segments multiplied the work by 5.6, and the 40-house network in 1000 / 30 Ω·m took 4.2 times the solve before wave 3 with numba and 9.7 times without. The near image pairs of "point" are those of audit W3R2A-01.

docs.text:

docs.text:

  • Wilton, D. R., Rao, S. M., Glisson, A. W., Schaubert, D. H., Al-Bundak, O. M., & Butler, C. M. (1984). Potential integrals for uniform and linear source distributions on polygonal and polyhedral domains. IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation AP-32(3), 276–281 (closed-form potentials of uniform sources).
  • Grover, F. W. (1946). Inductance Calculations: Working Formulas and Tables. Van Nostrand; Dover reprint (the double integrals of \(1/r\) over parallel and inclined filaments).

Architecture decision: ADR-0015. Implementation: groundfield.solver._line_kernel (private) behind Engine.kernel.

docs.title: Performance and scaling
docs.text:
This page tells you what a groundfield solve costs in time and memory, which part of the computation the cost comes from, and which settings to change first. Read it before a large study — a whole TN network, a sweep of hundreds of cells, a three-dimensional fem solve — or when a solve is slower than expected. Recipes for running large studies (parallel sweeps, Monte Carlo, speeding up large networks) are in the how-to guides.

At a glance: measured costs

Task Size Time, memory galvanic TN network, 30 houses, homogeneous, point kernel \(N\) = 3687 0.26 s, 115 MiB the same, 80 houses \(N\) = 9712 1.98 s, 773 MiB the line kernel (default) on such networks 1.1 … 1.9 times the point kernel 30 houses, two-layer soil, 11 frequencies, point kernel \(N \approx\) 3 700 2.6 … 9.8 s inductive TN network, 30 houses, Sommerfeld earth return, 4 frequencies 338 inductive branches 12.2 s fem, axisymmetric model (ring, rod, ring with rod) 7 341 … 223 112 nodes 0.20 … 2.0 s fem, 3-D model (AP1 station) 1.2 … 1.4 million nodes 75 … 140 s, 4.3 GB

Measured as described below; the fem numbers are those of the fem page.

docs.title: Where the cost is
docs.text:
A solve of the image family has three parts:

  1. Reaction matrix. For \(N\) segments the kernel is evaluated for every pair: \(O(N^2)\) time and, if the matrix is kept, \(8N^2\) bytes. In two-layer soil every pair carries the Tagg / Sunde series, so the cost grows with the number of image terms, which depends only on the contrast \(\lvert K\rvert\) (20 terms at \(\lvert K\rvert = 0.5\), 277 at \(\lvert K\rvert = 0.94\) for the default tolerance; table on the image_2layer page). An electrode through the layer interface switches every pair to the spectral kernel of ADR-0007, which is slower and needs more memory per depth group.
  2. Network solve. The unknowns are one current per owner (each straight wire, and its part in each soil layer for a wire through the interface), one potential per node and one current per finite branch — a small dense system. A purely galvanic world is solved once and reused for every frequency; with inductive conductors one complex solve per frequency follows, which is cheap against the assembly.
  3. Earth-return assembly of inductive conductors: one integral per pair of conductor sub-segments, the dominant cost of inductive worlds with the default sommerfeld model.

The mom family solves for one current per segment: its dense LU is \(O(N^3)\) and dominates for large \(N\). mom_sommerfeld adds one quadrature per distinct pair argument.

fem meshes the soil instead. Its cost is set by the node count of the finer of its two mesh levels, not by \(N\): about 4 GB per million nodes for the axisymmetric model and 2.9 GB per million nodes for the 3-D model, whose conjugate gradients run once per port and level. Both refuse a mesh above FemOptions.max_nodes / max_nodes_3d (2 million nodes) before it is built (ResourceLimitError); the fem page has the measurements.

docs.title: Memory model
docs.text:
The kernels never build (N, N, 3) difference tensors. The reaction matrix is materialised once per solve while it fits a budget of 1 GiB — \(8N^2\) bytes, i.e. up to \(N\) = 11 585 segments in homogeneous soil, \(16N^2\) and \(N\) = 8 192 for the two-layer series — and applied with the same BLAS calls as before, which keeps results bit-identical. Beyond the budget the kernels work in row blocks of 4 MiB with \(O(N\cdot\text{block})\) memory; results then differ at round-off (about \(10^{-15}\)). Field evaluation (FieldResult.potential) runs in pieces of at most 16 MiB, so a 200 × 200 grid of field points costs memory proportional to the grid, not to grid times sources.

The resource limit of the engine, Engine.max_segments (default diagnostics.HARD_LIMIT, 20 000 segments or nodal unknowns), stops a world before anything of size \(N\) is allocated (ResourceLimitError); raise it per engine to solve a larger world on purpose. SOFT_LIMIT (5 000) marks the size where solves take minutes rather than seconds on a typical laptop; every Engine.solve at or above it emits a UserWarning that says so (solve_mutual_matrix and solve_mutual_field check the limit but emit no notice; fem emits it from the count of its display segments, which is not its problem size — that is its mesh). The size of that notice belongs to the engine as well, Engine.warn_segments (default SOFT_LIMIT, read at solve time), so a workstation can move it up together with max_segments.

Measurements and audit trail

Up to 0.15.0 the difference tensors needed 96 bytes per segment pair, 1.25 GB for a 30-house network and a MemoryError at 80 houses (finding 10.56). The resource limit is finding 10.06, the notice's entry points are audit D2A-09, and Engine.warn_segments is user decision Q31.

docs.title: What to change first
docs.text:
In order of effect on a typical study:

  1. Earth-return model of inductive conductors. The Sommerfeld assembly dominates inductive studies; keep the default Engine.sommerfeld_assembly="tabulated", the faster and, by the measurements below, more accurate choice ("exact" integrates every segment pair and costs 17–25 times as much on the TN networks below). Leave conductors without an inductance_model where their inductance is not the question — then no assembly runs at all.
  2. Segment length. Cost and memory grow with \(N^2\). With the line kernel straight wires are exact at any segment length, so ds only needs to resolve the geometry (corners, rings, the distance between neighbouring wires and to a layer interface); a convergence study (convergence_study) shows when it does.
  3. Parallel cells of a sweep or Monte Carlo study (sweep(n_jobs=...)).
  4. numba (extra fast) for the line kernel's far field and the two-layer series; for catalogue sweeps in high-contrast two-layer soil Engine.image_far_field = "point" (point-form far images, 3e-6 … 4.3e-4 on networks).
  5. Contrast and electrodes through the interface set the cost of two-layer worlds; the series length follows from \(\lvert K\rvert\) alone.
  6. fem only where it is needed as a reference: the axisymmetric model takes seconds, the 3-D model minutes and gigabytes per solve.

docs.title: Measured in this release
docs.text: How the numbers were measured: synthetic AP1-like networks of the review's performance study (R8 workloads) — a substation with a 4 × 4 m ring and three rods, 10 to 80 houses with their foundations on both sides of four streets, PEN cables with service drops, 100 Ω·m or 500/100 Ω·m with \(h_1\) = 5 m, ds = 0.5 m — built with the layout builder. The release work-streams ran v0.15.0 and the release candidate back to back in separate processes, one BLAS thread, on a shared machine with two cores; times are wall-clock (best of two for the short ones), memory is the tracemalloc peak, which is deterministic. Wall-clock ratios vary with the machine load; memory ratios do not. The scripts belong to the release evidence; the memory gates are part of the test suite (tests/test_kernel_performance.py), the timing gates run with --run-benchmark.

docs.title: Galvanic solves (point kernel, bit-identical to v0.15.0)
docs.text:
Workload \(N\) v0.15.0 time / memory 2026.11 time / memory W1: 30 houses, homogeneous, 50 Hz 3687 2.7 s / 1247.6 MiB 0.26 s / 115.0 MiB W1-80: 80 houses, homogeneous 9712 MemoryError (8.4 GiB of tensors) 1.98 s / 773.2 MiB W2a: 30 houses, two-layer, rods inside layer 1, 11 frequencies 3669 94.8 s / 1235.5 MiB 9.8 s / 218.7 MiB W2: 30 houses, two-layer, rods through \(h_1\), 11 frequencies 3690 4.2 s / 1249.7 MiB 2.6 s / 510.2 MiB W4: potential of W1 on a 50 × 50 grid 3687 0.81 s / 844.1 MiB 0.16 s / 15.5 MiB W4-200: potential of W1 on a 200 × 200 grid 3687 — 1.6 s / 17.0 MiB \(Z_G\) (solve_mutual_matrix), 20 houses, two-layer 2466 82.7 s / 604.1 MiB 2.65 s / 146.0 MiB Measurements and audit trail

The gains come from component-wise row-block kernels instead of tensors, one reaction-matrix assembly per solve instead of two, the two-layer series summed into one matrix before the product (optionally compiled with numba, bit-identical) and the direct assembly of \(Z_G\) instead of applying the kernel to an identity matrix (\(O(N^3)\) per image term; findings 10.56–10.59, 10.62). The W2 peak was the grouped spectral correction of the cross-layer path; since wave 3 of the 2026.11 work a large depth group is planned once from the range of its distances and evaluated in row chunks (bit-identical), and beyond the budget the path works in row blocks like the series path (see Electrodes through the layer interface below).

docs.title: The default line kernel
docs.text:
The exact line kernel (kernels, ADR-0015) adds the exact near-pair integrals and the quadrupole far field over all pairs. Its cost relative to the point kernel, measured on the release state:

Workload \(N\) point: time / memory line: time / memory ratio (time) \(Z_\text{in}\), line vs point 16 house grids, homogeneous 1920 0.043 s / 38.8 MiB 0.165 s / 47.7 MiB 3.8 (5.8 without numba) — 16 house grids, 500 / 100 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m 1920 0.332 s / 64.4 MiB 0.519 s / 69.7 MiB 1.6 (1.4 without numba) — W1: 30 houses, homogeneous 3668 0.83 s / 113.4 MiB 1.55 s / 155.7 MiB 1.9 +0.35 % W1-80: 80 houses, homogeneous 9668 6.19 s / 758.3 MiB 6.94 s / 856.2 MiB 1.1 +0.27 %

Install the extra fast (numba) for the compiled far field; kernel="point" reproduces the old numbers and cost.

Measurements and audit trail

The 16-house rows are the release state (best of three rounds of fresh processes, interleaved, with other agents on the machine, load 6 … 13); the homogeneous one is the case documented with Engine.kernel. The W1 rows were measured under a machine load of about 5.6 on two cores (numba installed), so their absolute times are about three times those of the galvanic table above; the ratio and the memory are the meaningful columns. The networks differ slightly from the v0.15.0 table (\(N\) = 3668 instead of 3687) because the layout builder now joins PEN cables at junction nodes instead of 5 cm rods.

docs.title: Far images in two-layer soil
docs.text:
In two-layer soil every Tagg/Sunde image within reach carries the far-field term of the line kernel. Its cost follows the image density: high contrasts and thin top layers put hundreds of images within reach, and with long pieces below a thin top layer the Galerkin integrals of their near image pairs add to it (each long piece is within 7.5 segment lengths of every short segment's image; the near-pair criterion of the kernel). Engine.image_far_field = "point" keeps far images as point sources and leaves out their far-field term; the near image pairs stay Galerkin integrals on both paths, so on the cross-layer path it takes 0.49 … 0.94 of the default's time. Headline numbers (line kernel, ds = 0.5 m, 50 Hz, numba installed; † the cross-layer path):

world \(N\) default "point" 16 house grids, 500 / 100 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 5 m 1920 0.54 s 0.48 s AP1 station, 40 % penetration † 2711 1.35 s 0.96 s TN network, 40 houses, 1000 / 30 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 1.5 m † 4877 4.03 s 1.99 s the same without numba † 4877 9.46 s 2.33 s

"point" moves networks by 3e-6 … 4.3e-4 against the default: a choice for catalogue sweeps, not for fields near the interface.

Measurements and audit trail

Audit W3A measured that the cost of the far-image term followed the longest segment of the world and the image density; since then an image is evaluated on the pairs whose longer segment reaches it, the reaction matrix's part on its upper half, with one division per evaluation. Engine.image_far_field = "point" is the author's decision of 2026-11-15; its near image pairs on both paths are audit W3R2A-01.

Line kernel, ds = 0.5 m, 50 Hz, best of three solves, one fresh process per row, the four trees of a row run one after the other (other agents on the machine, load 10 … 18; the times of stream fw3xl measured before its last commit, which changed the summation of the sparse image corrections and nothing else; peaks of the final code). The rows marked † solve on the cross-layer path (wires at or below \(h_1\); the TN network in 1000 / 30 Ω·m through its transformer rods); their "before wave 3", "now" and "point" columns were measured again after audit W3R2A-01 (stream fw3r2a, load 4 … 9), the "wave 3" column is that of stream fw3xl:

docs.title: Electrodes through the layer interface
docs.text:
The ADR-0007 path of image_2layer (wires at or below \(h_1\)) costs one spectral evaluation per pair of segment depths; large depth groups are planned once and evaluated in row chunks. Its peak memory is that of the series path: 16 house grids entirely below \(h_1\) = 0.5 m need 21.9 bytes per segment pair (the series path 18.3), and beyond the matrix budget the path works in row blocks with memory linear in \(N\) (36 house grids, \(N\) = 4320: 34.8 MiB in block mode). On the AP1 station of the roadmap with 40 % penetration (\(N\) = 2711) it takes 1.35 s with the line kernel (2.17 s without numba) and 0.96 s with image_far_field="point"; the same world with 4 m rods that stay in the top layer solves on the series path in 1.27 s.

Measurements and audit trail

The AP1 station of the roadmap — a 4 × 4 m ring at 0.6 m and three 6 m rods from 0.6 m through \(h_1\) = 5 m (500 / 100 Ω·m), 60 houses with foundations (10 × 10 m, 2 × 2 meshes at 0.8 m) at 5 … 40 % penetration, PEN cables, ds = 0.5 m, 50 Hz — before and after wave 3 of the 2026.11 work (best of three, numba installed, a shared machine; memory: tracemalloc peak):

penetration \(N\) line kernel before → after point kernel before → after peak before → after the same world with 4 m rods (series path) 5 % 311 0.82 → 0.43 s — 19.4 → 20.8 MiB 0.06 s, 8.5 MiB 10 % 671 0.84 → 0.50 s 0.85 → 0.42 s 27.8 → 28.5 MiB 0.11 s, 18.7 MiB 20 % 1031 0.89 → 0.62 s — 42.5 → 39.6 MiB 0.22 s, 25.0 MiB 40 % 2711 1.28 → 1.65 s 1.14 → 0.70 s 278.3 → 136.6 MiB 1.27 s, 127.1 MiB

The spectral amplitudes are eliminated in closed form (one LAPACK solve per quadrature node before, half the time of the path): the point kernel, which sees only that change, is 1.6 … 2.0 times faster. The line kernel carries the layered correction in line form now (a rod through the interface no longer depends on the segment length); since audit W3A its far-field terms cost about what the closed-form amplitudes saved (1.35 s at 40 % penetration, 1.29 s before wave 3; 2.17 s without numba). Before wave 3, 16 house grids entirely below \(h_1\) = 0.5 m needed 41.2 bytes per segment pair, and the 36 house grids 1008 MiB without row blocks (finding 10.56).

docs.text:
Workload v0.15.0 2026.11, sommerfeld_assembly="exact" 2026.11, "tabulated" (default) W3: 2 houses, Neumann PEN, Sommerfeld earth return, 11 f 35.3 s 1.9–2.1 s 1.2–1.5 s W3: 30 houses, same ≈ 3600 s (estimate) 242 s 7.8–9.1 s W3c: 30 houses, carson_series 16.4 s 3.3 s — TN generator, 8 houses, Neumann PEN (78 inductive branches), 4 f — 16.6 s 1.0 s TN generator, 30 houses, same (338 inductive branches) — 306 s 12.2 s

The tabulated assembly shares one table of the spectral integral per pair of depth groups and frequency, and agrees with a converged reference better than the per-pair rule (substation impedance \(5\cdot 10^{-10}\) against \(1.1\cdot 10^{-8}\) on W3; input impedance of the 8-house TN network \(2\cdot 10^{-10}\) against \(1.2\cdot 10^{-8}\)). carson_series is an approximation for long parallel lines, not a replacement of sommerfeld (earth return), and no faster than necessary to be a check.

Measurements and audit trail

CPU times of the W3 rows measured by the coupling work-stream, of the TN rows by the stream that made the tabulated assembly the default (user decision Q16; TnNetworkGenerator, homogeneous 100 Ω·m, ds = 1 m, 50/250/550/1000 Hz). The per-pair path gains from one multi-frequency assembly per solve (geometry, λ grid and Bessel tables once per pair; bit-identical) and the resolved λ grid (finding 10.60). carson_series moved by its own fix (F32).

docs.text:
• mom_sommerfeld, three layers. The depth-group tabulation of the reflected kernel (default) took a 40 m grid in 1000/30/200 Ω·m soil at ds = 1.25 m from 66.6 s to 0.30 s and a village of eleven rings (\(N\) = 273) from 34.1 s to 1.25 s, within \(10^{-6}\) of the quadrature (benchmark B12).
  • sweep(n_jobs=...). Parameter cells run in a process pool with one BLAS thread per worker; the result is bit-identical to n_jobs=1 when the parent also runs a single BLAS thread. The review measured 1.98 times the throughput on two workers. The LU factorisation is 0.2–1.5 % of a solve, so BLAS threads are not the lever; parallel cells are.
  • Import. import groundfield loads its heavy dependencies lazily: 223 ms instead of 798 ms, 346 instead of 1169 modules.
  • fem. The axisymmetric model takes 0.20 s, 0.58 s and 2.0 s for a ring, a 3 m rod and a ring with a central rod in two layers (7 341 / 28 934, 18 868 / 74 871 and 56 079 / 223 112 nodes at levels 0 / 1). The 3-D model takes 26 s and 1.8 GB for a ring of 12.6 m (600 000 nodes at the finer level) and 75 … 140 s and 4.3 GB for the AP1 station (28 m of wire, 1.2 … 1.4 million nodes); FemOptions.max_nodes_3d (2 million nodes) refuses meshes of more than about 6 GB before they are built. Details and conditions on the fem page.

The tabulation of mom_sommerfeld is finding 10.61, the parallel sweep finding 10.64, the lazy import finding 10.72.

docs.title: Sources, junctions and the measurement loop
docs.text:
This page explains how groundfield feeds a grounding system — current and voltage sources with two terminals, nodes without soil contact (junctions) — which of the three impedances of a result to read, and how the fall-of-potential measurement is wired. Read it before you set up a fault or a measurement study, or when two impedances of one result disagree.

A grounding system is never fed in isolation. A fault current enters at one point and returns through a remote source; a measurement instrument injects between the earth electrode and an auxiliary electrode and reads the voltage against a probe; cable joints and instrument terminals are nodes without soil contact.

docs.title: Mathematical and physical context
docs.text:
The engines solve a linear network: the soil multiport of the electrodes, the branches of the conductors and the nodes that connect them (see the engine family). Current sources enter as impressed node currents. Voltage sources enter as a fixed potential difference between their terminals whose current is an additional unknown (modified nodal analysis). Every quantity is therefore linear in the source values, and results of several sources superpose.

The potential reference is remote earth: \(\varphi \to 0\) far away from all electrodes. The potential of an electrode is therefore its earth potential rise (EPR) against remote earth, and a voltage between two points — a touch voltage, a measured reading — is a difference of such potentials.

docs.title: Two-terminal sources
docs.text:
A current source has two terminals:

  • attached_to — the node where the current \(I\) enters (an electrode, a junction or, through its cluster, a bonded group);
  • return_to — the node where it leaves again; None means the return through remote earth.

The solver injects \(+I\) at attached_to and \(-I\) at return_to (groundfield.solver._pipeline.inject, shared by every backend). The current balance holds to round-off, and a two-terminal source equals the superposition of two one-terminal injections (tests/test_two_terminal_sources.py). A manual counter-source at the return electrode, as generators used before, now warns as a double count.

Sources are validated before any work is done (World.check, called by every solve): unknown node names raise with a did-you-mean suggestion, magnitudes must be finite, a current source must not be 0 A, a source whose two terminals end in one cluster (a short circuit) raises, and so do voltage sources without internal resistance that form a loop (the message names the sources of the loop).

Measurements and audit trail

Up to 0.15.0 return_to was stored but ignored, so an auxiliary electrode carried no current and the station potential did not depend on its distance (finding 10.16, F01). The validation of voltage-source loops is finding 10.66.

docs.title: Voltage sources
docs.text:
A VoltageSource drives attached_to against return_to (or against remote earth) with the voltage \(U\) behind an internal impedance \(Z_q = R + j\omega L\) (internal_resistance_ohm, internal_inductance_h; 0 by default, the ideal source) — an instrument that drives a test voltage, or the source voltage of a fault loop behind the impedance of the feeding transformer and line. With the potentials \(\varphi_a\) and \(\varphi_r\) of its two terminals and its current \(I\) the source imposes

\[ \varphi_a - \varphi_r = U - Z_q I , \]

the terminal voltage is the source voltage less the drop across the internal impedance. The current is solved for and reported like the impressed current of a current source (result.sources[k].current); input_impedance() \(= U/I - Z_q\) is the impedance the source sees, without its own \(Z_q\).

For one source the answer is the 1 A current-source solve scaled by

\[ I = \frac{U}{Z_q + Z_\text{in}} , \]

\(Z_\text{in}\) the input impedance of the network at the source's terminals. This is the fault current \(I_F = U_q/(Z_q + R_F + T)\) of a fault study, with \(U_q\) the source voltage, \(R_F\) a fault resistance and \(T\) the input impedance of the network, and a voltage source saves that step. With several voltage-driven terminals in one solve the scaling would need the transfer matrix of all of them; the result is their superposition, and the input impedance of each is then an apparent one. A series resistance written as a junction at the terminal, a lumped conductor to the electrode and the ideal source at the junction gives the same solution as internal_resistance_ohm to round-off (sources).

Measurements and audit trail

Up to 0.15.0 voltage sources were dropped with a warning (finding 10.51); they are solved since 2026.11. Before 2026.11 the junction pattern above was the only way to give a source a series resistance.

docs.title: Junctions
docs.text:
A junction (create_junction(world, position=...)) is a network node without soil contact: conductors may start and end at it and sources may attach to it, but it leaks no current. Junctions model cable joints of a PEN conductor and the terminals of a measurement instrument. A junction must reach the soil through its conductors; a dangling junction raises. The solve reports its potential in result.metadata["junction_potentials"].

Measurements and audit trail

Junctions replace the 5 cm pseudo-rods that the layout builder used for PEN joints up to 0.15.0: those were small electrodes, and depending on the penetration they leaked several per cent of the test current (finding 10.38).

docs.title: Three impedances
docs.text:
A result offers three impedances. They coincide for a single electrode fed against remote earth and differ as soon as conductors connect the fed cluster to other electrodes:

Impedance Definition Accessor What it is input \(Z_\text{in} = (\varphi_a - \varphi_r)/I_s\) result.input_impedance(source) the driving-point impedance of the whole connected system cluster \(Z_c = \varphi_c / I_{c,\text{leak}}\) result.cluster_impedance(name) the local spreading impedance of the fed cluster electrode \(Z_e = \varphi_e / I_{e,\text{leak}}\) result.grounding_impedance(name) one electrode of a cluster over its own leakage

Here \(I_s\) is the source current, \(\varphi_a\) and \(\varphi_r\) are the potentials of the clusters the source attaches to and returns at, \(\varphi_c\) is the length-weighted cluster potential and \(I_{c,\text{leak}}\) the sum of the leakage currents of the cluster's electrodes; \(\varphi_e\) and \(I_{e,\text{leak}}\) are the potential and the leakage of one electrode. For a return through remote earth the input impedance is the EPR per injected ampere.

The split factor \(s = I_{c,\text{leak}}/I_s\) is the share of the injected current that leaks through the fed cluster itself. For a one-terminal source \(\varphi_a = \varphi_c\) and \(\varphi_r = 0\), so

\[ Z_\text{in} = \frac{\varphi_c}{I_s} = \frac{I_{c,\text{leak}}}{I_s}\, \frac{\varphi_c}{I_{c,\text{leak}}} = s\,Z_c \]

(tests/test_impedance_quantity.py::test_split_factor_links_input_and_cluster_impedance).

In a TN network the station's cluster leaks only a part of the current — the rest flows through the PEN conductors into the house foundations — so \(s < 1\) and the cluster impedance can exceed the input impedance by a large factor. For an engineer the input impedance is the quantity of interest: it is what a fall-of-potential measurement approaches and what a fault sees. It is the default (quantity="input") of sweep, convergence_study and the rho-f exporters (rho_f_from_field_result, rho_f_standard_from_results); quantity="cluster" and quantity="electrode" give the other two. Every fit records the quantity it represents.

Measurements and audit trail

The input impedance is the default since 2026.11 (findings 10.18, 10.19). Before, sweep reported the cluster impedance and the exporters the electrode impedance; quantity="cluster" and quantity="electrode" reproduce those semantics.

docs.title: The fall-of-potential measurement
docs.text:
The classical measurement of a grounding impedance injects a current \(I\) between the earth electrode E and an auxiliary electrode H at the distance \(D\), and reads the voltage between E and a probe S placed between them at the distance \(x\) from E. For a hemispherical electrode E of radius \(r_E\) in homogeneous soil, with H far enough away to act as a point source, the reading is

\[ \frac{\varphi_E - \varphi_S}{I} = \frac{\rho}{2\pi}\Bigl[\frac{1}{r_E} - \frac{1}{D} - \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{D - x}\Bigr] , \]

the true resistance \(\rho/(2\pi r_E)\) plus the potential that the return current at H and the injected current at E impose on the probe. The correction vanishes when \(1/(D - x) = 1/x + 1/D\), that is for \((x/D)^2 + x/D - 1 = 0\) or \(x/D = (\sqrt5 - 1)/2\): the reading equals the remote impedance when the probe sits at 61.8 % of the distance to H (Tagg 1964). tests/test_two_terminal_sources.py::test_fall_of_potential_follows_the_61_8_percent_rule checks that groundfield reproduces this rule. The finite size of a real earthing system leaves a residual error at 61.8 %, and for an extended system such as a whole LV network the electrical centre is not known; the fall-of-potential tutorial shows how far the auxiliary electrode must be.

The TN network generator builds the measurement as it is wired in the field:

  • two junctions at the instrument, meas_H and meas_S, at the position of the substation and the height of the leads;
  • the feed lead from meas_H to the auxiliary electrode, the probe lead from the probe electrode to meas_S;
  • one two-terminal source attached_to=<station>, return_to="meas_H";
  • the reading generators.measured_impedance(result) \(= (\varphi_E - \varphi_S)/I\).

With junctions, resistive leads do not change the reading (tests/test_measurement_loop.py::test_resistive_leads_do_not_change_the_reading) and inductive leads shift it by their coupling without shorting it. Leads that run towards the same side are laid side by side (touching), because two coincident conductors have no finite mutual inductance. The leads run horizontally at MeasurementLeadConfig.depth_m below the surface; a depth of 0 places them 0.1 m above ground.

input_impedance of the measurement source is the two-pole impedance between E and H — the loop impedance including the auxiliary electrode and the feed lead — not the reading; measured_impedance is the reading.

Measurements and audit trail

Up to 0.15.0 the leads were wired to the station itself: the probe lead short-circuited the instrument and the feed lead closed the loop through the metal (finding 10.17).

docs.title: Validity
docs.text:
• The source model is an impressed current (ideal) or an impressed voltage behind a lumped internal impedance \(R + j\omega L\) (no frequency dependence of \(R\) and \(L\) themselves; a source with a frequency-dependent impedance needs one solve per frequency with its values).
  • Two-terminal sources, junctions and voltage sources are supported by every backend — the image family, the mom family and fem (registry capabilities two_terminal_sources, junctions, voltage_sources).
  • Measured readings include the coupling of the leads only if the leads are modelled as inductive conductors (inductance_model="neumann").
Corrected statement

Earlier versions of this page said that fem ignores return_to and rejects junctions and voltage sources. That held for the equivalent-hemisphere fem before user decision Q37; the conforming fem runs the shared network pipeline and its registry entry declares all three capabilities.

docs.title: Validation and benchmarks
docs.text:
Generated page

Every number on this page comes from one run of the engine benchmark suite, measured on 2026-11-16 with groundfield 2026.11.0 (Python 3.12.16, NumPy 2.4.4, SciPy 1.17.1, numba installed: yes; Darwin arm64), and from the bounds in tests/benchmarks/tolerances.py. The page is written by python scripts/generate_validation_page.py; tests/test_validation_page.py checks that it matches the stored measurements and, with --run-benchmark, that a fresh run reproduces them.

Suite result of that run: 71 passed, 7 skipped (pytest tests/benchmarks --run-benchmark; the skipped tests are combinations a benchmark does not apply to).

docs.title: Kernel of the image family
docs.text:
The image family assumes a uniform current per unit length on each straight wire of an electrode (a wire line of a grid, an arm of a star, a straight run of a polyline; user decision Q30 of 2026.11). For that model the resistance of a straight wire and of a ring has a closed form, so the error of the kernel can be separated from the error of the ansatz. Signed deviation from the exact uniform-current resistance (kernel="line" is the default since 2026.11, kernel="point" reproduces 0.15.0):

Against the thin-wire solution of the same rod (33.1957 Ω, the B2 reference, which lets the current vary along the rod) the line kernel stays at +0.92 % for every segment length: that is the error of the uniform-current ansatz, not of the kernel. The point kernel lies at −0.79 % … −0.30 %, closer by accident — its kernel error has the opposite sign and partly cancels the ansatz error.

docs.text: mom on the same discretisation is the reference: mom_sommerfeld integrates the same layered Green's function numerically (a kernel check), image_2layer replaces the computed current distribution by a uniform one (an ansatz check), fem solves the electrodes as solid bodies in a volume mesh (an independent method; the difference is the deficit of the point kernel of mom).

docs.title: Field quantities near the electrode
docs.text:
