docs.title: Regenerating this page
docs.text:
python scripts/generate_validation_page.py --measure   # about 1–3 min
python -m pytest tests/test_validation_page.py         # page up to date

The benchmark tests themselves (pytest tests/benchmarks --run-benchmark) fail when a value leaves its bound; this page only reports them. A change of a bound or of a measured value therefore shows up here after --measure, and the test of the page fails until the page is regenerated.

docs.title: Engines
docs.text:
This page helps you choose the numerical engine (the backend) for a study and tells you where each engine must not be used. Start with the decision path; the tables below it give the accuracy and the cost behind each choice, cited from the validation page, the engine pages, the performance page and the known limitations. The second half of the page explains the physics the engines share and where they differ.

All engines solve one physical problem: the quasi-static current field of electrodes and conductors in horizontally layered soil, below 1 kHz. They share the data model (World), the solve pipeline and the network equations, so the same world can be solved by any of them and the results compared. They differ in the soils they accept, in how they represent the current on the wires, in accuracy and in cost.

docs.title: Decision path
docs.text:
How many distinct soil layers?
│
├── three or more ─────────────────────────────────────────▶ mom_sommerfeld
│                                                             (impedances only:
│                                                              no field quantities)
└── one or two
    │
    ├── touch, step or mesh voltages within about 5 m of a
    │   grid, a star, a strip end or a bonded group of
    │   electrodes; the current distribution along wires ─────▶ mom
    │
    └── everything else: impedances, networks, frequency
        sweeps, rho-f samples, potentials away from the wires ─▶ image (default;
                                                                 two layers run
                                                                 image_2layer)

Check a result once with a second method:
    image  next to  mom              same kernels, other current model
    mom    next to  mom_sommerfeld   same discretisation, other Green's function
    fem                              independent reference for one cluster

image is the right engine for most work: it is exact for its model, the cheapest for large networks, and its model error is about 1 % on impedances. That model, one uniform current per straight wire, misplaces the current along a wire, so surface potentials next to the ends and corners of extended electrodes need mom. Three or more layers need the numerical Green's function of mom_sommerfeld. fem shares nothing with the integral engines but the network solve; it is the independent check of a single earthing system, not a tool for networks.

Question Engine Why Impedance, potentials, rho-f samples in homogeneous or two-layer soil image (default; forwards to image_2layer) closed form, exact line kernel, cheapest for large networks Touch, step and mesh voltages near grids, stars, strip ends, bonded clusters mom one current per segment; the image family errs by up to tens of per cent there Three or more distinct layers mom_sommerfeld the only integral engine with that Green's function Is the uniform current ansatz good enough here? mom next to image same kernels, one current per segment Is the image series right for this soil? mom_sommerfeld next to mom same discretisation, independent kernel A reference that shares no kernel with the integral engines fem (experimental) volume PDE; about 1e-4 for coaxial rods and rings, about 2e-3 in 3-D

docs.title: Accuracy against references
docs.text:
Every engine is compared with references that do not use a groundfield solver (closed forms, an independent thin-wire solver, high-precision quadrature, the solid electrodes of fem) in the benchmark suite B1–B13 of the validation page. Typical deviations, signed where the sign is known:

Case and reference image, line kernel mom fem Rod 3 m, 100 Ω·m; thin-wire solution 33.1957 Ω (B2) +0.92 % −0.63 … −1.4 % (ds 0.5 … 0.125 m) 7.3e-5 (solid rod) Ring r = 2 m at 0.8 m; closed form 12.4816 Ω (B3) −0.24 % (ds 0.5 m), −1.5e-4 (ds 0.125 m) −1.2 % 5.7e-5 (solid torus) Ring with three bonded 4 m rods; 3-D fem (B10), homogeneous / two-layer +0.81 % / +1.97 % (point kernel) −0.6 % / −0.8 % reference (estimate 3.9e-3 / 4.3e-3) Rods and rings in the top layer of two-layer soil; mom (B6) within 0.37 % (point kernel) reference +0.57 … +1.3 % Grids 10 m 2 × 2 … 40 m 8 × 8; one current per segment +0.36 … +0.70 % — — Stars of 3 / 4 / 8 arms of 10 m; one current per segment +1.8 / +3.5 / +10.5 % — — Touch / step voltage at a grid corner, 20 m 4 × 4; mom +6.4 % / −11 % reference — Touch / step voltage at a star tip, 4 arms of 10 m; mom +10 % / −23 % reference —

How to read it:

  • image is exact for its own model. For a straight wire the line kernel reproduces the closed-form resistance of a uniform line current to about 1e-6 at any segment length; a ring converges with the square of the segment length (kernel of the image family). What remains is the error of the ansatz: about 1 % on impedances of rods, rings, grids and rectangles, more on stars, and up to tens of per cent on surface potentials next to grid corners and star tips — with the step voltage under-estimated, the non-conservative direction (field quantities).
  • mom resolves the current distribution but not the absolute value. Its point-source near field leaves impedances 0.6 … 1.9 % low and drifts as the segments get shorter. Its strength is the shape of the current and of the surface potential, which is why it is the reference for field quantities and for the current model of the image family.
  • mom_sommerfeld checks the kernel. It reproduces the Tagg/Sunde series of mom to 1.2e-8 on the two-layer worlds of B6 and the three-layer kernel to 2.3e-13 of a 30-digit quadrature (B5); its tables for three layers move a grid's impedance by 1.5e-10 (B12). Its discretisation error is that of mom.
  • fem is the independent reference. The axisymmetric model agrees with Weber's disc to 3.1e-4 and with the thin-wire rod and ring to better than 1e-4 (B1–B3); the 3-D model agrees with the axisymmetric one to about 2e-3 away from layer interfaces and other wires, and reports an error estimate of 3 … 5e-3.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Wall-clock time of one world.solve at 50 Hz with 0.5 m segments and the default options, after a warm-up solve; peak memory of the process where it matters. Measured for this page with the code of this release on a shared Apple-silicon machine (macOS arm64, numba installed, one BLAS thread, load 8 … 15); the times vary with the machine's load, the ratios between the engines less so. The networks are those of the how-to speed up large studies: a station ring and n houses with 10 m × 10 m mesh foundations on a PEN chain.

World Segments image mom mom_sommerfeld fem rod 3 m, 100 Ω·m 6 1 ms < 1 ms < 1 ms 0.64 s (axisymmetric) ring r = 2 m, 100 Ω·m 26 3 ms < 1 ms < 1 ms 0.23 s (axisymmetric) grid 20 m 4 × 4, 100 Ω·m 400 0.03 s 5 ms 4 ms — the same grid, 300 / 100 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 2 m 400 0.08 s 0.03 s 0.25 s — the same grid, 300 / 100 / 1000 Ω·m 400 — — 0.05 s — 30 houses, 100 Ω·m 2426 0.19 s 0.17 s — — 30 houses, 300 / 100 Ω·m, \(h_1\) = 2 m 2426 0.71 s 0.47 s — — 80 houses, 100 Ω·m 6426 1.5 s, 0.6 GiB 2.0 s, 1.7 GiB — — 120 houses, 100 Ω·m 9626 2.6 s, 1.0 GiB 5.8 s, 3.6 GiB — — 30 houses, inductive PEN, 11 frequencies 2426 4.9 s 9.5 s — —

What the table and the performance page show:

  • Up to a few thousand segments image and mom take a second or less. The line kernel of the image family integrates near pairs exactly, which costs about what the dense LU of mom costs.
  • mom grows faster. Its LU is \(O(N^3)\) and it holds more of the dense system in memory (3.6 GiB against 1.0 GiB at 9 626 segments); with inductive conductors it factorises once per frequency (twice the time of image for 11 frequencies above).
  • image_2layer pays for contrast and thin top layers. The image series needs 20 terms at \(\lvert K\rvert\) = 0.5 and 277 at 0.94; a 40-house network takes 3.2 s in 500 / 100 Ω·m with \(h_1\) = 5 m and 4.0 s in 1000 / 30 Ω·m with \(h_1\) = 1.5 m, where Engine.image_far_field = "point" brings it to 2.0 s for catalogue sweeps.
  • mom_sommerfeld integrates every distinct pair. In two-layer soil it costs several times mom (0.25 s against 0.03 s above); for three layers its depth-group tables make it fast (a 40 m grid at 1.25 m segments in 0.30 s instead of 66.6 s).
  • fem is a reference, not a production engine. The axisymmetric model takes a fraction of a second for a rod or a ring and about 17 s for eight rings with a central rod (a million nodes). The 3-D model takes 26 s and 1.8 GB for a ring of 12.6 m, 75 … 140 s and 4.3 GB for the AP1 station (28 m of wire), and 2 … 3.5 minutes and up to 3.8 GB for the ring with three rods of B10.
  • Inductive conductors add the earth-return assembly, the same for every engine and the dominant cost of inductive studies (12.2 s for a generated 30-house TN network with a Neumann PEN at four frequencies).

Every engine stops before allocating anything when a world has more than Engine.max_segments segments (default 20 000, ResourceLimitError) and notes from 5 000 segments on that the solve may take minutes.

docs.title: Where each engine must not be used
docs.text:
Each row names what goes wrong, how large the error is, what the code tells you and what to use instead. The entries of the known limitations give the measurements; warnings and errors describes every class. Three limits hold for every engine: the model is quasi-static and validated below 1 kHz, the soil is linear and horizontally layered, and potentials in the soil (touch and step voltages, plots, field exports) are available for one and two layers only (NotImplementedError for three or more).

image and image_2layer (current ansatz, soil layers):

Do not use it for Error Signal Instead touch, step and mesh voltages within 5 m of grids, stars, strip ends, open polylines, bonded clusters grid corner +6.4 % / −11 %, star tip +10 % / −23 % (touch / step) UniformCurrentFieldWarning mom impedances of stars with many arms +3.5 % (4 arms), +10.5 % (8 arms) none mom three or more distinct layers not supported BackendCapabilityError mom_sommerfeld a layer contrast with \(\lvert K\rvert\) > 0.94 (2000 / 30 Ω·m) series truncated at 300 terms SeriesTruncationWarning raise image_max_terms rod ends within one wire radius of a layer interface +22 % with the tip at the interface InterfaceContactWarning axisymmetric fem (solid rod) horizontal wires within a few wire radii of an interface +3.6 % at 2 radii over a layer 33 times more conductive InterfaceContactWarning axisymmetric fem for rings

docs.title: Check your choice
docs.text:
Before a long run, gf.diagnose(world, engine) collects the checks that need no solve: resolution, segment budget, thin wires, close and interpenetrating wires, rod ends and wires at a layer interface, mixed coordinates and overlapping cables (read and act on warnings). After it, gf.compare_engines runs the world through a second engine and gf.convergence_study refines the segment length:

import groundfield as gf

world = gf.create_world(soil=gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=100.0, rho_2=300.0, h_1=2.0))
gf.create_electrode(world, "grid_mesh", name="grid", corner=(-10.0, -10.0, 0.5), size=(20.0, 20.0), n_x=4, n_y=4)
gf.create_source(world, attached_to="grid", magnitude=1.0)

print(gf.diagnose(world, gf.create_engine()) or "no findings")
report = gf.compare_engines(world, engines={"image": gf.create_engine(), "mom": gf.create_engine(backend="mom")})
print(f"image against mom: {report.deviations['grid']:.2%}")   # 0.92%
study = gf.convergence_study(world, gf.create_engine(), segment_lengths=[1.0, 0.5, 0.25])
print(study[["segment_length_m", "abs_Z"]])                     # 4.8005 Ω at every length

The grid's wires are straight, so the line kernel of image gives the same impedance at every segment length; mom reads 0.9 % lower, the size of its point-kernel bias. Which pair checks what:

  • image against mom checks the current model (the same kernels).
  • mom against mom_sommerfeld checks the Green's function (the same discretisation).
  • Neither pair checks the discretisation itself; that is what the convergence study and the references of the benchmark suite do.
  • Two names that run the same computation (a deprecated alias and its target) are reported as such by compare_engines: their agreement is not evidence.

docs.title: Mathematical and physical context
docs.text:
Below 1 kHz the soil is a conductor whose displacement current is negligible (\(\omega\varepsilon\rho \ll 1\)) and whose skin depth \(\delta = \sqrt{2\rho/(\omega\mu_0)}\) — about 500 m for 100 Ω·m at 1 kHz, more at lower frequencies and higher resistivities — is large against the extent of the electrodes. The galvanic part of the problem is therefore stationary current flow at each frequency. With the conductivity \(\sigma = 1/\rho\) piecewise constant in depth and a current density \(q\) injected by the electrodes, the potential \(\varphi\) satisfies

\[ -\nabla\cdot\bigl(\sigma(z)\,\nabla\varphi\bigr) = q \quad\text{in the soil } (z > 0),\qquad \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial z}\Big|_{z=0} = 0,\qquad \varphi \to 0 \text{ for } |\mathbf r|\to\infty . \]

In words: current is conserved in the soil, no current crosses the soil surface into the air, and the potential vanishes at remote earth. \(\varphi\) and the normal current density \(\sigma\,\partial\varphi/\partial z\) are continuous at every layer interface (\(z\) points into the soil). Frequency enters through the conductors only: their longitudinal impedance (resistance, skin effect, partial inductances and the earth-return correction, see earth return) makes the network equations complex and frequency dependent, while the soil kernel stays real. A galvanic world is therefore solved once and reused for every frequency.

The Green's function of this problem is the potential of a unit point current at depth \(z_s\), observed at horizontal distance \(s\) and depth \(z\) in the top layer. It is the Sommerfeld integral

\[ G(s, z; z_s) = \frac{\rho_1}{4\pi}\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-\lambda|z-z_s|} + e^{-\lambda(z+z_s)} + \Gamma_1(\lambda)\bigl[e^{-\lambda(2h_1-|z-z_s|)} + e^{-\lambda(2h_1-z-z_s)}\bigr]} {1-\Gamma_1(\lambda)\,e^{-2\lambda h_1}}\;J_0(\lambda s)\,\mathrm d\lambda , \]

a superposition of cylindrical waves \(J_0(\lambda s)\) over the horizontal wavenumber \(\lambda\). Here \(\rho_1\) and \(h_1\) are the resistivity and the thickness of the top layer, and \(\Gamma_1(\lambda)\) is the reflection coefficient of the stack below the first interface, built bottom-up from the interface coefficients \(K_i = (\rho_{i+1}-\rho_i)/(\rho_{i+1}+\rho_i)\). For one layer \(\Gamma_1 = 0\) and \(G\) is the point source plus its air image; for two layers \(\Gamma_1 = K_1\) is constant and the denominator expands into the Tagg / Sunde image series; for three and more layers no closed form exists and the integral is evaluated numerically. The engines differ in how they evaluate \(G\) and in how they discretise the electrodes.

docs.title: Two current models
docs.text:
All integral engines discretise every wire into straight segments of length at most Engine.segment_length (and split them at layer interfaces). They then differ in the unknowns:

  • Uniform current per straight wire (image, image_2layer). Each straight wire of an electrode — a full wire line of a grid, an arm of a star, a straight run of a polyline (user decisions Q30 and Q44 of 2026.11), and each electrode per soil layer it reaches — carries one leakage current, spread uniformly per unit length over its segments; the wires of an electrode are ideally bonded. The unknowns are a handful per electrode, the reaction matrix is reduced with length weights to a wire-by-wire multiport matrix, and the solve is cheap. The ansatz is exact for a ring by symmetry and good for impedances of compact electrodes (grids about 1 % above one current per segment); it misplaces current along each wire — towards the tips of a star and the ends of a strip — which matters for surface potentials near the electrode (touch and step voltages) more than for impedances.
  • One current per segment (mom, mom_sommerfeld). Point matching (collocation): one pulse current per segment, the potential matched at every segment midpoint. This resolves how the current distributes along and between electrodes; it uses a point-source near field, which leaves it 1–2 % below the exact thin-wire solution and drifting under refinement (see mom).

fem is not a third current model of the same problem: it solves the field in the soil by finite elements, the electrodes as the solid bodies they are where the world is axisymmetric and as smoothed line sources in three dimensions otherwise (experimental, see fem).

docs.title: Network equations
docs.text:
Electrodes bonded by ideal conductors form a cluster with one potential; finite conductors (lumped, distributed, inductive) are branches between nodes; junctions are nodes without soil contact. Every engine of the integral family assembles the same augmented nodal system — multiport relation between leakage currents and node potentials, Kirchhoff's current law at every node, and Ohm's law along every branch:

\[ \begin{bmatrix} Z & -C & 0 \\ C^{\top} & 0 & B^{\top} \\ 0 & B & -Z_b(\omega) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf I_e \\ \boldsymbol\varphi_n \\ \mathbf I_b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf 0 \\ \mathbf I_\text{in} \\ \mathbf 0 \end{bmatrix}, \]

with \(Z\) the soil reaction (multiport) matrix, \(C\) the owner-to-node incidence, \(B\) the branch-to-node incidence and \(Z_b\) the branch impedance matrix; \(\mathbf I_e\) are the leakage currents, \(\boldsymbol\varphi_n\) the node potentials, \(\mathbf I_b\) the branch currents and \(\mathbf I_\text{in}\) the injected source currents. The first row says that the soil turns leakage currents into potentials, the second that current is conserved at every node, the third that each branch obeys Ohm's law. Sources inject \(+I\) at attached_to and, if set, \(-I\) at return_to (two-terminal sources, see sources and measurement). A node without a source floats: it takes the potential the field imposes with zero net current, which keeps transfer impedances reciprocal.

An impressed voltage source (VoltageSource, since 2026.11) is added by modified nodal analysis: its current \(I_v\) becomes one more unknown, which enters Kirchhoff's current law at attached_to and return_to, and one more row fixes \(\varphi_a - \varphi_r + Z_q I_v = U\) (\(\varphi_r = 0\) for remote earth; \(Z_q = R + j\omega L\) the internal impedance of the source, zero for an ideal source). With the terminal incidence \(S\) and the diagonal matrix \(Z_q(\omega)\) of the internal impedances the system grows by one block row and column,

\[ \begin{bmatrix} Z & -C & 0 & 0 \\ C^{\top} & 0 & B^{\top} & -S \\ 0 & B & -Z_b(\omega) & 0 \\ 0 & S^{\top} & 0 & Z_q(\omega) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf I_e \\ \boldsymbol\varphi_n \\ \mathbf I_b \\ \mathbf I_v \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf 0 \\ \mathbf I_\text{in} \\ \mathbf 0 \\ \mathbf U \end{bmatrix}, \]

and the solution of a world without voltage sources is unchanged. A reactive \(Z_q\) makes the system complex at \(f > 0\), so such a world is solved per frequency also without inductive conductors. The mom family borders its segment-level system the same way.

docs.title: The registered backends
docs.text:
Backends are registered in groundfield.solver.registry with their solve function, declared capabilities and options model (ADR-0014). Engine.solve resolves the requested name, checks the world against the capabilities before any work is done (soil layer count, concrete shells, explicitly requested kernel; BackendCapabilityError names a backend that can solve the world), forwards image to image_2layer for a two-layer soil, and writes the metadata core (backend, effective backend, kernel, version, frequencies, segments, soil kind, earth model, solve time, series controls, provenance) into every result. The table is generated from the registry:

Name Status What it runs Soil layers Kernel (default first) return_to, junctions, voltage sources Concrete shells Conductor models Options image current Homogeneous soil, closed-form image-charge sum; forwards two_layer → image_2layer, multi_layer → image_nlayer 1, 2 line, point yes, yes, yes yes distributed, inductive, lumped, skin — image_2layer current Two-layer soil, Tagg / Sunde image series 2 line, point yes, yes, yes yes distributed, inductive, lumped, skin — image_nlayer deprecated name of image Layered soil routed to image (n = 1) or image_2layer (n = 2) 1, 2 line, point yes, yes, yes yes distributed, inductive, lumped, skin — cim deprecated name of image Deprecated name of the image auto-dispatch (10.76) 1, 2 line, point yes, yes, yes yes distributed, inductive, lumped, skin — mom current Method of moments, point-matching collocation 1, 2 point yes, yes, yes yes distributed, inductive, lumped, skin — mom_sommerfeld current Method of moments with Sommerfeld quadrature, any n 1, 2, ≥ 3 point yes, yes, yes yes distributed, inductive, lumped, skin MomSommerfeldOptions bem deprecated name of mom Deprecated name of 'mom' (10.76) 1, 2 point yes, yes, yes yes distributed, inductive, lumped, skin — fem experimental Conforming finite elements: axisymmetric (rods and rings on one axis) or three-dimensional (any electrodes; fem3d extra) 1, 2, ≥ 3 none (volume mesh) yes, yes, yes yes distributed, inductive, lumped, skin FemOptions

Backend-specific settings live in Engine.options, keyed by backend name (MomSommerfeldOptions, FemOptions); the image-series controls image_max_terms (default 300) and image_series_tol (default 1e-6) are common Engine fields because every layered engine and the post-solve field evaluation read them.

docs.title: Deprecated names
docs.text:
Three names of earlier releases are deprecated aliases since 2026.11; they keep working, emit a DeprecationWarning naming the replacement, and will be removed no earlier than 2027.5.

  • cim ran the complex-image method: approximate \(\Gamma_1(\lambda)\) by a sum of exponentials (matrix-pencil fit), which turns the Sommerfeld integral into a finite sum of complex images. For one and two layers the closed forms are exact and no fit was ever used on a solve path; the three-layer kernel was structurally incomplete and has raised since 0.11.0. cim now runs the image auto-dispatch, which gives the numbers cim gave on every world it accepted. The fit itself, groundfield.solver.cim.fit_complex_images, remains available for studies of the spectral reflection coefficient; it reports convergence only when the maximum error on an independent grid meets the tolerance.
  • bem was described as a boundary-element collocation but assembled the same reaction matrix as mom (to 4e-16) and now runs mom.
  • image_nlayer routed a layered soil with one or two distinct layers to image / image_2layer and rejected three. image does the routing itself; a real image series for \(n \ge 3\) (Stefanescu's construction) is not implemented (ADR-0002), use mom_sommerfeld.

Layer stacks are canonicalised before they reach a backend: zero-thickness layers are dropped and adjacent layers of equal resistivity merged, so TwoLayerSoil(ρ, ρ, h) and MultiLayerSoil([ρ, ρ, ρ]) are solved as the homogeneous soil they are (benchmark B9).

docs.title: fem — conforming finite elements, axisymmetric and 3-D (experimental)
docs.text:
This page explains how the fem engine computes the current field in the soil with finite elements, how accurate its two models are, what they cost and where they must not be used. Read it when you use fem as the reference for the integral engines (image, image_2layer, mom, mom_sommerfeld), or when you need to know why it refused a world.

At a glance

Soil any number of horizontal layers Electrodes every kind, bare or encased (ADR-0012) Axisymmetric model rods on one vertical axis and rings around it, meshed as the solid cylinders and tori they are 3-D model every other world (optional fem3d extra); thin wires as smoothed line sources Accuracy axisymmetric about 1e-4; 3-D about 2e-3 away from layer interfaces and other wires Far field exact monopole Robin condition on a box 1000 lengths away Extrapolation Richardson over two nested mesh levels, with a reported error estimate Network the shared pipeline of the integral engines Status experimental (ExperimentalBackendWarning once per process), a reference backend

In short

  • Two models. With FemOptions.model="auto" (the default) fem takes the axisymmetric model for any set of rods on one vertical axis and horizontal rings centred on it (a rod, a ring, a ring with a central rod) and the three-dimensional model for every other world: strips, polylines, stars, meshes and grids, rods and rings side by side, several clusters, galvanic distributed conductors. model="axisymmetric" refuses the other worlds, model="3d" forces the 3-D model.
  • Axisymmetric accuracy. The port resistance lies within about 1e-4 of independent references at the default settings, in any horizontally layered soil and at any contrast; within 5.1e-5 for a ring wire within 1.05 radii of an interface, up to a layer contrast of 1000.
  • 3-D accuracy. Within about 2e-3 of the axisymmetric model away from layer interfaces and other wires. Wires that run beside each other are kept at least \(1.5\,R\) apart (\(R\) = source_radius, 6 cm by default; a smaller \(R\) for closer wires, BackendCapabilityError where none fits). Next to a strongly contrasting interface the thin-wire error of the integral engines applies (+9.2e-3 three wire radii above a 1000 / 30 Ω·m interface). Layer contrasts are tested up to about 300.
  • Cost. Axisymmetric: 0.2 … 2 s for a ring, a rod or a ring with a central rod. 3-D: seconds to a few minutes and up to 4.3 GB in the measured worlds (a 12.6 m ring 26 s and 1.8 GB, the AP1 station 75 … 140 s and 4.3 GB).
  • Use it as the independent reference where the integral engines approximate: the uniform current of the image family, the point kernel of mom, the thin wire next to an interface, each wire's own concrete shell at the junctions of a foundation.
  • Do not use it for networks (by default the 3-D model takes at most 100 ports and 2 million nodes), for layer contrasts above about 300 in the 3-D model, or for wires beside each other closer than 3.3 radii of the thickest bare wire (refused). The full list is under Validity range.

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
fem solves the volume form of the stationary current-flow problem: it meshes the soil around the electrodes and computes the potential in the whole soil volume, instead of integrating a Green's function over the wires as the integral engines do. Its two models share nothing with the integral engines but the network solve. That makes fem the independent reference for the image family, mom and mom_sommerfeld where they make their approximations: the uniform current of the image family, the point kernel of mom, the thin wire of both next to an interface, each wire's own concrete shell at the junctions of a foundation (ADR-0016).

The physical model and its assumptions:

  • Quasi-static soil. The soil carries a stationary conduction current; the earth part of the solve is the same at every frequency of the engine. The conductor branches of the network (resistance, inductance, skin effect, earth return) are evaluated per frequency, as in the integral engines.
  • Horizontally layered soil. Any number of layers, each with a constant resistivity, an insulating soil surface, and the potential zero far away.
  • Electrodes are perfect conductors, each at its own potential. The axisymmetric model takes a rod, a ring and a ring with a central rod — any set of rods on one vertical axis and rings around it — as the solid bodies they are: a rod is the solid cylinder of its wire_radius with flat end faces, a ring the solid torus of its wire_radius. The current density along and around them follows from the field (more at the rod ends, more on the side of a ring that faces a conductive layer). The three-dimensional model represents every wire by a smoothed line source with an analytic correction for its radius.
  • Concrete. An encased wire carries its own thin concrete shell (the coefficient \(C\) of ADR-0012) in both models; the 3-D model can resolve the concrete as a volume instead (FemOptions.concrete_resistivity).

The options are the fields of FemOptions:

Option Default Meaning model "auto" "axisymmetric", "3d", or the automatic choice refinement 0 level of the coarser of the two meshes extrapolate True solve two levels and extrapolate r_far_factor 1000 size of the truncation box in characteristic lengths far_field "robin" monopole Robin condition; "dirichlet" grounds the box max_nodes 2 000 000 node limit of the axisymmetric model max_nodes_3d 2 000 000 node limit of the 3-D model max_ports_3d 100 port limit of the 3-D model source_radius None (6 cm) disc radius \(R\) of the smoothed line sources growth 0.5 growth of the 3-D element size away from the wires concrete_resistivity None resolve the concrete as a volume (3-D)

docs.title: Mathematical and physical context
docs.text: The field equation, the ports, the concrete shells and the network solve hold for both models; the discretisation below is that of the axisymmetric model, and the three-dimensional model has its own section (below).

docs.title: The field equation
docs.text:
The stationary current field obeys

\[ - abla\cdot igl(\sigma(z)\, abla\varphi igr) = 0 \quad ext{in the soil},\qquad rac{\partial\varphi}{\partial z}\Big|_{z=0} = 0,\qquad \varphi o 0 ext{ far away}, \]

with the potential \(\varphi\), the depth \(z\) (positive downwards) and the conductivity \(\sigma = 1/ ho\), piecewise constant in depth. The first equation is the conservation of charge for the conduction current \(\mathbf J = -\sigma abla\varphi\), the second says that no current crosses the soil surface into the air, and the third puts the reference at remote earth.

For a body of revolution about a vertical axis the field is the same in every meridian plane, and the problem reduces to the meridian half-plane \((s, z)\), \(s\) the distance from the axis:

\[ - rac{1}{s} rac{\partial}{\partial s}\Bigl(s\,\sigma\, rac{\partial\varphi}{\partial s}\Bigr) - rac{\partial}{\partial z}\Bigl(\sigma\, rac{\partial\varphi}{\partial z}\Bigr) = 0 . \]

It is the same conservation law in cylindrical coordinates; the factor \(s\) weights each point of the half-plane with the circumference \(2\pi s\) of the circle it stands for.

docs.title: Ports and the port conductance matrix
docs.text:
Every electrode is a perfect conductor at its own potential \(U_k\) — a port. The port conductance matrix \(G\) relates the port currents to the port potentials,

\[ \mathbf I = G\,\mathbf U , \]

and is the earth part of the solve: symmetric (reciprocity) and positive definite (the soil dissipates power for every non-zero \(\mathbf U\)). By the minimum-energy principle the discrete \(G\) of a mesh that holds the electrodes exactly (a rod is a rectangle of mesh lines) is larger than the exact one, so its resistance lies below the exact one: the true potential minimises the dissipated power among all potentials with the port values, and the finite elements search a smaller set. A ring's O-grid inscribes a polygon in the wire's circle, so for rings this is observed, not guaranteed (see Numerics).

docs.title: Encased electrodes
docs.text: An encased electrode (concrete_shell_coefficient_ohm_m \(= C\) in Ω·m, concrete shells) keeps its metal at \(U_k\) and leaks through its shell surface \(r_b\) = wire_radius: every metre adds the radial resistance \(C\), applied locally as the surface conductance \(1/(2\pi r_b C)\) per unit area between the metal and the soil at each point of the surface. That is Sunde's cylindrical shell, exact for a shell thin against the scale on which the leakage current varies; the current may redistribute, so the shell adds at least \(C/L\) to a wire of length \(L\) (for a ring \(C/(2\pi r)\)), as in mom.

docs.title: Discretisation of the axisymmetric model
docs.text:
• Graded tensor mesh. Vertical lines \(s = s_i\) and horizontal lines \(z = z_j\) through every feature — the rod surfaces and end faces, the layer interfaces, the soil surface, the axis and the truncation box — graded away from each feature, \(h(x) = \min_f (h_f + 0.2\,|x - x_f|)\) (\(h\) the line spacing at the coordinate \(x\), \(h_f\) the spacing at the feature \(x_f\)). The cells inside a rod are removed, so the rod is a rectangle of mesh lines. The edges of its end faces are re-entrant corners of the conductor; with a spacing of \(0.002\,a\) there (\(a\) the wire radius) the convergence stays of second order, also for a rod tip on an interface. Each cell is split into two linear triangles; the weight \(2\pi s\) is integrated exactly.
  • Coincident features. Mesh features closer than 1e-9 of max(1 m, x) are one line (\(x\) the coordinate of the feature): a run keeps the coordinate of its physical feature (an interface, a rod end, the soil surface), so only mesh lines move; an interface is cut at its own line, and a triangle of zero area is refused as an internal error.
  • O-grid for the ring wire. A square block of up to three wire radii around the wire's cross section is filled by an O-grid that conforms to the tensor lines on its boundary and is inscribed in the wire's circle (32 chords at level 0). The block keeps clear of the soil surface, the axis, the other electrodes and of every interface more than \(1.05\,a\) from the wire axis; a nearer interface — a ring on it or within its radius — is cut into the block's elements, so every element lies in one layer.
  • Ring wires next to an interface. A ring wire within \(1.05\,a\) of an interface gets a finer block: the gap between the wire and the interface, and the narrow wedge where the interface cuts the wire near its edge, make the field vary over \(\sqrt{2a\,|d - a|}\) (\(0.14\,a\) at \(d = 1.01\,a\), \(d\) the distance of the wire axis from the interface). The interface cuts the wire at an edge of the conductor on a material interface, or touches it in a contact zone that shrinks with the contrast. The O-grid of such a block is therefore graded towards the points where the interface cuts the wire at a narrow angle (0.7 a or farther from the axis) or comes closest to it — the rays geometrically in angle, the first layers geometrically in radius, from cells of 1e-3 wire radii, both bisected with the level — and the block has 32 intervals per side. The default lies within 5.1e-5 of independent boundary elements of the solid torus at contrasts 3 … 1000 on either side, cut or touching (60 cases; 3.2e-5 at 100), refinement=1 within 1.9e-5, and the error estimate (3.9e-4 … 1.5e-3) lies above the error in all 113 cases of the sweep at both refinements. A ring touching a 1000 times more conductive layer takes 38 317 / 151 807 nodes, 1.8 s and 0.76 GB (refinement=1: 604 307 nodes, 11 s, 2.8 GB). A ring on the interface (\(d = 0\)) reads −1.2e-5 against the same model.
  • Truncation. A box at r_far_factor = 1000 characteristic lengths (the electrodes' depth and radius, or the depth of the deepest interface times the layer contrast \(\max\rho/\min\rho\) if larger, since a resistive bottom keeps the current in the layers above it over that distance) with the Robin condition \(\partial_n\varphi = -(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r/r^2)\,\varphi\), the exact Dirichlet-to-Neumann map of the monopole far field on any boundary: far away the potential is that of a point source, \(\varphi \propto 1/r\) (\(r\) the distance from the electrodes, \(\mathbf n\) the outward normal of the box), for which this relation holds exactly on any surface. The graded mesh reaches the box with a few dozen extra lines.
  • Ports. The surface nodes of a bare electrode are one unknown; \(G\) is the Schur complement of the stiffness matrix onto the ports, one sparse LU factorisation for all of them.

docs.title: Network, sources and results
docs.text:
The soil model hands an EarthPorts record (port conductance matrix, display segments with their leakage per port volt) to the network solve of the integral backends (ADR-0014), with \(Z = G^{-1}\) as the multi-port matrix. Lumped and isolated distributed conductors, inductive branches with their earth-return models (earth_inductive_model), the skin effect, junctions, return_to and voltage sources with their internal impedance are honoured exactly as there, at every frequency of the engine; the soil part is quasi-static and the same at every frequency. Floating electrodes take their transfer potential.

The result reports every electrode's potential and current, the port resistance matrix (metadata["fem_port_resistance"], ports in world order metadata["fem_ports"], and per level), the mesh size and time per level (fem_mesh) and the box size (fem_r_far). Its point sources are the display segments of the engine's segment_length (rods cut at the interfaces) with the model's leakage distribution, so FieldResult.potential, the touch-voltage helpers and the exports work as for the other backends (homogeneous and two-layer soil). The field of those point sources is the exact field of the model's leakage, and the nodal field of the mesh converges to it (at most 0.96 %, 0.21 %, 0.062 % at levels 0, 1, 2 along the surface 1 … 100 m from a 3 m rod). Next to a rod the equipotential current distribution differs from the uniform one of the image family: the surface potential 1 … 3 m from the rod lies 0.08 … 0.36 % below that of image, the touch voltage at 1 m (per ampere) 1.4 % below. The solve runs the coordinate check (MixedCoordinatesWarning) and solves projected coordinates in a local frame.

docs.title: The three-dimensional model
docs.text: The three-dimensional model needs the optional fem3d extra (scikit-fem, BSD-3; pyamg, MIT; see Install the optional extras). It meshes the soil in tetrahedra and represents every wire by a smoothed line source, so the mesh never has to resolve a wire radius of a few millimetres; what the mesh does not resolve is added analytically. Layer interfaces, and resolved concrete, enter as partially penalised immersed elements instead of mesh planes.

docs.title: Wires as smoothed line sources
docs.text:
Every electrode is a chain of straight pieces along its wire axis (a ring a polygon of 1° chords), every leaking piece of a galvanic distributed conductor one more. A piece leaks the current density \(j(s)\) in A/m (\(s\) the position along the wire), spread over the disc of radius \(R\) (FemOptions.source_radius, default 6 cm) perpendicular to the axis with the bump density

\[ \eta(r) = \frac{3}{\pi R^2}\Bigl(1 - \frac{r^2}{R^2}\Bigr)^2 , \]

\(r\) the distance from the wire axis: a smooth profile of unit integral over the disc, so the current leaves the wire as if from a soft cylinder of radius \(R\). The wire sees the \(\eta\)-weighted disc average \(\Pi(s)\) of the potential. Its field is smooth, so the mesh needs no resolution of the wire radius \(a\). What lies inside the disc is added analytically as a radial resistance per unit length between the metal and that average,

\[ U - \Pi(s) = \bigl(C + \Delta C(s)\bigr)\,j(s), \qquad \Delta C = \frac{\rho}{4\pi}\sum_k \bigl[\Phi_k(s; a) - \Phi_k(s; r_\eta)\bigr], \]

with the shell coefficient \(C\) of an encased wire, \(\Phi_k(s; c)\) the integral of the reduced kernel \(1/\sqrt{d^2 + c^2}\) over piece \(k\) (closed form; \(d\) the distance from the point \(s\) to the points of the piece) and \(r_\eta = 0.5442\,R\) the energy radius of the bump. The first equation is Ohm's law per metre of wire: the metal at \(U\) lies above the disc average by the current density times the shell and the soil inside the disc; the second is that soil's resistance, the potential the pieces produce on the wire surface minus what the smoothed source already gives. The sum runs over what the mesh does not resolve:

  • the observer's own wire whole: its polyline as far as it has turned by at most 90° along the wire (a ring's polygon, a strip, the corners of a loop), and every piece on the same axis line that belongs to the observer's port or to a wire that meets it — the next piece of a galvanic conductor, a rod cut into touching pieces, the surface image of a rod whose head reaches the surface;
  • of the rest of its electrode — a part of the own polyline that has turned by 150° or more along the wire (an arm folded back, the far side of a narrow loop or a small ring, the other arm of a narrow V, the next arm of a meander or the next winding of a spiral, which run the same way again after a full turn), the other wires of a mesh or a star — and of every other surface image only the part within \(1.5\,R\) of the point; between 90° and 150° of turn the own polyline counts by the weight \((150° - T)/60°\) whole and by the rest of the weight within \(1.5\,R\);
  • of a wire of another port the part within \(1.5\,R\) (on the observer's axis line the whole piece) only where the two wires meet, that is, where their surfaces touch: a rod on a ring, a T-joint, a crossing, a galvanic conductor and the electrode it is attached to. Wires that touch are one conductor and carry about the same current where they meet. Where two wires have just stopped touching, this window term fades out linearly with the gap between their surfaces, from 1 at contact to 0 at a gap of \(a_1 + a_2\), so the correction is continuous. Any other wire of another port carries its own current, which the observer's correction cannot know, and counts nothing.

The turn \(T\) is the sum of the angles at the corners passed along the chain from the observer's piece, along a closed chain the shorter way round. The blend between 90° and 150° makes the correction continuous in the turn: a V whose turn passes 120°, a meander arm tilted by a fraction of a degree and a spiral wound as one polyline or as bonded windings all agree with mom and image (measurements in the note below).

Each wire reaches its radius from its axis perpendicular to it, up to a flat end. Two wires that cross therefore touch where their axes come within \(a_1 + a_2\) (the window fades out between \(a_1 + a_2\) and \(2(a_1 + a_2)\)); a wire that ends at another touches it where its end face reaches the other's surface; two wires end to end on one axis touch only where the gap between their ends is zero (to 1e-9 m). An encased wire reaches its outer shell radius \(r_b\), which is what the soil sees: two encased wires of different ports whose shells touch count as one conductor in the radius correction, so their separate port entries are not resolved.

Farther than \(1.5\,R\) the disc average of a smoothed line is its line field (the 2-D mean-value property of the radial bump), so the mesh already gives the exact field: for two parallel wires the exact correction is below \(10^{-3}\) of the self term from \(1.5\,R\) on, and the surface image of a horizontal wire (\(2z \ge 2.5\,R\) away) never counts. Far inside a straight wire \(\Delta C\) is Sunde's radial resistance \(\frac{\rho}{2\pi}\ln(r_\eta/a)\) of the soil between the wire and the disc; near an end, a corner or a junction it carries the 3-D geometry. The squared distance from a piece's axis is taken from the cross product, which stays accurate on long pieces off the coordinate axes.

Measurements: the turn rule

The blended turn rule against the earlier rule of a 120° direction test, mom and image (evidence h00 of stream fw4r3b, one run each, another agent running):

world base (120° direction rule) now mom (ds 0.025 m) image S-meander, third arm tilted by 1e-4 rad, \(Z\) +4.65e-4 −1.24e-4 −1.26e-4 −1.19e-4 spiral of 3 windings (pitch 0.15 m), one polyline / bonded windings − 1 +2.08e-3 +5.9e-5 0 0 V of 0.5 m arms, turn 119.9° → 120.1°, \(Z\) −1.26e-3 +3.30e-4 +3.44e-4 +3.48e-4

An L corner (turn 90°) and a square loop are unchanged to the last bit. The far chords of a ring now count by their weight: rings of \(r\) = 1 / 0.3 m move by −4.4e-7 / −6.9e-6 in \(Z\) (to −1.839e-3 / −5.00e-4 against the solid torus, from −1.839e-3 / −4.93e-4). A rule that clipped the own polyline by its distance from the observer's axis line also clipped the curved continuation of a ring and moved rings away from the solid torus (−1.19e-3 for \(r\) = 0.3 m, −2.0e-3 for \(r\) = 1 m; evidence g02 of stream fw4r2b), so it was not taken.

docs.title: Wires beside each other
docs.text:
The disc of a smoothed source reaches \(R\) from its axis. Where another wire runs within \(1.5\,R\) of it, the mesh no longer gives that wire's exact field and the radius correction has no term for it. The 3-D model therefore keeps wires that run beside each other at least \(1.5\,R\) apart, as it keeps every disc in the soil and in one layer: it takes \(R\) = (their axis distance) / 1.5 for the whole world (wires end to end: their gap / 5). Two wires run beside each other where

  • a point of one lies within \(1.5\,R\) of the side of the other (its nearest point is not an end of that wire) and the two run within 30° of parallel: wires side by side, concentric or diagonal rings, an arm of the same polyline folded back beside the point, a galvanic conductor in the trench of an earthing strip; or
  • the whole of one electrode's wire lies within \(1.5\,R\) of another wire it does not meet (a small ring around a rod's head); or
  • two wires that do not meet lie in line, end to end — the gap runs within 30° of both axes and within \(a_1 + a_2\) of both axis lines — with a gap below \(5\,R\): stacked rods of two electrodes.

Wires end to end keep their gap at \(5\,R\), not \(1.5\,R\), because the measured error of their transfer entry falls with \(R\) / gap: at \(1.5\,R\) it read 1.5 … 2.0 times its estimate, at \(3\,R\) still 1.15 … 1.18 times for 8 mm rods 10 … 18 cm apart, at \(5\,R\) it lies within the estimate in every measured case. Stacked 8 mm rods up to 8.8 cm apart are therefore refused; from 10 cm on every port entry, the transfer entry included, and the bonded value lie within their estimates, and from a gap of 30 cm on \(R\) stays 6 cm.

Measurements: stacked rods

Stacked rods (\(a\) = 8 mm, 1.5 m each, 100 Ω·m) against the axisymmetric model, two ports, default options (evidence h07, h12 of stream fw4r3b; base 4f443f5 in brackets):

Every entry, the transfer entry included, and the bonded value lie within their estimates, as do 2 mm rods 6 and 10 cm apart (R12 −2.33e-3 / −2.44e-3 against 4.57e-3 / 4.58e-3). From a gap of 30 cm on the solve is that of round 3 to the last bit.

The distance is that of the two wire axes, independent of how the check samples them. Left alone are wires that meet at 10° or more: the collinear pieces of a galvanic conductor, a rod cut into touching pieces, a rod on a ring, a T-joint, a corner, a crossing, a conductor's attachment, and a V or a branch of 10 … 30°. Two straight wires that meet at an angle \(\theta\) come within \(1.5\,R\) of each other only within \(1.5\,R/\sin\theta\) of where they meet, and there the window term counts the other wire, whose current agrees with the observer's. Wires that meet at less than 10°, nearly parallel or touching along their length (a cable laid on a strip, the service drops of TnNetworkGenerator laid in a row at the touching distance), run beside each other like wires that do not meet. They are refused before meshing where they are closer than 3.3 radii of the thickest bare wire, and the message names their distance and the angle at which they meet: two bonded parallel strips 8 mm apart (\(a\) = 5 mm) are refused, as a V of 9°. Touching wires that run together are not one conductor. Crossings at more than 30° are left alone as well: near them a point crosses the other wire within a few \(R\). A V whose arms do not touch (a rounded apex, a second strip starting beside the first) still runs beside: a V of 10° whose second arm starts 3 cm beside the apex takes \(R\) = 2 cm.

A V of two 4 m arms meeting at the apex, as two bonded strips and as one polyline, agrees between the two representations to 2e-5 from 10° to 35°, and its ratios to mom and image continue the trend of the wider angles down to 10°; below 10° it is refused (see above).

Measurements: a V of two 4 m arms

A V of two 4 m arms meeting at the apex (5 mm wire, 0.8 m deep), as two bonded strips (two ports) and as one polyline, against mom and image (evidence h03 of stream fw4r3b):

One \(R\) serves the whole world (the disc quadrature, the energy radius and the mesh size around the wires use it), so the closest pair refines the whole mesh: the nodes grow as \(1/R\). The smallest \(R\) is 2.2 radii of the thickest bare wire of the world, wherever that wire lies (the energy radius must exceed 1.2 of its radii): wires beside each other closer than 3.3 such radii, axis to axis, and wires end to end closer than 11, are refused before meshing with BackendCapabilityError naming the distance and the integral engines (stacked 8 mm rods up to a gap of 8.8 cm). Two 4 mm strips 4 cm apart are refused next to a rod of 20 mm radius elsewhere in the world, and solved at \(R\) = 2.67 cm without it. Where the finer mesh exceeds max_nodes_3d, ResourceLimitError says why \(R\) is small.

Two coaxial rings 4.5 … 10 cm apart lie within 1.8e-3 of the solid tori of the axisymmetric model in every entry of their port matrix and inside both error estimates; 3 cm apart they would need 2.02 million nodes and are refused (ResourceLimitError). Rings diagonal to each other 1.6 … 2.05 wire radii apart in \(s\) and \(z\) (axes 11 … 14.5 mm apart), which model="auto" sends to the 3-D model when the axisymmetric mesh block has no room, and a small ring 0.75 radii above a rod head are refused before meshing, naming the integral engines; mom lies within 0.07 … 0.18 % of boundary elements of the solid bodies there.

docs.title: Mesh, layers and concrete
docs.text:
• Isotropic mesh. A grid of \(8\times8\times4\) cubes on the truncation box, six Kuhn tetrahedra each, refined by a deterministic conforming longest-edge bisection until every element is below \(1.5\,(R/2 + g\max(0, d - R))\), \(d\) the distance from the nearest wire and \(g\) = FemOptions.growth (0.5): fine around the wires, growing linearly with the distance beyond the disc. The elements keep an aspect ratio of at most 2. (A graded tensor grid carries its fine lines to the box as slabs; the multigrid stalls on them.)
  • Layer interfaces are no mesh planes. An element that an interface cuts is an immersed element: its shape functions are linear on either side of the plane, continuous across it and carry the flux \(\sigma\,\partial_z\varphi\) across it; the faces the interface crosses get the consistency and penalty terms of the partially penalised method (Lin, Lin & Zhang 2015), so a layered field is reproduced exactly. Nodes within 30 % of their shortest edge of an interface are moved onto it. Elements four times larger than the layer they cut (far from the electrodes) take the laminate conductivity.
  • Concrete shells. By default every encased wire carries its own coefficient \(C\) — the model of the image family and mom, so fem compares with them directly. With FemOptions.concrete_resistivity \(= \rho_c\) the concrete is a volume: a square prism of conformal radius \(r_b\) = wire_radius (side \(s = r_b/0.59017\), the same resistance to the soil as a circular shell) around every straight encased wire along x, y or z, the metal radius \(r_a\) following from \(C = \frac{\rho_c}{2\pi}\ln(r_b/r_a)\), the radial resistance of a cylindrical shell. Where wires meet, the prisms share their concrete (see Concrete shells). The square keeps the resistance to the soil, but in the shell-dominated limit (\(\rho_c \gg \rho\)) its concrete is 3.8 % less resistive than the circular shell: the concrete between the bar and a nearly equipotential prism surface is set by the square's inner conformal radius at its centre, \(0.5394\,s = 0.914\,r_b\) (for a 5 mm bar with 5 cm cover \(\ln(50.3/5)/\ln(55/5) = 0.962\); Schwarz–Christoffel and a least-squares Green's function agree). One square side cannot match both radii.

docs.title: Solve
docs.text: The disc averages couple all nodes of a disc, so the coupling is never formed: conjugate gradients run on the operator, preconditioned by the smoothed-aggregation multigrid of the soil stiffness (pyamg, set up under a fixed seed of numpy's global random state, which is restored afterwards, so a result does not depend on the user's seed), one solve per port. The iterations grow with the layer contrast: 16 … 115 up to the contrast 33 of the AP1 soils, 384 … 530 at 100 and 1 225 … 1 264 at 333 at the finer level for a rod through the interface (both orders of the layers, each within its error estimate of the axisymmetric model). At 1 000 they do not converge in 3 000 iterations and the solve raises BackendCapabilityError naming the contrast, the axisymmetric model (any contrast) where it takes the world, and the integral engines (a multigrid of the stiffness plus the diagonal of the wire coupling gives the same counts). Without a layer contrast the refusal names its circumstances instead — resolved concrete and its contrast to the soil, or homogeneous soil, where 19 … 27 iterations are the rule.

docs.title: Numerics
docs.text: Both models solve two nested mesh levels and extrapolate. With the ratio \(r\) of the errors of the two levels (coarser over finer) and the error \(e_1\) of the finer level, second-order extrapolation errs by \(e_1(4 - r)/3\) and the reported estimate is \(e_1(r - 1)/3\), so the estimate bounds the error while \(r \ge 2.5\) (both levels on the same side of the converged value). At exact second order \(r = 4\): the extrapolated value is exact and the estimate equals the finer level's error.

docs.title: Axisymmetric model
docs.text:
Refinement and extrapolation. Level \(\ell\) bisects every interval of the level-0 lines \(\ell\) times (and doubles the O-grid). The tensor part of the spaces is nested, the O-grid of a ring is not (its layers move with the level, the inscribed polygon grows): one level converges at second order and, in every case tested away from interfaces, from below — observed, not guaranteed. By default fem solves levels 0 and 1 and extrapolates \(G\) with the observed second order (Richardson),

\[ G = G_1 + \frac{G_1 - G_0}{3} , \]

which removes the leading error: at second order the error of level 1 is a quarter of that of level 0, so their difference is three times the error left in level 1. metadata["fem_error_estimate"] is the largest relative difference of a port's resistance between the extrapolated and the finer level — about the finer level's error (0.88 … 0.99 of it in 36 cases, 0.94 … 1.07 for a ring that an interface cuts or comes within 1.05 radii of, 60 cases) and 10 … 130 times the error of the extrapolated value, which it bounds while both levels lie on the same side of the converged value and the finer level's error is at most 1/2.5 of the coarser one's (1/3.9 observed; 1/3.9 … 1/4.0 for a ring touching a 100 or 1000 times more conductive layer). FemOptions(refinement=k) starts at level \(k\); extrapolate=False solves one level, usually below the converged value, and reports fem_error_estimate as NaN.

Convergence. One level converges at an observed order of 1.95 … 2.00 in rods and rings, homogeneous, in two and three layers, through an interface and with a ring 1 cm above or on an interface; level 3 lies within 0.015 % of the reference, and the default extrapolation of levels 0 and 1 within 1.0e-5 … 7.0e-5 (table in the note).

Measurements: convergence of the axisymmetric model

One level without extrapolation; deviation from the independent reference; time on an M1 Pro core with other jobs running. The ring on \(h_1\) is re-measured with its graded block of audit W4R2A-02 (the script e05 of stream fw4int on the merged fixes: 24 488 … 1 543 200 nodes at levels 0 … 3, the level 3 in 30 s and 6.4 GB).

World level 0 level 1 level 2 level 3 observed order default (0/1 extrapolated) ring \(r\) = 2 m at 0.8 m, \(a\) = 8 mm, 100 Ω·m (closed form) −0.63 % −0.16 % −0.043 % −0.013 % 1.97 / 2.00 −5.7e-5 rod 0.5 … 3.5 m, \(a\) = 8 mm, 100 Ω·m (solid-rod FV) −0.42 % −0.11 % −0.027 % −0.0069 % 1.98 / 1.99 −1.4e-5 the rod through \(h_1\) = 2 m, 30 / 1000 Ω·m (FV) −0.40 % −0.10 % −0.025 % −0.0061 % 1.98 / 1.99 −1.0e-5 rod 0.5 … 5 m with its tip on \(h_1\), 1000 / 30 Ω·m (FV) −0.43 % −0.11 % −0.029 % −0.0075 % 1.96 / 1.95 −4.1e-5 ring (\(a\) = 5 mm) on \(h_1\) = 2 m, 30 / 1000 Ω·m (solid-torus boundary elements) −0.44 % −0.11 % −0.028 % −0.0070 % 1.98 / 2.00 −1.1e-5 the ring 1 cm above \(h_1\), 1000 / 30 Ω·m (Hankel ring + proximity) −0.69 % −0.18 % −0.049 % −0.015 % 1.98 / 1.96 −7.0e-5 ring in three layers 100 / 1000 / 30 Ω·m (Hankel ring) −0.48 % −0.12 % −0.034 % −0.011 % 1.97 / 2.00 −5.2e-5

Mesh size and cost. A ring has 7 341 / 28 934 nodes at levels 0 / 1, a 3 m rod 18 868 / 74 871, a ring with a central rod in two layers 56 079 / 223 112; the default solve takes 0.20 s, 0.58 s and 2.0 s (best of three), refinement=1 12 s for the last, level 3 of a rod through an interface 2.4 million nodes and 36 s (above the default max_nodes). The error estimate of the finer level (\(1.0 \ldots 1.7 \cdot 10^{-3}\) in these cases) is 0.88 … 0.99 of its actual error in 36 cases (0.88 for a rod head on a 30 / 10 000 Ω·m interface). The solve needs about 4 GB per million nodes of the finer mesh (0.82 / 3.15 / 5.15 GB at 0.20 / 0.80 / 1.22 million, measured with /usr/bin/time -l), so FemOptions.max_nodes (2 000 000 nodes, about 8 GB) refuses larger meshes before anything is assembled; the prediction counts the O-grid exactly and errs high (+0.7 … +11 % in five worlds).

Truncation. The truncation is converged: the box at 30, 100, 300 … 10 000 characteristic lengths moves a rod over 30 / 10 000 Ω·m by at most 4e-5 (5e-6 from 100 on), a grounded box (far_field="dirichlet") at the default size by 7e-5.

docs.title: Three-dimensional model
docs.text:
Levels and error estimates. The finer level is the red refinement of the coarser one (every tetrahedron into eight); the port conductance matrix is extrapolated with the second order, and the relative difference of a diagonal entry to the finer level is metadata["fem_error_estimate"] (3 … 5e-3 at the defaults). The levels are not asymptotic for every geometry (error ratios between the levels of 3.0 … 4.4), so the extrapolated value carries up to about 2e-3. By the rule above the estimate bounds the error while \(r \ge 2.5\): rods run at 3.3 … 4.4 and rings at 3.0 … 3.4, where the estimate is 2.1 … 4.4 times the error.

metadata["fem_error_estimate_transfer"] is the same for the transfer resistances, the largest relative difference of an off-diagonal entry (NaN for one port or one level). Where the model holds it bounds the error of the transfer entries with a margin of 1.06 … 6.3: two 3 m rods 10 m apart 1.06 against image and 1.8 … 1.9 against mom, 30 m apart 1.7 / 1.8, two coaxial rings 4.5 … 10 cm apart 2.3 … 2.6, and 6.3 on the coaxial analogue of benchmark B8 (rod 0 … 3 m on the axis, ring \(r\) = 2.5 m at 0.8 m, 1000 / 30 Ω·m with \(h_1\) = 5 m: 3.1e-3 against an error of \(R_{12}\) of −4.9e-4). In B8 itself it is 2.9e-3, with mom refined to ds = 1/32 m 1.5e-3 above fem and still falling. For two wires end to end the rule keeps the gap at \(5\,R\), where it bounds the error of \(R_{12}\) in every measured case with a margin of 1.24 … 2.6 (see Wires beside each other).

Resolved concrete converges at first order (\(r \approx 2\)): there the estimate is no bound. Next to a strongly contrasting interface the two levels can lie on either side of the solid wire's value, and the estimate does not see the thin-wire error (see Validation of the 3-D model).

Cost. A ring of 12.6 m (600 000 nodes at the finer level) takes 26 s and 1.8 GB, the AP1 station (28 m of wire, 1.2 … 1.4 million nodes) 75 … 140 s and 4.3 GB (fresh processes, one solve each, other jobs running). The solve adds about 2.9 GB per million nodes of the finer mesh (3.0 … 3.1 GB with the process itself), so FemOptions.max_nodes_3d (2 million nodes) refuses meshes of more than about 6 GB before they are built (ResourceLimitError). Every port costs one conjugate-gradient solve per level, about 0.9 s per port and level at 600 000 nodes, so max_ports_3d (100) limits the ports. metadata["fem_peak_memory_gb"] is what the solve added to the peak resident memory of the process — in a fresh process the memory the solve needs, less (down to zero) when an earlier computation of the process already needed more — and metadata["fem_process_peak_memory_gb"] that peak itself, the figure /usr/bin/time -l reports. Both are in GiB.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Every number is checked against a second method that shares no code with fem (references in tests/benchmarks/references.py, tests in tests/test_fem.py): Weber's disc, the thin ring in closed form, a Hankel-transform thin ring for any number of layers, the exact 2-D proximity correction of a wire next to an interface, a cell-centred finite-volume model of the solid rod on its own grid, and axisymmetric boundary elements of the solid rods and tori. The integral engines follow within their documented biases: the uniform current of the image family lies about 1 % above a rod's equipotential solution, the point kernel of mom 0.2 … 2 % below.

docs.title: Validation of the 3-D model
docs.text:
Two methods each: the axisymmetric model where the world allows it, closed forms and the integral engines otherwise.

Against the axisymmetric model (defaults of the 3-D model, levels 0/1 extrapolated): every case — rods and rings in homogeneous soil, rods through and above an interface, a ring above an interface, a ring in three layers — lies within 2.0e-3 of the axisymmetric model and inside its own error estimate. The free ends of a wire read slightly high, a wire without ends (a ring) about 2e-3 low: the two mesh levels are not yet in the asymptotic range for every geometry (error ratio between the levels 3.0 … 3.4 for rings, 3.3 … 4.4 for rods). A ring \(r\) = 1 m (\(a\) = 5 mm) reads −1.62e-3 … −1.83e-3 at 0.06, 0.1, 0.3 and 0.8 m deep, and two coaxial rings 1.0 m and 1.1 m as two ports −1.19e-3 / −1.48e-3 / −1.57e-3 in \(R_{11}\) / \(R_{22}\) / \(R_{12}\) against an estimate of 3.9e-3 (image, the exact thin rings, agrees with the axisymmetric model to 3.7e-4); closer rings with the source radius they need are under Wires beside each other.

Measurements: the 3-D model against the axisymmetric model

Two 2 m rods (\(a\) = 8 mm) in 100 Ω·m: the port matrix is symmetric to round-off (\(\lvert R_{12}/R_{21} - 1\rvert \le 1.1\cdot10^{-16}\)), and the transfer resistance tends to the point-source value, \(R_{12} = 0.949\) / \(0.994\,\rho/(2\pi d)\) at \(d\) = 5 / 20 m. Encased braces and concrete shells. The house mesh of the generators (10 m, 2 × 2 cells, 5 mm bar, 5 cm cover, 100 Ω·m; source_radius 0.1 m, growth 0.6, 1.5 million nodes): encasing its braces raises \(Z\) by +49.1 / +318.2 % at \(\rho_c\) = 1 000 / 5 000 Ω·m (mom +49.6 / +321.3 %), and the owner model of the image family lies +1.6 / +2.8 % above the 3-D model with bare braces, +0.14 / +0.03 % with encased ones. On straight bars, an L, a T-joint and a crossing the per-wire shell of the 3-D model agrees with image to 0.01 … 0.21 % and with mom to 0.06 … 0.28 %.

Resolved concrete (concrete_resistivity) reads the conductance per metre 2.8 … 4.6 % high at the default levels: in the shell-dominated limit the square prism's concrete is 3.8 % less resistive than the circular shell (see Mesh, layers and concrete), and its prism faces and edges converge at first order. So it serves differences on one mesh: against each wire's own shell a junction of a foundation acts like a few cm of wire, at most about \(2\,r_b\), sign not settled, and the house mesh of the generators changes by about 1 % or less (60 m with 4 corners, 4 T-joints and a crossing: 0.35 … 0.85 % with every sign aligned, from the extrapolated junctions of both decompositions, 0.5 … 1.2 % from the finer level alone). The junction numbers are not converged: one refinement of the prism faces moved the corner by about 5 cm, the conductance and the impedance decomposition differ in sign for the corner and the T-joint, and the T-joint and the crossing were not refined (Concrete shells).

docs.title: Validity range
docs.text:
What fem accepts, what happens outside, and what to do instead. The same limits, with their remedies, are collected in Known limitations; the warnings and errors are described in the warnings reference.

Condition Limit Outside Instead Axisymmetric electrodes rods on one vertical axis, horizontal rings centred on it, not touching the 3-D model; BackendCapabilityError with model="axisymmetric" model="auto" Ring wire, axisymmetric top deeper than 5 % of the wire radius; room for its mesh block the 3-D model — 3-D wires the disc of radius source_radius in the soil and in one layer (a bare wire at least about 2.8 radii from an interface) BackendCapabilityError an integral engine 3-D wires beside each other at least \(1.5\,R\) apart, so at least 3.3 radii of the thickest bare wire BackendCapabilityError before meshing an integral engine 3-D wires end to end gap at least \(5\,R\), so at least 11 radii of the thickest bare wire BackendCapabilityError before meshing an integral engine 3-D wires meeting at less than 10° treated as running beside each other BackendCapabilityError closer than 3.3 radii an integral engine 3-D wire next to an interface axis outside the reach of the interface (3.9 wire radii at a contrast of 33) InterfaceContactWarning; thin-wire error (+9.2e-3 at 3 radii, 1000 / 30 Ω·m) the axisymmetric model where it applies Soil any number of horizontal layers; any contrast in the axisymmetric model, up to about 300 tested in the 3-D model 3-D: BackendCapabilityError when its conjugate gradients do not converge the axisymmetric model or the integral engines 3-D ports at most max_ports_3d = 100 (electrodes and leaking pieces of galvanic conductors) ResourceLimitError before meshing coarser discretize_segment_length, or raise the limit Mesh size max_nodes (about 8 GB), max_nodes_3d (about 6 GB), 2 000 000 nodes each ResourceLimitError before the mesh is built raise the limit with the memory at hand Resolved concrete (3-D) straight wires along x, y or z; concrete in the soil; a cover the smoothed source reaches beyond BackendCapabilityError concrete_resistivity=None Per-wire concrete shells every wire, both models — — Conductors lumped, inductive, skin effect, isolated distributed chains; galvanic distributed chains in the 3-D model — — Electrodes every electrode in the soil, below the surface plane (\(2z > a\)) ValueError — fem3d extra installed for the 3-D model ImportError install the extra Frequency quasi-static soil; conductor branches per frequency — —

Accuracy. The axisymmetric model reaches a port resistance within about 1e-4 at the default (within 5.1e-5 for a ring wire within 1.05 radii of an interface, up to a contrast of 1000); raise FemOptions.refinement for more. The 3-D model reaches about 2e-3 away from interfaces and other wires (wires beside each other at least \(1.5\,R\) apart), the error estimate being a bound while the ratio of the two levels' errors is at least 2.5; next to a strongly contrasting interface the thin-wire error applies (see Validation of the 3-D model). For more, take a smaller source_radius or growth with a larger max_nodes_3d (refinement multiplies its nodes by eight: the AP1 station would need about 11.5 million), or one of the integral engines as the second method.

docs.title: Guards
docs.text:
What the dispatch and the axisymmetric model check before they solve:

  • The 3-D model instead (FemOptions.model="auto"): an electrode other than a rod or a ring; a rod or a ring off the common axis; a galvanic distributed conductor (it leaks along its route); rods that touch or overlap on the axis, a ring that touches a rod or another ring, a ring wire that reaches within 5 % of its radius to the soil surface (the solid torus must fit), a ring without room for its mesh block (within about a wire radius, diagonally, of a rod's end edge). With FemOptions.model="axisymmetric" these worlds are refused (BackendCapabilityError, naming the backends whose own checks accept the world).
  • The common axis has a tolerance of 1e-3 of the smallest wire radius or surface gap between two electrodes in the meridian plane (at least 1e-12 of the world's size). The resistance is even in the offset \(\delta\), so the axisymmetric reading is off by \(\kappa(\delta/L)^2\): \(|\kappa| \le\) 6e-4 for \(L\) the wire radius and \(\le\) 1.1e-2 for \(L\) the gap (image and mom on the same discretisations, three worlds), below 1e-6 at the tolerance; for coaxial rods end to end with a gap \(g \le a\) the overlap of the end faces changes linearly in \(|\delta|\) in the parallel-plate picture, which with \(d\ln Z/d\ln g\) = 0.02 … 0.10 estimates 6e-6 … 1.3e-5 at the tolerance: below about 1e-5 (an estimate that errs high, the offset being at most 1e-3 g).
  • Error (ValueError, before anything else): an electrode, driven or passive, at or above the soil surface, in the surface plane (\(2z \le a\)) or reaching above it, and a galvanic distributed conductor out of the soil — what every backend refuses. A rod with its head at \(z = 0\) is the ordinary driven rod.
  • Error (ResourceLimitError): the node count of the finer mesh, predicted from its lines before anything is assembled, above FemOptions.max_nodes (2 000 000 nodes, about 8 GB; level 3 of a rod, 2.4 million, needs it raised). The display segments of the point sources count against Engine.max_segments like the segments of every backend (a unit error of segment_length fails before anything is allocated).
  • The remedy of every refusal comes from the other backends' own checks: a backend that a setting of the engine would let solve the world is named with that setting (a larger Engine.max_segments, a finer segment_length), and if none is left the message says that no backend solves the world yet.

docs.title: Guards of the 3-D model
docs.text:
• ImportError naming the fem3d extra if it is missing.
  • BackendCapabilityError before meshing: a wire so close to the soil surface or a layer interface that its disc cannot lie in the soil and in one layer; wires that run beside each other closer than 1.5 times the smallest source radius (3.3 radii of the thickest bare wire of the world, axis to axis), or lie end to end without touching closer than 5 times it (see Wires beside each other; wires that meet at less than 10° count as running beside each other), naming the wires, their distance and the integral engines; resolved concrete around a wire that is not straight along x, y or z (rings, oblique strips), whose concrete would reach the surface, or whose cover is so thin that the smoothed source does not reach beyond the metal (a 5 mm bar with 5 mm cover), naming concrete_resistivity=None. After meshing: conjugate gradients that do not converge (layer contrasts above the tested 300, such as a rod through a 1 / 1000 Ω·m interface), naming the contrast, the axisymmetric model where it takes the world, and the integral engines.
  • ResourceLimitError before anything is meshed: the display segments above Engine.max_segments (a unit error of segment_length), more ports than FemOptions.max_ports_3d (100) — every electrode and every leaking piece of a galvanic distributed conductor is a port and costs one conjugate-gradient solve per level, about 0.9 s per port and level at 600 000 nodes, so the message names the estimated time (coarsen the conductor's discretize_segment_length, or raise the limit to solve the world on purpose) — and the predicted finer mesh above FemOptions.max_nodes_3d; after the coarser mesh, its exact refinement above that limit. Where the source radius was limited by wires beside each other, the message says so.
  • ValueError: a source_radius that does not reach beyond the bare wire (it must be at least 2.2 wire radii).
  • InterfaceContactWarning (the solve goes on): a horizontal wire whose axis lies within the reach of a contrasting layer interface (3.9 wire radii at a contrast of 33; the table of the reach is under the warning). The smoothed line source shares the thin-wire error of the integral engines there (+9.2e-3 against the solid torus 3 radii above a 1000 / 30 Ω·m interface, beyond the error estimate), so the dispatch warns before the 3-D model runs, as the integral engines do; the axisymmetric model solves the wire as a solid torus and does not warn. A bare wire closer than about 2.8 radii to an interface is refused (its disc would not lie in one layer).

docs.title: Literature
docs.text:
