  • Weber, H. (1873). Ueber die Besselschen Functionen und ihre Anwendung auf die Theorie der elektrischen Ströme. J. reine angew. Math. 75 (the disc electrode, \(R = \rho/(4b)\)).
  • Givoli, D. (1992). Numerical Methods for Problems in Infinite Domains. Elsevier (Dirichlet-to-Neumann truncation; the monopole map is its lowest mode).
  • Strang, G., & Fix, G. (2008). An Analysis of the Finite Element Method, 2nd ed. Wellesley-Cambridge Press (minimum-energy principle and one-sided convergence).
  • Richardson, L. F. (1911). The approximate arithmetical solution by finite differences of physical problems. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 210.
  • Smythe, W. R. (1968). Static and Dynamic Electricity, 3rd ed. McGraw-Hill (images in a plane interface and in a circular cylinder).

Architecture decision: ADR-0016 (the conforming model; ADR-0002 for the engine family). API: groundfield.solver.fem.solve_fem; FemOptions; equivalent_hemisphere_radius (deprecated) and FemReductionWarning (never emitted) are kept for compatibility.

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
The history of the model and the audits behind the numbers above, kept as provenance.

History of the model
  • Up to 2026.11 fem reduced every cluster to an equivalent hemisphere; that reduction and its rules are gone (ADR-0016). Since 2026.11 (user decision Q37) it has the two conforming models of this page: the axisymmetric model (part A) and the three-dimensional model (part B). The resolved concrete of the 3-D model, where the prisms of meeting wires share their concrete, is user decision Q40.
  • The coordinate check of the solve (MixedCoordinatesWarning) is user decision D5.
Audit trail of the axisymmetric model
  • One-sided convergence of rings (audit W4A-09): the O-grid of a ring inscribes a polygon in the wire's circle, so the resistance below the exact one is observed for rings, not guaranteed.
  • Coincident features (audits W4R2A, W4R3A-01): before the rule that features closer than 1e-9 of max(1 m, x) are one line, a ring axis picometres off an interface read +35 … +44 % or failed.
  • Ring wires next to an interface (audits W4A-01, W4R2A-02): with the default block the levels converged at first order and not monotonically there (up to −6.0e-3 next to a layer 33 times more conductive, the error estimate below the error in 7 of 14 cases; audit W4A-01). With 64 intervals per side the default lay within 3.3e-4 at contrast 33, but not beyond it: touching a 1000 times more conductive layer it read −1.6e-2 with an estimate of 1.1e-2, the levels converged at about first order (audit W4R2A-02). The graded block of 32 intervals per side replaced it and takes fewer nodes than the 64-interval block (evidence e05, e07 of stream fw4r2a). The boundary elements of that comparison are the auditor's (W4R2A), and the 113 cases of the estimate check are audit W4R2A's sweep.
  • Error estimate (audit W4A-02 and the auditors' cases): the 36 cases of the ratio 0.88 … 0.99 are auditor W4A's, the 60 cases of the ratio 0.94 … 1.07 audit W4R2A's. extrapolate=False reports fem_error_estimate as NaN since audit W4A-02.
  • Memory and node prediction (audit W4A-10; evidence e02 of stream fw4axi): 0.82 / 3.15 / 5.15 GB at 0.20 / 0.80 / 1.22 million nodes; the prediction errs high by +0.7 … +11 % in five worlds.
  • The 3-D model instead (audit W4A-03): a ring without room for its mesh block goes to the 3-D model.
  • The common axis (audits W4A-08, W4R2A-06): up to audit W4A-08 the tolerance was 1e-9 of the world's size (3 nm): a rod 1 µm off a ring's axis went to the 3-D model (40.7 s, 2.35 GB, −1.43e-3; evidence e01 of stream fw4axi). The estimate for coaxial rods end to end at the tolerance is audit W4R2A-06's.
  • Refusals (audits D2A-06, R2A-07, R2A-03, R2A-04): the surface checks every backend shares, and the remedy named from the other backends' own checks.
  • Validation references: the finite-volume model of the solid rod is adapted from audit A3; the boundary elements of the solid rods and tori are auditor W4A's (audit W4A-11).
  • B8 and B10 (evidence e01 of stream fw4int): run once outside the suite. The value at \(h_1\) = 5 m was re-run in g04 of stream fw4r2b, the other soils by auditor W4R2B, as are the coaxial rod and ring in the three soils. Up to audit W4R2B-05 the page read mom's coarse value as fem's deviation.
Audit trail of the three-dimensional model
  • Wires that meet (audits W4R3B-01, W4R3B-04): up to these audits the axes had to come within the smaller wire radius. Two crossing strips whose surfaces still overlapped stopped meeting, so a 2 m cross jumped by −7.5e-4 in \(Z\) between axis gaps of 4.9 and 5.1 mm (mom −1.6e-5); it now moves by −2.4e-5. And two stacked rods with an end gap below the radius met, so the other rod counted whole with the observer's current. Auditor W4A's small ring 0.75 radii above a rod's head stays 0.49 mm from the rod's end face although the axes are 15.2 mm apart, within \(a_1 + a_2\) = 16 mm.
  • Far terms (audit W4B-01): up to this audit the surface images and every wire within \(20\,R\) counted: shallow wires read up to +1.9e-3 high, two rings 10 cm apart +4.6e-3. The 3-D validation rows were re-measured after it (evidence f04, f06, f07, f12 of stream fw4fem3d): the rows against the axisymmetric model moved by at most 3e-5, the AP1 station by −0.9e-4 … −1.1e-4 against the first version. A ring \(r\) = 1 m drifted before from +2.4e-4 to −1.85e-3 with its depth through the surface-image term; two coaxial rings 1.0 m and 1.1 m read +4.6e-3 in \(R_{11}\) before (evidence f08, f09 of stream fw4fem3d).
  • Distance from the axis (audit W4R2B-01): the difference \(|\mathbf r|^2 - (\mathbf r\cdot\mathbf e)^2\) cancelled on long pieces off the coordinate axes and clipped the observer's own piece from about 7 m on: a 20 m oblique strip read −3.8e-4.
  • The turn rule (audits W4R2B-02, W4R3B-03): it replaces two earlier rules. Up to audit W4R2B-02 an exactly parallel test was used: a folded arm tilted by 1e-6 rad counted whole, so a hairpin's impedance jumped by +1.41e-3 for a tilt of 1e-4 rad. Up to audit W4R3B-03 a piece counted whole where its direction was within 120° of the observer's: the third arm of an S-meander, which runs the same way as the first, 0.20 m beside it, counted whole as soon as it was tilted, and a V jumped where its turn crossed 120°.
  • Wires beside each other (audits W4R2B-03, W4R3B-01, W4R3B-02, W4R3B-05, W4R2A-01): counting the other wire's near field with the observer's current, as up to audit W4R2B-03, read two coaxial rings 7.5 cm apart +4.35e-3 in a port entry, above the estimate; up to then the port entries read +4.35e-3 at 7.5 cm and +1.0e-2 at 6 cm (auditor W4R2B). Stacked rods 1 cm apart read +1.57e-2 in a port entry and −7.3e-2 in the transfer entry, against estimates of 4.9e-3 / 4.5e-3 (audit W4R3B-01; base values in brackets in the stacked-rod table); up to audit W4R3B-01, at \(R\) = 6 cm for a gap of 3 cm, the transfer entry read −2.9e-2 against an estimate of 4.5e-3. The gap of \(5\,R\) for wires end to end is the coordinator's decision on the stream's open point. Up to audit W4R3B-02 a V narrower than 30° was refused, with the distance of the sample point nearest the apex, 0.65 mm for 10°; the worlds of the V table below 30° were refused then. Without the 10° limit, as one conductor, the bonded pair of strips read −1.30e-2 against one strip of the pair's mean radius \(\sqrt{aD}\), image −1.16e-2, and a V of 5° / 2.5° lay on the trend of the wider ones, fem / image − 1 = −1.49e-2 / −1.41e-2 (evidence h03, h05 of stream fw4r3b). The refusal radius is that of the thickest bare wire of the world since audit W4R3B-05. Auditor W4R2A's rings diagonal to each other read +11.4 … +14.3 % against the solid tori before, and auditor W4A's small ring 0.75 radii above a rod head +0.80 % (estimate 0.66 %); both are refused since audits W4R2A-01 and W4R2B-03; the mom comparison there is auditor W4R2A's.
  • Square prism (audit W4B-04): the inner conformal radius and the 3.8 % of the shell-dominated limit.
  • Iterations and contrast (audits W4B-03, W4R2B-06; evidence f13 of stream fw4fem3d): the counts at 33, 100 and 333 and the refusal at 1 000; the refusal names its circumstances without a layer contrast since audit W4R2B-06.
  • Error estimates (audit W4R2B-05; evidence f04 of stream fw4fem3d, the ratios recomputed in g05 of stream fw4r2b; the transfer margins from g04 of stream fw4r2b and h00, h07, h11 of stream fw4r3b): fem_error_estimate_transfer was added because the estimate covered the diagonal only.
  • Cost and memory (audit W4B-09; evidence f06, f15 of stream fw4fem3d): fem_peak_memory_gb and fem_process_peak_memory_gb.
  • Resolved concrete (audit W4R2B-04; audit W4B-05; evidence f12 of stream fw4fem3d): the refusal of a cover so thin that the smoothed source does not reach beyond the metal, and the junction numbers that are not converged.
  • Next to a contrasting interface (audits W4B-02, W4A-07; evidence f10, f13 of stream fw4fem3d): the estimate does not see the thin-wire error, so the dispatch warns before the 3-D model runs.

docs.title: image — homogeneous soil
docs.text:
This page explains the default engine for homogeneous soil: the physical model, the equations it solves, how accurate its results are and where it must not be used. Read it before you rely on image for touch and step voltages next to a grid, a star or a bonded cluster.

At a glance

Soil HomogeneousSoil; a TwoLayerSoil is forwarded to image_2layer Green's function point source plus its air image, closed form Current model one uniform leakage current per straight wire (user decision Q30) Kernel exact line source in Galerkin form (default); kernel="point" for the midpoint point source Unknowns one current per straight wire, node potentials, branch currents Accuracy exact for its model; impedances about 1 % from per-segment mom on grids, a few per cent on stars; near-field quantities up to tens of per cent (Validation) Status default engine; cim and image_nlayer are deprecated names that run it

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
image is the classical grounding calculation of Sunde, Tagg and Dwight. It computes the stationary current field of buried electrodes and the potentials and impedances that follow from it, under these assumptions:

  • Soil. A homogeneous, isotropic half-space of resistivity \(\rho\) (in Ω·m), bounded at \(z = 0\) by insulating air. Depth \(z\) counts positive downwards.
  • Quasi-static field. No displacement current, and a skin depth large against the electrode (frequencies below 1 kHz, see the engine family). The galvanic solution is then independent of the frequency: one solve serves every frequency of a galvanic world.
  • Thin wires. The wire radius \(a\) is small against the segment length. The current flows on the wire axis and the potential is observed on the wire surface.
  • Uniform current per straight wire. Every straight wire of an electrode leaks one current that is uniform along its length: a grid has one current per full wire line, a star one per arm, a polyline one per straight run (a building outline one per side). Rods, strips and rings are one wire each. The wires of an electrode are ideally bonded, so they share one potential, and every result is reported per electrode (user decisions Q30 and Q44).
  • Average potential. The potential of a wire is the average of the field over the wire (Galerkin testing), not the value at one point.

For this model image is exact. What remains is the error of the model itself, chiefly the uniform current, which the Validation section quantifies.

docs.title: Green's function of the half-space
docs.text:
A point current \(I\) (in A) injected at \(\mathbf r_s = (x_s, y_s, z_s)\) with \(z_s > 0\) produces the potential \(\varphi\) (in V) that satisfies

\[ \nabla^2\varphi = -\rho I\,\delta(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_s), \qquad \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial z}\Big|_{z=0} = 0 . \]

The first equation says that the injected current is the only source of the field; the second that no current crosses the soil surface into the air. The image construction solves the problem in closed form: a second source of the same sign at the mirror point \(\mathbf r_s' = (x_s, y_s, -z_s)\) makes the normal derivative vanish on \(z = 0\), so

\[ \varphi(\mathbf r) = \frac{\rho I}{4\pi}\left( \frac{1}{\lvert\mathbf r - \mathbf r_s\rvert} + \frac{1}{\lvert\mathbf r - \mathbf r_s'\rvert}\right). \]

Physically, the insulating surface doubles the potential of a source at the surface: the current that would flow into the upper half-space is reflected back into the soil.

docs.title: Potential of a straight wire
docs.text:
A straight segment of length \(L\) from \(A\) to \(B\) that leaks the current \(I\) uniformly along its length produces, at a point \(X\) with the end-point distances \(R_1 = \lvert X - A\rvert\) and \(R_2 = \lvert X - B\rvert\),

\[ \varphi_\text{line}(X) = \frac{\rho I}{4\pi L} \ln\frac{R_1 + R_2 + L}{R_1 + R_2 - L}. \]

This is the line integral of the point-source potential along the segment. It holds for any orientation of the segment; its air image is the mirrored segment. Since \(R_1 + R_2\) is constant on prolate spheroids with foci \(A\) and \(B\), the equipotentials of a uniformly loaded segment are those spheroids.

docs.title: Current model and discretisation
docs.text:
Every electrode is cut into straight segments no longer than Engine.segment_length (rings into chords, meshes and grids into their wire pieces between crossings). The unknown currents belong to owners: an owner is one straight wire of an electrode. Owner \(o\) of total length \(L_o\) leaks the current \(I_o\), distributed uniformly per unit length, so its segment \(k\) of length \(L_k\) carries

\[ I_k = I_o\,\frac{L_k}{L_o}. \]

Let \(K_{kl}\) (in 1/m) be the reaction coefficient: \(\rho/(4\pi)\) times \(K_{kl}\) is the average potential on segment \(k\) per ampere leaked uniformly by segment \(l\), air image included. The potential of owner \(o\) is the length-weighted average of its segment potentials, with the same weights \(L_k/L_o\) that distribute its current. With the weight matrix \(W\), \(W_{ko} = L_k/L_o\) for \(k \in o\) and zero otherwise, the owner multiport matrix is

\[ Z_{oo'} = \frac{\rho}{4\pi}\sum_{k \in o}\sum_{l \in o'} \frac{L_k}{L_o}\,K_{kl}\,\frac{L_l}{L_{o'}} = \frac{\rho}{4\pi}\,\bigl(W^\top K W\bigr)_{oo'} . \]

\(Z_{oo'}\) is the average potential of wire \(o\) per ampere leaked by wire \(o'\). This is the Galerkin reduction dual to the uniform-current ansatz: the same weights distribute the current and average the potential, so \(Z_{oo'} = Z_{o'o}\) whenever \(K\) is symmetric, and the multiport matrices of the engine are reciprocal.

docs.title: Source kernel
docs.text:
\(K\) uses the exact line-source kernel by default (Engine.kernel=None resolves to "line" for this family). Every pair of segments is the double integral of the reduced kernel \(1/\sqrt{\lvert\mathbf x - \mathbf y\rvert^2 + a^2}\) over both segments: the current on the axis seen from the surface, which keeps the self term finite. For a straight wire the result is then independent of the segment length. The legacy point kernel (kernel="point") places each segment's current at its midpoint and uses the collocation self term \(2\ln(L/a)/L\); its grounding resistance converges to a value about 1–2 % below the uniform-current solution, at every segment length. The kernels page derives both and shows where the difference comes from.

A concrete encasement enters as the coefficient \(C\) (in Ω·m) of the electrode, the radial resistance of the shell times its length: every segment adds \(C/L_k\) to its diagonal entry (concrete shells).

docs.title: Network solve
docs.text:
The owner multiport matrix enters the augmented nodal system of the engine family:

  • electrodes bonded by ideal conductors share a node potential, and all owners of an electrode belong to its node;
  • finite conductors are branches with their resistance, internal and partial inductance and earth-return correction;
  • junctions are nodes without soil contact;
  • a current source injects \(+I\) at attached_to and \(-I\) at return_to;
  • a voltage source adds its current as an unknown and fixes \(\varphi_a - \varphi_r + Z_q I = U\) (modified nodal analysis), with the potentials \(\varphi_a\) and \(\varphi_r\) of its two terminals and its internal impedance \(Z_q\).

Source-free clusters float with zero net current. A lone passive electrode then carries no current (under the uniform ansatz its leakage would have to be zero everywhere) and reports the potential the field imposes; a bonded group of passive electrodes exchanges current between its members to stay one equipotential. The reported potential of an electrode is the length-weighted average over its wires, which equals the potential of its cluster. The impedances that can be read from the result (input, cluster and electrode impedance) are explained on sources and measurement.

docs.title: Field evaluation after the solve
docs.text:
FieldResult.potential(points) superposes the segment sources with the kernel of the solve:

  • with the line kernel, the exact line potential near a segment and the point form plus its quadrupole term farther away;
  • with the point kernel, point sources with a 1 mm distance floor.

Surface potentials next to a wire are therefore correct with the default kernel. The point form misses the field above a wire by several per cent when the segment length is comparable to the distance (kernels).

docs.title: Numerics
docs.text:
Convergence. With the line kernel a straight wire gives the same resistance at every segment length: the generated kernel check below shows a 3 m rod and a 10 m strip within about \(10^{-6}\) of their exact uniform-current resistance at every segment length it tests. A ring converges like the square of the segment length, because its chords approximate the circle (−0.24 % at 0.5 m, −1.5e-4 at 0.125 m for a ring of radius 2 m). The point kernel converges as well, but to a value 1–2 % below the uniform-current solution, so a segment-length study cannot reveal that offset (kernels). convergence_study runs such a study for any world.

Cost. The reaction matrix needs one kernel evaluation per pair of segments: \(O(N^2)\) time for \(N\) segments and \(8N^2\) bytes. It is kept in memory while it fits 1 GiB (\(N \le 11\,585\)) and evaluated in row blocks beyond. The network system has one unknown per straight wire, node and finite branch and is small. A galvanic world is solved once for all frequencies; inductive conductors add one complex solve per frequency. The line kernel takes 3.8 times as long as the point kernel for 16 house grids (\(N\) = 1920) with numba installed, 5.8 times without (kernels). Engine.max_segments (default diagnostics.HARD_LIMIT = 20 000 segments) stops a larger world before anything of size \(N\) is allocated. FieldResult.potential works in row blocks of at most 16 MiB, so large grids of field points do not allocate (points × sources × 3) tensors. Timings of whole networks are on the performance page.

Error estimates. The engine reports no error estimate of its own: within its model and with the line kernel the discretisation error is essentially the chord error of curved wires (the far-form remainder of the kernel stays near \(10^{-6}\) in the kernel check). The model error (the uniform current) is estimated by a second engine on the same world: compare_engines with mom, or diagnose() for the warnings that apply.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Two effects make up the accuracy of image, and they differ in size:

  • Impedances are accurate to about a per cent on grids and a few per cent on stars against mom on the same discretisation (one current per segment, same point kernel). Rings and single rods are exact by symmetry or nearly so.
  • Field quantities next to the electrode (touch, step and mesh voltages within a few metres of a grid corner or a star tip) can be off by about ten per cent next to a grid corner and by tens of per cent next to a star tip, with the step voltage under-estimated — the non-conservative direction for a safety assessment.

The generated tables below give the measured values; the kernel check at their end compares both kernels with the exact uniform-current resistance. References and all cases are on the validation page.

docs.title: Field quantities and the uniform-current ansatz
docs.text:
The uniform-current ansatz is impedance-grade, not field-grade. The impedance averages the potential over the electrode, and a wrong current distribution changes that average only to second order. A surface potential next to a grid corner or the tip of a star arm depends on the local current density, which the ansatz gets wrong: a real grid leaks more current at its corners and edges than in its interior, a star more at its tips. One current per wire line lets the outer lines of a grid carry more than the inner ones; along each wire, and along each arm of a star, the current is still uniform.

In the near-field table below the touch voltage has its feet 1 m outside the corner or tip, and the step starts at the surface point above the corner or tip and reaches 1 m outwards. The warning text and groundfield.postprocess.safety quote the step from 1 m to 2 m outside instead, next to the touch voltage at 1 m: at the grid corner the image family reads +6 % / −8 % with the default line kernel (+5 % / −8 % with the point kernel).

The safety helpers therefore warn: touch_voltage, step_voltage, touch_voltage_envelope and touch_voltage_at_part emit UniformCurrentFieldWarning when a result of the image family is evaluated within 5 m (NEAR_FIELD_DISTANCE_M) of a grid, mesh, star, strip, open polyline or a bonded multi-electrode cluster. For a safety assessment of such geometries solve with mom (or compare both); for impedances, rho-f samples and far-field potentials the image family is the right tool.

docs.title: Validity range
docs.text:
Condition Limit Behaviour outside Soil HomogeneousSoil; two layers go to image_2layer BackendCapabilityError for three distinct layers Frequency quasi-static, \(f < 1\) kHz not checked Thin wire \(a \ll\) segment length; \(L \le a\) rejected, \(L < 5a\) reported by diagnose() ValueError Burial every segment in the soil, \(2z > a\) ValueError naming the electrode Shallow segments, point kernel \(L \le 4z\) ShallowSegmentWarning with the bias Field quantities within 5 m of grids, stars, strip ends, bonded clusters ansatz error up to tens of per cent UniformCurrentFieldWarning Size Engine.max_segments, default 20 000 segments ResourceLimitError before allocation

Notes on the rows:

  • Frequency. The galvanic kernel is frequency independent, so the limit is not checked; above about 1 kHz the quasi-static model itself no longer holds.
  • Burial. The mirror image of a wire must not touch the wire itself, so a wire at depth \(z\) needs \(2z > a\).
  • Shallow segments. The point form of a segment's own image is biased high when the segment is longer than four times its depth; the warning quotes the bias in per cent. The default line kernel is not affected.
  • Field quantities. Use mom for touch, step and mesh voltages next to such electrodes, or compare both engines (Validation).
  • Size. The reaction matrix is kept in memory up to \(N = 11\,585\) segments and evaluated in blocks beyond; raise Engine.max_segments to solve a larger world on purpose.

What to use instead, and the other limits of the family: known limitations; the warnings: warnings reference.

docs.title: Literature
docs.text:
• Dwight, H. B. (1936). Calculation of resistances to ground. Electrical Engineering 55(12), 1319–1328 (the uniform-current, average-potential closed forms of groundfield.references.dwight1936).
  • Sunde, E. D. (1968). Earth Conduction Effects in Transmission Systems. Dover, New York, ch. 2–3 (image construction, average-potential method).
  • Tagg, G. F. (1964). Earth Resistances. George Newnes, London.
  • Heppe, R. J. (1979). Computation of potential at surface above an energized grid or other electrode, allowing for non-uniform current distribution. IEEE Transactions on Power Apparatus and Systems PAS-98(6), 1978–1989 (why the uniform-current ansatz misplaces surface potentials).
  • IEEE Std 80-2013. IEEE Guide for Safety in AC Substation Grounding (mesh and step voltage of grids; groundfield.references.ieee80).

Architecture decisions: ADR-0001, ADR-0015. API: groundfield.solver.image.solve_image (called through Engine.solve).

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
One current per straight wire (user decisions Q30 and Q44)

Before 2026.11 the uniform current belonged to the whole electrode. Since user decisions Q30 and Q44 it belongs to every straight wire of an electrode. With one current for the whole grid, the 20 m grid with 4 × 4 meshes read +3.9 % against mom, and the touch and step voltages 1 m and 1 m … 2 m outside its corner read +20 % / −21 % (now +6 % / −8 % with the line kernel, +5 % / −8 % with the point kernel). The generated tables are measured with one current per straight wire.

Kernel default (ADR-0015)

The exact line kernel is the default of the image family since 2026.11. The point kernel was the only kernel up to 0.15.0 and reproduces its numbers (kernel="point").

docs.title: image_2layer — two-layer soil
docs.text:
This page explains the default engine for two-layer soil: how the layer interface enters the Green's function, how electrodes in, at and through the interface are treated, how accurate the results are and which geometries next to the interface need care. Read the image page first; everything said there about the current model, the network solve and the field-grade limits applies here too.

At a glance

Soil TwoLayerSoil, or a MultiLayerSoil whose canonical stack has two layers; backend="image" forwards here Green's function Tagg / Sunde image series inside a layer; the two-layer Sommerfeld kernel of ADR-0007 once an electrode reaches the interface Current model one uniform leakage current per straight wire and soil layer (user decision Q30) Kernel exact line source (default); kernel="point" reproduces 0.15.0 Accuracy exact for its model; the current-model error of image; thin-wire limits right at the interface Status default for two-layer soil

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
The two-layer soil is an upper layer of resistivity \(\rho_1\) and thickness \(h_1\) over a half-space of resistivity \(\rho_2\). It is the simplest soil that captures the first-order effect of stratification — a dry or frozen top layer over wet ground, weathered soil over rock — without the identification problem of more layers, and it is the soil model of the AP1 catalogue. image_2layer solves it with the classical image series and the uniform-current model of image:

  • Soil. Two homogeneous, isotropic layers with a horizontal interface at depth \(h_1\), insulating air above; depth \(z\) counts positive downwards.
  • Quasi-static field, thin wires and average potential as for image.
  • Current model. One uniform leakage current per straight wire, and per soil layer for a wire that crosses the interface: a rod driven through \(h_1\) is one owner per layer, so its current density may differ above and below the interface.
  • Electrodes anywhere in the soil: in the top layer (image series), at or below the interface (Sommerfeld kernel).

docs.title: Reflection at the interface
docs.text:
The interface reflects the current field with the coefficient

\[ K = \frac{\rho_2 - \rho_1}{\rho_2 + \rho_1} \in (-1, 1). \]

\(K < 0\) (a conductive subsoil) draws current downwards and lowers the grounding impedance; \(K > 0\) (a resistive subsoil) pushes current into the top layer and raises it. For \(K = 0\) the soil is homogeneous.

docs.title: From the Sommerfeld integral to the image series
docs.text:
For a point current \(I\) at depth \(z_s\) and a field point at depth \(z\) and horizontal distance \(s\), both in the top layer, the potential is the Sommerfeld integral (the static limit of Sommerfeld's half-space problem; the general stack is on the mom_sommerfeld page)

\[ \varphi = \frac{\rho_1 I}{4\pi}\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-\lambda\lvert z-z_s\rvert} + e^{-\lambda(z+z_s)} + K\bigl[e^{-\lambda(2h_1-\lvert z-z_s\rvert)} + e^{-\lambda(2h_1-z-z_s)}\bigr]} {1 - K\,e^{-2\lambda h_1}}\,J_0(\lambda s)\,\mathrm d\lambda , \]

with the spatial frequency \(\lambda\) (in 1/m) and the Bessel function \(J_0\). The numerator holds the direct field, its air image and the first reflection at the interface; the denominator sums the reflections back and forth between the surface and the interface. For two layers the reflection coefficient is the constant \(K\), so three steps give a closed form:

  1. expand the denominator in a geometric series, \(1/(1 - K e^{-2\lambda h_1}) = \sum_{m\ge0} K^m e^{-2m\lambda h_1}\);
  2. multiply out: every term is \(K^n e^{-\lambda d}J_0(\lambda s)\) with a vertical distance \(d\) of \(2nh_1 \pm (z - z_s)\), \(2nh_1 + z + z_s\) or \(2nh_1 - z - z_s\);
  3. integrate each term with Lipschitz' integral \(\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda d}J_0(\lambda s)\,\mathrm d\lambda = 1/\sqrt{s^2+d^2}\), which is the potential of a point source at distance \(\sqrt{s^2 + d^2}\).

The result is the image series

\[ \varphi = \frac{\rho_1 I}{4\pi}\Biggl[\frac{1}{r_0^+} + \frac{1}{r_0^-} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} K^n\Bigl(\frac{1}{r_n^{++}} + \frac{1}{r_n^{+-}} + \frac{1}{r_n^{-+}} + \frac{1}{r_n^{--}}\Bigr)\Biggr], \qquad r_n^{\sigma\tau} = \sqrt{s^2 + (z - \sigma\,2nh_1 - \tau z_s)^2}, \]

with \(\sigma, \tau \in \{+1, -1\}\) and \(r_0^{\pm} = \sqrt{s^2 + (z \mp z_s)^2}\): the source and its air image, plus four images of weight \(K^n\) per order \(n\) at the depths \(\pm 2nh_1 \pm z_s\) (Stefanescu 1930; Tagg 1964; Sunde 1968). Each order is one more round trip of the current field between the surface and the interface. For \(K = 0\) only the \(n = 0\) pair remains and the result is that of image bit for bit.

docs.title: Electrodes in the top layer
docs.text:
Every segment carries the source, the air image and the image series. With the exact line kernel (default) all of them are line sources, treated like the direct pairs of the kernels page:

  • image pairs closer than six segment lengths are exact Galerkin integrals, blended into the far form up to 7.5 segment lengths;
  • beyond, the point form with the quadrupole term of the segment average, tapered off between 60 and 120 segment lengths of vertical distance, where it falls below the remainder of the far form;
  • the exact integral of an image pair takes the image's potential at the transverse distance \(\max(\rho_\perp, a)\) of the wire from the image's axis (\(\rho_\perp\) the distance of the two axes, \(a\) the wire radius): its average over the wire's circumference.

A straight wire then reproduces its uniform-current resistance at any segment length (Numerics). The point kernel sits about 1–2 % low, as in homogeneous soil.

docs.title: Electrodes that reach the interface
docs.text:
A rod driven through \(h_1\), or any wire at or below the interface, needs the Green's function with source and field point in different layers. As soon as one segment reaches the interface, image_2layer evaluates every pair with the two-layer Sommerfeld kernel of groundfield.coupling.layered_green (ADR-0007):

  • segments are first split at \(h_1\);
  • the reaction matrix is the homogeneous kernel scaled with the resistivity of the source layer, plus a layered correction \(\Delta Z\) evaluated by spectral quadrature, grouped by depth;
  • for a pair in different layers the direct term carries the transmitted resistivity \(2\rho_1\rho_2/(\rho_1+\rho_2)\), which keeps the matrix reciprocal;
  • with the line kernel \(\Delta Z\) is in line form as well: in two-layer soil it is an exact superposition of images in every layer combination (Sunde), and its images get the treatment of the Tagg / Sunde images above — the far quadrupole term over all pairs, the Galerkin integral for pairs within six segment lengths blended up to 7.5, the Galerkin self images on the diagonal — on top of the spectral values between midpoints.

Physically the leakage current density of a rod through the interface scales roughly with the conductivity of the layer it is in. Such an electrode is therefore one owner per layer, all in the electrode's cluster — the same model as two rods bonded at \(h_1\): the current density may differ above and below the interface, and the reported potential is the length-weighted average over the whole electrode. Every interface cut is kept, however short the piece beyond it: the Galerkin self term and the line kernel's parallel-pair integral are evaluated without cancellation for such pieces, so the impedance is continuous in the depth of a rod tip.

The diagonal entry of a segment is the layered correction at the wire radius, \(s = a\), with the interface image exchanged for its Galerkin integral; its closed-form \(1/R\) terms are evaluated at that radius (the default regularisation of layered_green, a clamp at \(h_1/200\), is meant for coincident points). The diagonal then equals the image solution to \(10^{-13}\), a ring is continuous through \(h_1\) (4.1826 Ω 1 µm above, 4.1805 Ω at \(h_1\)), and pairs closer than \(h_1/200\) are regularised at the 1 mm of the point forms they combine with.

docs.title: Truncation of the series
docs.text: The weights decay geometrically, so the neglected tail after order \(n\) is bounded by \(\lvert K\rvert^{n+1}/(1 - \lvert K\rvert)\). The series (one ImageSeries object shared by the solver, FieldResult.potential and solve_mutual_*) stops at the first \(n\) whose tail bound is below Engine.image_series_tol (default \(10^{-6}\)), or at Engine.image_max_terms (default 300) with a SeriesTruncationWarning. The number of terms depends only on \(\lvert K\rvert\), about \(\ln(\text{tol})/\ln\lvert K\rvert\); the generated table in the validation section lists it for typical contrasts — the default cap covers the AP1 corner soil 1000 / 30 Ω·m. metadata["series"] records the controls of the solve, and the post-solve field evaluation uses the same controls.

docs.title: Convergence with the segment length
docs.text:
With the line kernel a straight wire reproduces its exact uniform-current resistance at any segment length:

  • a 10 m strip at 0.5 m in 1000 / 50 Ω·m with \(h_1\) = 1 m: within 3.6e-6 from 2 m to 0.125 m segments, not monotonically; 0.1 m above \(h_1\) within 3.8e-6;
  • a ring 1 cm above a 1000 / 30 Ω·m interface: within 0.004 % of its exact thin ring;
  • the surface potential above the strip: within 8e-6 of the closed-form image sum;
  • a 75 m strip below a 0.5 m top layer: within 1.1e-5 at every segment length from 0.5 to 37.5 m in 500 / 100 and 1000 / 30 Ω·m (within 4.1e-6 from 1 m); over a more resistive lower layer, 100 / 500 Ω·m, +1.2e-4 at 0.5 m and +4.8e-5 at 1 m (the far terms of an image series that does not alternate);
  • a 6 m rod from 0.6 m through \(h_1\) = 5 m in 500 / 100, 1000 / 30 and 30 / 1000 Ω·m: within 6.7e-7 from 2 m to 0.125 m segments, and within 1.4e-6 of the exact two-owner value;
  • for wires in the upper layer, where both paths apply, the cross-layer path reproduces the series to 1.8e-7.

About 2e-6 of the strip's rest is the reduced kernel that the soil-surface image keeps. The point kernel converges to a value 1–2 % low.

docs.title: Far images in point form
docs.text:
Engine(image_far_field="point") (the author's decision of 2026-11-15) leaves out the dense far term: the far Tagg / Sunde images and the far images of the layered correction are point sources, while the near image pairs — within 7.5 segment lengths, a segment's own images included — stay Galerkin integrals blended into the point form, on the series and the cross-layer path alike. It saves the far-image work (cost on the kernels page) and against the default moves

  • networks by 3e-6 … 4.3e-4 (16 house grids 0.4 m above a 1000 / 10 Ω·m interface: 4.3e-4; 16 house grids with a 75 m bare conductor in two pieces below a 0.5 m top layer: within 4e-6),
  • single wires near the interface by up to 4e-4 and the surface potential above them by up to 0.8 %.

A wire on the interface is up to 3e-4 apart on the two paths in this form (the default: 1.3e-6), because the far terms the point form leaves out are split differently between the two decompositions. The continuous switch and the transverse distance of near image pairs stay, so "point" is not the result of the earlier code: within the upper layer it differs from it by up to 2.3e-4. metadata["series"] records the form, the post-solve field evaluation and solve_mutual_* use it, and any value other than "quadrupole" or "point" raises ValueError.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: The series path costs the image terms of every pair: their number grows with the contrast (table below). The cross-layer path costs one spectral evaluation per pair of segment depths. Large depth groups (all house grids at one depth, for example) are planned once and evaluated in row chunks, so the path needs the memory of the series path — the reaction matrix, \(16N^2\) bytes, within the budget and row blocks beyond it. The boundary-value system of the spectral amplitudes is eliminated in closed form, vectorised over the quadrature nodes. Timings: kernels and performance.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Against mom on the same segments, electrodes in the top layer agree to 0.37 % (B6) and a rod through the interface to 0.38 % (B7): the difference is the uniform-current ansatz (both run with the point kernel in that comparison). For straight wires the line kernel reproduces the exact uniform-current resistance (kernel check at the end of the generated block). The field-grade limits of the ansatz next to grids and stars are those of image. Next to the interface the thin-wire model itself has limits, measured against a solid-rod and a solid-torus model (Validity range).

Generated from the benchmark run measured on 2026-11-16 with groundfield 2026.11.0 (Python 3.12.16, NumPy 2.4.4, SciPy 1.17.1, numba installed: yes; Darwin arm64); bounds from tests/benchmarks/tolerances.py. Details and all cases: Validation and benchmarks.

docs.title: Validity range
docs.text:
Condition Limit Behaviour outside Soil two distinct layers; \(\rho_1 = \rho_2\) is solved as homogeneous BackendCapabilityError for three distinct layers (use mom_sommerfeld) Contrast \(\lvert K\rvert < 1\); terms grow like \(\ln(\text{tol}) / \ln\lvert K\rvert\) SeriesTruncationWarning at image_max_terms Electrodes anywhere in the soil; at or through \(h_1\) via the slower Sommerfeld path — Rod ends head and tip more than one wire radius from \(h_1\) InterfaceContactWarning Horizontal wires next to \(h_1\) axis outside the reach of the interface (3.9 wire radii at contrast 33) InterfaceContactWarning Point kernel near \(h_1\) horizontal wires at least 0.6 segment lengths from \(h_1\) PointKernelInterfaceWarning; within 0.387: BackendCapabilityError Thin wire, burial, shallow segments as for image ValueError / ShallowSegmentWarning Field quantities near grids, stars, strip ends uniform-current ansatz, see image UniformCurrentFieldWarning Frequency quasi-static, \(f < 1\) kHz —

The two thin-wire limits at the interface and the point-kernel limit are explained below. What to do instead, and the other limits of the family: known limitations of the current ansatz and kernels and of the soil layers; the warnings and their reach: warnings reference.

docs.title: Rod ends at the interface: a limit of the thin-wire model
docs.text:
The thin wire has no end face. A rod that ends exactly at \(h_1\) is a wire entirely in the upper layer; one that reaches past it by a fraction of its radius touches the lower layer through a short piece only. The solid rod is continuous in between, because its flat end face carries the contact. Against an axisymmetric finite-volume model of the solid rod (4.5 m, \(a\) = 8 mm, 1000 / 30 Ω·m) the line kernel reads:

Tip below \(h_1\) Solid rod Thin wire −16 mm 190.2 Ω +3.3 % −8 mm 188.9 Ω +3.9 % −1 mm 182.8 Ω +7.2 % 0 161.4 Ω +21.4 % +1 mm 156.3 Ω −4.6 % +4 mm 148.5 Ω −1.2 % +8 mm 141.2 Ω +0.7 % +16 mm 130.2 Ω +2.1 %

The point kernel and mom behave alike (+19.0 … +20.5 % at 0). Every segment backend therefore warns with InterfaceContactWarning when a rod head or tip lies within one wire radius of an interface, and diagnose() lists it under interface_contact. Keep rod ends a few wire radii from an interface, or bracket the result by moving the end by ±2 wire radii; fem models the solid rod.

docs.title: Horizontal wires next to the interface
docs.text: A horizontal wire has the same kind of limit: next to a more conductive layer the solid wire's current crowds to its near side, which the current on the axis cannot follow. A ring (\(a\) = 5 mm) reads +1.2 % at 3 wire radii, +3.6 % at 2 and +8.6 % at 1.5 radii above a layer 33 times more conductive, against the solid torus of the axisymmetric fem. Within the reach of the interface — 3.9 radii at that contrast, tabulated under InterfaceContactWarning in the warnings reference — the solve warns with InterfaceContactWarning as well.

docs.title: Point kernel next to the interface
docs.text:
With kernel="point" (and in the mom family, which shares the point form) a horizontal wire just below or above \(h_1\) needs segments much shorter than twice its distance to the interface:

  • 5 cm below \(h_1\), a ring of radius 3 m gives 29.7 Ω at ds = 0.5 m against 54.7 Ω at ds = 0.025 m, while the line kernel gives 55.6–55.7 Ω at every segment length (tests/test_cross_layer_line_kernel.py);
  • above \(h_1\) the point form takes the image of a segment in the interface as a point source: a ring 1 µm / 1 cm above \(h_1 = 5\) m read −1931 / −57.9 Ω (line kernel 4.18 / 15.18 Ω).

On either side of the interface a wire closer than 0.387 segment lengths therefore raises BackendCapabilityError, and one within 0.6 segment lengths warns with PointKernelInterfaceWarning. The default line kernel needs no such care.

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
Line-source images (wave 3 of the 2026.11 work, audit W3A-02)

Before wave 3 of the 2026.11 work, far images were point sources (which Engine.image_far_field = "point" offers in its own form today), and on the cross-layer path only the interface image of near pairs in one layer was a Galerkin integral. The reduced kernel of direct pairs, applied to images, left out \(a^2/(2d^2)\) of an image \(d\) away; audit W3A-02 replaced it by the transverse distance. Measured before against now:

  • the 10 m strip at 0.5 m in 1000 / 50 Ω·m: up to +5.1e-4 before; 0.1 m above \(h_1\): +6.8e-5 with the reduced kernel on the images;
  • the ring 1 cm above a 1000 / 30 Ω·m interface: +1.60 % against its exact thin ring before (now −0.004 %); the point-kernel example ring 1 cm above \(h_1 = 5\) m: line kernel 15.42 Ω before audit W3A-02, 15.18 Ω now;
  • the surface potential above the strip: up to 0.94 % before (the alternating series of a more conductive lower layer amplifies the error of its far images);
  • the rod through the interface: 1.3e-4 … 2.4e-4 over the segment lengths before; the cross-layer path against the series in the upper layer: up to 6.2e-4 before.
Point form of the far images (audits W3R2A-01, W3R2A-02, user decision D2)

Up to audit W3R2A-01 the cross-layer path kept the line form of the interface image only, as before wave 3; the own surface and transmitted images of a segment below the interface were point sources, and the 75 m strip below a 0.5 m top layer read −1.0e-3 at a segment length of 2.5 m and −58 % at 37.5 m (16 house grids with a 75 m bare conductor in two pieces: +1.1 % against the default). The point form keeps the continuous switch of user decision D2, which blends up to 7.5 segment lengths where the base switched at six in one step; hence its difference of up to 2.3e-4 from the code before wave 3. Audit W3R2A-02 added the ValueError for other values of image_far_field.

Series length and memory (findings 10.25, 10.56)

Up to 0.15.0 the post-solve field evaluation capped the series at 100 terms (finding 10.25); it now uses the controls of the solve. Before finding 10.56 the cross-layer path needed 41 instead of 18 bytes per segment pair for 16 house grids below \(h_1\), and had no row blocks; one LAPACK solve per quadrature node took half the time of the path before the closed-form elimination.

Rods through the interface (finding 10.15, audits A2S-01, A3S-01)

Up to 0.15.0 one uniform density ran across the interface, which put a 12 m rod through \(h_1 = 5\) m in 1000 / 30 Ω·m soil 566 % above the per-segment mom solution (tests/test_cross_layer_owners.py); since 2026.11 the electrode is one owner per layer (finding 10.15).

Earlier in 2026.11, cuts that would leave a piece shorter than the wire diameter were dropped, which ignored the contact with the other layer: a 4.5 m rod in 1000 / 30 Ω·m read 195.0 Ω with its tip 15.9 mm into the lower layer and 128.6 Ω at 16.1 mm (second adversarial audit, A2S-01).

The default regularisation of layered_green clamps the closed-form \(1/R\) terms at \(h_1/200\) (25 mm for \(h_1 = 5\) m). On the diagonal it took 68–84 % of the layered correction of every piece within \(h_1/400\) of the interface: a ring of radius 3 m at \(h_1 = 5\) m read −5.29 Ω, and the contact values of a rod tip were 10–32 % low (third adversarial audit, A3S-01). The diagonal is now evaluated at the wire radius.

Horizontal wires next to the interface (audits W4A-07, W4R2A-04)

The ring next to a layer 33 times more conductive was measured against the solid torus of the axisymmetric fem in audit W4A-07; the reach of the interface, 3.9 radii at that contrast, comes from audit W4R2A-04.

docs.title: mom — point-matching method of moments
docs.text:
This page explains the engine that solves for one current per segment: the integral equation behind it, the point-matching scheme, why it is the check of the image family's current model rather than an accuracy reference, and its limits. Read it when you use mom for touch and step voltages near grids and stars, or to cross-check image and image_2layer.

At a glance

Soil homogeneous or two layers (a MultiLayerSoil whose canonical stack has at most two layers) Green's function the kernels of the image family: point source plus air image, Tagg / Sunde series, the Sommerfeld kernel of ADR-0007 across the interface Current model one pulse current per segment Testing delta at the segment midpoints (point matching, collocation) with a point-source near field Kernel point only (an explicit kernel="line" raises BackendCapabilityError) Accuracy resolves the current distribution; absolute impedances 0.2 … 2 % low, drifting under refinement (Numerics) Status current; bem is a deprecated name that runs it

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
mom solves the same physical problem as the image family — the quasi-static current field of thin-wire electrodes in homogeneous or two-layer soil, see image and image_2layer — but drops the uniform-current ansatz. Each segment carries its own leakage current, so the solve resolves how current distributes along an electrode (end and corner effects), between the electrodes of a bonded cluster and across a layer interface.

Its role in the family is to check the current model of the image family on the same kernel and discretisation. It is not an accuracy reference for impedances at the 1 % level, which its point-source near field does not reach.

docs.title: The integral equation
docs.text:
With the Green's function \(G(\mathbf r, \mathbf r')\) of the soil (the potential at \(\mathbf r\) per ampere injected at \(\mathbf r'\), homogeneous or two-layer, see image and image_2layer) the potential on the surface of a thin wire is the integral of the leakage current density \(\iota(l)\) (in A/m, \(l\) the arc length) along all wires,

\[ \varphi(\mathbf r) = \int_{\text{wires}} G(\mathbf r, \mathbf r')\,\iota(l')\,\mathrm dl' . \]

Every point of an electrode must sit at the potential of its cluster, so the left-hand side is known on the wires and \(\iota\) is the unknown: a Fredholm integral equation of the first kind. Physically, the current distributes itself so that the metal is an equipotential.

docs.title: Method of moments with point matching
docs.text:
The method of moments (Harrington 1968) expands \(\iota\) in basis functions and enforces the equation with test functions. mom uses the simplest choice:

  • basis: one constant current \(I_j\) per segment \(j\) (pulse functions);
  • testing: the equation at the segment midpoints (delta functions) — point matching, or collocation.

The reaction matrix, the potential at midpoint \(i\) per ampere on segment \(j\), is

\[ Z_{ij} = \frac{\rho}{4\pi}\,K_{ij},\qquad K_{ij} = \begin{cases} \text{potential at midpoint } i \text{ of a unit point source at midpoint } j, & i \ne j,\\[2pt] 2\ln(L_i/a_i)/L_i + \text{images}, & i = j, \end{cases} \]

with \(L_i\) the length and \(a_i\) the wire radius of segment \(i\). The off-diagonal uses the point kernel of the soil (its images included); the diagonal uses the potential of the uniformly loaded segment on its own surface (the Galerkin self term for very short segments, \(L < 2.99\,a\)). The matrix is assembled directly, entry by entry.

This is not a Galerkin scheme. Galerkin testing would average the potential over each segment and integrate each source along its segment (the exact line kernel of the image family does exactly that, for a uniform current). metadata["solver"] = "point_matching" says so.

docs.title: Network solve
docs.text:
The segment currents \(\mathbf I_\text{seg}\) and the node potentials \(\boldsymbol\varphi_n\) enter the bordered system

\[ \begin{bmatrix} Z & -C \\ C^{\top} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf I_\text{seg} \\ \boldsymbol\varphi_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf 0 \\ \mathbf I_\text{in} \end{bmatrix}, \]

with the incidence matrix \(C\) (\(C_{in} = 1\) if segment \(i\) belongs to node \(n\)) and the injected node currents \(\mathbf I_\text{in}\), plus one row and column per finite conductor branch, as in the engine family. The first block row says that every midpoint of a node sits at the node potential, the second that the segment currents of a node add up to its injected current. \(Z\) is symmetric; the bordered matrix as assembled is not, and is solved with a dense LU.

Every node with soil contact is an unknown, also without a source: a source-free cluster floats with zero net current, so transfer impedances are reciprocal (B8) and passive networks carry their equalising currents. The node potential is reported as the mean of its segment potentials, which point matching makes equal.

mom runs the shared pipeline of the image family (discretise, inject, topology, branches; ADR-0014): two-terminal sources (return_to), voltage sources (one current unknown and one constraint row each), junction nodes and inductive conductors behave exactly as with image.

docs.title: Concrete-encased wires
docs.text: A concrete-encased wire (concrete_shell_coefficient_ohm_m \(= C\), in Ω·m; ADR-0012) adds the radial resistance of each segment's shell, \(C/\Delta s_k\) for a segment of length \(\Delta s_k\), to the segment's diagonal entry, and the drop \(C I_k/\Delta s_k\) to its potential: the reported potential is that of the metal. With one owner per segment the image family solves the same system: the two agree to \(7\cdot10^{-16}\) with shells, in homogeneous, two-layer and cross-layer soil, and a ring, whose current stays uniform, rises by exactly \(C/(2\pi r)\) (to \(10^{-14}\); see concrete shells).

docs.title: Accuracy of the point-matching scheme
docs.text:
The point-source near field underestimates the coupling of neighbouring segments of the same wire. For a collinear neighbour of length \(\Delta s\), the exact potential at the midpoint is the line integral \(\frac{1}{\Delta s}\int_{\Delta s/2}^{3\Delta s/2}\mathrm dx/x = \ln 3/\Delta s\) per unit current; the point source gives \(1/\Delta s\) (−9 %). The self image of a shallow segment is a point image, too. Both errors scale with the near-field terms themselves, so mom does not converge to the thin-wire limit under refinement: the B2 rod lies below the independent thin-wire Galerkin solution and the gap grows as the segments get shorter (generated table below). Consequences:

  • mom against image with kernel="point" isolates the effect of the current model: both use the same kernel, so their difference is the ansatz (validation: B6, B10, B13 and the field quantities).
  • mom against image with the default line kernel mixes the ansatz with the 1–2 % kernel difference.
  • Absolute impedances at the 1 % level are better taken from the image family with the line kernel where the ansatz holds (rings, rods, compact electrodes), or from a convergence study (convergence_study).

ShallowSegmentWarning is emitted when a segment is longer than four times its depth, because the point self image is then biased high.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text: The matrix is dense, \(N \times N\) for \(N\) segments, and its LU factorisation costs \(O(N^3)\): it dominates for large \(N\), and an inductive world needs one factorisation per frequency. Memory and timings are on the performance page.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
mom resolves the current distribution that the image family assumes uniform, so near-field quantities next to grid corners and star tips are its strength (the comparison table is on the image page). Its absolute impedances carry the point-kernel deficit: the B2 rod 1.4 % below the thin-wire limit at the finest segment length, the B3 ring 1.2 % below its closed form. Reciprocity holds to \(10^{-8}\).

Generated from the benchmark run measured on 2026-11-16 with groundfield 2026.11.0 (Python 3.12.16, NumPy 2.4.4, SciPy 1.17.1, numba installed: yes; Darwin arm64); bounds from tests/benchmarks/tolerances.py. Details and all cases: Validation and benchmarks.

docs.title: Validity range
docs.text:
Condition Limit Behaviour outside Soil one or two distinct layers BackendCapabilityError for three distinct layers (use mom_sommerfeld) Kernel point BackendCapabilityError for an explicit kernel="line" Concrete shells thin shell per segment, \(C/\Delta s\) on the diagonal (ADR-0012) — Horizontal wires near \(h_1\), point form at least 0.6 segment lengths from \(h_1\), on either side PointKernelInterfaceWarning; within 0.387: BackendCapabilityError Rod ends at an interface head and tip more than one wire radius away (+21 % with the tip at \(h_1\)) InterfaceContactWarning Horizontal wires next to an interface axis outside the reach (3.9 wire radii at contrast 33; +3.6 % at 2 radii) InterfaceContactWarning Size dense \(N \times N\) matrix, one LU per inductive frequency, \(O(N^3)\) memory and time (performance) Frequency quasi-static, \(f < 1\) kHz —

The interface limits are those of every thin-wire engine: the point form of the interface image needs short segments next to \(h_1\), and the thin wire has no end face and no current crowding to its near side; they are explained on the image_2layer page. What to do instead, and the other limits: known limitations of the current ansatz and kernels and of the soil layers; the warnings: warnings reference.

docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
Assembly, naming and passive clusters (findings 10.29, 10.31, 10.59)
  • Up to 0.15.0 the reaction matrix was extracted by applying the image-family operator to an identity matrix, an \(O(N^3)\) product per image term with bit-identical entries; it is now assembled directly (finding 10.59).
  • Since review pass 10 the documentation and metadata["solver"] = "point_matching" call the scheme point matching, not Galerkin (finding 10.31).
  • Up to 0.15.0 passive clusters were dropped from the unknowns and read back as an unweighted field mean, which broke reciprocity; every node with soil contact is now an unknown (finding 10.29).
Concrete shells (since 2026.11)

Up to 2026.11 mom rejected concrete-encased electrodes. Since then it carries the per-segment shell term of ADR-0012.

docs.title: mom_sommerfeld — layered Green's function by quadrature
docs.text:
This page explains the engine for soils of three and more layers: the layered Green's function as a Sommerfeld integral, how the integral is evaluated without silent truncation, what it costs and where its limits are. Read it when your soil model has more than two layers, or when you want the kernel reference for two-layer soil.

At a glance

Soil any number of layers (canonical stack; equal adjacent layers merged) Green's function the Sommerfeld integral with the recursive reflection coefficient, evaluated numerically Current model one pulse current per segment, point matching (the scheme of mom) Kernel point only Options MomSommerfeldOptions: lambda_max_factor, epsabs, epsrel, max_osc_panels, tabulate Accuracy the kernel to \(10^{-9}\) or better; the point-matching deficit of mom on impedances Status current; the only engine for three or more distinct layers

docs.title: What it solves
docs.text:
mom_sommerfeld computes the quasi-static current field of thin-wire electrodes in a horizontally stratified half-space: layers \(i = 1 \dots n\) of resistivity \(\rho_i\) and thickness \(h_i\), the last one infinite, insulating air above. It evaluates the layered Green's function without expansion or fit: the reflection coefficient \(\Gamma_1(\lambda)\) of the whole stack enters the Sommerfeld integral as it is, and the integral is computed by quadrature for every pair of segments.

That makes it the reference for the kernel: on two-layer soil it must reproduce the Tagg / Sunde series of mom on the same discretisation, and for three and more layers it is the only kernel there is. The discretisation and the current model are those of mom (one current per segment, point matching), so it is not an independent check of the point-matching scheme.

Concrete-encased wires carry the per-segment shell term of mom (ADR-0012). On two-layer soil the two engines agree to about \(10^{-8}\) with and without shells where neither engine warns; under SeriesTruncationWarning (a truncated series) they can differ by 9 %. An encased ring in three layers rises by exactly \(C/(2\pi r)\) over the bare ring of the outer radius (\(C\) the shell coefficient, \(r\) the ring radius).

docs.title: The Sommerfeld integral of a layered soil
docs.text:
The potential of a point current \(I\) at depth \(z_s\) in the top layer, observed at horizontal distance \(s\) and depth \(z\) in the top layer, is

\[ \varphi = \frac{\rho_1 I}{4\pi}\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-\lambda\lvert z-z_s\rvert} + e^{-\lambda(z+z_s)} + \Gamma_1(\lambda)\bigl[e^{-\lambda(2h_1-\lvert z-z_s\rvert)} + e^{-\lambda(2h_1-z-z_s)}\bigr]} {1 - \Gamma_1(\lambda)\,e^{-2\lambda h_1}}\,J_0(\lambda s)\,\mathrm d\lambda , \]

with the spatial frequency \(\lambda\) (in 1/m) and the Bessel function \(J_0\). It is the static limit of Sommerfeld's (1909) half-space problem: the potential is decomposed into cylindrical waves \(J_0(\lambda s)\), each of which is reflected by the stack below the top layer with the coefficient \(\Gamma_1(\lambda)\). The numerator holds the direct field, its air image and the first reflection; the denominator sums the reflections back and forth between the surface and the first interface.

docs.title: The reflection coefficient of the stack
docs.text:
The reflection coefficient seen from the top layer is built bottom-up from the interface coefficients \(K_i = (\rho_{i+1}-\rho_i)/(\rho_{i+1}+\rho_i)\) of the interfaces \(i = 1 \dots n-1\):

\[ \Gamma_{n-1} = K_{n-1},\qquad \Gamma_i(\lambda) = \frac{K_i + \Gamma_{i+1}(\lambda)\,e^{-2\lambda h_{i+1}}} {1 + K_i\,\Gamma_{i+1}(\lambda)\,e^{-2\lambda h_{i+1}}}. \]

Each step combines the reflection at interface \(i\) with what comes back, attenuated by the round trip \(e^{-2\lambda h_{i+1}}\) through layer \(i+1\), from the stack below it. Short wavelengths (large \(\lambda\)) see only the first interface, \(\Gamma_1(\infty) = K_1\); long wavelengths see the deep layers. \(\Gamma_1\) is therefore constant only for two layers: for \(n = 2\) the integral expands into the image series of image_2layer, for \(n \ge 3\) no closed form exists.

docs.title: Electrodes and layers
docs.text: For \(n = 2\) with every segment in the top layer the diagonal of the reaction matrix is the series diagonal of mom, and the off-diagonal entries are quadratures; a world with an electrode at or below the interface is delegated to the two-layer Sommerfeld kernel of groundfield.coupling.layered_green (ADR-0007). For \(n \ge 3\) every segment must lie in the top layer.

docs.title: Quadrature
docs.text:
The integrand does not decay for two points at the same depth: the direct term \(e^{-\lambda\lvert z-z_s\rvert}J_0(\lambda s)\) with \(z = z_s\) converges only through the oscillation of \(J_0\), and a truncation at \(\lambda_\text{max}\) leaves an error of order \(\sqrt{2/(\pi\lambda_\text{max}s)}\) that no quadrature tolerance can remove. The kernel is therefore split with Lipschitz' integral \(\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda d}J_0(\lambda s)\,\mathrm d\lambda = (s^2+d^2)^{-1/2}\):

  1. the direct term (\(d = \lvert z - z_s\rvert\)), its air image (\(d = z + z_s\)) and the leading interface reflection with \(\Gamma_1(\infty) = K_1\) (\(d = 2h_1 - z - z_s\)) are taken in closed form;
  2. the remainder decays at least like \(e^{-\lambda d_\text{rem}}\) with a strictly positive length \(d_\text{rem}\), even when both points sit on the interface, so its truncation error is bounded by \(e^{-\lambda_\text{max}d_\text{rem}}\);
  3. the remainder is integrated with Gauss–Legendre panels on a grid graded towards \(\lambda = 0\) (exponentials and \(\Gamma_1\)), with a geometric family down to the scale \((1-\Gamma_1(0))/(2h_1)\) of the reflection multiplier (which collapses for \(\lvert K_1\rvert \to 1\)), and subdivided at the half period \(\pi/s\) of \(J_0\);
  4. the grid is refined until two successive grids agree within \(\max(\varepsilon_\text{abs}, \varepsilon_\text{rel}\lvert G\rvert)\), \(G\) the kernel value.

Failing that is reported, never silent: SommerfeldConvergenceWarning names the achieved and the requested tolerance; a capped oscillation budget (max_osc_panels) counts as non-convergence; metadata["converged"], ["converged_per_frequency"] and ["n_unconverged_entries"] record it. Distances are floored at 1 mm like in the image family; keep segment midpoints a few millimetres clear of an interface, where the floor would saturate the interface term.

docs.title: Cost: distinct pairs and depth-group tables
docs.text: Every distinct argument \((s, \lvert z-z_s\rvert, z+z_s)\) is integrated once. For \(n \ge 3\) the pairs of a depth class in the top layer share one function \(G(s)\) of the horizontal distance alone; with tabulate=True (the default, option of MomSommerfeldOptions) its smooth quadrature remainder is tabulated on 64 log-spaced nodes per decade of \(s\) and interpolated with a cubic spline in \(\ln s\), while the closed-form terms stay exact. Each table is checked at eight interval midpoints against the pointwise quadrature to \(10^{-7}\) of \(\lvert G\rvert\), refined once, and dropped in favour of pointwise quadrature when it fails. Benchmark B12 bounds the effect on the assembled matrix and the impedance by \(10^{-6}\) (generated table below); the measured speed-up is on the performance page. The current model adds the dense LU of mom, \(O(N^3)\) for \(N\) segments.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The kernel is checked against independent references: the exact Tagg / Sunde series for two layers (B4, within 2.0e-10 over 1050 points) and mpmath quadrature for three layers (B5, within 2.3e-13). On the same segments it reproduces mom on two-layer soil to about \(10^{-8}\) (B6, B7, B11). Impedances carry the point-matching deficit of mom, which these checks do not measure.

Generated from the benchmark run measured on 2026-11-16 with groundfield 2026.11.0 (Python 3.12.16, NumPy 2.4.4, SciPy 1.17.1, numba installed: yes; Darwin arm64); bounds from tests/benchmarks/tolerances.py. Details and all cases: Validation and benchmarks.

Benchmark Measure Bound Worst measured Cases Status Note B4 Two-layer Sommerfeld kernel rel. kernel error, or SommerfeldConvergenceWarning 1e-9 2.0e-10 1 pass never silent (10.47); no warning for h_1 >= 0.2 m B5 Three-layer Sommerfeld kernel rel. kernel error 1e-10 2.3e-13 2 pass B6 Top-layer electrodes, two-layer soil abs(Z/Z_ref - 1) 1e-7 1.2e-8 10 pass kernel check B7 Rod through the layer interface abs(Z/Z_ref - 1) 1e-7 1.4e-10 2 pass kernel check B8 Two-port reciprocity abs(Z_AB/Z_BA - 1) 1e-7 4.4e-16 2 pass B9 Limits of the layered kernels (equal_rho_integral) abs(Z/Z_ref - 1) 1e-10 0 3 pass image_2layer, mom, mom_sommerfeld, cim, bem B9 Limits of the layered kernels (layer_limit_integral) abs(Z/Z_ref - 1) 0.1 % 5.1e-4 2 pass physical limit B11 Grid refinement abs(Z/Z_mom - 1) at ds = 5 m 1e-7 7.5e-10 1 pass kernel check B12 Three-layer grid max abs(Z_ij,tab / Z_ij - 1) and abs(Z_g1,tab / Z_g1 - 1) 1e-6 6.9e-9 4 pass depth-group tabulation of the reflected kernel (10.61)

docs.text:
Condition Limit Behaviour outside Soil any canonical stack — Electrodes, \(n \ge 3\) every segment in the top layer ValueError Electrodes, \(n = 2\) anywhere (cross-layer path of layered_green) — Quadrature converged within epsrel / epsabs (defaults \(10^{-7}\) / \(10^{-9}\)) SommerfeldConvergenceWarning, metadata["converged"] = False Interface distance segment midpoints more than about 1 mm from an interface interface term saturated by the 1 mm floor Line kernel not supported BackendCapabilityError Concrete shells thin shell per segment, as in mom — Size dense matrix, one quadrature per distinct pair argument seconds to minutes (performance) Frequency quasi-static, \(f < 1\) kHz —

The thin-wire limits next to an interface (rod ends, horizontal wires, the point form near \(h_1\)) are those of mom. What to do instead, and the other limits: known limitations of the current ansatz and kernels and of the soil layers; the warnings: warnings reference.

docs.title: Literature
docs.text:

  • Watson, G. N. (1944). A Treatise on the Theory of Bessel Functions, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press, §13.2 (Lipschitz' integral).
  • Sunde, E. D. (1968). Earth Conduction Effects in Transmission Systems. Dover, New York, sect. 3.5 (the layered-earth integral and its recursive reflection coefficient).
  • Lucas, S. K., & Stone, H. A. (1995). Evaluating infinite integrals involving Bessel functions of arbitrary order. Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 64 (panel quadrature between the zeros of \(J_0\)).
  • Zou, J., Du, X., & Zhou, C. (2015). Fast calculation of the Green function of a point current source in a horizontal layered soil with a new complex path. IEEE Transactions on Magnetics 51(3) (a complex contour, an alternative to the analytic extraction; not implemented).
