docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
Concrete shells against mom (since 2026.11; audits W2B-07, W2R2-09)

Since 2026.11 concrete-encased wires carry the per-segment shell term of mom (ADR-0012). On two-layer soil the two engines agree with and without shells:

  • \(10^{-9}\) … \(1.5\cdot10^{-8}\) for a 10 m grid in four soils (audit W2B-07);
  • \(9\cdot10^{-8}\) with the layer interface 0.2 m below the wires, under PointKernelInterfaceWarning, and 9 % for a truncated series under SeriesTruncationWarning (audit W2R2-09);
  • the shell increments agree to \(1.4\cdot10^{-10}\), the agreement of the two kernels.
Convergence reporting and tabulation (findings 10.47, 10.61)

SommerfeldConvergenceWarning and the converged metadata were added by finding 10.47, so a quadrature that does not converge is never silent. The depth-group tabulation with its midpoint check and fallback is finding 10.61.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This page shows how to install groundfield for use (from PyPI, with the optional extras you need) and for development (from a Git checkout with Poetry). When it is installed, continue with the quickstart.

groundfield runs on Python 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14 on any operating system. The core dependencies are numpy, scipy, pydantic, sympy, pandas and matplotlib.

docs.title: From PyPI
docs.text:
pip install groundfield

Check the installation:

python -c "import groundfield; print(groundfield.__version__)"

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
The core package solves every engine except the three-dimensional model of fem. Four extras add features:

Extra Installs Needed for fast numba compiled kernels for the two-layer image series and the far field of the exact line-source kernel; same results, shorter solve times fem3d scikit-fem, pyamg the three-dimensional model of the experimental fem backend: every world that is not rods on one axis and rings around it (fem) geo requests, shapely, pyproj building footprints from OpenStreetMap (Overpass), WGS84 → local coordinates, polygon geometry (Geo / OSM, ADR-0011) groundinsight groundinsight live groundinsight.BusType objects and writing into the groundinsight SQLite store; the JSON export works without it (IO and groundinsight, ADR-0008) 
pip install "groundfield[fast]"                            # recommended for large studies
pip install "groundfield[fast,fem3d,geo,groundinsight]"    # all extras

A missing extra is not an error until you call a function that needs it: then groundfield raises an ImportError that names the extra to install (import groundfield.geo itself works without geo). Without fast, every kernel runs in numpy. The how-to guide install the optional extras shows how to check what an environment has.

docs.title: From a Git checkout (development)
docs.text:
The project uses Poetry (2.x) and a committed lock file:

git clone https://github.com/Ce1ectric/groundfield.git
cd groundfield
poetry install                     # package + dev group
poetry install --extras "geo fast" # optional extras
poetry install --all-extras        # every extra, fem3d included

The dev group contains pytest (with pytest-cov and pytest-xdist), ruff, mypy, ipykernel, and groundinsight, requests, shapely and pyproj, so the bridge and OSM tests run end to end.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
poetry run pytest -n auto                  # full suite, parallel
poetry run pytest -m "not slow"            # skip long-running tests
poetry run pytest --run-benchmark tests/benchmarks   # engine benchmark suite
poetry run pytest --run-network            # tests that query Overpass

The markers finding, slow, network, benchmark and golden are registered in pyproject.toml; pytest --finding 10.28 selects the tests of one review finding.

docs.title: Code standards
docs.text:
poetry run ruff format .
poetry run ruff check --select F,E9,B,W605 .   # blocking subset in CI
poetry run mypy                                # report only for now

The same checks run as pre-commit hooks (.pre-commit-config.yaml; install pre-commit with pipx, then pre-commit install). Docstrings follow the NumPy convention.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
poetry install --with docs
poetry run mkdocs serve           # live preview on http://127.0.0.1:8000
poetry run mkdocs build --strict  # what CI runs

The docs group contains MkDocs with Material, mkdocstrings, mkdocs-jupyter (renders the tutorial notebooks with their stored outputs) and mike (versioned deployment). Python code blocks in the Markdown pages are executed by the test suite, so a snippet that no longer matches the API fails CI; see the how-to guide on contributing to the documentation for the rules.

docs.title: Versions and releases
docs.text:
Releases use calendar versioning YYYY.M.MICRO in its PEP 440 form: 2026.11.0 is the first release of November 2026, 2026.11.1 the second, 2027.1.0 the first of January 2027. Releases up to 0.15.0 used semantic versioning. Deprecated names keep working for at least two releases and six months; see Deprecations.

For maintainers: cutting a release

The release tool lives in the repository and is not installed with the package:

python scripts/release.py calver --dry-run   # all checks, prints the plan
python scripts/release.py calver             # writes, commits, tags
git push origin main
git push origin vYYYY.M.MICRO

The tool validates everything before it writes (clean tree, branch up to date with its upstream, the three version sources pyproject.toml, src/groundfield/__init__.py and CITATION.cff agree, non-empty [Unreleased] block, no unmerged changelog.d/ fragments), then commits chore(release): vX and creates the annotated tag. It never pushes. The tag starts the release workflow (tests, tag/version check, build, PyPI trusted publishing) and the documentation workflow, which deploys the docs of that version with the alias latest. python scripts/release.py set 2026.11.0rc1 sets an explicit version, e.g. a release candidate.

docs.title: Working with the sister projects
docs.text:
groundfield, groundinsight and groundmeas can share one Poetry environment through path dependencies, which is useful when changing the interface between them:

[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies]
groundinsight = { path = "../groundinsight", develop = true }
groundmeas = { path = "../groundmeas", develop = true }

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Quickstart: a first earthing impedance, touch voltage and plot in a few minutes.
  • Tutorials: the package step by step, as executed notebooks.
  • Examples: three complete case studies of real earthing systems.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: This page takes you from an empty Python session to the numbers of a typical earthing study: the earthing impedance of a rod, a ring and a grid in homogeneous and in two-layer soil, the earth potential rise and the touch voltage of a fault, a potential profile with a plot, and the impedances of two earthing systems joined by a PEN conductor. Every code block runs as it stands, in the order of the page (later blocks reuse earlier objects); the comments show what it prints. Install the package first (installation).

docs.title: 1. A rod in homogeneous soil
docs.text:
A driven rod of 3 m in soil of 100 Ω·m, fed with 1 A:

import groundfield as gf

world = gf.create_world(soil=gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0))                       # 100 Ω·m
gf.create_electrode(world, "rod", name="rod", position=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), length=3.0)
gf.create_source(world, attached_to="rod", magnitude=1.0)                         # 1 A

result = world.solve(gf.create_engine(frequencies=[50.0]))
print(f"{result.input_impedance()[0].real:.2f} Ω")    # 35.99 Ω

What each line does:

  • Soil. HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0) is a half-space of resistivity \(\rho = 100\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}\) below an insulating air space. All inputs are SI units (m, Ω·m, A, Hz).
  • World. The World holds the physical model: soil, electrodes, conductors and sources.
  • Electrode. Coordinates are \((x, y, z)\) in metres with \(z\) the depth, positive downwards. A rod's position is its upper end; this one runs from the surface to 3 m. The wire radius defaults to 5 mm.
  • Source. 1 A RMS injected at the rod. Without return_to the current returns through remote earth, the potential reference (\(\varphi \to 0\) far away).
  • Engine and solve. The Engine holds the numerics. The default backend image solves the problem in closed form; the result holds one value per frequency, here one. With 1 A the impedance in ohms is also the earth potential rise in volts.

Dwight's formula for a rod, \(R = \frac{\rho}{2\pi L}\bigl(\ln\frac{4L}{a} - 1\bigr)\) with length \(L\) and wire radius \(a\), is a quick plausibility check:

from groundfield.references import dwight1936

print(f"{dwight1936.rod(rho=100.0, length=3.0, radius=0.005):.2f} Ω")   # 35.99 Ω

The two agree to about 0.01 %: both assume a uniform current along the rod. A real rod leaks more current near its ends, and its resistance lies about 1 % lower; choosing an engine explains when that matters.

docs.title: 2. A rod, a ring and a grid in two soils
docs.text:
A small helper builds one earthing system per call, so that the same electrode can be solved in different soils:

def earthing_system(kind, soil, current=1.0):
    """A world with one earth electrode named "earth", fed with `current` in A."""
    world = gf.create_world(soil=soil)
    if kind == "rod":
        gf.create_electrode(world, "rod", name="earth", position=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), length=3.0)
    elif kind == "ring":
        gf.create_electrode(world, "ring", name="earth", center=(0.0, 0.0, 0.8), radius=3.0)
    else:  # a grid of 20 m × 20 m with 4 × 4 meshes, 0.5 m deep
        gf.create_electrode(
            world, "grid_mesh", name="earth", corner=(-10.0, -10.0, 0.5), size=(20.0, 20.0), n_x=4, n_y=4
        )
    gf.create_source(world, attached_to="earth", magnitude=current)
    return world


soils = {
    "homogeneous": gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0),
    "two-layer": gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=100.0, rho_2=300.0, h_1=2.0),
}
engine = gf.create_engine(frequencies=[50.0])
impedances = {}
for kind in ("rod", "ring", "grid"):
    impedances[kind] = [earthing_system(kind, soil).solve(engine).input_impedance()[0].real for soil in soils.values()]
    print(f"{kind:5s} {impedances[kind][0]:6.2f} Ω {impedances[kind][1]:6.2f} Ω")
# rod    35.99 Ω  51.41 Ω
# ring    9.41 Ω  13.81 Ω
# grid    2.37 Ω   4.80 Ω

TwoLayerSoil is a top layer of resistivity \(\rho_1 = 100\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}\) and thickness \(h_1 = 2\,\mathrm{m}\) over a half-space of \(\rho_2 = 300\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}\). The more resistive lower layer raises every impedance, and the more so the larger the electrode: the current of a large electrode spreads deeper into the soil. The rod gains 43 %, the ring 47 %, the 20 m grid more than doubles. The engine needs no change: image forwards a two-layer soil to image_2layer, the Tagg/Sunde image series.

docs.title: 3. A fault: earth potential rise and touch voltage
docs.text:
Feed the grid in the two-layer soil with an earth-fault current of 100 A. The touch voltage next to a grid depends on how the current crowds to its edges and corners, so solve it with mom, which computes one current per wire segment (the default image assumes one uniform current per straight wire and warns near grids):

grid = earthing_system("grid", soils["two-layer"], current=100.0)   # 100 A
fault = grid.solve(gf.create_engine(backend="mom", frequencies=[50.0]))

epr = abs(fault.electrode_potentials["earth"][0])
_, u_touch = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(fault, grid, electrode="earth", distance=1.0)
u_step = abs(gf.step_voltage(fault, position=(10.0, 10.0, 0.0), direction=(1.0, 1.0, 0.0), world=grid))
u_tp = gf.permissible_touch_voltage_en50522(0.5)   # fault cleared after 0.5 s
print(f"EPR {epr:.0f} V, touch voltage up to {abs(u_touch).max():.0f} V, step voltage {u_step:.0f} V")
print(f"permissible touch voltage {u_tp:.0f} V")
# EPR 476 V, touch voltage up to 129 V, step voltage 54 V
# permissible touch voltage 225 V
  • The earth potential rise (EPR) is the potential of the grid against remote earth: here \(4.76\,\Omega \times 100\,\mathrm{A}\) (mom reads the impedance 0.9 % below image).
  • The touch voltage \(U_T = U_E - \varphi(\text{feet})\) is the EPR \(U_E\) of the touched metal minus the surface potential where a person stands, 1 m away. touch_voltage_envelope puts the feet 1 m outside the grid's footprint, on 24 directions and on the arc around each corner; the largest value lies off the corners.
  • The step voltage is the difference of the surface potential over 1 m; here from the point above a corner outwards.
  • The comparison with the permissible touch voltage of EN 50522 (Figure 8, Table B.4; 225 V for 0.5 s) leaves out body, footwear and surface-layer resistances, which is conservative; permissible_prospective_touch_voltage_en50522 adds them.

With the default image engine the same envelope reads 9 % higher and the call warns with UniformCurrentFieldWarning. For impedances the two engines agree within 1 %; for field quantities near extended electrodes mom is the reference (choosing an engine). Every result scales linearly with the source current.

docs.title: 4. A potential profile and a plot
docs.text:
FieldResult.potential evaluates the potential at any point of the soil or its surface. Along a line at \(y\) = 2.5 m, through the middle of a row of meshes:

import numpy as np

x = np.array([0.0, 11.0, 20.0, 50.0])                       # m from the centre
points = np.column_stack([x, np.full_like(x, 2.5), np.zeros_like(x)])
for xi, phi in zip(x, fault.potential(points).real):
    print(f"x = {xi:4.0f} m: {phi:4.0f} V ({phi / epr:.0%} of the EPR)")
# x =    0 m:  460 V (97% of the EPR)
# x =   11 m:  400 V (84% of the EPR)
# x =   20 m:  233 V (49% of the EPR)
# x =   50 m:   95 V (20% of the EPR)

Inside the grid the surface stays close to the EPR, which keeps touch voltages there small; outside it the potential falls off towards remote earth, and the touch voltage grows with it. Two plotting functions show the same as figures:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

gf.plot_potential_profile(fault, start=(0.0, 2.5, 0.0), direction=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0), distance=50.0)
gf.plot_surface_potential(fault, grid)
plt.show()

The first draws the curve of the table above, the second a colour map of the surface potential over the grid and its surroundings with the electrode drawn on top. The plotting guide shows the other plots (geometry, cross-sections, current sharing, sweeps).

docs.title: 5. Two earthing systems joined by a PEN conductor
docs.text:
A substation ring earth and the rod earth of a house 40 m away, joined by a PEN conductor, in the two-layer soil; a current of 1 A is injected at the substation and returns through remote earth.

world = gf.create_world(soil=gf.TwoLayerSoil(rho_1=100.0, rho_2=300.0, h_1=2.0))
gf.create_electrode(world, "ring", name="substation", center=(0.0, 0.0, 0.8), radius=3.0)
gf.create_electrode(world, "rod", name="house", position=(40.0, 0.0, 0.0), length=3.0)
gf.create_conductor(world, name="pen", start="substation", end="house", cross_section=95e-6)
gf.create_source(world, attached_to="substation", magnitude=1.0)

result = world.solve(gf.create_engine(frequencies=[50.0]))
print(result.input_impedance()[0])                # (11.2695+0j) Ω
print(result.cluster_impedance("substation")[0])  # (14.1034+0j) Ω

The conductor is a 95 mm² copper PEN (cross_section in m²): a branch with resistance \(R = \rho_\text{Cu}\,\ell/A\) between the two electrodes, with the copper resistivity \(\rho_\text{Cu}\), the length \(\ell\) and the cross-section \(A\). Without cross_section it would be an ideal connection and both electrodes would form one galvanic cluster.

docs.title: Three impedances of one solve
docs.text:
Z_in = result.input_impedance()[0]
Z_substation = result.cluster_impedance("substation")[0]
Z_house = result.cluster_impedance("house")[0]
share = result.electrode_currents["substation"][0]   # leakage current, A
print(f"{Z_in.real:.2f} Ω, {Z_substation.real:.2f} Ω, {share.real:.0%} at the substation")
# 11.27 Ω, 14.10 Ω, 80% at the substation
Method Definition What it describes input_impedance(source) \((\varphi_a - \varphi_r)/I_s\) what an earth tester or a fault sees at the feeding point: the whole connected system cluster_impedance(electrode) \(\varphi_c / \sum_{e \in c} I_e\) the local earthing system: one galvanic cluster and only the current it leaks itself grounding_impedance(electrode) \(\varphi_c / I_e\) the share of one electrode; equal to the cluster impedance for a cluster of one electrode

\(\varphi_a\), \(\varphi_r\) are the potentials of the feeding and the return node (zero for a return through remote earth), \(I_s\) the source current, \(\varphi_c\) the length-weighted potential of a cluster and \(I_e\) the current an electrode leaks into the soil. Here 20 % of the test current flows through the PEN to the house earth, so the substation ring alone (14.10 Ω) is seen as 11.27 Ω at the feeding point. Because the PEN resistance is only a few milliohms, the input impedance is the parallel connection of the two cluster impedances:

print(abs(1 / (1 / Z_substation + 1 / Z_house) - Z_in))   # 0.0003 Ω

Which one you need depends on the question: the input impedance for a measurement or a fault loop (it is the default of sweep, convergence_study and the rho-f fits), the cluster impedance to characterise one earthing system on its own. The sources and measurement page explains the definitions in detail.

docs.title: 6. Check the result with a second method
docs.text:
Every number from a field model should be checked against an independent computation. Two quick checks: solve the same world with a second backend, and refine the discretisation.

report = gf.compare_engines(
    world,
    engines={"image": gf.create_engine(), "mom": gf.create_engine(backend="mom")},
    rel_tolerance=0.05,
)
print(report.summary())     # largest deviation 1.1 % (house cluster): consistent

fine = world.solve(gf.create_engine(segment_length=0.25))
print(fine.input_impedance()[0])   # (11.2758+0j) Ω, +0.06 % at half the segment length

The two methods differ in the current model: mom solves for one current per segment by point matching with midpoint point sources, image_2layer assumes a uniform current per unit length on each straight wire and integrates it with the exact line-source kernel. Agreement within about 1 % is expected (the point kernel reads 1–2 % low, see source kernels).

Values asserted by the test suite

The code blocks on this page are executed by the documentation tests; these assertions keep the numbers quoted in sections 5 and 6 in step with the code.

assert abs(Z_in - 11.2695) < 5e-4 and abs(Z_substation - 14.1034) < 5e-4
assert abs(share.real - 0.799) < 1e-3
assert abs(1 / (1 / Z_substation + 1 / Z_house) - Z_in) < 1e-3
assert report.is_consistent and max(report.deviations.values()) < 0.012
assert abs(fine.input_impedance()[0] - 11.2758) < 5e-4

docs.title: How-to guides
docs.text:
Short, task-oriented recipes for readers who know what they want to do. Each guide assumes you know the basic workflow (soil → world → electrodes → source → engine → solve) from the quickstart or the first tutorials. The code blocks are complete and are executed by the test suite (tests/test_doc_snippets.py), so what you copy is what CI ran.

Guide Task Install the optional extras OpenStreetMap ingest, groundinsight bridge, compiled kernels, the 3-D fem model (fem3d) Run sweeps and Monte Carlo studies parameter grids, stochastic networks, parallel workers Speed up large studies segment budget, kernel and earth-return choices, many excitations Plot results geometry, surface potential, profiles, cross-sections, current sharing, sweeps Model the inductive coupling of cables and leads Neumann inductance, earth-return models, skin effect Assess touch voltages touch points at accessible metal parts, transferred potential, open-air grids, EN 50522 limits Export to CSV, VTK and ParaView tables with provenance, geometry and field files Work with OpenStreetMap offline Overpass cache, building filters, coordinates Read and act on warnings diagnose(), the common warnings and what to do about them Contribute to the documentation page types, tutorial notebooks, the snippet markers, local build

Which engine to use for a task, and where each engine must not be used, is on choosing an engine; the theory behind the engines and the validation numbers are in the explanation section; every public name is in the reference.

docs.title: Assess touch voltages
docs.text:
This guide computes the touch voltages of an installation at its accessible metal parts and compares them with the permissible values of EN 50522. Read it when you verify an earthing system for an earth fault: a station, a transferred potential at a house, an open-air grid.

EN 50522 assesses the touch voltage \(U_T\) between an accessible conductive part and the feet of a person who touches it, standing 1 m away from the part, against the permissible touch voltage \(U_{Tp}(t_f)\) of the fault duration \(t_f\). groundfield returns the prospective (open-circuit) value

\[ U_T = U_\text{part} - \varphi(\text{feet}), \]

the potential of the touched part less the soil potential at the feet, as a phasor in V for the source current of the solve.

Prerequisites: the basic workflow of tutorial T01. The steps define the touch points, evaluate a transferred potential, sample the meshes of an open-air grid and compare the results with the permissible values.

docs.title: 1. Define the touch points
docs.text:
The touched parts are the metal parts above ground: the housing or the door of a station, a mast, a fence post, a cable cabinet, a house connection box. gf.touch_voltage_at_part takes one part — its horizontal position and the electrode or junction it is bonded to — and puts the feet on the circle of radius distance (1 m) around it. exclude removes the foot positions inside outlines where nobody can stand (the housing itself); directions keeps only the given sides, for example the outside of a fence.

A compact substation: a housing of 3 m × 2.5 m inside a ring earth of 2.5 m radius, 100 A of earth-fault current into the station earth at 50 Hz, 100 Ω·m.

import math

import groundfield as gf

world = gf.create_world(soil=gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0))
gf.create_electrode(world, "ring", name="station", center=(0.0, 0.0, 0.6), radius=2.5)
gf.create_source(world, attached_to="station", magnitude=100.0)
result = gf.create_engine(frequencies=[50.0]).solve(world)

housing = [(-1.5, -1.25), (1.5, -1.25), (1.5, 1.25), (-1.5, 1.25)]  # outline in m
angles, u_door, feet = gf.touch_voltage_at_part(
    result, world, position=(0.0, -1.25), bonded_to="station",  # door in the south wall
    exclude=[housing], return_points=True,
)
_, u_fence = gf.touch_voltage_at_part(
    result, world, position=(0.0, -4.0), bonded_to="station",  # fence post, bonded
    directions=[(0.0, -1.0)],  # people stand outside the fence
)
u_e = abs(result.electrode_potentials["station"][0])
print(f"earth potential rise {u_e:.0f} V")
print(f"door: {abs(u_door).max():.0f} V (largest of {len(u_door)} foot positions)")
print(f"fence post: {abs(u_fence[0]):.0f} V")

Of the 24 positions around the door, the 11 inside the housing are dropped; the two on the wall line are kept. The door is inside the ring, where the surface potential is high, so its touch voltage (447 V) is lower than 1 m outside the ring; the bonded fence post outside the ring has 784 V.

docs.title: 2. Evaluate a transferred potential over the PEN
docs.text:
A part bonded to a node far from the faulted earth carries that node's potential into an area of low potential rise (EN 50522, 3.6). A house 40 m away without an earth electrode of its own is connected to the station by the PEN conductor of the low-voltage cable, which ends on a junction at the service connection box:

gf.create_junction(world, name="service_box", position=(40.0, 0.0, 0.7))
gf.create_conductor(
    world, name="pen", start="station", end="service_box",
    resistivity=2.83e-8, cross_section=150e-6,  # aluminium, 150 mm²
)
result = gf.create_engine(frequencies=[50.0]).solve(world)

house = [(40.0, -4.0), (50.0, -4.0), (50.0, 4.0), (40.0, 4.0)]
_, u_box = gf.touch_voltage_at_part(
    result, world, position=(40.0, 0.0), bonded_to="service_box", exclude=[house]
)
print(f"service connection box: {abs(u_box).max():.0f} V of {u_e:.0f} V")

No current flows on the PEN, so the box carries the station potential, while the soil at the house is almost at remote earth: 96 % of the earth potential rise is a touch voltage there.

docs.title: 3. Sample the meshes of an open-air grid
docs.text:
touch_voltage_envelope puts the feet 1 m from the nearest wire of an electrode, all around it — a proxy where the touched parts are not known. It walks 24 equally spaced directions from the centre and, by default (corners=True), nine more feet on the arc around every corner of the convex hull of its wires, where the touch voltage is largest: equally spaced directions alone miss the corners of a non-square grid (a 60 m × 40 m grid read 12 … 28 % low, case study E03). By default it samples nothing inside the footprint, because there stands the station, the house, the steel structure or the mast. Over an open-air grid, such as a substation yard, people walk over the grid and the surface potential sags inside the meshes: interior="meshes" adds the centre of every mesh (the mesh voltage of IEEE Std 80), of a ring, and of the cells of a foundation built from bonded wires; interior=True also the inside of a closed polyline. Use the modes only where the inside is accessible open ground.

Near grids the image backend's uniform current is not field-grade (UniformCurrentFieldWarning), so the yard is solved with mom:

yard = gf.create_world(soil=gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0))
gf.create_electrode(
    yard, "grid_mesh", name="grid", corner=(0.0, 0.0, 0.5), size=(20.0, 20.0), n_x=2, n_y=2
)
gf.create_source(yard, attached_to="grid", magnitude=100.0)
yard_result = gf.create_engine(backend="mom", segment_length=0.5, frequencies=[50.0]).solve(yard)

_, outside = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(yard_result, yard, electrode="grid")
# corners=False: the 24 equally spaced feet first, then the mesh centres
_, inside = gf.touch_voltage_envelope(
    yard_result, yard, electrode="grid", interior="meshes", corners=False
)
print(f"1 m outside: {abs(outside).max():.1f} V; mesh centres: {abs(inside[24:]).max():.1f} V")

The value to assess is the largest of both, here 1 m outside a corner.

The feet stand 1 m from the nearest wire of the whole foundation (anchor="footprint", the default). anchor="connection_point" puts them on a circle round the electrode's connection point instead. That point is the centre of a hand-built grid mesh, but a corner of a rectangular foundation of the generators — the start of its local −y side, the electrode named after the foundation — so the circle goes round that corner: 100 A into a generated 20 m × 5 m ring at 0.8 m in 100 Ω·m give 229.71 V there against 161.76 V round its centre (default engine, 0.5 m segments). Keep the default for generated foundations.

Background and audit trail

anchor="connection_point" keeps the rule of 0.15.0. The connection point of a generated foundation is a corner since 2026.11: for meshes since audit A2G-04, for rectangles without cross-braces since user decision Q38. With 0.15.0, round the centre of one grid mesh, the same case gave 156.07 V (audits D3A-03, R4B-09).

docs.title: 4. Compare with the permissible touch voltage
docs.text:
permissible_touch_voltage_en50522(t_f) follows Figure 8 / Table B.4 of EN 50522:2022 up to 10 s and returns 80 V beyond, the value the standard allows for current-flow durations considerably longer than 10 s. Pass math.inf for an earth fault that is not cleared, as in a resonant-earthed network. With footwear or a resistive surface layer, permissible_prospective_touch_voltage_en50522 adds the body current times the additional resistances (Annex B.4):

u_tp_cleared = gf.permissible_touch_voltage_en50522(0.5)  # cleared after 0.5 s
u_tp_uncleared = gf.permissible_touch_voltage_en50522(math.inf)
u_vtp = gf.permissible_prospective_touch_voltage_en50522(math.inf, R_F1=1000.0, rho_s=100.0)
for part, u in (("door", abs(u_door).max()), ("service connection box", abs(u_box).max())):
    print(f"{part}: {u:.0f} V against U_Tp = {u_tp_cleared:.0f} V (0.5 s), "
          f"{u_tp_uncleared:.0f} V (not cleared), U_vTp = {u_vtp:.1f} V (1000 Ω shoes, not cleared)")

What you get: each part's largest touch voltage against \(U_{Tp}\) for a cleared and an uncleared fault and against \(U_{vTp}\) with footwear. Both parts exceed the limits by far at 100 A: the earthing system of this example needs more than a ring (EN 50522, 5.4.2 and Annex E, describe the verification steps and the measures).

docs.title: Contribute to the documentation
docs.text:
This guide shows how to write or change a page of this documentation — a tutorial notebook, a how-to page, an explanation or reference page — so that its code runs, its numbers are checked and the strict site build passes. Read it before you open a pull request that touches docs/.

Prerequisites: a checkout of the repository with poetry install --with dev,docs (pytest, ruff and nbclient from the dev group; MkDocs, mkdocs-jupyter and with it nbconvert from the docs group).

docs.title: 1. Pick the kind of page
docs.text:
The documentation follows the Diátaxis scheme: four kinds of pages, each with one job.

Section Job Form docs/tutorials/ teach by doing, with checks executed Jupyter notebooks docs/how-to/ solve one task Markdown with executed code blocks docs/reference/ describe every public name mkdocstrings pages, tables docs/explanation/ explain the physics and the methods Markdown with equations, generated validation tables

Three rules hold everywhere: English; every number comes from code that runs (a notebook cell, an executed block, a generated table) or cites the test or evidence file it comes from; and every page about a module or an engine states the mathematical-physical context, not only the API.

docs.title: 2. Write or change a tutorial notebook
docs.text:
• One notebook per tutorial, docs/tutorials/TNN_short_name.ipynb, listed in docs/tutorials/index.md and in the navigation (mkdocs.yml).
  • Narrative first: what we compute and why, the physics in two or three sentences with the formula where it helps, then the code.
  • Cross-check the key numbers with a second method (a closed form, a limit, a second engine, a convergence study) and put the checks into assert cells, so the notebook fails when a number drifts.
  • No network: OpenStreetMap data comes from a cache file under docs/tutorials/data/; files the notebook writes go to a temporary directory.
  • The notebook runs top to bottom in less than 120 s on a laptop and is committed with its outputs: the site renders the stored outputs (mkdocs-jupyter with execute: false). Execute it in place from the notebook's directory, then format the code cells:
cd docs/tutorials
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace T01_first_grounding_impedance.ipynb
ruff format T01_first_grounding_impedance.ipynb
  • tests/test_tutorials.py checks without executing anything that every tutorial is committed with its outputs and without errors, stays below 1.5 MB, needs no network and has at least three assert statements. With the marker slow it executes every tutorial with nbclient (300 s per notebook) and fails on an error, a failed assert or a deprecation warning in the outputs:
python -m pytest -m slow tests/test_tutorials.py

docs.title: 3. Write or change a how-to page
docs.text:
Code blocks in Markdown pages (and in README.md) are executed by tests/test_doc_snippets.py, page by page, blocks in document order in one namespace, in a temporary working directory. A block either runs or is marked; the markers are HTML comments and invisible on the site:

<!-- skip-doctest: needs the Overpass API (network) -->
```python
footprints, projector = gf.query_and_project(51.9, 10.8, 150.0)
```

<!-- doctest-module: my_factories.py -->
```python
def network(seed): ...
```

<!-- doctest-allow-warnings: UniformCurrentFieldWarning -->
```python
gf.touch_voltage_envelope(result, world, electrode="grid")
```

<!-- doctest-check
assert abs(z_in.real - 33.50) < 0.01
-->
  • skip-doctest: reason — an illustrative fragment; the reason is mandatory.
  • doctest-module: name.py — the block is written to that file in the working directory (which is on sys.path), for code that must be importable, e.g. by the worker processes of sweep(n_jobs=...).
  • doctest-allow-warnings: A, B — the block may emit these warnings. Any other warning that comes from groundfield or from the block itself fails the page — in particular a deprecated name.
  • doctest-check — a hidden check, executed in the page's namespace. Every how-to page needs at least one assert.

Run the harness for one page while you write it:

python -m pytest tests/test_doc_snippets.py -k how-to/plot-results

A how-to page opens with the task it solves and who needs it, lists its prerequisites, then gives the steps in order, says what the reader gets and how to check it, and ends with links to the tutorial, explanation and reference pages of the topic.

docs.title: 4. Write or change an explanation or reference page
docs.text:
• Generated blocks. The validation page and the blocks between <!-- generated:begin <name> --> and <!-- generated:end <name> --> on the engine pages are written by scripts/generate_validation_page.py from the stored measurements (docs/explanation/validation/measurements.json) and the bounds in tests/benchmarks/tolerances.py. Do not edit them by hand: change the bound or the benchmark and render again.
python scripts/generate_validation_page.py            # render from the stored measurements
python scripts/generate_validation_page.py --measure  # run the benchmarks, then render
python scripts/generate_validation_page.py --check    # exit 1 if a generated file is stale
  • Purpose first. Each page opens with one or two sentences: what the page is for and who should read it. Introduce each symbol where it first appears and give each equation one sentence that says what it means physically.
  • Provenance out of the reading flow. Audit ids, finding numbers, long measurement lists and the history of a number are the provenance of a statement: keep them, but in a collapsible block (??? note "Measurements and audit trail", from pymdownx.details), a footnote or a closing provenance section. Never delete a measured limit; the limit itself stays in the text.
  • Math. $…$ inline and $$…$$ on their own lines; inside a Markdown table no | in math (write \lvert … \rvert), no escaped underscores, no math in headings.
  • Tables with short cells and at most about six columns; put long explanations in the text below.
  • Pinned phrases. tests/test_explanation_pages.py, tests/test_docs_*.py and the tests of several modules assert phrases of these pages — for example the headings every engine page carries (## Mathematical and physical context, ## Validity range, ## Validation, ## Literature) and the measured limits of the known limitations. Run them after a rewrite, and keep the fact a failing test protects.

docs.title: 5. Build the site locally
docs.text:
poetry install --with docs
poetry run mkdocs serve          # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
poetry run mkdocs build --strict # what CI runs: every warning is an error

--strict fails on broken links, unknown cross-references and malformed docstrings. Link to other pages with relative paths to the source file (../reference/glossary.md, ../tutorials/T03_interconnected_systems_and_impedances.ipynb) and to API objects with mkdocstrings references ([FieldResult][groundfield.FieldResult]); do not use reST roles such as :class: in Markdown pages. Math uses $...$ and $$...$$.

The published site is versioned with mike: every release gets its own version of the documentation, latest points to the newest release and dev to the main branch. The deployment runs in CI; you do not need mike locally to write pages.

How to check it: before you push, run the docs tests and the strict build:

python -m pytest -q tests/test_doc_snippets.py tests/test_docs_*.py tests/test_explanation_pages.py tests/test_validation_page.py
python scripts/generate_validation_page.py --check
poetry run mkdocs build --strict

docs.title: Export to CSV, VTK and ParaView
docs.text:
This guide writes the numbers of a solve to CSV tables for spreadsheets and other tools, and the geometry and the surface potential to VTK files for a 3-D viewer such as ParaView. Read it when results have to leave Python.

groundfield.io writes plain tables (CSV) and legacy VTK files. Every CSV starts with # key: value lines that record where the numbers come from (groundfield version, UTC time, backend, frequency and the solve provenance), and no writer overwrites an existing file unless you pass overwrite=True. For complete, lossless result files use gf.save_result instead (tutorial T10).

docs.title: 1. Solve the world to export
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

import groundfield as gf

world = gf.create_world(soil=gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0), name="station")
gf.create_electrode(world, "ring", name="ring", center=(0.0, 0.0, 0.6), radius=4.0)
for k, (x, y) in enumerate([(4.0, 0.0), (-4.0, 0.0)]):
    gf.create_electrode(world, "rod", name=f"rod_{k}", position=(x, y, 0.6), length=3.0)
    gf.create_conductor(world, name=f"bond_{k}", start="ring", end=f"rod_{k}")
gf.create_source(world, attached_to="ring", magnitude=100.0)
result = gf.create_engine(segment_length=0.5, frequencies=[50.0, 250.0]).solve(world)
out = Path("export")
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

docs.title: 2. Write and read tables
docs.text:
gf.save_cluster_impedances_csv(result, out / "clusters.csv")
gf.save_electrode_table_csv(result, out / "electrodes.csv", world=world, frequency_index=1)
gf.save_potential_path_csv(result, out / "profile.csv", start=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), direction=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0), distance=50.0, n=101)

table, header = gf.read_csv_with_provenance(out / "electrodes.csv")
print(header["backend"], header["frequency_hz"], "Hz")
print(table[["name", "cluster_root", "abs_I", "share_of_cluster_pct"]])

What you get: three CSV files in export/, and the electrode table read back with its header. gf.read_csv_with_provenance returns the table and the header lines as a dictionary; the hidden check asserts the backend and frequency of the header and that the current shares add up to 100 %. The potential path holds one row per point and frequency (columns s, x, y, z, frequency_Hz, phi_re, phi_im, abs_phi). Other tools read the files with pandas.read_csv(path, comment="#"); write a plain CSV without the header with provenance=False. A second write to the same path raises FileExistsError:

try:
    gf.save_cluster_impedances_csv(result, out / "clusters.csv")
except FileExistsError as exc:
    print("FileExistsError:", exc)
gf.save_cluster_impedances_csv(result, out / "clusters.csv", overwrite=True)

docs.title: 3. Write VTK files
docs.text:
Two writers produce legacy VTK files (ASCII, double precision):

  • gf.export_geometry_vtk(world, path) — every electrode and conductor as poly-lines;
  • gf.export_field_vtk(result, path, extent=..., z=..., n=...) — the potential on a horizontal grid at depth z as a structured-points data set with the scalar fields of the complex potential.
geometry = gf.export_geometry_vtk(world, out / "geometry.vtk")
field = gf.export_field_vtk(result, out / "surface_potential.vtk", extent=(-30.0, 30.0, -30.0, 30.0), z=0.0, n=(121, 121))
print(geometry.read_text().splitlines()[:4])
print(field.read_text().splitlines()[:5])

What you get: two ASCII VTK files; the header lines printed above start with # vtk DataFile.

docs.title: 4. Open them in ParaView
docs.text:
1. File → Open both files, Apply.
  2. The coordinates are those of groundfield: \(z\) is the depth and points downwards. To see the electrodes below the surface, add a Transform filter with scale (1, 1, -1) to both data sets.
  3. Colour the field data set by the real part of the potential (or its magnitude); add Contour for equipotential lines and Tube on the geometry for visible wires.
  4. For several frequencies, export one field file per frequency_index.

docs.title: Model the inductive coupling of cables and leads
docs.text:
This guide switches on the inductive model of cables, PEN conductors and measurement leads, chooses the earth-return model, checks it against the classical per-metre formulas and adds the skin effect. Read it when a study has long conductors, or frequencies above 50 Hz, where the series impedance of the conductors matters.

Below 1 kHz the soil is quasi-static, but cables are not: a PEN conductor, a cable shield or a measurement lead has a series impedance \(R' + j\omega L'\) per metre (\(R'\) its resistance and \(L'\) its inductance per metre, \(\omega = 2\pi f\)) and couples magnetically to every other conductor.

Prerequisites: the basic workflow of tutorial T01 and conductors between electrodes as in tutorial T03.

docs.title: 1. Switch the inductive model on
docs.text:
Inductance is a property of a conductor with a cross section (a branch); the earth-return model is a property of the engine:

import math

import numpy as np

import groundfield as gf


def two_cables(gap, rho=100.0):
    # Cable A carries 1 A between its end rods; cable B, `gap` metres away, is passive.
    world = gf.create_world(soil=gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=rho))
    for name, y in (("A", 0.0), ("B", gap)):
        gf.create_electrode(world, "rod", name=f"{name}_start", position=(0.0, y, 0.6), length=1.5)
        gf.create_electrode(world, "rod", name=f"{name}_end", position=(100.0, y, 0.6), length=1.5)
        gf.create_conductor(
            world,
            name=f"cable_{name}",
            start=f"{name}_start",
            end=f"{name}_end",
            conductor_type="pen",
            resistivity=2.82e-8,  # aluminium, Ohm m
            cross_section=50e-6,  # m^2
            coupling_to_soil="isolated",  # insulated: a branch without leakage
            inductance_model="neumann",  # self and mutual inductance (Neumann integrals)
            discretize_segment_length=5.0,  # sub-branches of 5 m
        )
    gf.create_source(world, attached_to="A_start", return_to="A_end", magnitude=1.0)
    return world


frequencies = [50.0, 250.0, 1000.0]
engine = gf.create_engine(segment_length=0.5, frequencies=frequencies, sommerfeld_assembly="tabulated")
induced = {}
for gap in (0.5, 5.0, 50.0):
    result = engine.solve(two_cables(gap))
    potentials = result.electrode_potentials
    induced[gap] = np.array([potentials["B_start"][k] - potentials["B_end"][k] for k in range(len(frequencies))])
    print(f"gap {gap:4.1f} m: |U_B| = {np.round(np.abs(induced[gap]), 4)} V per A at {frequencies} Hz")

What you get: the voltage induced along the passive cable B per ampere in cable A. It is almost purely imaginary (about +90° against the current in cable A), grows with frequency and falls with the distance between the cables; the hidden check asserts all three.

docs.title: 2. Choose the earth-return model
docs.text:
The earth-return model is the engine option earth_inductive_model:

Model Earth Use it for "sommerfeld" (default) half-space or layered earth, real geometry every quantitative study "carson_series" homogeneous earth, long parallel wires long parallel cables in homogeneous soil "perfect_mirror" a perfect magnetic mirror a fast diagnostic baseline only
  • "sommerfeld" evaluates the Sommerfeld/Pollaczek integral of the conducting half-space or of the layered earth over the real segment geometry; conductors in or above the surface plane are handled.
  • "carson_series" applies Carson's (1926) per-metre correction for infinitely long parallel wires over homogeneous earth, on the anti-parallel image. It is tiled per metre of overlap for near-parallel horizontal pairs (\(\lvert\cos\varphi\rvert > 0.99\), \(\varphi\) the angle between the two wires: an inclination below 8.1°), across the surface through the field transmitted into the soil. Every other pair and every inclined segment gets the Sommerfeld correction of the same earth, so the result steps at 8.1°. Do not use it for layered soil, nor for networks of short cables: on generated LV networks at 1 kHz it gives a reactance X 9 … 15 % above "sommerfeld".
  • "perfect_mirror" treats the earth as a perfect magnetic mirror, independent of frequency. With conductors on both sides of the soil surface the solve warns: its additive image has no basis for such pairs.

With "sommerfeld" the correction is assembled from shared tables (sommerfeld_assembly="tabulated", the default; the examples on this page spell it out): it agrees with the per-pair assembly ("exact") to far below the model accuracy and is much faster on networks with many inductive segments (see Speed up large studies).

docs.title: 3. Check a model against the per-metre formulas
docs.text:
For a long straight cable the series impedance per metre approaches the conductor–earth loop impedance of an infinite line, given by Pollaczek's integral (groundfield.references.pollaczek) and, for a line on the surface, by Carson's formula (groundfield.references.earth_return). The comparison needs lines much longer than the skin depth of the earth, \(\delta = \sqrt{2\rho/(\omega\mu_0)}\) (about 160 m at 1 kHz in 100 Ω·m), and the end effects of the finite line must cancel: we take the difference of an 800 m and a 1600 m line. The line carries no leakage, so its series impedance is \((\varphi_\mathrm{start} - \varphi_\mathrm{end}) / I_\mathrm{end}\).

from groundfield.references.pollaczek import loop_impedance_conductor_earth

RHO, F = 100.0, 1000.0


def line_impedance(length):
    world = gf.create_world(soil=gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=RHO))
    gf.create_electrode(world, "ring", name="start", center=(0.0, 0.0, 0.8), radius=2.0)
    gf.create_electrode(world, "rod", name="end", position=(length, 0.0, 0.5), length=3.0)
    gf.create_conductor(
        world,
        name="line",
        start="start",
        end="end",
        cross_section=95e-6,
        coupling_to_soil="isolated",
        inductance_model="neumann",
        discretize_segment_length=50.0,
    )
    gf.create_source(world, attached_to="start", magnitude=1.0)
    result = gf.create_engine(segment_length=2.0, frequencies=[F], sommerfeld_assembly="tabulated").solve(world)
    p = result.electrode_potentials
    return (p["start"][0] - p["end"][0]) / result.electrode_currents["end"][0], world.conductors[0]


(z_800, line), (z_1600, _) = line_impedance(800.0), line_impedance(1600.0)
z_per_m = (z_1600 - z_800) / 800.0
reference = loop_impedance_conductor_earth(
    RHO,
    RHO,
    10.0,  # homogeneous earth: equal layers, thickness irrelevant
    F,
    depth=0.5 * (line.start[2] + line.end[2]),
    gmr=line.wire_radius * math.exp(-0.25),  # geometric mean radius of a solid wire
    r_internal=line.resistivity / line.cross_section,
)
print(f"groundfield: z' = {z_per_m * 1e3:.5f} Ohm/km")
print(f"Pollaczek:   z' = {reference * 1e3:.5f} Ohm/km")
print(f"X' {z_per_m.imag / reference.imag - 1:+.1e}, R' {z_per_m.real / reference.real - 1:+.1e}")

What you get: the per-metre impedance of the line and Pollaczek's value with their relative deviations. The reactance agrees closely (the hidden check asserts within 0.5 %); the earth-return resistance converges more slowly with the line length (within 2 %), because the current in the earth spreads over the skin depth beyond the ends of the line.

docs.title: 4. Add the skin effect
docs.text:
By default a conductor uses its DC resistance and the DC internal inductance. resistance_model="skin" uses the exact solution for a solid round conductor instead (Bessel functions), so the resistance rises and the internal inductance falls with frequency. For a check, at low frequency the classical expansion \(R_\mathrm{ac}/R_\mathrm{dc} \approx 1 + \frac{1}{48}(r/\delta_c)^4\) with the skin depth of the conductor \(\delta_c = \sqrt{2\rho_c/(\omega\mu_0)}\) must hold:

world = gf.create_world(soil=gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0))
gf.create_electrode(world, "rod", name="a", position=(0.0, 0.0, 0.6), length=2.0)
gf.create_electrode(world, "rod", name="b", position=(200.0, 0.0, 0.6), length=2.0)
pen = gf.create_conductor(
    world,
    name="pen",
    start="a",
    end="b",
    conductor_type="pen",
    resistivity=2.82e-8,
    cross_section=150e-6,
    coupling_to_soil="isolated",
    inductance_model="neumann",
    resistance_model="skin",
    discretize_segment_length=10.0,
)
r_dc = pen.resistivity / pen.cross_section
radius = math.sqrt(pen.cross_section / math.pi)
for f in (50.0, 550.0, 1000.0):
    ratio = pen.internal_impedance_per_length(f).real / r_dc
    delta_c = math.sqrt(2.0 * pen.resistivity / (2.0 * math.pi * f * 4e-7 * math.pi))
    print(f"{f:6.0f} Hz: R_ac/R_dc = {ratio:.5f} (low-frequency expansion {1 + (radius / delta_c) ** 4 / 48:.5f})")

The solver adds the difference to the DC convention to every branch of the conductor, so engine.solve(world) now sees a frequency-dependent resistance. At 50 Hz the effect is negligible for typical PEN cross sections; it matters for harmonics up to 1 kHz.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• A conductor without inductance_model is purely resistive.
  • Two conductors closer than the sum of their radii — cables in one trench drawn on one axis, a service drop along its main — couple as wires touching side by side.
  • A concentric cable is a core drawn on the axis of a thicker conductor with conductor_type="cable_shield": the core couples to the shield as a filament inside a tube, at the shield radius, and the shield carries no internal inductance of a solid wire. A 100 m coax with 5 mm core and 15 mm shield has a loop inductance of 26.97 µH, whatever sub-pieces discretize_segment_length cuts the two conductors into, also with the core drawn off or across the shield's axis. Two cables or leads that touch at a small angle, or wires leaving one junction, add up to the lumped pair the same way, also under "carson_series", whose correction of a tilted pair is integrated along the overlap. Without the marker two conductors on one axis are two separate cables touching each other; gf.diagnose(world) reports such pairs (category overlap, see Read and act on warnings).
  • A long conductor can stay lumped under "sommerfeld": its self term is integrated in one dimension along it, at a cost that grows at most linearly with the length (one lumped 2 km conductor at 50 Hz and 1 kHz: 1.1 s; 100 km: 10.6 s, within 0.25 GB). The spectral quadrature resolves the most distant points of a conductor up to \(2^{17}\cdot 2\pi\,(z + z')/30\), about 27 km per metre of \(z + z'\) (16 nodes per Bessel period up to 2.4 km, 8 beyond, at any frequency): 38 km for a conductor at 0.7 m, 33 km for one from a rod head at 0.5 m to a junction at 0.7 m. A longer conductor warns (SommerfeldResolutionWarning) and its result is not converged — the 100 km conductor above is solved in 10.6 s but warns.
  • For hand formulas of a cable or a line over layered soil (the complex-depth formulas of Dubanton and Deri), gf.penetration_depth(soil, frequencies) gives the equivalent complex depth and resistivity of any layer stack (Soil).
  • The leads of a measurement (tutorial T07) couple like cables; lay the probe lead at an angle to the feed lead.
  • Conductors that cross or lie in the soil surface are solved with "sommerfeld"; with the other two models their image is singular and the solve raises.
Background and audit trail
  • The coupling of touching conductors and of concentric cables follows user decisions Q32 and Q33.
  • The correction of "carson_series" for a tilted pair is integrated along the overlap since audit W1R3-07.
  • The resolution limit of long lumped conductors under "sommerfeld" (SommerfeldResolutionWarning) was documented in audit W3B-10.
  • sommerfeld_assembly="tabulated" is the default since 2026.11.

docs.title: Install the optional extras
docs.text:
This guide installs the optional parts of groundfield — OpenStreetMap footprints, the groundinsight bridge, compiled kernels and the three-dimensional fem model — and checks which of them your environment has. Read it when a function asks for an extra, or before you set up a machine for large studies.

Prerequisites: groundfield itself, installed as in the installation guide, which also covers Python versions, Poetry and the development setup. The core package needs only numpy, scipy, pydantic, pandas, matplotlib and sympy.

docs.title: The four extras
docs.text:
Extra Installs Needed for geo requests, shapely, pyproj OpenStreetMap building footprints groundinsight groundinsight live BusType objects and the groundinsight database fast numba compiled kernels (same results, faster solves) fem3d scikit-fem (BSD-3), pyamg (MIT) the three-dimensional model of fem
  • geo serves gf.geo, LvNetworkLayout.from_osm and the OSM placement of TnNetworkGenerator.
  • groundinsight serves gf.to_bustype (a live BusType) and save_bustype_to_db; the JSON export works without it.
  • fast compiles the kernels of the two-layer image series and of the line-source kernel; results are identical, solves are faster.
  • fem3d adds the three-dimensional model of the fem backend: every world its axisymmetric model cannot hold (strips, meshes, rods side by side, several clusters, galvanic distributed conductors, resolved concrete).

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install "groundfield[geo]"
pip install "groundfield[fem3d]"
pip install "groundfield[geo,groundinsight,fast,fem3d]"   # all extras

From a checkout with Poetry:

poetry install --extras "geo fast fem3d"
poetry install --all-extras

docs.title: 2. Check what is available
docs.text:
A missing extra is not an error until you call a function that needs it; then groundfield raises an ImportError that names the extra to install. To see what your environment has:

import importlib.util

import groundfield as gf

print("groundfield", gf.__version__)
extras = {
    "shapely": "geo",
    "pyproj": "geo",
    "requests": "geo",
    "groundinsight": "groundinsight",
    "numba": "fast",
    "skfem": "fem3d",
    "pyamg": "fem3d",
}
available = {module: importlib.util.find_spec(module) is not None for module in extras}
for module, extra in extras.items():
    print(f"{module:14s} [{extra}]: {'installed' if available[module] else 'missing'}")

What you get: one line per module, installed or missing, with the extra that provides it.

docs.title: 3. The compiled kernels need no setting
docs.text: With numba installed the compiled kernels are picked up automatically; there is nothing to configure. They return the same matrices bit for bit as the numpy path, so results do not depend on the extra — only the run time does. Compare both on your machine with the timing recipe in Speed up large studies.

docs.title: Without the fem3d extra
docs.text: fem keeps its axisymmetric model (rods on one axis, rings around it) with the core dependencies. A world that needs the three-dimensional model raises an ImportError that names the extra; FemOptions(model="axisymmetric") turns that into the axisymmetric model's own refusal, which names the backends that solve the world. The extra changes no other backend and no result of the axisymmetric model.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Installation: Python versions, Poetry, the development setup.
  • fem engine: the axisymmetric and the three-dimensional model.
  • Performance and scaling: measured run times with and without numba.
  • Work with OpenStreetMap offline: the geo extra in use.

docs.title: Work with OpenStreetMap offline
docs.text:
This guide builds and uses an on-disk cache of OpenStreetMap building footprints, so that a study runs without network access and reads the same map every time. Read it before you build a network from real buildings, in CI, behind a firewall or on the road.

groundfield.geo reads building footprints from OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API. Every answer is cached on disk, and a cached answer is used without any network access. That makes studies reproducible: the map changes, your cache does not.

Prerequisites: the geo extra (requests, shapely, pyproj; see Install the optional extras). Only step 1 needs the network.

docs.title: How the cache works
docs.text: query_buildings (and everything built on it: query_and_project, LvNetworkLayout.from_osm, the OSM placement of TnNetworkGenerator) builds the Overpass query text from centre, radius and timeout, and looks for the file <sha256 of the query>.json in cache_dir (default ~/.cache/groundfield/osm). If the file exists and is a valid Overpass answer, it is used; otherwise the query is sent and the answer is written there atomically. force_refresh=True sends the query again.

docs.title: 1. Prepare a cache while you are online
docs.text:
Run the query once with an explicit cache directory and keep the directory with your study (commit it, or copy it to the offline machine):

from pathlib import Path

import groundfield as gf

footprints, projector = gf.query_and_project(51.9136, 10.8432, 150.0, cache_dir=Path("osm_cache"))

Every later call with the same centre, radius and timeout reads osm_cache/ and never touches the network.

docs.title: 2. Or put an Overpass answer you got elsewhere into the cache
docs.text:
An answer saved from another tool (for example the Overpass web front-end, with the same query) can be put into the cache under the name groundfield expects. The query text comes from the public groundfield.geo.osm.build_query. Here a tiny two-building answer is written by hand to keep the example self-contained:

import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path

import groundfield as gf
from groundfield.geo import osm

LAT, LON, RADIUS = 51.9136, 10.8432, 150.0
payload = {
    "version": 0.6,
    "elements": [
        {
            "type": "way",
            "id": 1,
            "tags": {"building": "house"},
            "geometry": [
                {"lat": 51.91370, "lon": 10.84320},
                {"lat": 51.91370, "lon": 10.84335},
                {"lat": 51.91379, "lon": 10.84335},
                {"lat": 51.91379, "lon": 10.84320},
                {"lat": 51.91370, "lon": 10.84320},
            ],
        },
        {
            "type": "way",
            "id": 2,
            "tags": {"building": "garage"},
            "geometry": [
                {"lat": 51.91350, "lon": 10.84300},
                {"lat": 51.91350, "lon": 10.84308},
                {"lat": 51.91353, "lon": 10.84308},
                {"lat": 51.91353, "lon": 10.84300},
                {"lat": 51.91350, "lon": 10.84300},
            ],
        },
    ],
}
cache = Path("osm_cache")
cache.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
query = osm.build_query(LAT, LON, RADIUS, timeout_s=osm.DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_S)
(cache / f"{hashlib.sha256(query.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()}.json").write_text(json.dumps(payload))

footprints, projector = gf.query_and_project(LAT, LON, RADIUS, cache_dir=cache)
for fp in footprints:
    print(fp.osm_id, fp.building_use, f"{fp.area_m2():.1f} m2")

What you get: the two footprints of the cached answer, with their OSM ids, building use and area, read without any network access. The cache key contains the timeout (timeout_s) and, for other endpoints than the default, the endpoint URL: use the same values offline as online.

docs.title: 3. Filter the buildings
docs.text:
Every building=* way is a footprint by default, garages and sheds included. Buildings without electrical service usually have no foundation earth electrode connected to the PEN; drop them with exclude_building_tags (the documented set gf.geo.NON_SERVICE_BUILDING_TAGS contains garage, shed, carport, hut, ruins and similar) and very small outlines with min_area_m2:

from groundfield.geo import NON_SERVICE_BUILDING_TAGS

kept, _ = gf.query_and_project(LAT, LON, RADIUS, cache_dir=cache, exclude_building_tags=NON_SERVICE_BUILDING_TAGS)
print([fp.building_use for fp in kept])

docs.title: 4. Convert coordinates
docs.text:
Footprints are projected into local east/north metres around the query centre. The returned Projector converts in both directions, so you can place a substation or a probe from GPS coordinates:

x, y = projector.to_xy_m(51.9137, 10.8433)
lat, lon = projector.to_lat_lon(x, y)
print(f"x = {x:.2f} m, y = {y:.2f} m -> back: {lat:.6f}, {lon:.6f}")

LvNetworkLayout.from_osm(..., cache_dir=...) accepts the same cache and offers lat_lon_to_xy / xy_to_lat_lon; tutorial T06 builds a whole network from a cached answer.

docs.title: Limits and safety
docs.text: Requests are bounded: the radius is at most 10 km, the timeout an integer of at most 900 s, the response is capped in size, and malformed answers or Overpass error remarks raise OverpassError and are never cached. A cache file that cannot be read is fetched again with a warning.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Tutorial T06: a whole TN network from a cached answer.
  • ADR-0011: the footprint data model, the projection, the Overpass query and its cache.
  • API: Geo / OSM and the generators.

docs.title: Plot results
docs.text:
This guide draws the standard figures of a grounding study — the geometry, the surface potential, profiles and cross-sections, the current sharing and sweeps — with the plot helpers of groundfield. Read it when you need a first look at a result or a figure for a report.

All plot helpers return matplotlib objects (a Figure or an Axes) and are available as flat names (gf.plot_world) and in the gf.plot namespace. Potential plots draw the real part of the complex potential by default and say so in the label; pass component="imag", "abs" or "phase" for the other parts.

Prerequisites: matplotlib (part of the core install); plot_world_3d draws with matplotlib as well.

docs.title: 1. Solve a world to plot
docs.text:
A substation earth (ring and four rods) measured with an auxiliary electrode 200 m east and a voltage probe at 61.8 %, built with the layout builder; 1 A at 50 Hz in 100 Ω·m.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import groundfield as gf
from groundfield.generators import LvNetworkLayout

layout = LvNetworkLayout.from_footprints([], substation_xy=(0.0, 0.0))
layout.add_auxiliary_electrode(distance_m=200.0, direction_deg=0.0)
layout.add_voltage_probe(inline_fraction=0.618)
world = layout.to_world(soil=gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=100.0))
result = gf.create_engine(segment_length=0.5, frequencies=[50.0]).solve(world)
print([e.name for e in world.electrodes])

docs.title: 2. Plot the geometry
docs.text:
fig = gf.plot_world(world, title="Top view")  # plane="xy" (default)
fig_side = gf.plot_world(world, plane="xz", extent=(-10.0, 15.0, -1.0, 5.0), title="Side view, depth downwards")
ax = layout.plot(figsize=(9, 4))  # the layout view with anchors and the measurement loop
fig_3d = gf.plot_world_3d(world)

docs.title: 3. Map the surface potential
docs.text:
fig = gf.plot_surface_potential(result, world, extent=(-20.0, 220.0, -40.0, 40.0), n=120)
fig_abs = gf.plot_surface_potential(result, world, extent=(-15.0, 15.0, -15.0, 15.0), n=100, component="abs")

With an auxiliary electrode the potential is strongly negative near it and only moderately positive around the substation. The layout's own plot uses a colour scale with equal resolution above and below zero (two_slope=True, the default); symmetric=True and log=True are the alternatives:

fig = layout.plot_surface_potential(result, world, padding_m=30.0, n=120, levels=31)
fig_log = layout.plot_surface_potential(result, world, padding_m=30.0, n=120, log=True, cmap="viridis")

docs.title: 4. Draw profiles and cross-sections
docs.text:
A profile along a line at several depths, the radial decay around an electrode, and a vertical cross-section through the measurement axis:

fig = gf.plot_potential_profile(result, start=(-30.0, 0.0, 0.0), direction=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0), distance=260.0, depths=(0.0, 1.0))
fig_r = gf.plot_potential_radial(result, around="substation_ring_0", world=world, r_max=60.0, depths=(0.0, 0.5, 1.0), log_x=True)
fig_xz = gf.plot_potential_contour(result, world=world, plane="xz", y=0.0, extent=(-20.0, 220.0, 0.0, 30.0), n=120)

plane="xz" holds y fixed, plane="xy" holds z fixed (depth positive downwards). Without extent the window follows the electrodes.

docs.title: 5. Show where the current goes
docs.text:
fig = gf.plot_current_sharing(result, world, by="electrode")
table = gf.electrode_current_table(result, world)
print(table[["name", "abs_I", "share_of_cluster_pct"]].head())

How to check it: the electrode currents of a three-pole set-up add up to zero, because the test current returns through the auxiliary electrode; the hidden check of this page asserts it.

docs.title: 6. Plot sweeps and convergence studies
docs.text:
gf.plot_sweep_lines and gf.plot_sweep_heatmap take the table of gf.sweep (see Run sweeps and Monte Carlo studies); gf.plot_convergence the table of gf.convergence_study (tutorial T09):

df = gf.convergence_study(world, gf.create_engine(frequencies=[50.0]), segment_lengths=[0.5, 0.25, 0.125])
fig = gf.plot_convergence(df, response="abs_Z")
plt.close("all")

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Every helper takes frequency_index for multi-frequency results.
  • Save a figure with fig.savefig("name.png", dpi=150); in scripts call plt.show() or close figures with plt.close("all") in loops.
  • For publication plots, use the helpers for a first look and then plot the numbers yourself: result.potential(points) returns the complex potential at any (M, 3) array of points.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Tutorial T07: the fall-of-potential measurement behind the example world.
  • Export to CSV, VTK and ParaView: the same quantities as files, for other tools.
  • Postprocess API: every plot helper with its options.

docs.title: Speed up large studies
docs.text:
This guide makes large solves — networks of many houses, fine discretisations, inductive conductors at many frequencies — fast enough, with the levers in the order in which they usually matter, and shows how to measure each one on your own machine. Read it before a study whose single solves take more than a few seconds.

The cost of a solve grows with the number of wire segments \(N\) (the reaction matrix has \(N^2\) entries and the solve is a dense \(N \times N\) system), with the number of inductive conductor segments, and with the earth-return model. Measured run times of this release are on the performance page.

Prerequisites: the basic workflow of tutorial T01. All blocks of this page build on the test network of step 1 (a ring station and six house grids joined by a PEN cable).

docs.title: 1. Count the segments before you solve
docs.text:
gf.expected_segments(world, engine) predicts the discretisation exactly as the solver will do it, per electrode and in total, without solving. gf.world_statistics(world) summarises the geometry.

import time

import numpy as np

import groundfield as gf
from groundfield.diagnostics import HARD_LIMIT


def network(n_houses=6, inductive=False, rho=100.0):
    world = gf.create_world(soil=gf.HomogeneousSoil(rho=rho))
    gf.create_electrode(world, "ring", name="station", center=(0.0, 0.0, 0.6), radius=2.0)
    previous = "station"
    for k in range(n_houses):
        gf.create_electrode(
            world, "grid_mesh", name=f"house_{k}", corner=(30.0 * (k + 1) - 5.0, 8.0, 0.8), size=(10.0, 10.0), n_x=1, n_y=1
        )
        gf.create_conductor(
            world,
            name=f"pen_{k}",
            start=previous,
            end=f"house_{k}",
            conductor_type="pen",
            resistivity=2.82e-8,
            cross_section=50e-6,
            coupling_to_soil="isolated",
            inductance_model="neumann" if inductive else None,
            discretize_segment_length=5.0 if inductive else None,
        )
        previous = f"house_{k}"
    gf.create_source(world, attached_to="station", magnitude=1.0)
    return world


world = network()
for ds in (2.0, 1.0, 0.5):
    count = gf.expected_segments(world, gf.create_engine(segment_length=ds))
    print(f"segment_length {ds:3.1f} m: {count['total']:5d} segments")
print("hard limit:", HARD_LIMIT)

What you get: the segment count per segment length and the limit it is checked against. Halving the segment length doubles \(N\) and roughly quadruples the matrix work. A world above the engine's limit is rejected with ResourceLimitError before anything large is allocated.

docs.title: Raise or lower the resource limit
docs.text:
The limit bounds the number of leakage segments and the size of the dense nodal system (current owners, nodes and branches, every conductor sub-piece included). It belongs to the engine: max_segments=None (the default) uses the module constant HARD_LIMIT (20 000), a positive integer sets the limit for this engine only. The dense reaction matrix takes \(8N^2\) bytes, so check the memory of the machine before you raise the limit — 40 000 segments need 12 GiB for the matrix alone. A lower limit is a cheap guard for batch runs: a world that a unit error has blown up fails at once instead of filling the memory. Every segment backend, solve_mutual_matrix and solve_mutual_field honour the limit, gf.diagnose reports against it, and the result records it:

from groundfield.diagnostics import ResourceLimitError, check_segment_budget

guarded = gf.create_engine(segment_length=0.5, max_segments=200)
try:
    check_segment_budget(world, guarded)  # what guarded.solve(world) checks first
except ResourceLimitError as error:
    print("refused:", str(error).split(" (")[0])
large = gf.create_engine(segment_length=0.5, max_segments=50_000)
print("limit:", gf.expected_segments(world, large)["limit"])
result = large.solve(world)
print("checked against:", result.metadata["max_segments"])

Changing groundfield.diagnostics.HARD_LIMIT changes the default of every engine of the process; max_segments is the per-engine setting.

docs.title: Move the size notice
docs.text:
Below the limit, every Engine.solve at or above a second size emits a UserWarning that the solve time may run from seconds to minutes ("budget: ...", an info finding of gf.diagnose); solve_mutual_matrix and solve_mutual_field do not emit it, and for the experimental fem the segment count is not its problem size (the mesh of each cluster is). That size belongs to the engine as well: warn_segments=None (the default) uses the module constant SOFT_LIMIT (5 000), a positive integer sets it for this engine only and is counted like the limit (segments and nodal unknowns). On a workstation that solves 10 000 segments quickly, raise it together with max_segments; on a small machine, lower it. The two are not checked against each other: a notice above the hard limit never appears, because the world is refused first.

quiet = gf.Engine(segment_length=0.5, max_segments=50_000, warn_segments=12_000)
early = gf.Engine(segment_length=0.5, warn_segments=400)
for label, engine in (("quiet", quiet), ("early", early)):
    notices = [d for d in gf.diagnose(world, engine, proximity=False).by_category("budget")]
    print(label, engine.warn_segments, [d.severity for d in notices])

docs.title: 2. Choose the segment length from a convergence study
docs.text:
Use the coarsest segment length that is converged for the quantity you need — tutorial T09 shows how. With the default line-source kernel, network impedances are usually converged at 0.5–1 m; compare two values on a representative world before a large run:

z = {ds: gf.create_engine(segment_length=ds).solve(world).input_impedance()[0].real for ds in (1.0, 0.5)}
print(f"1.0 m: {z[1.0]:.5f} Ohm, 0.5 m: {z[0.5]:.5f} Ohm, change {z[0.5] / z[1.0] - 1:+.2e}")

How to check it: the change printed above is the convergence of the input impedance; the hidden check of this page asserts that it is below 1e-3 for this network.

docs.title: 3. Kernel and compiled extension
docs.text:
The exact line-source kernel (default of the image family) costs a few times the point kernel per solve, but it is converged at much coarser segments, so it is usually the faster way to a given accuracy. Install the fast extra (numba) for compiled kernels with identical results. Measure both kernels on your machine:

for kernel in (None, "point"):
    engine = gf.create_engine(segment_length=0.5, kernel=kernel)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    result = engine.solve(world)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f"kernel {result.metadata['kernel']:5s}: {elapsed:.3f} s, Z_in = {result.input_impedance()[0].real:.5f} Ohm")

What you get: the time and the input impedance per kernel; result.metadata["kernel"] records the kernel a result was solved with. On this network the point kernel reads 0.6 % below the line kernel (on single rods, rings and strips 1–2 %, at every segment length; see Kernels). In a fresh process the first line-kernel solve also compiles the numba kernels, about a second once; the earlier blocks of this page have done that already, so time a second solve when you run the block on its own.

docs.title: 4. Many excitations: one matrix instead of many solves
docs.text:
When you need the response to an injection at each of many earth electrodes — the mutual grounding-impedance matrix \(Z_G\) of a site — gf.solve_mutual_matrix assembles the reaction matrix once and solves all excitations with it, instead of one full solve per electrode. Its off-diagonal is the Galerkin reaction of the leakage distributions, which is reciprocal and reproduces a solve of the clusters joined by branches; probe points are not needed (offdiag="probe" samples the potential at points instead). It expects a world with the earth electrodes only (no cables between them):

electrodes_only = network()
electrodes_only.conductors.clear()
electrodes_only.sources.clear()
anchors = [e.name for e in electrodes_only.electrodes]
engine = gf.create_engine(segment_length=1.0)

start = time.perf_counter()
z_g = gf.solve_mutual_matrix(electrodes_only, engine, anchors)
t_matrix = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
diagonal = []
for name in anchors:
    single = electrodes_only.model_copy(deep=True)
    gf.create_source(single, attached_to=name, magnitude=1.0)
    diagonal.append(engine.solve(single).cluster_impedance(name)[0])
t_solves = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"{len(anchors)} excitations: one matrix {t_matrix:.2f} s, {len(anchors)} solves {t_solves:.2f} s")
print("largest difference on the diagonal:", f"{np.max(np.abs(np.diag(z_g) - diagonal)):.1e} Ohm")

How to check it: the diagonal of \(Z_G\) equals the cluster impedances of the single solves (the printed difference; the hidden check asserts below 1e-9 Ω), and \(Z_G\) is symmetric.

docs.title: 5. Frequencies and the earth-return model
docs.text:
• Put all frequencies into one engine: the soil problem is assembled once, and the earth-return correction of inductive conductors is built for the whole frequency set at once.
  • The Sommerfeld correction of inductive conductors is interpolated from tables per pair of depth groups by default (sommerfeld_assembly="tabulated") instead of integrated per segment pair ("exact"). The two agree to far below the accuracy of the model, and the tables are the closer of the two to a converged reference; compare them on your network:
inductive = network(inductive=True)
frequencies = [50.0, 250.0, 550.0, 1000.0]
z_assembly = {}
for assembly in ("exact", "tabulated"):
    engine = gf.create_engine(segment_length=1.0, frequencies=frequencies, sommerfeld_assembly=assembly)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    z_assembly[assembly] = np.array(engine.solve(inductive).input_impedance())
    print(f"{assembly:9s}: {time.perf_counter() - start:.2f} s, Z_in(1 kHz) = {z_assembly[assembly][-1]:.6f} Ohm")
print(f"largest relative difference: {np.max(np.abs(z_assembly['tabulated'] / z_assembly['exact'] - 1)):.1e}")

The difference in run time grows with the number of inductive segments (on an 8-house TN network with an inductive PEN, 78 inductive branches and four frequencies: 16.6 s CPU per-pair, 1.0 s tabulated). carson_series is cheaper still, but it is a long-parallel-wire approximation: for cables that run at an angle to each other or are short it can be far off, so it is no general substitute for sommerfeld (see Model the inductive coupling of cables and leads).

docs.title: 6. Parallel sweeps
docs.text: Independent solves of a parameter study run in parallel with gf.sweep(..., n_jobs=...); see Run sweeps and Monte Carlo studies.

docs.title: 7. Memory
docs.text:
The image-family kernels never build per-pair difference tensors, switch to row blocks for very large matrices, and evaluate result.potential on large grids in blocks, so memory grows with \(N^2\) for the reaction matrix itself and not with the number of field points. If memory is the limit, reduce \(N\) (segment length, fewer electrodes per solve) first.

Changes since 0.15.0
  • sommerfeld_assembly="tabulated" is the default since 2026.11; up to 0.15.0 the default was the per-pair assembly "exact".
  • solve_mutual_matrix takes the Galerkin reaction as its off-diagonal since 2026.11; offdiag="probe", which samples the potential at probe points, was the definition up to 0.15.0.
  • The default kernel of the image family is the exact line source since 2026.11 (ADR-0015); kernel="point" reproduces the numbers of 0.15.0.
