In a project, put the check into a test so that it runs with every change, for example with pytest (a sketch — paths and names are yours):

# tests/test_study_reference.py
import groundfield as gf
from my_study import build_world, ENGINE, check_reference

def test_station_impedance_is_unchanged():
    result = ENGINE.solve(build_world())
    ok, worst = check_reference(result, "reference/station.json")
    assert ok, f"input impedance moved by {worst:.2e}"

When a check fails after an upgrade, read the "numbers that change" section of the release notes before you accept new reference values.

docs.title: T10 — Reproducible studies
docs.text:
A number in a report or a dissertation is only as good as the ability to produce it again. This tutorial shows the tools groundfield offers for that: seeds that pin a stochastic realisation, network plans and world JSON that pin the geometry, the provenance record of every solve, versioned result files, and regression checks that tell you when an upgrade changes your numbers.

You will learn

  • how to make a stochastic network reproducible, and what to store;
  • what result.metadata["provenance"] records;
  • how to save and load results losslessly (gf.save_result, gf.load_result);
  • how to re-run a study in a fresh process and verify that it gives the same numbers;
  • how to guard a study with a reference ("golden") check.

Runtime: about 15 s (one solve runs in a separate Python process).

docs.title: 1. Pin the realisation
docs.text:
The configuration below has two random axes: the resistivity and the thickness of the upper soil layer. Three things reproduce a realisation:

  • the seed — TnNetworkGenerator(cfg, seed=...), or sample_world(rng=seed), draws everything from one stream;
  • the resolved configuration that sample_world returns — the same configuration with every distribution replaced by its drawn value;
  • the network plan (generator.plan()) — the pure-data description of the sites, electrodes, cables and sources, from which materialise_plan rebuilds the world.

gf.world_fingerprint (SHA-256 of the canonical world JSON) tells whether two worlds are identical.

docs.title: 2. Provenance of every solve
docs.text: Every result records how it was made: the versions of groundfield, Python and the numerical libraries, the platform, the complete engine configuration, the fingerprint of the solved world and the UTC time.

docs.title: 3. Save and load results
docs.text: gf.save_result writes one standard-JSON file with a small envelope (format, schema_version, written_by, provenance, result). No pickle is involved, so a result file can be read anywhere and does not execute code when loaded; the write is atomic and refuses to overwrite unless asked to. gf.load_result restores the result losslessly — complex values, infinities and the metadata included — and rejects files of a newer schema with ResultFormatError.

docs.title: 4. Re-run in a fresh process
docs.text: The strongest everyday check of reproducibility is to repeat the computation from the stored inputs in a new Python process and compare. We store the world and the engine as JSON, run a short script with the same interpreter, and load its result file.

docs.title: 5. A reference ("golden") check for your study
docs.text: Store the key numbers of a study once, together with the inputs and a tolerance, and check them whenever you upgrade groundfield or change your environment. The check below compares the input impedance at every frequency with a relative tolerance and reports the worst deviation.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Store the seed and the configuration — or the network plan or world JSON — with every study; compare worlds with gf.world_fingerprint.
  • result.metadata["provenance"] records versions, engine and world fingerprint; gf.save_result / gf.load_result keep results losslessly in standard JSON.
  • Re-run from stored inputs in a fresh process, and guard key numbers with a reference check and a stated tolerance.

This is the last tutorial. The how-to guides cover individual tasks (sweeps and Monte Carlo, plots, exports, warnings), the explanation section the theory behind every engine.
